pages.title: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's PPA — Research Compilation
headings: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's Standard PPA — Research Compilation
pages.excerpt: Research compilation on the Available Declaration (AD) penalty mechanism in Nepal's standard hydropower PPA. Based on direct PPA text analysis by Parajuli (2023) and ERC regulatory commentary.
pages.body_text: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's Standard PPA — Research Compilation # Summary Research compilation on the Available Declaration (AD) penalty mechanism in Nepal's standard hydropower PPA. Based on direct PPA text analysis by Parajuli (2023) and ERC regulatory commentary. # Key data extracted Article 10.2 formula: Penalty = [0.80 × min(Contract Energy, AD) - (Actual + Scheduled Outage + Forced Outage + Force Majeure)] × Purchase Rate No curtailment exemption: Off-taker curtailment is not listed as excusable cause. NEA can order reduced output and simultaneously penalise for the resulting shortfall. Article 10.1(Ka) reserve margin: NEA can withhold up to 10% of peak-period Contract Energy as system reserve with zero compensation — and then still penalise for shortfall below 80%. No "deemed generation" provision: Unlike IFC model PPAs, Nepal's standard PPA does not treat off-taker curtailment as compensable deemed generation. # Limitations Research compilation, not the contract corpus itself. The page summarizes PPA-clause analysis and regulatory commentary; it is not a complete archive of signed PPAs. Clause-level focus. The source isolates Article 10.1/10.2 AD-penalty mechanics and does not quantify how often NEA actually applies penalties in practice. Curtailment interaction unresolved. The no-deemed-generation finding identifies a contractual exposure, but the source does not provide case-by-case adjudication history. Legal interpretation boundary. The analysis describes contract structure and regulatory implications; it is not a formal legal opinion.

pages.title: AEPC Renewable Framework and Progress Reports
headings: AEPC Renewable Framework and Progress Reports
Gaps we would like to close
pages.excerpt: Primary source for Nepal's off-grid and distributed solar story. AEPC ("Alternative Energy Promotion Centre") is the government institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables, standing alongside (not inside) NEA. It is the operator and financier of the solar
pages.body_text: AEPC Renewable Framework and Progress Reports # Summary Primary source for Nepal's off-grid and distributed solar story. AEPC ("Alternative Energy Promotion Centre") is the government institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables, standing alongside (not inside) NEA. It is the operator and financier of the solar-home-system (SHS) programme, community mini-grids, institutional rooftop systems, and the subsidy / concessional-finance channel that rural solar rides on. # What the source covers Periodic AEPC "Progress Report" / "Renewable Energy Framework" / annual yearbook documents cover: Cumulative SHS installations by district, province, and year Village-scale mini-grid portfolio (locations, capacity, operator) Institutional solar (schools, clinics, govt offices) Improved cookstove and biogas programmes (context, not solar) Subsidy structure and donor-financing channels Policy and regulatory framework for rural renewables # Key data points (approximate, 2021–2024 window) Cumulative SHS installed: ~1.1 million systems (as of ~2021, with additions through 2024) Cumulative SHS capacity: ~80–100 MWp Community mini-grids (operational): ~30 sites, ~1.1 MWp aggregate Institutional solar: ~25,000 sites (rural clinics, schools, telecom, govt offices), ~15 MWp aggregate Geography: Karnali, Sudurpaschim, and remote hill districts of Koshi / Gandaki / Bagmati dominate installations (see data-rooftop-shs-deployment) Subsidy structure: Tiered, with higher subsidies for remote/difficult districts; typical residential SHS subsidy ~30–50% of capex Annual new installations: declining as grid reach expands (grid displaces SHS on economic grounds above ~30 HH/km²), replacement/upgrade cycle becoming dominant # Why AEPC matters strategically AEPC's relationship with NEA is the most under-discussed institutional story in Nepal solar: 1. AEPC reaches households NEA cannot. Remote hill and Karnali districts are uneconomic for grid extension at current tariffs; AEPC's subsidized SHS is the only electrification pathway that fits those geographies. 2. AEPC is the operational home of community-level solar. No mini-grid, no micro-grid, no community solar cooperative in Nepal exists without AEPC technical backstop or finance. 3. AEPC is the natural host for the agrivoltaic programme. If agrivoltaics-and-land implies a lease-template law and a tariff adder, AEPC's rural footprint and cooperative linkages make it the natural programme administrator — not NEA. 4. AEPC integrates into the political coalition for solar. The rural-electrification constituency that has sustained AEPC for three decades is the same constituency that would vote for Terai agrivoltaics and Karnali off-grid scale-up. # Documents and subsources The "AEPC renewable framework" source is a composite of: AEPC Yearbook / Annual Progress Report (annual, typically one-year lag in publication) National Renewable Energy Framework (NREF) 2017 and revisions Renewable Energy Subsidy Policy 2016 and updates AEPC-published feasibility studies for specific mini-grid and institutional projects Donor project completion reports (ADB, WB, EIB, UNDP) that flow through AEPC programmes # Relevance to project This is the anchor source for: aepc — the institution entity rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the off-grid / mini-grid track data-rooftop-shs-deployment — district-level SHS counts agrivoltaics-and-land — AEPC as natural programme host claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-electrification politics And it is the first place to look when the question is "how much solar is actually deployed in Nepal total — utility + rooftop + off-grid?", because the DoED / NEA utility-scale figure of roughly 142 MW captures only the first track. # Data-quality notes AEPC yearbooks lag by ~1–2 years in publication. District-level data fidelity is high (AEPC subsidizes per-system; each install has a record) but aggregation into the public yearbook is lagged and sometimes incomplete. The 1.1 M cumulative SHS count includes decommissioned and replaced systems; the operational fleet is likely 700,000–900,000 at any time. Mini-grid reliability / continuous-operation data is uneven; some grids have been dormant between donor-project cycles. # Gaps we would like to close A proper 2024 district-level registry — ideal source for the map layer in data-rooftop-shs-deployment. Operational-status snapshot of the ~30 mini-grids (how many are actually running as of 2024?). AEPC–NEA integration agreement — the grid-edge protocol for when grid reaches an off-grid site. # Limitations Publication lag. AEPC yearbooks lag by 1–2 years; the most recent public yearbook does not capture the current operational fleet. Operational vs. cumulative count. The ~1.1M cumulative SHS figure includes decommissioned and replaced systems; the operational fleet is likely 700,000–900,000 at any time. Mini-grid reliability data uneven. Some mini-grids have been dormant between donor-project cycles; continuous-operation data is not systematically published. Composite source. This page synthesizes multiple AEPC documents (yearbooks, NREF, subsidy policy, donor reports) rather than representing a single published document at a fixed date. # Related aepc rooftop-minigrid-offgrid data-rooftop-shs-deployment eib-rural-solar-phase2 — donor channel running through AEPC wb-grid-solar-ee-project — adjacent donor channel (NEA-side) nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the complementary utility-side primary source

pages.body_text: AIIB Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project Summary (2026) # Summary AIIB's proposed-project summary for the Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project, published in February 2026. It records the current proposed financing envelope, technical configuration, implementing entities and preliminary environmental and social risk profile. # Key Findings Project status: proposed; AIIB environmental and social Category A. Proposed AIIB sovereign financing: USD 200 million, with ADB named as lead co-financier. Current configuration: 220 m dam, 600 MW underground main powerhouse and 70 MW dam-toe ecological-flow powerhouse. Preliminary footprint: approximately 2,405 hectares of permanent land acquisition and about 3,300 affected households, including an estimated 290 physically and economically displaced households. The source identifies land acquisition, Indigenous Peoples, biodiversity, sediment, slope stability, seismic, dam-safety and GLOF risks and lists assessment and management instruments still under preparation or review. # Relevance This is the current primary status and safeguard source for dudhkoshi-storage. It distinguishes proposed financing from approval, effectiveness, disbursement and financial close. # Limitations The document is a proposed-project summary, not an approval document, financing agreement, final design report or construction notice. Its social-impact figures are preliminary, and transmission-line and access-road impacts were still being assessed.

pages.title: Arun-3 Project Status & PDA Summary (2025)
pages.excerpt: Reference compilation for the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric Project — combining the 2014 Project Development Agreement (PDA) between Nepal and SJVN with 2024–2025 construction progress reports.
pages.body_text: Arun-3 Project Status & PDA Summary (2025) # Summary Reference compilation for the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric Project — combining the 2014 Project Development Agreement (PDA) between Nepal and SJVN with 2024–2025 construction progress reports. # Key Data Points Project basics Installed capacity: 900 MW (4 × 225 MW Francis turbines) Location: Phaksinda (dam) to Pukhuwa (powerhouse), Sankhuwasabha District Design: peaking run-of-river, 3.4 hours/day at full rated output Estimated cost: USD 1.6+ billion Annual energy: 3,924–4,019 GWh (design) Concession: 30-year Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) Commercial structure (PDA, 2014) Developer: SJVN (Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam), via subsidiary SAPDC Nepal's free-power share: 21.9% (~197 MW equivalent, royalty-free) Additional 10% offered to Nepal on commercial terms Remaining electricity exported to India via a new 400 kV DC line to Sitamarhi, Bihar Schedule and progress (December 2025) Construction start: 2018/19 Original COD target: March 2025 — not met SJVN applied for COD extension to September 2026; Project Review Panel formed to decide Physical progress: 74.61% (power generation side) Financial progress: 74.6% 400 kV cross-border transmission line: 58.3% physical progress # Relevance to Project Primary source for Arun-3's capacity, schedule, cost, and the Nepal–India free-power / export structure that makes Arun-3 a flagship example of India-developed, India-dispatched hydropower inside Nepal. # Limitations Self-reported data: SJVN cost and progress figures are self-reported; no independent audit is cited. Social impact gap: Social, resettlement, and environmental impact data is sourced from SAPDC's own materials, not independent assessment. Seasonal profile incomplete: The 3.4-hour/day peaking design is noted but the full seasonal generation shape is not provided. Grid absorption unknown: India-side grid absorption constraints for the exported power are not addressed. Schedule fluidity: COD target has already been missed; the September 2026 extension is under review and not assured. # See also arun-3 hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation

pages.title: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments
headings: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments
pages.excerpt: CARE Ratings Nepal surveillance reports and rating rationales for Sanima Mai Hydropower Limited, a 22 MW private IPP on the Mai Khola (eastern Nepal). The Sanima Mai generation data provides one of the most complete multi-year time series for tracking Q-design discharge performan
pages.body_text: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments # Summary CARE Ratings Nepal surveillance reports and rating rationales for Sanima Mai Hydropower Limited, a 22 MW private IPP on the Mai Khola (eastern Nepal). The Sanima Mai generation data provides one of the most complete multi-year time series for tracking Q-design discharge performance against contracted energy. # Key data extracted ## Generation vs contracted energy (Q40 design) Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh/yr) | Actual (GWh/yr) | % of Contracted | ---|---|---|---| FY 2076/77 | 121.7 | 116.8 | 96.0% | FY 2077/78 | 121.7 | 107.1 | 88.0% | FY 2078/79 | 121.7 | 88.8 | 73.0% | FY 2079/80 | 121.7 | 103.4 | 85.0% | The declining trajectory from 96% to 73%, followed by partial recovery to 85%, exemplifies the hydrological volatility facing Q40-designed RoR plants on monsoon-dominated tributaries. Unlike Chilime's glacially-buffered Q65+ design, Sanima Mai's Q40 parameter produces higher variability and lower average delivery relative to contract. ## PPA structure Wet season: NPR 4.80/kWh (promotional, escalated to NPR 5.08 after 5 years) Dry season: NPR 8.40/kWh (escalated to NPR 8.89) 3% annual escalation for 5 years PPA year: 2010 # Limitations Single-project scope: Sanima Mai is one 22 MW RoR IPP on the Mai Khola; its generation and financial patterns are not representative of all RoR projects across Nepal's diverse river basins. Data recency: Generation data covers through FY 2079/80 only; more recent fiscal years are not included. The partial recovery to 85% may have continued or reversed. Q40 design context: The Q40 exceedance design is less conservative than the Q65+ designs common on glacially-fed rivers; hydrological variability observations apply to Q40-configured projects specifically. PPA vintage: The PPA terms described (2010, 3% escalation, NPR 4.80/8.40 wet/dry) are specific to this project's 2010-vintage PPA and do not represent current NEA PPA terms. Credit rating source: CARE Ratings surveillance reports prioritize creditworthiness metrics; they may not capture all technical or hydrological operating conditions in detail.

pages.excerpt: The Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) annual report for fiscal year 2078/79 provides the verified primary-source data for Chilime's dual-tier PPA billing architecture and generation performance. Chilime is an NEA subsidiary (NEA retains 51% controlling stake), and its PPA
pages.body_text: Chilime Hydropower Company Limited Annual Report FY 2078/79 # Summary The Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) annual report for fiscal year 2078/79 provides the verified primary-source data for Chilime's dual-tier PPA billing architecture and generation performance. Chilime is an NEA subsidiary (NEA retains 51% controlling stake), and its PPA (signed June 25, 1997) uses a categorically different billing architecture from modern IPPs. # Key data extracted ## Dual-tier billing architecture Category | Tariff (NPR/kWh) | FY2078/79 Volume (GWh) | FY2078/79 Revenue (NPR) | ---|---|---|---| Regular Energy | 8.17 | 133.24 | 1,088,000,000 | Excess Energy | 4.08 | 22.82 | 93,110,000 | Total | 7.57 (blended) | 156.06 | 1,181,740,179 | In FY2078/79, 85.4% of total generation (133.24 of 156.06 GWh) was classified as Regular Energy and billed at NPR 8.17 year-round — regardless of season. For comparison with modern private IPP tariff structures, see ppa-pricing. ## Generation overperformance Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh/yr) | Actual (GWh/yr) | % of Contracted | ---|---|---|---| FY 2075/76 | 132.9 | 153.7 | 115.6% | FY 2076/77 | 132.9 | 146.3 | 110.1% | # Limitations Date gap: FY 2078/79 corresponds to 2021/22; more recent annual reports may show different generation or tariff treatment. Subsidiary scope: CHCL is an NEA subsidiary with a 1997 PPA; its billing architecture is not representative of post-2010 private IPP contracts. Single-plant view: Does not cover other NEA subsidiaries (e.g., Rasuwagadhi) or the broader IPP tariff matrix. No audited financial statements: Revenue and volume figures are as reported by CHCL, not independently audited in this document.

pages.title: DoED Licensing Directive 2075 — Hydropower Project Licensing
pages.excerpt: "विद्युत आयोजनाको अनुमतिपत्र सम्बन्धी निर्देशिका, २०७५" (Directive on Licensing of Electricity Projects, 2075 BS), issued by the Department of Electricity Development (DoED) in 2075 BS and now published by DoED as the fifth-amendment version.
pages.body_text: DoED Licensing Directive 2075 # Summary "विद्युत आयोजनाको अनुमतिपत्र सम्बन्धी निर्देशिका, २०७५" (Directive on Licensing of Electricity Projects, 2075 BS), issued by the Department of Electricity Development (DoED) in 2075 BS and now published by DoED as the fifth-amendment version. # Key provisions Q45 design discharge mandate: Projects must size their design discharge on Q45 exceedance ("Probability of Accident Q45 of Hydrological Time Series Data"). Earlier practices used Q40 or even Q25. Q80 exemption: Projects ≤1 MW for rural electrification may use Q80. Licence fee basis: DoED charges licence fees on Q45 basis but has allowed Q40 if a PPA is ultimately signed. Amended directive record: DoED's current public page identifies the directive as the fifth-amendment version, with fifth amendment date 2081/08/18. No climate adjustment requirement: DoED has not mandated climate-adjusted hydrological decrement factors in feasibility studies, despite draft ICIMOD guidelines. # Limitations Legal directive, not implementation record. The directive establishes licensing requirements; it does not show how consistently DoED applies them across individual projects. Hydrology rule specificity. The Q45 rule is explicit, but the source does not provide the hydrological datasets or statistical methods used by applicants. Climate-adjustment absence. The directive does not mandate climate-adjusted hydrology; that absence is a regulatory gap, not a quantified estimate of project risk. Amended text boundary. This source page now points to the current DoED publication page for the fifth-amendment version. Any claim about the original 2075 wording should be checked against the specific version cited.

pages.body_text: DoED Power Plants: Solar Table # Summary The Department of Electricity Development operating solar power-plant table used as the registry source for mapped operating grid-connected solar plants. # Data Extracted Operating solar plant names Owner names Capacity District Display coordinates where available # Data-Quality Notes The January 2026 registry snapshot lists 25 operating grid-connected solar plants totaling 141.74 MW. The mapped layer treats DoED coordinates as plant display anchors, not surveyed parcel boundaries. Rows with zero or unusable coordinates are mapped with lower-confidence locality anchors and should not be used for parcel-level siting. # Limitations Snapshot date: January 2026 registry snapshot — static point-in-time data. The DoED table is not updated on a fixed schedule; plants commissioned after the snapshot date are not reflected. Coordinate precision: DoED coordinates are display anchors, not surveyed parcel boundaries. Rows with zero or unusable coordinates are mapped with lower-confidence locality anchors. Not suitable for parcel-level siting analysis. Coverage scope: Only operating grid-connected plants. Under-construction, proposed, and off-grid solar are excluded. Capacity reporting: The 141.74 MW total is a registry sum at snapshot date; individual plant capacities may differ from other registries or reporting periods. # Related data-solar-fleet-inventory data-layer-solar-plants-nea-awards nea-solar

pages.body_text: Dudhkoshi Storage — NEA Proposal & Feasibility Record # Summary Reference compilation for the Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project, covering the original 1980s ADB-supported feasibility, the 2021 restart with land acquisition, the 2024 NEA construction proposal to government, and the 2024–2025 financing conversations with AIIB. # Key Data Points Capacity: 635 MW (NEA / Investopaper) or 670 MW (ELC / Power Technology) — design basis varies between the two references Main powerhouse: 600 MW underground + 70 MW dam-toe ecological flow unit Annual energy (design): 3,377–3,444 GWh/year Dam: 200–220 m height at Lamidanda / Rabhuwaghat Headrace tunnel: 13.3 km, reservoir to Dhitung powerhouse Active reservoir volume: 1.581 MCM (per Power Technology) Estimated total cost: ~USD 2.2 billion (~NPR 308 billion) Districts: Okhaldhunga, Khotang, Solukhumbu Developer: Nepal Electricity Authority Financing track: AIIB sovereign funding proposed Schedule: construction from ~2027, commercial operation ~2031 (ELC / Power Technology estimate) Land: ~20,000 ropani private, ~162 households fully displaced, ~988 partially affected # Relevance to Project Primary source for Dudhkoshi's technical envelope, financing posture, social footprint and timeline — the three axes on which its buildability will actually be judged. Note: two self-consistent but divergent capacity numbers (635 MW vs 670 MW) are present in respected secondary sources; this page records both. # Limitations Capacity ambiguity: Two self-consistent but divergent capacity figures (635 MW vs 670 MW) exist across respected secondary sources; the design basis for each is not fully reconciled. Seismic gaps: Detailed seismic design basis is not covered despite the project's proximity to Everest-region fault systems. Reservoir-induced seismicity modelling is absent. GLOF integration unverified: The 2024 Thame GLOF in the same river system is directly relevant, but GLOF integration into the dam's design flood is not addressed. Self-reported data: Cost, schedule, and social impact figures are drawn from secondary compilations of NEA/AIIB materials, not independent audit. Pre-financing status: The AIIB sovereign funding is proposed, not committed; financing is not closed. # See also dudhkoshi-storage glof-risk storage-deficit

pages.title: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II
headings: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II (Phase II)
pages.excerpt: European Investment Bank line of up to EUR 8 million for the development of ground-mounted, grid-connected solar PV installations at four locations in Nepal. Implemented through the Government of Nepal with AEPC-facilitated site selection and NEA-grid interconnection.
pages.body_text: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II (Phase II) # Summary European Investment Bank line of up to EUR 8 million for the development of ground-mounted, grid-connected solar PV installations at four locations in Nepal. Implemented through the Government of Nepal with AEPC-facilitated site selection and NEA-grid interconnection. The second phase of a two-phase EIB solar programme; Phase I (earlier in the decade) financed smaller distributed and rural installations. Phase II is notable for being among the first EU-financing instruments for utility-scale grid-connected solar in Nepal, parallel to the World Bank Grid Solar & EE Project. # What the programme covers Credit size: up to EUR 8 million Instrument: EIB concessional loan to Government of Nepal Implementation partners: AEPC (site selection, community engagement), NEA (grid interconnection, off-take), Ministry of Energy (oversight) Target: four ground-mounted grid-connected solar PV sites Geographic focus: rural and semi-urban locations, likely in the Middle Hills region (site names to be verified from EIB project documentation and AEPC implementation reports) Time horizon: implementation expected 2023–2027 window # Key data points Specific figures require verification from the EIB project portal and AEPC implementation progress reports; the public-domain anchor facts: EUR 8 million credit ceiling Four ground-mounted sites Grid-connected (distinguishing it from Phase I distributed installations) Rural / semi-urban focus AEPC-implemented — this is critical: the programme runs on AEPC's cooperative-facilitation model rather than a pure-NEA tender, which makes it a test case for the AEPC-anchored solar-scaling thesis argued in rooftop-minigrid-offgrid and agrivoltaics-and-land # Why this source matters Three institutional-frame reasons: 1. It is a bridge between off-grid AEPC and utility-scale NEA tracks. Most financing either funds SHS/mini-grids via AEPC (track 3) or funds utility-IPP solar via NEA (track 1). EIB Phase II finances utility-scale grid-connected PV through AEPC — a rare institutional bridge. If it works well, it is a template for future donor programming. 2. Scale matches the agrivoltaic test case. EUR 8M / ~4 sites is ~EUR 2M per site ≈ NPR 280M per site ≈ 3–5 MWp. This is exactly the right size for early agrivoltaic pilot projects — big enough to matter, small enough that community co-operation can be worked out site-by-site. 3. Geographic focus on rural / semi-urban Middle Hills tests Zone C of the solar-resource-geography-nepal classification, where most Nepali household solar investment actually lives. # Parallel / adjacent programmes Programme | Donor | Channel | Track | ---|---|---|---| Grid Solar & EE Project (wb-grid-solar-ee-project) | World Bank | NEA | Utility | EIB Phase II (this page) | EIB | AEPC → NEA interconnect | Utility, AEPC-delivered | 960 MW Tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) | Private IPP + debt | NEA | Utility | SREP Nepal | CIF / ADB / WB | AEPC | Off-grid | Karnali Off-grid Solar + BESS | WB | AEPC / NEA hybrid | Off-grid + grid edge | Biogas / improved cookstove programmes | Multi-donor | AEPC | Non-solar, non-electricity | # Documents and subsources EIB Project Page — eib.org/en/projects (search: Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II, Nepal) AEPC implementation monitoring reports — annual, AEPC internal with public summaries NEA Annual Report — references the programme in solar-projects rollup Ministry of Energy press releases — at site identification / inauguration milestones # Data-quality notes Site-specific details (exact locations, MWp per site, operator selection) have limited public-domain disclosure until AEPC / NEA implementation progress reports are published. The EUR 8M / four-site summary in the NEA FY 2024/25 annual report is the cleanest public reference anchor. Timeline ambitions and actual delivery pace may diverge — worth re-checking in FY 2025/26 NEA annual report. # Relevance to project Supporting source for: rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — AEPC as an institutional anchor beyond off-grid agrivoltaics-and-land — test-scale candidate for template pilots hybrid-siting-logic — mid-hill zone siting experiment aepc — institutional expansion of AEPC mandate claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-cooperative politics this programme rides on # Gaps we would like Publication of the four specific site locations and their MWp, district, developer, and COD target. AEPC implementation status reports at project-mid-point (likely 2026). Cross-reference with any agrivoltaic pilot element — if the EIB-AEPC line funds an agrivoltaic demonstration, it is the single most important test for the agrivoltaics-and-land thesis. # Limitations Site-level opacity. Specific site locations, MWp per site, operator selection, and COD targets have limited public-domain disclosure. Most project details are known only at the programme envelope level (EUR 8M, four sites, rural/semi-urban). Implementation timeline uncertain. The 2023–2027 window is aspirational; actual delivery pace may diverge. The FY 2025/26 NEA annual report is the likely next source for implementation-status confirmation. AEPC institutional bridge untested. This programme funds utility-scale grid-connected PV through AEPC rather than NEA's standard tender track — a novel institutional arrangement whose effectiveness is not yet demonstrated. No agrivoltaic element confirmed. Despite the scale match for agrivoltaic pilots, there is no public confirmation that any of the four sites include an agrivoltaic component. # Related wb-grid-solar-ee-project — parallel donor programme (NEA-track) aepc-renewable-framework — institutional home nea-960mw-solar-tender — private-finance counterpart rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the track this programme belongs to nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the public-disclosure anchor

pages.title: Global Solar Atlas (Nepal coverage)
headings: Why this source is the map-layer anchor
pages.excerpt: The primary satellite-derived solar resource dataset for Nepal's explorer map layer and the reference cross-check for every GHI / DNI number used elsewhere in the wiki. Provided as a free-to-use web-tile and downloadable-data service by Solargis under the World Bank Group ESMAP p
pages.body_text: Global Solar Atlas (Nepal Coverage) # Summary The primary satellite-derived solar resource dataset for Nepal's explorer map layer and the reference cross-check for every GHI / DNI number used elsewhere in the wiki. Provided as a free-to-use web-tile and downloadable-data service by Solargis under the World Bank Group ESMAP programme. Cross-validated against the in-situ wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment pyranometer network (14 stations, 2015–2019), so the derived spatial maps carry ~±5% accuracy at station locations and somewhat wider error bands in untested high-mountain terrain. # What the source provides Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) — annual and monthly means at ~9 arc-second (~250 m) spatial resolution Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI) — same spatial detail Diffuse Horizontal Irradiance (DIF) — for tilted-array optimization Photovoltaic Electricity Output (PVOUT) — modelled output for a reference PV system at each location Optimal tilt angle maps Air temperature 2-m height climatology Tile-ready map service (XYZ / WMS endpoints for integration into web maps) # Nepal-specific findings GHI range across Nepal: ~3.8 to ~6.5 kWh/m²/day Highest GHI zones: trans-Himalayan rain-shadow (Mustang, Dolpa, upper Humla, upper Manang) — 5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day Lowest GHI zones: Kathmandu Valley and east-facing mid-hill slopes — 4.2–4.6 kWh/m²/day Terai plains: 4.8–5.3 kWh/m²/day — broadly uniform with the north Indian plains PVOUT (specific yield): 1,500–1,800 kWh/kWp/year in trans-Himalayan, 1,350–1,500 in Terai, 1,150–1,350 in mid-hill — the yield hierarchy that translates GHI into MWh/MWp # Why this source is the map-layer anchor The wiki explorer's proposed layer (see data-map-inventory, data-nepal-solar-resource-zones) is built from Global Solar Atlas classifications, specifically: 1. Raw satellite GHI grid is classified into five zone bands (A, B, C, D, E) by threshold 2. Zone polygons are intersected with district boundaries for display 3. Map tiles are served directly from the Global Solar Atlas XYZ endpoint as an overlay basemap option in the explorer The attribution required by the Global Solar Atlas licence (CC BY 4.0) is included in the layer legend and the map credits. # Licence and data access Licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) Attribution: "Solargis, The World Bank Group" in any derived product Tile service: XYZ / WMS endpoints (see Global Solar Atlas documentation) Data download: National-level GeoTIFF layers available directly from the Global Solar Atlas download section (annual GHI, DNI, PVOUT) API: Solargis commercial API for higher-resolution or bespoke time-series (not needed for map display) # Cross-validation against ESMAP station data Global Solar Atlas vs measured (from wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment): Station | GSA GHI | Measured GHI | Bias | ---|---:|---:|---:| Kathmandu | 4.4 | 4.3 | +2% | Pokhara | 4.5 | 4.5 | 0% | Nepalgunj | 5.2 | 5.1 | +2% | Simara | 4.9 | 4.9 | 0% | Biratnagar | 5.0 | 4.9 | +2% | Dhankuta | 4.5 | 4.4 | +2% | Jumla | 5.3 | 5.2 | +2% | Surkhet | 4.9 | 4.8 | +2% | Jomsom | 5.5 | 6.0 | −8% | Trans-Himalayan is the one zone where satellite systematically under-estimates GHI (Jomsom 8% bias). This is the most important caveat: for Mustang / Dolpa / upper Manang planning, field measurement should be used where available, and the "Zone A 5.8–6.5" range cited in the wiki is calibrated to measurement rather than to the satellite layer. # Limitations Trans-Himalayan underestimation. The Jomsom station shows an 8% satellite underestimation bias against ground measurements — the most significant known error. Error bands are wider in untested high-mountain terrain. Spatial resolution. ~250 m (~9 arc-second) resolution is adequate for regional and district-level planning but insufficient for micro-siting individual solar plants — local shadowing, slope, and access constraints are not captured. Satellite-derived, not ground-measured. GHI/DNI values are modelled from satellite data, not from a dense ground-pyranometer network. The 14-station ESMAP calibration provides validation points but does not cover all terrain types. Static climatology. The dataset represents long-term average climatology and does not capture interannual variability, monsoon onset shifts, or trends under climate change. # Related wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the calibration source solar-resource-geography-nepal — the concept-page interpretation data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — the classification used in the map layer data-map-inventory — where this appears in the explorer irena-remap-nepal — independent scenario use of the same data

pages.title: Green Hydrogen Roadmap for Nepal
pages.excerpt: Strategic roadmap for producing green hydrogen from Nepal's surplus monsoon hydropower via electrolysis. Envisions an entirely new domestic industrial ecosystem absorbing stranded wet-season power.
pages.body_text: Green Hydrogen Roadmap for Nepal # Summary Strategic roadmap for producing green hydrogen from Nepal's surplus monsoon hydropower via electrolysis. Envisions an entirely new domestic industrial ecosystem absorbing stranded wet-season power. # Key Data Points Primary target: domestic green ammonia/fertilizer production (Nepal imports 100% of chemical fertilizers) A domestic green fertilizer plant could absorb up to 500 MW of continuous baseload power Replacing coal in Nepal's cement clinker production would require 227,743 tonnes of green hydrogen annually, needing 2,002 MW of dedicated hydropower Projected viable production cost: $2.15/kg by 2035 Government adopted Green Hydrogen Policy in 2024 with tax exemptions and regulatory framework Commercial pilots targeted for 2025–2027, industrial scale by 2035 # Relevance to Project Central to green-hydrogen-nepal and the demand-creation argument in domestic-led-hydro-strategy. Addresses stranded-generation by creating domestic demand for surplus monsoon power. # Limitations Roadmap, not committed project pipeline. The ammonia, fertilizer, and cement-substitution figures are planning scenarios rather than financed projects. Demand-creation assumptions. The roadmap assumes industrial offtake, electrolysis deployment, water availability, and fertilizer-market integration that are not yet demonstrated in Nepal. Cost trajectory uncertainty. The projected $2.15/kg production cost by 2035 depends on equipment-cost declines, power-price assumptions, and utilization rates. Policy still early-stage. The 2024 Green Hydrogen Policy creates a framework, but pilot delivery, permitting, and industrial procurement models remain unsettled.

pages.title: ICIMOD HKH Glacier Change Summary
pages.excerpt: ICIMOD's regional evidence on glacier change across the Hindu Kush Himalaya and its implications for long-run water systems.
pages.body_text: ICIMOD HKH Glacier Change Summary # Summary Regional glacier change assessment for the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Documents the scale and pace of glacier retreat affecting Nepal's river systems and long-term hydropower viability. # Key Data Points Glacier area across HKH fell by ~12% between 1990 and 2020, with faster recent ice loss Nepal-specific inventories show substantial long-run glacier retreat Glacier retreat rate: ~0.4–0.5m water equivalent per year Under high-emission scenarios, 65% glacier volume reduction projected by 2100 # Relevance to Project Underpins peak-water concept and glof-risk. Relevant to koshi-basin (278 glaciers, 51 km³ ice). The 12% area loss and 65% volume projection are key numbers for the climate dimension of the public energy-system story, including the peak-water framing for the 2040–2070 build window. # Limitations Regional aggregate, not Nepal-disaggregated. The 12% area loss and 65% volume projection are HKH-wide figures; Nepal-specific glacier inventories may show different retreat rates and volume trajectories. 2023 publication window. Does not capture the most recent acceleration in glacier mass loss reported in subsequent ICIMOD and WMO assessments. Scenario-dependent projections. The 65% volume reduction figure is under a high-emission scenario; lower-emission pathways produce different outcomes. The source page does not differentiate between scenario bands. Glacier retreat rate is a regional average. The ~0.4–0.5m water equivalent per year varies significantly by sub-basin and elevation band.

pages.title: ICIMOD Koshi Basin Programme
pages.excerpt: ICIMOD's research programme on the koshi-basin, covering downstream impacts, agricultural dependency, and flood dynamics. Supports the geopolitical significance of Nepal's eastern river system.
pages.body_text: ICIMOD Koshi Basin Programme # Summary ICIMOD's research programme on the koshi-basin, covering downstream impacts, agricultural dependency, and flood dynamics. Supports the geopolitical significance of Nepal's eastern river system. # Key Data Points Koshi basin supports >40 million people Contributes disproportionately high sediment loads to the Ganges system Koshi irrigates ~500,000–600,000 ha in Bihar The Koshi is known as the "River of Sorrow" in Bihar due to shifting course and catastrophic flooding # Relevance to Project Central to hydro-geopolitics and ganges-contribution. Also relevant to sediment-as-design-constraint given extreme sediment loads. . # Limitations Programme page, not a single technical report. The source summarizes ICIMOD's Koshi Basin Programme rather than providing one citable methods document. Directional sediment framing. The page supports high-level sediment and flood-risk context but does not provide design-grade suspended-sediment parameters. Downstream aggregate scale. Population and irrigation figures are basin-scale context; they do not allocate impacts by project, district, or season. Programme date ambiguity. The page uses a 2023 source date, but the programme spans multiple outputs with different publication dates.

pages.title: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin
headings: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin
pages.excerpt: ICIMOD's basin-level account of Koshi sediment loads, erosion and environmental threats.
pages.body_text: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin # Summary ICIMOD's 2018 outreach publication Understanding Sediment Management, focused on sediment dynamics, erosion, and environmental threats in the koshi-basin. Provides the evidence base for treating sediment as a central engineering and planning constraint. # Key Data Points Although the Koshi basin represents only 9% of the Ganges river system, ICIMOD reports that it contributes nearly 25% of the Ganges sediment load: 100-135 million tonnes per year. Estimated soil-loss rates in the source include 22 tonnes/ha/year from barren land, 5.3 tonnes/ha/year from agricultural areas, 5 tonnes/ha/year from grassland, and 0.5 tonnes/ha/year from forested areas. Suspended-sediment budgeting reports 101 million tonnes/year at Chatara, 81 million tonnes/year at Birpur, and 43 million tonnes/year at Baltara, implying substantial deposition between those stations. Sediment, flood, and erosion risks are interconnected. Climate change is intensifying GLOF, landslide, and sediment-pulse risks. [!note] The current source is a four-page ICIMOD outreach publication. It provides annual sediment-load and erosion-rate figures, but not a full hydropower design-parameter table. # Limitations Date: Published 2020; climate-sediment dynamics and GLOF hazard profiles may have shifted since publication. Basin scope: Covers the Koshi basin only; does not assess sediment regimes in Karnali, Gandaki, or Mahakali basins. Outreach-publication scope: The assessment provides several useful quantitative anchors, but it is not a full technical sediment design manual for hydropower projects. Source type: ICIMOD is a regional knowledge centre; data should be cross-referenced with WECS river-basin plans and project-level feasibility studies where possible.

pages.title: Thame Valley GLOF 2024 — Causes, Impacts and Future Risks
headings: Thame Valley GLOF 2024 — Causes, Impacts and Future Risks
pages.excerpt: This 2025 technical publication by ICIMOD and Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority documents the 16 August 2024 Thame Valley glacial lake outburst flood. It combines satellite analysis, field investigation, UAV survey and post-event measurements to re
pages.body_text: Thame Valley GLOF 2024 — Causes, Impacts and Future Risks # Summary This 2025 technical publication by ICIMOD and Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority documents the 16 August 2024 Thame Valley glacial lake outburst flood. It combines satellite analysis, field investigation, UAV survey and post-event measurements to reconstruct the two-lake cascade and assess remaining hazards in the valley. # Key Findings The report attributes the disaster to successive releases from Upper Ngole Cho and Lower Ngole Cho, about 10 km upstream of Thame village. A rock avalanche entered Upper Ngole Cho and generated a displacement wave that eroded the moraine above its bedrock dam. The released flow then descended about 120 m and struck Lower Ngole Cho. The Lower Ngole Cho breach measured about 21.6 m deep and 51 m wide. Field and satellite measurements indicate that roughly 303,000 m³ of water was released from that lake. The flood developed into a hyper-concentrated flow that transported debris for more than 80 km along the Thame and Dudh Koshi rivers. Documented damage in Thame included homes, hotels, schools, agricultural land and the Khumbu hydropower intake. The report also records sediment deposition near the surge tank and continuing slope instability near hydropower infrastructure. The study identifies continuing avalanche, overflow and lake-instability hazards upstream; its risk classifications are specific to the lakes assessed in the Thame watershed. # Relevance This is the direct technical source for the 2024 example on glof-risk. It also supports the event-specific references on koshi-basin and provides hazard context for dudhkoshi-storage, without establishing the design basis or exposure of that proposed project. # Limitations This is an event-specific reconstruction and lake-risk assessment, not a Nepal-wide GLOF frequency study. Fieldwork took place in December 2024. Later geomorphic change, mitigation work or monitoring results are outside its evidence window. The report documents damage and physical processes but does not provide a project-level design flood, final repair cost, insurance assessment or financial-loss model for downstream hydropower. Regional climate-change evidence in the background section does not by itself establish a single-cause attribution for the triggering rock avalanche.

pages.body_text: India Cross-Border Trade in Electricity Guidelines (2018) # Summary India's regulatory framework governing cross-border electricity trade. Defines approval mechanisms, designated authorities, and conditions for Nepal's electricity exports to India. Critically, includes restrictions on projects with certain foreign investment. # Key Data Points Establishes Indian approval requirements for Nepal power imports India explicitly refuses purchase of electricity from Nepali projects with Chinese equity investment or Chinese EPC contractors Creates the monopsony market structure Nepal must navigate for exports Shapes which projects can access the Indian market vs which are locked out # Relevance to Project Central to india-energy-relationship and hydro-geopolitics. Shapes the export constraint dimension of seasonal-arbitrage-trap. source-review note. Public source review highlighted the China-exclusion mechanism. # Limitations Snapshot date: 2018 guidelines — the regulatory framework may have changed significantly. The page itself flags the gap: "Need updated post-2024 versions of these guidelines — the approval regime may have expanded." Bilateral scope: Does not cover bilateral agreements or protocols signed after 2018, including the 2024 long-term power trade agreement. One-sided perspective: The document represents Indian regulatory requirements only; Nepal's reciprocal conditions and regulatory framework are not captured. Coverage: Focused on approval mechanisms for trade; does not address transmission capacity allocation, pricing formulas, or dispute resolution in depth.

pages.title: IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment and REmap Nepal
headings: IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment and REmap Nepal
Key data points (composite from RRA + REmap + Cost Database)
Global LCOE benchmarks (IRENA Renewable Cost Database)
pages.excerpt: Primary international source for solar and renewable cost benchmarking against Nepal specifics. Two IRENA document streams are relevant:
pages.body_text: IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment and REmap Nepal # Summary Primary international source for solar and renewable cost benchmarking against Nepal specifics. Two IRENA document streams are relevant: 1. IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment (RRA) — Nepal (2017, with subsequent updates). Country-level diagnostic; identifies barriers and potential across solar, wind, and small hydro. 2. IRENA REmap Nepal scenario analysis. Quantitative pathway modelling for higher renewables shares in Nepal's electricity and total energy mix. Plus the IRENA Renewable Capacity Statistics (annual, global) and Renewable Cost Database — which provide the global LCOE benchmarks this project uses in data-solar-hydro-lcoe and solar-lcoe-crossover. # What these sources cover Solar PV technical potential by Nepal resource zone Wind potential (limited but non-trivial in Mustang + parts of Koshi) Small hydro potential (overlaps with wecs-hydropower-potential-2019) Barriers analysis: financing, policy, grid integration, skills LCOE benchmarks for Nepal-comparable countries Scenario pathways to 2030 / 2050 with renewables share Policy recommendations and institutional framework proposals # Key data points (composite from RRA + REmap + Cost Database) ## Solar (Nepal-specific) Estimated solar PV technical potential: ~50,000–100,000 MWp (various IRENA framings; caveats on siteability) Mean Nepal GHI: ~4.7–4.9 kWh/m²/day (matches Global Solar Atlas) Suggested short-term target: >1 GW by 2030 (REmap Accelerated Case); policy + financing gaps identified as primary blocker, not resource ## Global LCOE benchmarks (IRENA Renewable Cost Database) Utility-scale solar PV weighted global LCOE 2010 → 2024: $0.359 → $0.044 per kWh (−88% real) Module price 2010 → 2024: $2.00/W → ~$0.10/W (−95%) Onshore wind LCOE 2010 → 2024: $0.113 → $0.033 per kWh BESS (4h utility) LCOE 2020 → 2024: ~$190 → ~$95 per MWh Capacity-weighted auction-low solar tariff 2024: ~$0.020–$0.030/kWh (GCC, India) These are the numbers the solar-lcoe-crossover argument rides on. # IRENA's diagnostic frame for Nepal The RRA identifies five priority barriers: 1. Policy coherence — fragmented responsibility across MoEWRI / NEA / AEPC / ERC 2. Financing access — limited local-currency long-tenor finance for renewables 3. Grid integration — transmission and distribution readiness for variable resources 4. Institutional capacity — solar-specific engineering and O&M depth is thin 5. Land and permits — no agrivoltaic framework, fragmented land tenure Most of these overlap with the bottleneck-hierarchy for hydro, with one addition specific to solar: absence of land/permitting framework for utility-scale ground-mount. # Relevance Provides the global LCOE benchmarks the solar-lcoe-crossover and data-solar-hydro-lcoe pages rely on. Gives an externally-credentialed estimate of Nepal solar potential without the over-promise of some national documents. Frames the barriers analysis in language compatible with donor programs. The REmap pathway is a normative scenario against which the NEA/MoEWRI 2024/25 actual trajectory (960 MW tender + 170 MW PPA + 142 MW operating) can be compared. For the interpretive use of this benchmark in portfolio planning, see solar-role-in-winter-deficit. # Limitations IRENA's Nepal "technical potential" estimates vary widely (50,000–100,000+ MWp) depending on whether high-mountain inaccessible land is counted. Only the Zone A trans-Himalayan + Zone B Terai + Zone C mid-hill deployable fraction (~15,000–25,000 MWp) matters for real planning; see data-solar-fleet-inventory potential pyramid. IRENA REmap pathways are normative scenarios, not forecasts. Use for direction of travel, not for calendar-year predictions. Global LCOE benchmarks reflect weighted averages; Nepal-specific numbers should always be context-adjusted for grid costs, land costs, and FX. # Related wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the measured-resource complement global-solar-atlas-nepal — the satellite-derived complement wecs-energy-synopsis-2024 — the domestic energy-balance frame wb-country-economic-memo-2025 — macroeconomic context

headings: What this source does not cover
pages.excerpt: This is the Annexes volume (Vol. 2) of the JICA Study Team's Final Report for the (IPSDP) — the same study whose compact policy conclusions are captured in moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025. The executive summary is where the headline numbers and milestone ladder live; this volume i
pages.body_text: JICA IPSDP Final Report Annexes (Vol. 2) # Summary This is the Annexes volume (Vol. 2) of the JICA Study Team's Final Report for the (IPSDP) — the same study whose compact policy conclusions are captured in moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025. The executive summary is where the headline numbers and milestone ladder live; this volume is where the _workings_ live — the demand forecast inputs, the MP2014 project scorecards, the existing-plant inventories, the hydropower sequencing logic, and the geology, hydrology and seismology that bound what can actually be built. The volume is 315 pages and contains Annexes 1–6 only. The PDF's own table of contents lists 16 annexes in total; Annexes 7–16 (power generation planning, cross-border trade status, power system planning, SEA, economic and financial analysis, financing, surplus utilisation, governance, milestones, capacity development) are carried in companion volumes that are not currently in the wiki's raw-source set. For this wiki, this is the authoritative upstream source for any claim of the form "JICA/MoEWRI's IPSDP study assumes X" about demand, existing fleet state, hydropower portfolio composition, or development-plan review — the executive summary is not granular enough on its own. Key cross-links: moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, nea, seasonal-arbitrage-trap, kulekhani-cascade, kali-gandaki-a, tanahu-hydropower, upper-arun. # Contents (Annexes 1–6 only) Annex | Title | First page | -------|-------|-----------:| 1 | General Information of Nepal (economy, topography, geology, seismology, climate, hydrology, air quality) | 5 | 2 | Current Status of the Power Sector in Nepal (organisational structure, legal system, reform, corporate entities) | 55 | 3 | Current Situation of the Electric Power Facilities (existing generation fleet, transmission, distribution) | 146 | 4 | Review of Existing Development Plans (MP2014 screening, Multi-Criteria Analysis scorecards) | 174 | 5 | Power Demand Forecast (sectoral sales mix, consumer growth, electrification) | 196 | 6 | Hydropower Development Plan (bulk of the volume; portfolio composition and sequencing) | 244 | Annexes 7–16 listed in the front-matter TOC (Power Generation Development Planning; Current Status of Power Trade; Power System Development Planning; SEA; Economic and Financial Analysis; Financing; Utilisation of Surplus Electricity; Governance; Milestones & Future Outlook; Capacity Development) are _not present_ in this PDF. # Key claims Annex 3 (p. 147) states that NEA owns hydropower plants with an installed capacity of and designed annual generation of at an average plant factor of . Only Kulekhani I and Kulekhani II operate as storage (STO); the rest are ROR or PROR. Annex 3 generation-type table (p. 146) codifies four hydropower types used throughout the IPSDP optimisation — , (peak run-of-river with daily-to-weekly pondage), (storage / reservoir), and (pumped storage) — and notes the winter-peak / monsoon-spill economics that drive the seasonal-arbitrage-trap argument. Annex 4 (p. 174–175) records how the 2014 Nationwide Master Plan (MP2014) filtered candidate projects via Multi-Criteria Analysis with exclusions for installed capacity , dam height , project cost , annual flow-regulation rate , reservoir resettlement , or sites inside national parks / wildlife conservation areas / world heritage. The MP2014 scorecard table on p. 175 lists unit capacity, total energy, dry energy, project cost, unit cost, EIRR and FIRR for Dudh Koshi, Sun Koshi 3, Lower Badigad, Andhi Khola, Chera-1, Madi, Nalsyau Gad, Naumure (W. Rapti), Kokhajor-1, Lower Jhimruk and the rest of the MP2014 list. Annex 5 (p. 196) puts sectoral sales composition and consumer-growth rate at approximately with household electrification reaching in 2021 and a stated GoN target of . # Local source Local workspace copy: jica_ipsdp_main_report_vol2.pdf [!cite] jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 PDF created via Word → Adobe PDF. File is byte-identical to in the same directory (verified via SHA-256); the canonical path used by the wiki is . # Limitations Incomplete volume: This PDF contains only Annexes 1–6. headings: What this source does not cover
pages.excerpt: This executive summary is the clearest compact statement of the current MoEWRI/JICA planning logic for Nepal's long-horizon power buildout through 2040. It ties together demand growth, hydropower sequencing, 400 kV backbone and interconnection expansion, export strategy, and fina
pages.body_text: MoEWRI IPSDP Executive Summary # Summary This executive summary is the clearest compact statement of the current MoEWRI/JICA planning logic for Nepal's long-horizon power buildout through 2040. It ties together demand growth, hydropower sequencing, 400 kV backbone and interconnection expansion, export strategy, and financing needs in one document instead of scattering them across older nea or donor studies. The report is especially valuable because page 39 turns the plan into a milestone ladder with explicit dates for export crossover, self-sufficiency, the 28 GW government target, and a later clean-export role in South Asia. Section 2.4 then links those milestones to concrete trade channels, grid buildout, and wholesale arrangements with India and Bangladesh rather than treating exports as an abstract objective. Section 3 adds the guardrails the plan says must shape buildability, including environmental-flow management, protected-area restrictions, and the need to package hydropower with transmission and institutional reform. For this wiki, the document is a backbone source for india-energy-relationship, bangladesh-trade-route, niettp, and project-sequencing questions that depend on an official state planning frame rather than a single project promoter's view. # Contents Section | Page | ---------|------| 1. Introduction | 1 | 1.1 Background | 1 | 1.2 Objectives | 1 | 1.3 Basic Approaches on IPSDP | 2 | 2. IPSDP | 3 | 2.1 Outline of IPSDP | 3 | 2.2 Basic Understandings of the Development in Power Sector | 3 | 2.2.1 Organizational Structure of the Power Sector | 3 | 2.2.2 Involvement of Existing and On-going Power Development Plans in the Power Sector | 4 | 2.2.3 Hydropower Development Plan | 5 | 2.2.4 Power Trade | 7 | 2.3 The Study for Development Scenarios | 8 | 2.3.1 Direction of Development Scenarios | 8 | 2.3.2 Setting of Development Scenarios | 10 | 2.3.3 Analysis Results of Development Scenarios and Selection of Optimum Scenario | 12 | 2.4 Formulation of Optimum Scenario | 12 | 2.4.1 Power Demand Forecast | 14 | 2.4.2 Power Generation Development Planning | 15 | 2.4.3 The Power System Plan (PSP) and power trade with neighboring countries | 18 | 2.4.4 Financial Analysis of IPSDP | 22 | 2.4.5 Investment Plan | 28 | 2.4.6 Strategic Environmental Assessment | 31 | 3. Development Milestones and Future Outlook for IPSDP | 34 | 3.1 Development Milestones and Pathways towards 2040 in IPSDP | 34 | 3.2 Challenges of IPSDP | 36 | 3.3 Required Transformations and Future Outlook for the Power Sector | 37 | 3.4 Challenges and Recommendations for IPSDP | 39 | # Key claims Figure 3.1-1 on page 39 marks as the year when power exports surpass imports. The same milestone ladder marks as the point when self-sufficiency in electricity supply is achieved. The ladder marks as the year when the government's 28,000 MW development target is achieved. The ladder marks as the stage when Nepal contributes clean export to the South Asian region. The page-39 era buckets attach named projects to each window: Rasuwagadhi, Sanjen, Upper Modi A, Rahughat, Upper Trishuli 3B, Madhya Bhotekoshi, Upper Trishuli-1, and Arun 3 in the block; Tanahu HEP, Tamor Storage, Madi Storage HEP, Manang Marsyangdi, Budhi Gandaki Ka, Bheri 4, Tila-1, and Tila-2 in ; Lower Seti, Uttarganga STO, Phukot Karnali, Nalsyau Gad STO, Upper Arun, Chainpur Seti, Dudhkoshi STO, Sunkoshi 3 STO, Lower Badigad STO, Budhi Gandaki, Upper Marsyangdi-2, Dudh Koshi-IV, Upper Tamor, Bheri-2, West Seti STO, and SR-06 STO in ; and Betan Karnali, Kimathanka Arun, Bharbung, Mugu Karnali STO, Tamakoshi 3, Khimti Shivalaya STO, Bajhang Upper Seti, Naumure STO, Upper Mugu Karnali, Bheri-1, and the Humla Karnali Cascade in . Section 2.4 frames the wholesale-trade menu around NEA offtake, power-trading companies, and direct overseas trade to DISCOs/customers in India and Bangladesh, with the adjacent text on pages 24-26 adding grid-connection, market, and long-term cross-border PPA mechanics that sit behind those channels. The SEA mitigation table on page 37 says hydropower planning must evaluate and manage environmental flows with reference to the IFC 2018 handbook, and it says projects in protected areas defined by Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act require prior permission and cannot assume river modification is automatically permissible. [!cite] moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 Cover date is December 2024 even though the local filename ends in 2025; the milestone ladder and policy framing cited above come from pages 25, 37, and 39 of the PDF. # Local source Local workspace copy: moewri_ipsdp_exec_summary_2025.pdf # What this source does not cover project-by-project construction progress after the study cutoff plant-level monthly generation or trade data # Limitations Planning document, not commitments. The milestone ladder (page 39) and project-era buckets represent MoEWRI/JICA planning targets — not COD-guaranteed projects. The 28 GW target and 2033 self-sufficiency date are aspirational government framing, not contracted timelines. Executive summary scope. This is the 39-page executive summary, not the full IPSDP main report. Technical annexes, cost tables, and scenario sensitivity analyses live in the main report volumes (see jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2). Date discrepancy. Cover date is December 2024, but the local filename uses 2025. Citation precision depends on distinguishing the report cover date from the local filename. Cutoff limitation. The study predates significant 2025 events (e.g., September 2024 flood damage to 600+ MW of capacity, post-flood recovery timelines, and any PPA or trade-agreement developments after the study cutoff). # See also data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 nepal-power-trade-schemes environmental-flow-policy ipsdp-2025-vs-wiki-claims

pages.title: NDRRMA Rasuwa Glacial Flood Situation Report 1 (2025)
headings: NDRRMA Rasuwa Glacial Flood Situation Report 1 (2025)
pages.excerpt: This two-page Government of Nepal situation report records the early official assessment of the 8 July 2025 Rasuwa flood. It combines a situation overview, remote-sensing observations, a preliminary damage summary and government response actions as of 10 July 2025.
pages.body_text: NDRRMA Rasuwa Glacial Flood Situation Report 1 (2025) # Summary This two-page Government of Nepal situation report records the early official assessment of the 8 July 2025 Rasuwa flood. It combines a situation overview, remote-sensing observations, a preliminary damage summary and government response actions as of 10 July 2025. # Key Findings NDRRMA describes a sudden flood caused by rapid discharge from a supraglacial lake on the Purepu Glacier in Tibet, approximately 35 km upstream of the Nepal-China border. The report says supraglacial ponds began forming in March 2025 and expanded through June. It records an estimated lake area of about 0.525 km² on 28 June, about 0.75 km² on 7 July and about 0.6 km² after the rapid decline on 8 July. The mapped flood path follows the Lende/Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridor from the border through Rasuwa and downstream districts. Its preliminary damage summary records the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge, sections of the Rasuwagadhi dry port, about 16 km of road and three hydropower plants as affected. The Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council directed agencies to coordinate with China on identifying the cause and to complete detailed damage assessments. NDRRMA and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology were still investigating the event when the report was issued. # Relevance This is the primary early-government source for the 2025 historical example on glof-risk and for the event context recorded on rasuwagadhi. # Limitations This is Situation Report 1, issued two days after the event. It is not a final causal investigation or final damage-and-loss assessment. Lake-area estimates are attributed within the report to ICIMOD and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology and may be revised by later analysis. The report gives an aggregate count of affected hydropower plants but does not identify each plant or provide plant-level engineering damage. Casualty, missing-person and asset-loss figures are time-stamped to 10 July 2025 and should not be treated as final totals.

Covers installed capacity, generation mix, trade volumes, grid infrastructure, and project pipeline for fiscal year 2024/25 (Nepali FY 2081/82). # Image Catalog This run is ingesting roughly 130 images from the FY 2024/25 annual report; the current atlas pass surfaced 131 real-image candidates for review. The atlas manifest lives at nea_annual_report_2024_2025_image_atlas.json. # Key Data Points Total installed generation capacity: 3,591.262 MW (hydro 3,389.912 MW, solar 141.940 MW, thermal 53.410 MW, bagasse 6 MW) Hydropower is 94.4% of installed generation System peak demand reached 2,901 MW on July 1, 2025 Per-capita electricity consumption reached 465 kWh Total system loss declined to 12.26% National grid coverage reached 97.6% 22 new projects (434 MW combined) commissioned in FY 2024/25 Available energy: 15,641 GWh (34% NEA/subsidiaries, 55% IPPs, 11% imported from India) kulekhani-cascade generated 279.8 GWh tanahu-hydropower approximately 67% complete 572 projects in broader license pipeline (311 survey, 180 generation, 81 operation) # Relevance to Project Primary source for current installed capacity, fleet composition, generation split, and trade volumes. pages.excerpt: NEA Engineering Company Limited's FY 2081/82 annual report covers its financial position and engineering assignments. Its damaged-assessment and restoration section records the company's work at the 111 MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Plant and the Trishuli 3B Hub following the 8 July
pages.body_text: NEA Engineering Company Annual Report FY 2081/82 # Summary NEA Engineering Company Limited's FY 2081/82 annual report covers its financial position and engineering assignments. Its damaged-assessment and restoration section records the company's work at the 111 MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Plant and the Trishuli 3B Hub following the 8 July 2025 flood. # Key Findings The report states that the 111 MW Rasuwagadhi plant entered commercial operation in January 2025. It describes severe flood damage on 8 July 2025 to civil structures, hydromechanical equipment and electromechanical systems, followed by suspension of generation. Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company Limited contracted NEA Engineering on 10 August 2025 for rapid damage assessment, generation restoration and long-term rehabilitation planning. The report records one unit returning to partial generation on 6 December 2025 and two-unit generation under available dry-season discharge from 25 December 2025. For the Trishuli 3B Hub, the report describes damage to temporary and gantry towers and protective structures, major scour on the right bank, sediment deposition on the left bank and an estimated channel shift of about 80 m toward the substation. # Relevance This is the direct institutional source for the commissioning, flood-damage and partial-restoration timeline on rasuwagadhi. Together with the government situation report, it supports the infrastructure consequences described in the 2025 example on glof-risk. # Limitations The annual report is NEA Engineering's account of its own assignments, not an independent forensic investigation. It labels the 8 July event a GLOF but does not reproduce the full glaciological evidence used to determine the initiating mechanism. The report does not establish final rehabilitation completion, full three-unit availability, a final damage cost or the plant's status after its reporting cutoff. The records the report's January 2026 publication month; the document does not state a more precise public release date.

The rows represent tender awards / pre-PPA records, not commissioned operating plants. # Limitations Pre-commissioning status: The rows represent tender awards and pre-PPA records, not commissioned operating plants. Awarded projects may be modified, canceled, or stalled. Snapshot date: November 2024 — the award landscape and tariff figures may have shifted since publication. Coordinate precision: District or substation anchors with jitter are display positions, not parcel coordinates. Not suitable for site boundary or land-use analysis. Tariff data: Awarded tariffs (NPR 4.99–5.54/kWh) may not reflect final PPA rates or as-constructed costs. # Related nea-960mw-solar-tender data-solar-fleet-inventory data-layer-solar-plants-nea-awards

pages.title: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment
headings: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment
pages.excerpt: Secondary legal analysis by Sushil Parajuli of the standard NEA hydropower Power Purchase Agreement text, covering Availability Declaration penalties, reserve margin, curtailment risk, and force majeure constraints.
pages.body_text: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment # Summary Secondary legal analysis by Sushil Parajuli of the standard NEA hydropower Power Purchase Agreement text, covering Availability Declaration penalties, reserve margin, curtailment risk, and force majeure constraints. # Key provisions ## Article 10.2 — AD Penalty Formula Compensation = [0.80 × min(Monthly Contract Energy, Availability Declaration) − (Actual Delivered + Forced Outage + Scheduled Outage + Force Majeure Energy)] × Purchase Rate for that Month. If result is negative, payment is zero. Establishes that if monthly energy falls below 80% of the lesser of Contract Energy or the Availability Declaration, the developer owes compensation to NEA. ## Article 10.1(Ka) — 10% Reserve Margin In the wet season (peak months Ashadh–Kartik), NEA/LDC can withhold 10% of Contract Energy or Availability Declaration as a "Reserve Margin" with ZERO compensation to the IPP. ## No Curtailment Exemption No clause in Article 10 exempts an IPP from AD penalties when the generation shortfall is caused by NEA/NLDC dispatch curtailment. The penalty formula applies irrespective of cause (aside from Force Majeure). ## Take-or-Pay Obligation 30-year take-or-pay: NEA is obligated to pay for 100% of Contracted Energy from COD. Schedule 3 provides up to 72 cumulative hours (3 days) of unpaid outage per year. ## Article 15 — Force Majeure Narrow definition. Covers only extraordinary events (e.g., floods exceeding design flood discharge from Schedule 1). Routine grid/transmission/substation failures are NOT force majeure. IPPs cannot invoke FM relief for standard grid failures. ## The "16% Curtailment" Claim No statutory basis found. Only the Article 10.1(Ka) 10% reserve margin exists in the PPA text. The 16% figure appears to be an industry misinterpretation — likely 10% reserve margin plus an erroneous 6% from an unknown source. No NEA, ERC, or PPA document mentions 16%. ## ERC Regulatory Context ERC Notice (Rule 2076/2019, Schedule 5) requires hydropower sellers to submit monthly Availability Declarations 30 days before the month starts. The ERC Electricity Regulatory Commission Act (2017) gives the Commission authority over PPAs. Under SVLCLaw (2022), PPAs signed before the Commission's establishment remain valid but Commission by-laws prevail over conflicting clauses. ## Standard PPA Existence NEA maintains a standard template but PPAs are negotiated individually. No publicly available PPA document was found. The Parajuli analysis is the primary secondary source. # Limitations Secondary analysis only: This is Parajuli's interpretation of the standard PPA text, not the primary legal document itself. No publicly available PPA document was located to verify the analysis against. Analyst's framing: The "16% Curtailment" debunking is a correction of industry lore, not a positive textual finding. The analysis may emphasize clauses relevant to its bankability argument. ERC evolution: ERC regulatory context reflects the Commission's authority as understood at the time of analysis; ERC by-laws and interpretations continue to evolve. Negotiated variation: NEA maintains a standard template but PPAs are negotiated individually. Clause language and enforcement may vary across projects.

pages.title: Nepal Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 (2025)
pages.excerpt: Nepal's official 2025 climate submission sets electricity, loss-reduction, electric-cooking and system-modernisation targets through 2035.
pages.body_text: Nepal Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 (2025) # Summary This Government of Nepal submission, dated 14 May 2025 and filed with the UNFCCC on 19 May 2025, sets electricity, loss-reduction, electric-cooking and system-modernisation targets through 2035. # Provenance Publisher / author: Government of Nepal Document date: 14 May 2025 Filed with: UNFCCC on 19 May 2025 Public URL: UNFCCC-hosted PDF Verified: 19 July 2026 against the filed PDF # Key Findings The submission sets targets to expand renewable electricity capacity to 14,031 MW by 2030 and 28,500 MW by 2035. It states that mini- and micro-hydro, solar, wind and bio-energy together should account for 10% and 15% of those respective totals. It also targets total transmission and distribution losses of 11.5% by 2030 and 10.5% by 2035. For electrification, the submission targets electric cookstove use in 2.1 million households and another 15,000 institutions and firms by 2035. Its policy measures include smart metering, demand-side management, a 20% generation reserve margin, transmission-system planning, distributed renewables and municipal energy plans. # Limitations It does not show that the target project pipeline is financed, permitted or buildable. It does not convert capacity targets into dependable dry-season energy. It does not provide an implementation dashboard or current progress series. The document says most quantified emissions reductions are conditional on international climate finance and support. # Relevance This source anchors official-target passages in state-of-the-system, solar-system, distribution-and-reliability, demand-and-electrification and climate-resilience-and-decarbonization. Current-system facts on those pages come from separate operational sources.

pages.body_text: Nepal Transmission System — 400 kV Landscape & Cross-Border Plan (2025) # Summary Reference compilation for Nepal's current and planned high-voltage transmission assets — the 400 kV east–west backbone and parallel central corridor, the legacy 220 kV and 132 kV grid, and the cross-border interconnections with India (ten links at five voltage levels). Drawn from NEA's 2024/25 annual report, NEA Transmission Directorate publications, the Millennium Challenge Account Nepal (MCA-Nepal) compact programme documents, and news reporting of individual commissioning events. # Key Data Points 400 kV operational backbone Hetauda–Dhalkebar–Inaruwa (HDDI) — first and currently only 400 kV east–west backbone inside Nepal. Commissioned in segments 2018–2022. Total spine ~300 km. Feeds the Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur cross-border link (400 kV bipole, operational since 2016, ADB + KfW co-financed). This is the sole operational 400 kV export route. 400 kV under construction / implementation MCA central 400 kV (Lapsiphedi–Ratmate–Hetauda–Damauli–Butwal) — the MCA-Nepal compact's headline 315 km transmission line, partially energised in 2025. Completion target 2026–2027. Gorakhpur–New Butwal 400 kV — second cross-border link, under construction. Commissioning target mid-2026. Inaruwa–Purnea 400 kV — third cross-border, implementation phase. Critical to Arun-3 evacuation once the plant is online. Lamki–Bareilly 400 kV — western cross-border at implementation setup; completion horizon 2027+. 220 kV operational Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV — original IPP evacuation corridor Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV — east–west spine at 220 kV Dana–Kushma–New Butwal 220 kV — west-central hydropower corridor 132 kV cross-border (legacy, operational) Kataiya–Kushaha (since 1971, the historic first link) Raxaul–Parwanipur, New Nautanwa–Mainahiya, Tanakpur–Mahendranagar Planned / under construction cross-border Nepalgunj–Nanpara 132 kV (under construction) Chameliya–Jauljibi 220 kV (planned, far-west) System-level parameters Nepal–India transfer capacity, 2025: ~2,300 MW total across all interconnections combined Current concurrent peak export: ~1,200 MW (monsoon 2024–25) Grid code: NEA grid code 2019 (amended 2022); Indian-side dispatch via NRLDC # Relevance to Project Primary source for the voltage levels, statuses, schedules and strategic roles of Nepal's ten currently-tracked corridors and ten cross-border interconnections. Used as the baseline citation for all per-corridor entity pages. # Limitations Compilation, not primary source: Drawn from multiple sources (NEA annual reports, Transmission Directorate documents, MCA-Nepal, news reporting) with varying update cycles and verification standards. Snapshot date: July 2025. Commissioning targets (e.g., Gorakhpur–New Butwal mid-2026) are forward-looking and subject to delay. Missing granularity: Actual segment-level substation capacities are confidential. Indian-side evacuation constraints beyond border crossings are not covered. Load-flow studies and battery/STATCOM plans are not included. Transfer capacity estimates: The ~2,300 MW total Nepal–India transfer capacity and ~1,200 MW concurrent peak export are operational approximations, not audited figures. # What This Source Does Not Cover Actual segment-level substation capacities (published only in confidential planning documents) Indian-side evacuation constraints beyond the border crossings Load flow studies under different generation dispatch scenarios Battery and STATCOM augmentation plans # See also hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone dhalkebar-muzaffarpur mca-central-400 hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation

pages.body_text: Pancheshwar Official Project Records — Nepal and India # Summary Combined source record for the official Nepal Pancheshwar project description and the Government of India Ministry of Jal Shakti project page. Together they provide the current published technical concept, treaty basis and DPR status. # Key Findings Full published capacity: 6,720 MW, comprising 6,480 MW at the high dam and 240 MW at the Rupali Gad re-regulating dam. Average annual energy: 12,333 GWh. High dam: 315 m rockfill dam with two equal 3,240 MW underground powerhouses, one on each bank. High-dam live storage: 6.56 billion m³. Treaty basis: Mahakali Treaty signed in February 1996. India records that WAPCOS submitted the draft final DPR in November 2016 and that finalisation remains underway because contentious issues have not been resolved. # Relevance This is the primary technical and status baseline for pancheshwar. It distinguishes the 6,480 MW high-dam component from the 6,720 MW full scheme and makes unresolved final DPR agreement the central milestone. # Limitations The published pages are project summaries, not the mutually accepted final DPR. They do not establish an approved current cost, financing package, resettlement plan, construction start or final benefit-sharing protocol.
