headings: Investigative Report: PPA Data Retrieval from ICRA & CARE Ratings Nepal
Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Financial Profile
Subsidiary vs. IPP Rate Differential (Document finding)
pages.excerpt: Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (15 pages) Original: Mission-based financial investigation sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119), CARE Ratings Nepal rating rationales, and statutory filings.
pages.body_text: Investigative Report: PPA Data Retrieval from ICRA & CARE Ratings Nepal Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (15 pages) Original: Mission-based financial investigation sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119), CARE Ratings Nepal rating rationales, and statutory filings. # Summary This investigation targets data gaps in Nepal's hydropower financial landscape, reconstructed from primary credit rating agency reports. It covers: Mission 1: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited (86 MW Solu Khola) — a documented private IPP financial profile Mission 2: Comparative PPA tariff matrix for five priority projects (Chilime, Sanima Mai, Rasuwagadhi, Trishuli 3A, Nyadi) Mission 3: Mathematical reconstruction of NEA subsidiary vs. private IPP rate differential (37.1% revenue advantage via Chilime anomaly) Mission 4: Insurance market quantitative verification (Sanima Mai pays 1.80% of gross revenue in non-life premiums) # Key Findings ## PPA Rate Matrix (VERIFIED) Project | Capacity (MW) | Wet Rate (NPR/kWh) | Dry Rate (NPR/kWh) | Entity Type | PPA Year | ---|---|---|---|---|---| Chilime | 22.1 | 4.08 (Excess) | 8.17 (Regular) | NEA Subsidiary | 1997 | Sanima Mai (Phase 1) | 22.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Private IPP | 2010 | Sanima Mai Cascade | 7.0 | 5.52 | 9.66 | Private IPP | 2013 | Rasuwagadhi | 111.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | NEA Subsidiary (via Chilime) | 2011 | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60.0 | N/A (Internal) | N/A (Internal) | NEA Owned | N/A | Upper Trishuli 3B | 37.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Subsidiary Corp | — | Nyadi | 30.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Private IPP | 2015 | ## Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Financial Profile Final build cost: NPR 172–175 million/MW (industry average often exceeds NPR 200–250M) FY 2080/81 revenue: NPR 2.648 billion Net profit: NPR 902.33 million (114.66% YoY growth) Gross margin: 95.54%; Net margin: 23.61% Plant Load Factor: 69.05%, achieving 87–89% of contracted energy Q-design: Aggressive Q41 model, 19.28% dry energy mix 10-bank syndicate led by Nepal Investment Bank, 76% debt-financed Promoter: Him Prasad Pathak — also controls Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki), Secretary at IPPAN ## Subsidiary vs. IPP Rate Differential (Document finding) Chilime's "Regular/Excess" billing architecture produces an effective blended rate of NPR 7.57/kWh vs. a typical private IPP's NPR 5.52/kWh — a 37.1% revenue advantage. Chilime classified 85% of its 156 GWh generation as "Regular" at NPR 8.17/kWh. ## Insurance Burden Sanima Mai Hydropower paid NPR 13.77 million in non-life premiums against NPR 764 million gross revenue = 1.80% of top-line. Within an ~15% OPEX envelope, insurance consumes over 10% of operating budget. # Data Gaps Marked SEBON IPO prospectuses are scanned-image PDFs — no automated parsing possible IPPAN's "800% premium surge" claim source inaccessible (server timeout) Specific OAGN paragraph condemning PPA favoritism for subsidiaries not isolated # Limitations Compilation nature: This is a reconstructed investigative report, not a primary rating agency publication. Individual claims should be traced to the underlying ICRA / CARE documents where possible. Scanned sources: SEBON prospectuses referenced are image-based PDFs; figures were manually transcribed and may contain transcription errors. Single-promoter focus: The Sahas Urja profile, while detailed, represents one successful promoter. It is not necessarily representative of average private IPP performance. Snapshot date: Financial data reflects FY 2080/81 or earlier; market conditions (tariffs, interest rates, construction costs) may have shifted. Inaccessible sources: Some referenced documents (e.g., IPPAN premium surge claim) were not retrievable at time of compilation. # See Also sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 ppa-pricing nea-triple-authority sahas-urja chilime rasuwagadhi upper-trishuli-3b

pages.title: "Mission 1: Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Benchmark IPP Success"
pages.excerpt: Source type: Research compilation — single-project deep-dive (4 pages) Original: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119) and corporate disclosures.
pages.body_text: Mission 1: Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) Source type: Research compilation — single-project deep-dive (4 pages) Original: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119) and corporate disclosures. # Summary Sahas Urja Limited is the critical positive benchmark in Nepal's private IPP landscape. The compilation presents profitability in a fixed-tariff environment as a function of capital efficiency and operational optimization, not anomalous PPA rates. # Corporate Details Entity: Private IPP, incorporated February 2014, converted to public September 2014 Asset: 86 MW Solu Khola (Dudh Koshi) Hydroelectric Project, Run-of-River Location: Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province Q-design: Q41 (~41% probability of exceedance) PPA: Signed February 25, 2015 | NPR 4.80 (wet) / 8.40 (dry) | 3% × 8 years escalation Contracted energy: 520.20 GWh/yr (100.27 GWh dry / 419.93 GWh wet = 19.28% dry mix) RCOD achieved: March 1, 2023 — retained all 8 escalations # Financial Performance (FY 2080/81) Metric | Value | ---|---| Build cost (final) | NPR 172–175 million/MW | Total project cost | NPR 14.7 billion | Electricity sales revenue | NPR 2.648 billion | Net profit | NPR 902.33 million (+114.66% YoY) | Gross profit margin | 95.54% | Net profit margin | 23.61% | Interest expense | NPR 805.9 million (down from NPR 1.165B) | Plant Load Factor | 69.05% (~87–89% of contracted) | Debt financing | 76% (10-bank consortium led by Nepal Investment Bank) | # Why It Works 1. Capital efficiency: ~NPR 173M/MW vs. industry average often exceeding NPR 200–250M/MW 2. Escalation retention: Achieved COD on time → all 8 annual 3% escalations intact 3. Scale: 86 MW means 19.28% dry energy mix still generates massive absolute NPR 8.40/kWh cash flows 4. Deleveraging: Interest expense dropped from NPR 1.165B to NPR 805.9M # Promoter Profile Chairman: Him Prasad Pathak Also controls: 51% stake in Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki PRoR, NPR 52.5B syndication) IPPAN: Secretary, Executive Committee — direct lobbying access to MoEWRI, ERC, NEA Prior projects: Upper Hugdi Khola (5 MW) # Limitations Single-project deep-dive. This compilation covers only Sahas Urja / Solu Khola. Findings on capital efficiency, escalation retention, and promoter profile are not necessarily representative of the broader IPP sector. Research compilation, not peer-reviewed. Assembled from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports and corporate disclosures — has not undergone independent verification or institutional fact-checking. Financial snapshot. Data reflects FY 2080/81 performance; does not capture subsequent operational or financial developments, deleveraging progress, or PPA rate adjustments. Promoter profile from public sources only. Promoter relationships and institutional connections are inferred from publicly available corporate disclosures and IPPAN listings, not from direct interviews. # See Also ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 sahas-urja ppa-pricing q-design-discharge

pages.title: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies
headings: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies
pages.excerpt: Multi-study compilation covering Kulekhani Reservoir sedimentation, including the primary DGPS bathymetric survey by Sangroula (NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010), InVEST/RUSLE catchment modeling by Bokan et al. (2021–2024), the ADB/World Bank post-completion review, and Mandal's (2021)
pages.body_text: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies # Summary Multi-study compilation covering Kulekhani Reservoir sedimentation, including the primary DGPS bathymetric survey by Sangroula (NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010), InVEST/RUSLE catchment modeling by Bokan et al. (2021–2024), the ADB/World Bank post-completion review, and Mandal's (2021) hydro-mechanical degradation study. Together these provide the most complete sedimentation evidence base for any single Nepali reservoir. # Primary DGPS Bathymetric Survey (Sangroula, NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010) Physical DGPS bathymetric mapping of Kulekhani Reservoir bed using echo sounders and differential GPS. Total gross storage lost: 20.4 MCM (23.9% of 85.3 MCM original) Active live storage lost: 14 MCM (19.1% of 73.3 MCM original) Average annual loss: 0.56% of total reservoir capacity over 27 years of operation Commissioning: December 1982 (Unit 1), May 1987 (Unit 2) # Source Document Sangroula, D.P. (2006, updated with DGPS surveys 2009/2010). Sedimentation and sustainability of the Kulekhani Reservoir: A Himalayan Case. Doctoral dissertation, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU). Associated with Hydro Lab Nepal. # InVEST/RUSLE Catchment Modeling (Bokan et al., 2021–2024) A DISTINCT study using spatial modeling, not physical bathymetry. Uses InVEST SDRmax model + RUSLE to calculate theoretical sediment yield from upstream catchment. Sedimentation rate: 13.3 t/ha/yr (2002) → 6.6 t/ha/yr (2010) → 4.8 t/ha/yr (2018) Total reservoir capacity measured at 61.66 MCM (April 2018) Confirms declining delivery rate trend — watershed management works Citation: Bokan, L.T. et al. Potential Sedimentation Rate and its Prioritization in Kulekhani Watershed Using InVEST Model (published 2024, modeling 2002–2018 data) # ADB Post-Completion Review (World Bank/ADB PCR) Loan 528-NEP / Credit 600-NEP 80% cost overrun, 21-month commissioning delay Key finding: NO sediment flushing system was designed — watershed management was completely unanticipated during appraisal Kulekhani served as the lesson that forced ADB/IDA to mandate catchment management plans and sediment flushing gates in all subsequent projects (Marsyangdi Cr. 1478-NEP, Tanahu) PCR URL: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/790631468289870058/pdf/multi-page.pdf # Hydro-Mechanical Degradation (Mandal 2021) Mandal, N.K. (2021). Pelton Runner Erosion Due To Cavitation: A Case Study Of Storage Hydropower Plant, Kulekhani First Hydropower Station Fine suspended quartz particles cause continuous abrasive pitting of Pelton turbine buckets Altered blade geometries trigger secondary cavitation — efficiency deteriorates even under low sediment concentrations Main inlet valves replaced multiple times since commissioning # Limitations Bathymetric survey date. The primary Sangroula DGPS survey is from 2009/2010 — sedimentation rates may have shifted in the subsequent 15+ years of operation. Multi-study compilation with different rigor levels. Combines a doctoral dissertation, spatial modeling (InVEST/RUSLE), an ADB/WB post-completion review, and a turbine-degradation case study — each with different methodologies and confidence levels. InVEST/RUSLE modeled, not measured. The Bokan et al. sedimentation rates (13.3 → 6.6 → 4.8 t/ha/yr) are model outputs, not physical sediment trap measurements. The declining trend is directionally consistent with the bathymetric survey but the absolute rates are model-derived. No post-2018 bathymetry. The most recent reservoir capacity measurement (61.66 MCM) is from April 2018. Current storage volume is uncertain.

pages.body_text: SEBON Hydropower Offering Records (Selected Issuers, 2018–2025) # Summary This source record indexes selected official Securities Board of Nepal (SEBON) prospectus, press-release and pipeline-status records for hydropower IPOs and rights issues. The individual prospectus pages and pipeline snapshots are primary regulatory disclosures; they establish that a filing, prospectus or review-stage application existed, but do not by themselves establish that an offer completed or how the proceeds were ultimately spent. # Key Findings SEBON's prospectus archive contains IPO records for Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut Company Limited (2018), People's Power Limited (2022), Terhathum Power Company Limited (2021), and a Rasuwagadhi Hydropower local offering (2022). SEBON's archive also contains a right-issue record for Ankhu Khola and right-issue prospectuses for Joshi Hydropower, People's Power and Terhathum Power in 2025. Ankhu Khola's approved right-issue prospectus states a 1:1.5 offer of 12 million shares at NPR 100, for NPR 1.20 billion. Its proceeds plan allocates NPR 800 million to equity in the 20 MW Ankhu Khola-2 project and NPR 400 million to partial repayment of the issuer's long-term bank loans. The prospectus lists NPR 1.227752064 billion of such loans before the planned repayment. This establishes the stated allocation, not the amount ultimately subscribed, allotted or applied. The SEBON right-share pipeline snapshot dated 13 December 2024 records the following review-stage terms: People's Power, 1:0.5 and NPR 316.3 million; Terhathum Power, 1:1 and NPR 400 million. The 16 October 2024 snapshot records Joshi Hydropower at 1:0.65 and NPR 241.41 million. SEBON subsequently published approved prospectuses for all three issues: People's Power on 7 July 2025, Terhathum Power on 29 June 2025 and Joshi Hydropower on 30 July 2025. Their proceeds plans state: - Joshi Hydropower: NPR 241.41 million total; NPR 155.71 million for bank principal and interest, NPR 56.835195 million to repay a promoter advance, and NPR 28.864805 million for repair and maintenance of damaged project structures. - People's Power: NPR 316.3 million total, directed to repayment of Nabil Bank's long-term project loan. The same later prospectus states that the company's earlier NPR 310 million IPO proceeds had been used to repay a Nabil Bank loan; this is an issuer statement in a regulatory filing, not a separately reconciled post-offer audit. - Terhathum Power: NPR 400 million total, directed to partial bank loan repayment: NPR 160 million to Machhapuchchhre Bank, NPR 120 million to Nabil Bank and NPR 120 million to Global IME Bank. The prospectus explains that an earlier plan to finance the 2 MW Khorunga Tangmaya project was amended so the rights cash would first repay bank debt, with staged borrowing intended to fund later construction. People's Power's official issuer site publishes an . That establishes closure of the subscription window, not the allotted amount, subscription rate or actual application of proceeds. Ankhu Khola's audited FY 2081/82 statements provide a post-offer reconciliation. The cash-flow statement records NPR 1.20 billion from the rights issue and NPR 134.642378 million of share premium. The share note records 10,249,752 shares taken up through the rights issue and 1,750,248 sold through auction, bringing paid-up capital from NPR 800 million to NPR 2.00 billion. Net borrowing repayment was NPR 482.416277 million, and total borrowings fell from NPR 1.256615440 billion to NPR 758.141433 million. Other-equity investments increased by NPR 135.225 million. These audited lines establish completion and substantial debt reduction, but they do not yet reconcile the full NPR 800 million prospectus allocation for Ankhu Khola-2 equity. People's Power's issuer-published unaudited third-quarter FY 2082/83 statement shows paid-up capital at NPR 948.9 million, up by exactly the NPR 316.3 million rights-offer amount from the NPR 632.6 million comparison period. It reports no long-term borrowing, compared with NPR 318.024 million in the corresponding prior-year quarter. This is balance-sheet evidence consistent with the planned loan repayment, but the quarterly statement is unaudited and does not contain a separate proceeds-application schedule. Terhathum Power's issuer-published unaudited third-quarter FY 2082/83 statement says the 1:1 rights issue was completed, unsubscribed shares were sold by auction with NPR 97.63 million of premium, and the proceeds were used to repay long-term bank borrowings. Paid-up capital doubled from NPR 400 million to NPR 800 million, while long-term borrowings fell from NPR 884.152207 million in the corresponding prior-year quarter to NPR 344.120399 million. The total debt reduction exceeds the offer amount and therefore should not be attributed entirely to rights cash. Joshi Hydropower's issuer site and the issue manager preserve the approved offer record, but no issuer, SEBON or NEPSE post-offer filing located in this pass establishes final allotment, actual application of proceeds or a subsequent audited loan balance. The pipeline snapshots label processing stages such as "reviewed and comment sent". Those stages must not be described as completed rights issues without a subsequent completion, allotment or financial-statement record. # Relevance These records provide the regulatory-document trail for the issuer-by-issuer inventory in ipo-hydropower-bailout. # Limitations The published PDFs are frequently Nepali-language and legacy-font encoded. The proceeds plans above have been checked at page level. Post-offer evidence is now available for Ankhu Khola, People's Power and Terhathum Power, but only Ankhu Khola's evidence is audited. A SEBON pipeline listing is an application-status record, not proof of an issued, allotted or fully subscribed security. The records do not provide a complete census of hydropower offerings, actual allocation of proceeds, debt-repayment outcomes or NRB bank-exposure data. # Official records SEBON prospectus archive Ankhu Khola IPO record Ankhu Khola right-issue record Ankhu Khola approved right-issue prospectus (PDF) Joshi Hydropower right-issue prospectus People's Power and Terhathum right-issue archive listing Joshi Hydropower approved right-issue prospectus (PDF) People's Power approved right-issue prospectus (PDF) Terhathum Power approved right-issue prospectus (PDF) People's Power official notices People's Power FY 2082/83 third-quarter statement (PDF) Ankhu Khola annual reports Ankhu Khola audited FY 2081/82 annual report Terhathum Power disclosures Terhathum Power FY 2082/83 third-quarter statement (PDF) Joshi Hydropower issuer reports Joshi Hydropower issue-manager offer document (PDF) SEBON right-share pipeline snapshot, 13 December 2024 (PDF) SEBON right-share pipeline snapshot, 16 October 2024 (PDF)

pages.body_text: Systemic Risk and Triple-Authority Research Compilation (2026) # Summary This page records the existence and evidentiary boundary of a legacy 17-page research compilation about NEA's institutional roles, hydropower project finance and securities offerings. The underlying file and its row-level source map are not present in the release corpus. The compilation is not peer-reviewed, audited or institutionally verified. It must not be used as a substitute for company accounts, signed PPAs, SEBON records, dispatch data or regulatory decisions. # Provenance Source type: legacy research compilation described as a Google Docs export. Author: not recorded in the repository. Document date: not recorded in the repository. Public URL or archived local file: not available. Verification status: provenance incomplete; claims require primary-source reconstruction. # Topics Recorded by the Compilation The potential conflict risk created by concentrating dispatch, purchasing and penalty administration around NEA. Hydropower IPO and rights-offer financing patterns. Availability-declaration clauses and possible project-finance effects. Differences between NEA-affiliated and private-project contracting. These are research topics, not findings established by this page. # Current Evidence Boundary The compilation's named-issuer and proceeds claims should be replaced by the bounded official record at sebon-hydropower-offering-records. Its standard-PPA discussion should be checked against nea-standard-ppa-clauses and, ultimately, signed project contracts. Its reported Barahi case cannot be checked because the underlying audited statement and adjudication record are absent. See barahi-hydropower. Its institutional thesis is treated as a conflict-risk hypothesis at nea-triple-authority, not as proof of discriminatory dispatch or a quantified project loss. # Limitations Missing source artifact: the described 17-page document is not archived in the release corpus. Missing authorship and date: provenance cannot be independently checked. No row-level source map: earlier issuer, market and project assertions cannot be reproduced from this page. No primary dispatch or penalty records: the compilation cannot establish operational discrimination or a sector-wide penalty effect. No verified named-project case: references to Barahi remain research leads only. # Related intervention-nea-structural-separation nea-triple-authority ad-penalties sebon-hydropower-offering-records ipo-hydropower-bailout

pages.body_text: SJVN Arun III HEP Project Record # Summary SJVN's official project record for the 900 MW Arun III HEP, read with its dated 2025--26 corporate disclosures. It distinguishes the public technical baseline, individual construction milestones and an announced schedule target from a verified project-wide completion forecast. # Key Findings Installed capacity: 900 MW. Design energy: 4,018.87 GWh in a 90%-dependable year. Generating configuration: four 225 MW units. The project includes a 217 km 400 kV evacuation component to the Nepal–India border. SJVN describes major works as in progress. A 23 May 2025 SJVN power-sale-agreement announcement describes commissioning in FY 2027/28 as the project's expectation. SJVN's May 2026 investor presentation instead lists expected commissioning in FY 2028/29 Q3. This later corporate schedule supersedes the earlier FY 2027/28 expectation for monitoring, but is still an announced target rather than a verified completion forecast. # Relevance This is the current technical baseline for arun-3. It supports component-aware monitoring of the generating works and evacuation line, without converting dated corporate milestones into a comparable completion percentage. # Limitations The current project page does not provide a single dated, package-defined physical-progress percentage. The later FY 2028/29 Q3 statement is an investor-presentation expectation, rather than a firm current commissioning commitment. Corporate review events do not substitute for package progress reports or an energisation record. # Primary Records Consulted SJVN Arun III HEP project page (current technical description). SJVN's 23 May 2025 power-sale announcement (FY 2027/28 expected commissioning statement). SJVN's May 2026 investor presentation (FY 2028/29 Q3 expected commissioning statement).

pages.body_text: Tanahu Hydropower Project Status (ADB, 2024–2026) # Summary Reference compilation for the 140 MW Tanahu Hydropower Project's construction progress and social-compliance posture, drawn from ADB's own project monitoring reports, two Accountability Mechanism complaints (2024 and 2025), and a later public construction-progress update. # Key Data Points Installed: 140 MW reservoir-type plant River: Seti (Gandaki basin) District: Tanahu Owner: Nepal Electricity Authority Financier: Asian Development Bank (primary), co-financiers Main civil works: 140 m high roller-compacted-concrete dam (Package-1), underground powerhouse (Package-2), main water conveyance tunnel Status (FY 2024/25): ~67% complete per NEA annual report Latest public progress check (April 2026): roughly 75% complete per tanahu-progress-2026 ADB monitoring visit: December 2024 — flagged buffer-zone demarcation, public-land acquisition and construction pace as open issues Accountability Mechanism complaints 2024 complaint: demarcation of buffer zones, free prior informed consent, land-for-land compensation, untitled-land registration 2025 complaint: filed 18 Feb 2025, deemed eligible for review 4 Apr 2025 # Relevance to Project Primary source for Tanahu's status, design basics and the unusually well-documented compliance issues that shape its completion schedule. The Accountability Mechanism filings are the reason Tanahu's delays are public and auditable — most Nepali storage projects lack that transparency layer. # What This Source Does Not Cover Dry-season energy contribution once the reservoir is in operation Plant-level cost escalation numbers (ADB figures redact subsidiary contractor detail) Coordination with downstream irrigation users on the Seti # Limitations Compilation, not primary project documents. Drawn from ADB monitoring reports and Accountability Mechanism filings — does not include the full PAD, EIA, or contractor progress reports. Construction progress is time-sensitive. The ~67% completion figure is from the NEA FY 2024/25 annual report; the ~75% figure is a later public update and should be refreshed before final publication or narration lock. Accountability Mechanism complaints are unresolved. Two complaints (2024 and 2025) are filed and eligible for review but not yet adjudicated. Their resolution may affect project timeline and cost. # See also tanahu-hydropower storage-deficit buildability

pages.body_text: UKHLL Annual Reports — Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited # Summary The audited annual reports of Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited (UKHLL), the NEA subsidiary that owns and operates the 456 MW Upper Tamakoshi Hydroelectric Project — Nepal's largest operating hydropower plant. The reports are available at utkhpl.org.np and provide the primary-source generation and financial data for the project. # Key data extracted (from research compilation of audited accounts) ## Generation data Fiscal Year | Generation (GWh) | % of Design (2,281 GWh) | Notes | ---|---|---|---| FY 2079/80 | 1,945.83 | 85.3% | | FY 2080/81 | 2,058.36 | 90.2% | Peak operational year | FY 2081/82 | 1,529.07 | 67.0% | 88-day flood shutdown (Sep 2024) | ## Financial data Total project cost: NPR 87–89.4 billion Effective D/E ratio at COD: 88:12 ICRA D default rating in FY 2081/82 (post-flood) Flood event damage: NPR 1.79 billion physical, NPR 1.43 billion business interruption Insurance claim: NPR 2.0–3.22 billion Rolwaling diversion: 212 GWh addition, dry-season peaking from 4 to 6 hours # Limitations Audit firm unconfirmed: The reports are described as "audited" but the specific audit firm and qualification opinions are not extracted. Post-flood data recency: The FY 2081/82 data (flood shutdown, ICRA D rating, insurance claim) is the most recent extracted; later fiscal-year data is not included. D/E ratio caveat: The effective 88:12 D/E ratio at COD is from UKHLL annual reports but cross-referencing against external debt-registrar data is not done. Insurance range: The insurance claim figure is reported as a range (NPR 2.0–3.22 billion) indicating uncertainty in the claim resolution.

pages.body_text: Upper Karnali Official Records — IBN and DoED (2022–2026) # Summary This source record combines two primary Government of Nepal records relevant to the Upper Karnali Hydroelectric Project: Investment Board Nepal's 2021/22 annual report and the Department of Electricity Development's registry updated 2 July 2026. Together they document a conditional financial-close extension and the project's current administrative registry listing. # Key Findings Investment Board Nepal records that the Government of Nepal approved a two-year extension of the financial-close deadline in July 2022, subject to conditions. The IBN record describes the developer as being in a process to meet the negotiation conditions; it does not report financial close as achieved. The DoED registry updated 2 July 2026 lists Upper Karnali HEP at 900 MW on the Karnali River, with GMR Upper Karnali Hydropower Limited as promoter. The DoED page places the project in its more-than-1-MW survey-licence table. That administrative listing establishes a current registry record, not construction, financing or PPA status. # Relevance These official records provide a primary institutional baseline for upper-karnali and distinguish a deadline extension or registry listing from achieved financial close, lender disbursement, executed offtake or construction commencement. # Limitations Neither record contains an executed financing agreement, lender effectiveness notice, construction notice to proceed, signed buyer PPA or tripartite transit approval. The IBN annual-report entry is historical and cannot establish the position after its reporting period. The DoED registry's licence category is administrative; it should not be inferred to be a physical delivery-stage classification. # Official Records IBN Annual Report 2021/22 (PDF) DoED more-than-1-MW hydropower registry

What This Source Does Not Cover
pages.excerpt: Reference compilation for the 900 MW Upper Karnali Hydroelectric Project — GMR-sponsored, repeatedly PDA-extended, and the canonical example of a stalled India-developed export project in Nepal.
pages.body_text: Upper Karnali — PDA, Financial Closure & Court Record # Summary Reference compilation for the 900 MW Upper Karnali Hydroelectric Project — GMR-sponsored, repeatedly PDA-extended, and the canonical example of a stalled India-developed export project in Nepal. # Key Data Points Project basics Capacity: 900 MW Districts: Surkhet, Dailekh, Achham (karnali-basin) River: Karnali Design annual energy: ~3,466 GWh Sponsor: GMR Upper Karnali Hydropower Limited (subsidiary of India's GMR Group) Bid won: International Competitive Bidding, 2008 Export orientation: 88% of output planned for international sale Commercial / PDA history Original PDA deadline missed repeatedly since 2014 Supreme Court of Nepal limited extensions; allowed a 186-day extension to compensate only for time lost during its own interim orders Bangladesh Power Development Board signed a PPA with GMR for 500 MW in principle; MOU in April 2017 for 300 MW; PPA planned for July 2017; in September 2021 Nepal proposed only 200 MW to Bangladesh — none of these have closed Recent financing development (2026) Government of Nepal cleared a path for financial closure GMR submitted investment commitments: INR 65 billion from India's IREDA; NPR 20 billion from Nepali banks Equity restructuring brought in SJVN and IREDA alongside GMR; NEA retains its originally-allocated stake # Relevance to Project Primary source for Upper Karnali's PDA history, export structure and the 2026 financial-closure path. Important because Upper Karnali is the reference case — alongside arun-3 — for India-developed Nepalese hydro, but with the opposite construction outcome: Arun-3 is building; Upper Karnali has been paperwork since 2008. # What This Source Does Not Cover Bangladesh-side transmission readiness (Bangladesh can only import what a new Nepal–India–Bangladesh corridor can carry) GMR Group's own financial condition and its effect on equity pace The downstream-irrigation objections that a 2014 high-level committee raised and never fully resolved # Limitations Paperwork since 2008. Despite repeated PDA extensions and the 2026 financial-closure path announcement, Upper Karnali has zero construction progress after 18 years. The source captures the paper trail, not operational reality. Financial commitments are announced, not disbursed. The INR 65 billion IREDA and NPR 20 billion Nepali bank commitments are investment proposals, not disbursed funds. Financial closure has been announced before without follow-through. Bangladesh PPA gap unaddressed. The source documents the history of Bangladesh PPA discussions without resolving whether the transmission corridor and tripartite agreements can actually deliver the promised 500/300/200 MW. # See also upper-karnali hydro-geopolitics karnali-basin

pages.title: Urja Khabar Generation Audit — IPP Generation vs Contracted
headings: Urja Khabar "Audit" of IPP Generation vs Contracted Energy
pages.excerpt: Kumar Pandey article in the January 2026 issue (Year 5, Issue 8) of Urja Khabar magazine. This is secondary reporting of a primary MoEWRI government study — not an independent Urja Khabar dataset. The source document is: "Statistics financially distressed hydropower projects oper
pages.body_text: Urja Khabar "Audit" of IPP Generation vs Contracted Energy # Summary Kumar Pandey article in the January 2026 issue (Year 5, Issue 8) of Urja Khabar magazine. This is secondary reporting of a primary MoEWRI government study — not an independent Urja Khabar dataset. The source document is: "Statistics financially distressed hydropower projects operated by IPP, Asadh 31, 2077" (mid-2020, Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation). By republishing this historical data in 2026, Pandey argues that the conditions producing mass IPP financial distress in 2020 have calcified rather than resolved. # Key data extracted ## Generation deficits (≥50 projects) Metric | Count | ---|---| 80% of contracted energy | 0 projects (sole exception: Chilime) | ## Financial distress classification (67 projects, mid-2020) Status | Capacity (MW) | Projects | ---|---|---| Interest & installment regular | 49.99 | 11 | Interest regular, installment irregular | 8.52 | 2 | Interest & installment irregular | 81.95 | 23 | On bank watchlist | 179.35 | 31 | An additional 40 projects under 10 MW (191 MW total) were not included in this classification, suggesting wider distress. ## Construction cost overruns (Table 9) Component | Increase | Primary cause | ---|---|---| Land acquisition | 105.0% | Policy issues | Civil construction | 34.9% | Conflict, blockades, loan delays | Project supervision/management | 38.1% | Conflict, blockades, time/cost | Interest during construction | 30.6% | Policy issues | Steel work | 22.8% | Inflation | Electromechanical | 7.8% | Inflation | ## Transmission-bottlenecked projects (18 named) Project | MW | Bottleneck | ---|---|---| Upper Syange | 2.4 | Khudi Hub Substation incomplete | Nyadi Khola | 30 | Khudi Hub Substation incomplete | Chepe Khola | 9.63 | 220 kV Marsyangdi Corridor incomplete | Super Chepe | 9.05 | Regional infrastructure delays | Dordi-1 | 12 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Upper Dordi | 25 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Super Dordi | 54 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Upper Chhyangdi Khola | 4 | 33 kV Udipur Mid-Marsyangdi line/transformer | Lower Modi | 20 | Isolated — forced to connect to New Modi Switching Substation | Theule Khola | 1.5 | Kusmi Shera Substation connection canceled by NEA | Down Piluwa | 10.3 | Forced to absorb 33/220 kV transformer cost at Baneshwor | Upper Khorunga | 7.5 | 33 kV common line not provided by state | Upper Hewa Small | 8.5 | Alternative evacuation provisions in limbo | Middle Tamor | 73 | Dhunge-Sanghu Substation incomplete | Sanjen Khola | 78 | New Bharatpur-Marsyangdi line incomplete | Gelun Khola Small | 3.2 | Chautara Substation connection pending | Thulo Khola | 21.3 | Rahughat Substation not constructed by NEA | Upper Rawa Khola | 3 | 33/11 kV Baksila Substation (now completed) | ## Regulatory penalties on distressed IPPs NEA penalties: up to 5% of income (rising to 11% after 15 years) for generation shortfalls or PPA non-compliance ERC/NEPSE/SEBON fees: ~1% of income Punishment for generation shortfalls often caused by NEA's own transmission failures ## The "32% claim" The "32% average generation" figure widely circulated in industry discussion does not appear in this article. The only ~33% figure in the Pandey article refers to administrative and operational costs consuming approximately 33% of revenue for affected small projects — not generation output. # Limitations Secondary reporting of a 2020 primary source. The underlying MoEWRI dataset is from mid-2020 (Asadh 2077); the January 2026 article republishes this data without a refreshed dataset. Conditions may have shifted substantially in the intervening period. No independent data collection. Urja Khabar did not conduct its own generation audit; it republished and interpreted a government study. The framing ("conditions have calcified") is Pandey's editorial argument, not a verified finding. Transmission bottleneck table may be partial. The 18 named projects represent Pandey's selection, not necessarily an exhaustive listing of all transmission-bottlenecked projects. The "32% generation" figure is a misconception. This widely circulated industry figure does not appear in the article; the article's ~33% figure refers to cost ratios, not generation output.

pages.title: Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited Disclosures (2026)
pages.excerpt: UTKHPL's official project-update pages, third-quarter statement and annual reports, checked in July 2026. They provide a primary company filing trail for the operating 456 MW Upper Tamakoshi plant.
pages.body_text: Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited Disclosures (2026) # Summary UTKHPL's official project-update pages, third-quarter statement and annual reports, checked in July 2026. They provide a primary company filing trail for the operating 456 MW Upper Tamakoshi plant. # Key Findings UTKHPL published its FY 2082/83 third-quarter financial report on 13 May 2026. It published combined sixteenth and seventeenth annual reports for FY 2079/80 and FY 2080/81 on 6 April 2026. The site identifies UTKHPL as the NEA-established implementing company and publishes company ownership information. The FY 2082/83 third-quarter statement reports NPR 7.718 billion in electricity-sales revenue, NPR 4.052 billion in finance costs and NPR 286.8 million in net profit for the quarter ending Chaitra 2082. The FY 2080/81 annual statements report NPR 8.679 billion in electricity-sales revenue and NPR 99.3 million in insurance expense. This is a single-project-year ratio of about 1.14%, not a sector-wide insurance-premium finding. The annual statements describe a 22 MW Rolwaling Khola project with 105.04 GWh of additional generation and a diversion expected to add 216.51 GWh to Upper Tamakoshi. They record an EPC award, a PPA application in process and construction ongoing at the report date. The May 2026 quarter reports NPR 2.103 billion of capital work in progress for Rolwaling. It does not provide a package completion percentage or a firm commissioning date. The FY 2080/81 annual statements say that property and lost-revenue insurance claims had been lodged after the September 2024 flood and remained in settlement processing at the report date; they do not establish an amount paid or the claim's later status. # Relevance This is the current company-disclosure source for upper-tamakoshi. It should control when older research compilations conflict with newer financial or operating filings. # Limitations The third-quarter statement is unaudited and published as a single image. The annual-report statements have an earlier reporting cut-off than the May 2026 quarter. Together they do not establish a current Rolwaling construction percentage, a stop/restart date, insurance settlement outcome, debt-restructuring agreement or reliable forward commissioning schedule. # Official Documents UTKHPL project updates FY 2079/80 and FY 2080/81 annual report (PDF) FY 2082/83 third-quarter statement

headings: VUCL Mugu Karnali Storage HEP Project Page
pages.excerpt: VUCL's official project page for the proposed 1,902 MW Mugu Karnali Storage HEP. It publishes the current salient design parameters and identifies NEA Engineering Company as design consultant.
pages.body_text: VUCL Mugu Karnali Storage HEP Project Page # Summary VUCL's official project page for the proposed 1,902 MW Mugu Karnali Storage HEP. It publishes the current salient design parameters and identifies NEA Engineering Company as design consultant. # Key Findings Project type: storage; installed capacity: 1,902 MW. Catchment area: 16,098.3 km²; design discharge: 793.45 m³/s. Dam height: 283 m. Reservoir storage: 4,843.2 MCM total and 2,238.95 MCM live. Generation configuration: eight Francis units at 242.67 MW each. Annual design energy: 6,291.8 GWh, comprising 2,415 GWh dry-season and 3,876.8 GWh wet-season energy. Evacuation concept: approximately 40 km of 400 kV double-circuit line. Published implementation duration: ten years; debt/equity assumption: 75:25. # Relevance This is the primary design source for mugu-karnali-storage. It corrects earlier wiki values of ten units, 5,883 GWh and an unsupported pumped-storage classification. # Limitations The parameters remain feasibility-stage values, not final construction quantities. The page's cost entry is written as “46,000 Crore” without enough currency and cost-basis context for safe conversion. It does not establish financing close, selected PPP ownership or construction start.

pages.title: World Bank Nepal Country Economic Memorandum (2025)
headings: World Bank Nepal Country Economic Memorandum (2025)
pages.excerpt: The World Bank's 2025 account of Nepal's growth constraints, including power-sector expansion, trade and enterprise reliability evidence.
pages.body_text: World Bank Nepal Country Economic Memorandum (2025) # Summary The World Bank's comprehensive economic assessment of Nepal with a significant energy/hydropower chapter. Provides the strongest international-institution perspective on Nepal's energy transition, trade patterns, and system constraints. # Key Data Points Hydropower capacity reached ~2,990 MW by end-2024 >70% of capacity added since 2018 came from IPPs IPPs accounted for 64% of total installed hydropower by 2024 >90% of hydropower is RoR or PRoR Trade shift: 2018 imported ~2,582 GWh / exported ~3 GWh → 2023 imported ~1,895 GWh / exported ~1,946 GWh Scheduled load shedding eliminated in 2018 76% of firms still reported regular power outages in 2022 >13% of firms reported sales losses above 10% from power cuts System losses: ~12.7% in 2024 September 2024 floods/landslides damaged 11 operational projects with >600 MW combined capacity # Relevance Key source for the IPP-driven growth story, the trade transformation timeline, and the reliability gap (load shedding gone but outages persist). The firm-level outage data (76%) is uniquely valuable for the reliability argument in stranded-generation. Trade shift data central to data-trade-time-series. # Limitations Snapshot date: Published March 2025; covers data through end-2024. Does not capture 2025 capacity additions or trade shifts. Firm-level data: The 76% outage figure and 13% sales-loss figure are from a World Bank enterprise survey (2022) — representative but not annual-update series. Trade data: The 2023 import/export figures are calendar-year approximations from the report narrative, not identical to NEA fiscal-year accounting.

pages.title: World Bank ESMAP Nepal Solar and Wind Resource Measurement
headings: World Bank ESMAP Nepal Solar and Wind Resource Measurement
Key findings (composite, from ESMAP final report)
For Nepal solar planning in general
pages.excerpt: World Bank ESMAP's Nepal solar and wind measurement programme and ground-station resource evidence.
pages.body_text: World Bank ESMAP Nepal Solar and Wind Resource Measurement # Summary The ground-measured solar and wind resource dataset for Nepal. Operated 2015–2019 under the World Bank ESMAP Renewable Energy Resource Mapping & Geospatial Planning programme, implemented on the ground through AEPC with technical delivery by Vaisala / 3TIER (solar) and DNV GL (wind). This is the only authoritative measured-data source for Nepal solar resource at the station-hour resolution — every satellite-derived estimate (including global-solar-atlas-nepal) is calibrated against and cross-validated with this dataset. # What the source covers 14 solar measurement stations deployed across Nepal's representative zones 4 wind measurement towers (lower priority; wind is constrained in Nepal) 10-minute and hourly meteorological and radiation data GHI, DNI, DIF, temperature, wind speed, humidity — the full solar-meteorological stack Validation campaign against Global Solar Atlas and MERRA-2 satellite datasets Open-data release through ESMAP Global Solar Atlas portal and AEPC national reports # Station network (solar — representative) Station (approximate) | Zone | Elevation (m) | Measurement period | GHI mean (kWh/m²/day) | ---|---|---:|---|---:| Jumla | E / A-border | 2,370 | 2015–19 | ~5.2 | Nepalgunj | B3 | 150 | 2015–19 | ~5.1 | Simara / Birgunj | B1 | 130 | 2015–19 | ~4.9 | Biratnagar | B2 | 80 | 2015–19 | ~4.9 | Pokhara | C2 | 820 | 2015–19 | ~4.5 | Kathmandu | C1 | 1,340 | 2015–19 | ~4.3 | Dhankuta | C3 | 1,100 | 2015–19 | ~4.4 | Surkhet | C4 | 700 | 2015–19 | ~4.8 | Jomsom (Mustang) | A | 2,730 | 2015–19 | ~6.0 | (+ 5 additional stations, detail in final report) | various | | | | Specific station coordinates, exact measurement periods, and precise GHI means require cross-reference with the ESMAP final report tables; the values here are representative. # Key findings (composite, from ESMAP final report) Nepal country-weighted GHI: 4.7–5.0 kWh/m²/day GHI range across stations: 4.3 (Kathmandu Valley) to 6.0+ (Jomsom / Mustang) Strongest seasonality in: mid-hill stations (Pokhara, Dhankuta) with 35–45% monsoon penalty Weakest seasonality in: trans-Himalayan stations (Jomsom) with 5–15% monsoon penalty Station-satellite validation: Global Solar Atlas is within ±5% of measured GHI at all stations; trans-Himalayan stations had largest satellite underestimate (~5–8%) Wind resource: limited utility-scale potential; best pockets in Mustang (annual mean >6 m/s at hub height) and selected Koshi gaps # Why this source matters ## For the wiki specifically Anchor citation for solar-resource-geography-nepal zone definitions Base data for data-nepal-solar-resource-zones district-level tables Validation reference for global-solar-atlas-nepal satellite-derived zones in the map layer Empirical grounding that distinguishes Nepal's measured resource from the theoretical resource estimates in less rigorous studies ## For Nepal solar planning in general It is the dataset that moves Nepal solar discussion from "we think Nepal has good sun" to "we measured it for four years across 14 representative sites and here is the spatial and seasonal structure." This is the empirical floor under claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro and the LCOE arguments downstream. # Data access Raw 10-min / hourly station data: ESMAP portal (historically), AEPC national archive (partial) Derived products: Global Solar Atlas tiles, Nepal national solar atlas (AEPC), IRENA REmap modelling Station reports: ESMAP Nepal final report (~2019–2020) # Relevance to project Primary source for: solar-resource-geography-nepal data-nepal-solar-resource-zones solar-hydro-complementarity — seasonality patterns data-solar-hydro-complementarity-profile — monthly shape Validation source for: global-solar-atlas-nepal irena-remap-nepal # Data-quality notes Station data is high-quality pyranometer-grade, calibrated, Vaisala-instrument-based. Spatial coverage is thin (14 stations across a country of Nepal's complexity); satellite products fill the interpolation gap but with systematic biases in high-mountain terrain. Temporal coverage (2015–2019) pre-dates the 2021–2024 atmospheric-aerosol shifts; there is a case for a refresh campaign, especially in the Indo-Gangetic-plain-adjacent Terai where dust aerosol has intensified. Post-2019 data is patchy; some stations continued under AEPC operation, others were decommissioned. # Gaps we would like A 2024/25 refresh campaign across at least 8 of the original 14 stations, to capture atmospheric-aerosol evolution. Publication of a per-station 10-year climatology with percentile bands (not just 10-year mean). Integration with cloud-cover indices (MODIS, Himawari) for operational forecasting value. # Limitations Spatial coverage thin. 14 stations across Nepal's terrain complexity leaves substantial interpolation gaps. Satellite products fill the gap but with systematic biases in high-mountain terrain. Temporal cutoff at 2019. The measurement campaign ended in 2019, pre-dating the 2021–2024 atmospheric-aerosol shifts. Terai stations in particular may now face dust-aerosol conditions not captured in the dataset. Post-2019 data patchy. Some stations continued under AEPC operation after 2019; others were decommissioned. There is no uniform post-campaign dataset. Station values are representative, not precise. The GHI means in the station table are approximate; exact values require cross-reference with the ESMAP final report tables. # Related global-solar-atlas-nepal — satellite-derived complement irena-remap-nepal — scenario-modelling use of this data aepc-renewable-framework — implementation partner solar-resource-geography-nepal — the narrative interpretation data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — the operational table

pages.title: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment
headings: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment
pages.excerpt: Regional-scale analysis of the Ganges basin covering water storage, flood management, and transboundary dynamics. Provides the valley-shape storage paradox that Public source review highlighted.
pages.body_text: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment # Summary Regional-scale analysis of the Ganges basin covering water storage, flood management, and transboundary dynamics. Provides the valley-shape storage paradox that Public source review highlighted. # Key Data Points Aswan High Dam (Egypt, 111m): 162 BCM storage — flat terrain allows massive reservoir Proposed Andhi Khola Dam (Nepal, 110m): only 0.9 BCM — steep V-shaped Himalayan valley Karnali Chisapani proposed gross storage: 28.2 BCM, usable live capacity only 16.2 BCM Nepal's annual water flow through territory: 175–225 BCM # Relevance to Project The valley-shape paradox (same dam height, 180x less storage) is one of the most powerful visualizations for explaining why Nepal's geography simultaneously enables hydropower and prevents easy storage. Central to storage-deficit and data-storage-comparison. # Limitations 2014 publication. Pre-dates the 2015 earthquake, post-earthquake hydrological assessments, and the 2021 Melamchi flood. Basin conditions, sedimentation rates, and infrastructure assumptions may have shifted. Regional focus, not Nepal-specific. The assessment covers the entire Ganges basin across four countries; Nepal-specific storage figures are extracted from a broader regional frame and may lack the granularity of a Nepal-only study. Karnali Chisapani figures are study-era estimates. The 28.2 BCM gross / 16.2 BCM live figures predate the most recent project feasibility iterations.

pages.title: World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project
headings: World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project
Component 1: Grid-Connected Solar PV Farms Development
Component 3: Institutional Capacity and Project Management
pages.excerpt: The institutional anchor for Nepal's first utility-scale, grid-tied solar farm and the financing channel that broke Nepal's "can we actually build solar at utility scale?" learning curve. IDA credit to the Government of Nepal, implemented by NEA under a World Bank project supervi
pages.body_text: World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project # Summary The institutional anchor for Nepal's first utility-scale, grid-tied solar farm and the financing channel that broke Nepal's "can we actually build solar at utility scale?" learning curve. IDA credit to the Government of Nepal, implemented by NEA under a World Bank project supervision framework. # What the project covers Three components: ## Component 1: Grid-Connected Solar PV Farms Development Pilot utility-scale solar farm development Output: 25 MWp ground-mounted grid-tied solar plant at Bidur / Trishuli, Nuwakot district (completed, commissioned 2022) — see bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp First NEA-owned, NEA-operated utility solar plant in Nepal Interconnection to the Trishuli 33 kV grid EPC via competitive procurement; O&M staff trained under the project ## Component 2: Distribution System Upgrading Substation upgrades, distribution line reinforcement Smart-meter pilot deployments Distribution loss reduction targets ## Component 3: Institutional Capacity and Project Management NEA capacity building for solar O&M, grid-integration studies, net-metering framework Technical assistance for future solar programmes (including what became the 960 MW tender) The "cumulative grid impact study for 960 MW solar" cited in nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 was delivered under this project's TA line # Key data points Credit size: IDA concessional loan (amount: in hundreds of millions of USD; specific number in PAD and ICR) Implementation period: approximately 2014–2023 Bidur / Trishuli 25 MWp: commissioned 2022; first ~40 GWh/yr generation Follow-on tender design capacity: provided the technical framework for the 960 MW national solar tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) # Why this project matters Three institutional firsts that changed what is operationally possible: 1. First NEA-EPC utility solar, closed on time. Broke the "NEA can't build renewables beyond hydro" narrative and put NEA's project-management bandwidth through the cycle once. 2. Established the PPA template for utility solar. The PPA structure, grid-interconnection specification, metering standard, and O&M protocol that subsequent IPP solar plants use are descendants of the Bidur/Trishuli precedent. 3. Demonstrated the site-to-grid latency. Planning → PPA → COD in ~5 years for the first plant; IPP plants now take ~2–3 years. The learning curve compression is the project's most valuable externality. # Parallel / follow-on donor programmes The WB Grid Solar & EE Project sits in a cluster of donor programmes on Nepal renewables: Programme | Donor | Focus | Target (approx.) | ---|---|---|---:| Grid Solar & EE | World Bank | Utility solar + grid upgrade | 25 MWp + distribution work | Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II | EIB | Ground-mounted grid-tied solar, 4 sites | up to EUR 8 M | Technical Assistance — Solar Tender Design | ADB / JICA (partial) | 960 MW tender grid studies | — | AEPC programmes (SHS, mini-grid) | ADB, SREP, WB, donor consortium | Off-grid + rural | ~100 MWp cumulative | Karnali off-grid solar + BESS | World Bank | Remote grid-absent districts | ~10 MWp target | Collectively these programmes have financed essentially all of Nepal's solar deployment to date; the 960 MW tender is the first programme of sufficient scale that private IPP finance dominates the capital stack rather than donor grants / concessional loans. # Documents and subsources Project Appraisal Document (PAD) — initial project design and rationale Implementation Status Reports (ISR) — periodic progress updates Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) — post-project evaluation Technical assistance outputs — solar tender design, grid impact studies, net-metering framework Bidur / Trishuli plant completion report (NEA + WB) # Data-quality notes Project-level disclosure is high (WB disclosure standards); credit amount, disbursement, and component performance are publicly documented. The 25 MWp Bidur/Trishuli plant's actual FY 2023/24 and FY 2024/25 generation numbers are in NEA annual reports and internal operational statistics. Grid impact study outputs have fed directly into the 960 MW tender design; that traceable chain is one of the cleanest "donor TA → national policy" examples in Nepal energy. # Relevance to project Primary source for: bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp — the flagship entity nea-960mw-solar-tender — the direct institutional descendant hybrid-siting-logic — Bidur/Trishuli is a near-hydro siting precedent rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — WB Grid Solar & EE Project touches both utility and distribution Cross-references: eib-rural-solar-phase2 — parallel programme aepc-renewable-framework — parallel programme on the off-grid side nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the implementation-side primary source # Limitations Credit amount imprecise. The exact IDA credit figure is described as "in the hundreds of millions of USD" — the precise number requires the Project Appraisal Document or Implementation Completion Report. Document collection, not a single source. This page synthesizes multiple underlying WB documents (PAD, ISRs, ICR, TA outputs) rather than representing a single published document at a fixed date. Generation data gap. The Bidur/Trishuli 25 MWp plant's actual FY 2023/24 and FY 2024/25 generation figures are in NEA annual reports and internal operational statistics, not in the WB project documents accessed for this page. Implementation period estimates. The ~2014–2023 window is approximate; precise approval, effectiveness, and closing dates are in the PAD and ICR. # Related bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp nea-960mw-solar-tender nea wb-country-economic-memo-2025 — macro frame wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022 — sector-reform frame this project sits inside

pages.title: World Bank Economics of Household Cooking Using Electricity in Nepal
headings: World Bank / CCAC Economics of Household Cooking Using Electricity in Nepal
pages.excerpt: A 2025 World Bank study of household electric-cooking economics that corroborates adoption as below one percent.
pages.body_text: World Bank / CCAC Economics of Household Cooking Using Electricity in Nepal # Summary 2025 World Bank policy research paper on household electric-cooking economics in Nepal. It is used here to verify that the latest reviewed source still describes electric-cooking adoption as below one percent of households rather than providing a newer annual uptake series. # Key Findings The report states that electricity has been used for cooking in less than one percent of Nepali households. It identifies unprocessed solid biomass as the primary cooking fuel for approximately 60% of households. It compares cooking technologies and fuels across Nepal's topographical regions from private and social-cost perspectives. It finds electricity cheaper than fossil fuels on average, but costlier than biomass from a private-cost perspective; when PM2.5 external costs are included, electricity becomes the cheapest option except for biogas. # Relevance Supports data-domestic-demand and intervention-electric-cooking-transition by confirming that the 0.5% electric-cooking statistic remains a low-adoption baseline rather than a superseded figure in the current reviewed source set. It also provides a primary analytical basis for comparing household cooking costs; it does not establish the design or outcome of a Nepal-wide electric-cooking programme. # Limitations Not an annual adoption series. The report corroborates sub-1% electric-cooking uptake but does not provide a newer nationally updated household share to replace the 2021 baseline. Economics focus. The report is primarily a cost-economics study, not a statistical yearbook or household energy census. Modelled economics, not a programme evaluation. It does not establish appliance prices, local feeder reliability, cooking-time load shape, subsidy incidence or results from a nationwide rollout.

pages.title: World Bank Nepal Power-Sector Evidence Record (2018–2025)
headings: World Bank Nepal Power-Sector Evidence Record (2018–2025)
pages.excerpt: A reconciled World Bank evidence record replacing a previously misidentified standalone reform-roadmap citation.
pages.body_text: World Bank Nepal Power-Sector Evidence Record (2018–2025) # Summary This record replaces an earlier misidentified citation to a standalone 2022 "Nepal Power Sector Reform Roadmap," for which no verified World Bank publication was located. It preserves two distinct World Bank evidence trails used by the wiki: the 2025 Nepal Country Economic Memorandum for the commonly cited hydropower-potential figures, and the 2018 Nepal Energy Development Policy Credit programme document for the documented power-market and institutional-reform work. # Key Findings The 2025 Country Economic Memorandum describes Nepal's hydropower potential as approximately 83,000 MW, of which 42,000 MW is considered economically viable (pp. 18 and 85–86). The 2018 Energy Development Policy Credit programme document records that a PPIAF/World Bank-supported Study on Power Market Reform Roadmap was completed in 2016. The same 2018 programme document records policy actions involving electricity regulation, the Nepal Power Trading Company, power-purchase rules and institutional reform. It does not identify a standalone 2022 report with the title previously assigned to this page. # Relevance The Country Economic Memorandum provides the World Bank provenance for the 42,000 MW economically viable figure used alongside WECS estimates in hydropower-potential-categories. The Energy Development Policy Credit document provides dated institutional context for pages discussing power-market and sector reform. # Limitations This is a combined source record maintained under a legacy slug. The 2018 and 2025 documents must be cited with their own dates and page locations rather than treated as one report. The 42,000 MW figure is a broad economic-potential benchmark, not a construction target, current project inventory or statement of firm energy. The 2018 programme document describes reform studies and policy actions at that time; it does not establish implementation status after its reporting period. # Official Documents World Bank, Nepal Country Economic Memorandum 2025 (PDF) World Bank, Nepal Energy Development Policy Credit programme document (2018, PDF)

pages.title: World Bank NIETTP Load-Shedding GDP-Cost Estimate
headings: World Bank NIETTP Load-Shedding GDP-Cost Estimate
pages.excerpt: World Bank project document for the Nepal-India Electricity Transmission and Trade Project that contains the specific load-shedding cost estimate used in the documentary verification pass.
pages.body_text: World Bank NIETTP Load-Shedding GDP-Cost Estimate # Summary World Bank project document for the Nepal-India Electricity Transmission and Trade Project that contains the specific load-shedding cost estimate used in the documentary verification pass. # Key Data Points The document describes Nepal's 2007-2017 electricity shortage period, including load shedding of up to roughly 14 hours per day. It states that load shedding cost Nepal an estimated 7% of GDP annually during that era. # Relevance This is the correct World Bank citation for the load-shedding cost claim. The World Bank Country Economic Memorandum 2025 supports the post-load-shedding reliability context but does not contain this exact GDP-cost estimate on the checked page. # Limitations The estimate describes the load-shedding era, not current outage costs. It should be cited as a World Bank project-document estimate, not as a new 2025 CEM finding.

pages.title: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic
headings: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic
pages.excerpt: The World Bank's national diagnostic of Nepal's water institutions, storage, resilience and investment needs.
pages.body_text: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic # Summary A water-sector-wide diagnostic covering storage requirements, irrigation, and the intersection of water management with energy. Provides the most authoritative estimate of Nepal's seasonal storage gap. # Key Data Points Nepal's storage volume requirement to satisfy annual seasonal water demand: 29.86 km³ Nepal effectively has none of this required seasonal storage at national scale JICA estimates Nepal will need at least 1,993 MW of storage hydropower by 2032 (BAU) or 3,154 MW (high demand) Nepal's active dam storage: ~85 MCM (one of the lowest in Asia) # Limitations Storage-gap framing: The 29.86 km³ requirement is a water-sector-wide estimate (irrigation + energy + other uses), not an electricity-only storage target. Active vs total storage ambiguity: The ~85 MCM active storage and 130–150 MCM total figures differ by boundary definition. Both are vanishingly small relative to need. 2023 cutoff: Post-2023 project progress, policy changes, and new studies (e.g., JICA IPSDP) may update the storage requirement estimates. JICA MW targets: The 1,993 MW (BAU) and 3,154 MW (high demand) storage hydropower figures are JICA study outputs, not verified construction plans. # Relevance to Project The 29.86 km³ requirement vs near-zero actual storage is the single most dramatic number for the storage-deficit argument. JICA's MW requirements give a concrete planning target. Data feeds into data-storage-comparison. . [!note] The 85 MCM active storage figure and the 130-150 MCM total figure likely differ in boundary — active vs total reservoir volume. Both are vanishingly small relative to the 29.86 km³ need.

pages.title: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990)
headings: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990)
pages.excerpt: "Methodology for Estimating Hydrological Characteristics of Ungauged Locations in Nepal" (WECS/DHM, 1990, Seq. No. 331, Ministry of Water Resources). The regulatory default methodology for feasibility studies on Nepal's vast number of projects on ungauged tributaries.
pages.body_text: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990) # Summary "Methodology for Estimating Hydrological Characteristics of Ungauged Locations in Nepal" (WECS/DHM, 1990, Seq. No. 331, Ministry of Water Resources). The regulatory default methodology for feasibility studies on Nepal's vast number of projects on ungauged tributaries. # Key points Empirical regionalization equations derived from DHM gauging data collected up to 1985. Simplistic regression: For example, instantaneous flood flows for a 2-year return period use a regression equation based solely on catchment area below 3,000 meters elevation. HYMOS dependence: Data processing and gap-filling have historically relied on HYMOS (version 4), a proprietary hydrological software system. Stationarity assumption: The models assume hydrological stationarity — that statistical properties of river flows remain constant over time. They do not capture cryospheric melt acceleration, shifting monsoon patterns, or increasing baseflow volatility. Partial update: DHM issued "Hydrological Estimation in Nepal" (June 2016), but the 1990 methodology remains the regulatory default for most feasibility studies. # Limitations Data age: Empirical regionalization equations are derived from DHM gauging data collected up to 1985; hydrological conditions may have changed significantly. Stationarity assumption: Models assume hydrological stationarity and do not capture cryospheric melt acceleration, shifting monsoon patterns, or increasing baseflow volatility. Simplistic regression: Instantaneous flood flows use regression equations based solely on catchment area below 3,000 m elevation, which may not capture complex Himalayan terrain. Proprietary dependence: Data processing and gap-filling historically rely on HYMOS (version 4), a proprietary software system that limits transparency and reproducibility. Partial update: DHM issued a 2016 update, but the 1990 methodology remains the regulatory default; newer hydrological insights are not systematically integrated.

pages.title: WECS Energy Sector Synopsis Report 2024
pages.excerpt: WECS's FY2079/80 full-energy balance, used to place grid electricity within Nepal's wider final-energy system.
pages.body_text: WECS Energy Sector Synopsis Report 2024 # Summary Covers Nepal's full energy balance for FY 2079/80 (~2022/23), including all energy sources (not just electricity). Provides the broader context for where grid electricity fits within Nepal's total energy system. This is the authoritative denominator for every "hydro share of total energy" claim. # Key Data Points (FY 2079/80) Total final energy consumption: 532.42 PJ (−16.81% YoY vs 640 PJ in FY 2078/79) Consumption by resource class: - Traditional biomass: 63.87% (340.04 PJ) — fuelwood, ag residue, animal dung - Commercial fuels: 25.80% (137.38 PJ) — coal, petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG, ATF, furnace oil - Grid electricity: 7.23% (38.49 PJ) — up from ~4.96% in FY 2078/79 (+21.18% YoY) - Modern renewables: 3.10% (16.50 PJ) — biogas, solar, micro-hydro, wind Coal consumption down −41.50% YoY; petroleum products down −16.14% YoY Sectoral shares: - Residential 60.75% (323,463 TJ) - Industrial 20.91% (111,306 TJ) - Transportation 10.43% (55,553 TJ) - Commercial 5.04% (26,835 TJ) - Construction/Mining 1.92% (10,222 TJ) - Agriculture 0.95% (5,040 TJ) Hydropower capacity referenced: 3,349 MW installed, 9,940.86 GWh generated (FY 2023/24) Transmission system: 5,742 circuit-km at 66 kV+; 8,867 MVA substation capacity # Correction note Earlier wiki pages cite grid electricity as 4.96% of final energy. That figure was the FY 2078/79 value that appears in this report's historical prose. The FY 2079/80 headline figure is 7.23%. Both are correct for their respective years; the 2.3-point jump in one year reflects real electrification growth. Full cross-tab decoded at data-final-energy-mix. # Local PDF status The local file at is now a real PDF copy of the report, verified locally as a 167-page PDF. The external above remains the canonical public URL. # Limitations Single-year snapshot: FY 2079/80 data; YoY comparisons (e.g., −16.81% total final energy) are sensitive to single-year anomalies such as fuel price shocks or demand disruptions. Local copy status: The repository copy has been verified as a 167-page PDF, but future extraction should still cross-check against the external . Biomass estimates: The 63.87% traditional biomass share relies on survey assumptions and stock-flow models, not metered consumption data. Grid-electricity share jump: The 4.96% → 7.23% jump in one year may reflect both real electrification growth and improvements in measurement coverage. # Relevance to Project The 7.23% grid-electricity share — and the fact that hydro is only ~6.8% of Nepal's total final energy — is one of the most revealing data points in the entire project. It collapses the "Nepal is a hydropower country" framing into the more honest "Nepal has a hydropower electricity system inside a biomass-and-petroleum energy system." Central to master-thesis, domestic-led-hydro-strategy, and energy-substitution-pathway. Feeds into nepal-energy-profile and data-final-energy-mix. .

pages.title: WECS Assessment of Hydropower Potential of Nepal (2019)
headings: WECS Assessment of Hydropower Potential of Nepal (2019)
pages.excerpt: Site Inspection during Safeguards
pages.body_text: WECS Assessment of Hydropower Potential of Nepal (2019) Site Inspection during Safeguards # Summary The revised national hydropower potential assessment. Supersedes the older 83,000 MW theoretical figure with updated screening. Provides basin-level gross and techno-economic potential breakdowns. # Key Data Points Revised gross potential: 72,544 MW (down from legacy 83,500 MW) Techno-economic potential: 32,680 MW Basin distribution of gross potential: - koshi-basin: 27,805 MW - karnali-basin: 20,385 MW - gandaki-basin: 19,803 MW - All remaining basins: ~4,551 MW ~94% of gross potential is in the three major Himalayan basins # Limitations Screening opacity: Full Multi-Criteria Analysis methodology and sensitivity parameters are not transparent in the public version. Gross vs techno-economic: The 72,544 MW gross potential is a theoretical ceiling; the 32,680 MW techno-economic potential is the more honest planning baseline. Legacy figure persistence: The older 83,000 MW figure remains politically prominent despite this revision. Exclusions: Does not account for climate-adjusted hydrology, sediment risk, or buildability constraints that would reduce realisable potential below techno-economic estimates. # Relevance to Project The definitive source for hydropower-potential-categories. Only surfaced the revised 72,544 MW figure — public summaries used the legacy 83,000 MW. The basin concentration data (94% in three basins) is central to the strategic argument. [!note] The legacy 83,000 MW figure remains politically prominent. The 2019 assessment's 72,544 MW is the more defensible current number, and 32,680 MW techno-economic is the more honest planning baseline.

pages.title: WECS River Basin Plans and Hydropower Development Master Plan (2024)
headings: WECS River Basin Plans and Hydropower Development Master Plan (2024)
pages.excerpt: WECS's 2024 basin-planning source for discharge, seasonality and hydropower-resource context.
pages.body_text: WECS River Basin Plans and Hydropower Development Master Plan (2024) # Summary The 2024 master planning document for Nepal's river basins. Provides basin-level discharge data, seasonal flow profiles, hydropower potential assessments, and strategic planning frameworks. This is the most authoritative recent basin-level reference. # Key Data Points koshi-basin: 27,818 km² in Nepal; 1,826.5 cumec average border flow; dry-season flows reduce to ~10x lower than peak gandaki-basin: 32,148 km² in Nepal; 1,952.3 cumec average border flow; ~80% of rainfall in four wet-season months karnali-basin: 43,153 km² in Nepal; 1,255.9 cumec average border flow; highest hydropower potential per WECS 75% or more of river flow occurs in the wet season (June–September) Storage and multipurpose projects treated as central to moving value from surplus to deficit basins Babai explicitly described as rain-fed; West Rapti, Kamala, Kankai as water-deficit / dry-season constrained # Relevance to Project Foundation for the hydrology evidence base. Provides the basin-level evidence for seasonal-mismatch and claim-timing-not-volume. [!warning] WECS explicitly warns that atlas flow numbers are model-derived (MIKE SHE / MIKE Hydro Basin) and may differ from DHM observations or project-specific studies. # Limitations Model-derived, not measured. Basin flow numbers are MIKE SHE / MIKE Hydro Basin model outputs, not DHM gauge observations. Values may differ from project-specific hydrological studies. Single planning document. The master plan represents WECS's planning framework at a point in time; it does not reflect subsequent basin-level developments, project-specific feasibility studies, or post-2024 hydrological events. Dry-season flow estimates are model projections. The ~10x wet-to-dry flow reduction cited for Koshi is a model estimate, not a multi-decadal gauge average. Interannual variability may be wider than implied.

headings: World Bank Dispute Resolution Agreement — Bharatpur–Bardaghat, 2023
pages.excerpt: The World Bank Accountability Mechanism records a mediated agreement between NEA and affected residents that allowed the last two Bharatpur–Bardaghat towers to proceed, while keeping the settlement terms confidential.
pages.body_text: World Bank Dispute Resolution Agreement — Bharatpur–Bardaghat, 2023 # Summary The World Bank Accountability Mechanism records the 2023 settlement of a dispute involving the Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV transmission line, Nepal Electricity Authority and affected residents in Dumkibas. The process used independent mediation through the World Bank's Dispute Resolution Service. # Key Findings Construction of the last two towers had been held up by the dispute. NEA and 63 community members reached an agreement after a year-long mediation process. The parties requested that the detailed settlement terms remain confidential. The published process record describes separate meetings, joint meetings, information exchange, option development and negotiated settlement. # Relevance The case is a bounded comparison for intervention-transmission-completion because it shows that a structured mediation process has resolved one Nepal transmission right-of-way dispute. # Transfer limitations It concerned a different 220 kV line, community, alignment and lender relationship. Access to the World Bank Accountability Mechanism was specific to a World Bank-financed project. Confidential settlement terms prevent comparison of compensation amounts or obligations. The case demonstrates a process option, not evidence that mediation will resolve Hetauda–Dhalkebar on the same terms or timeline. # Limitations The public record establishes the process and settlement outcome but not the confidential agreement's detailed commitments. # Source access World Bank Accountability Mechanism announcement 2024 follow-up report record
