An eastern Koshi-corridor buildout piece anchored on the Dhungesanghu and Basantapur substations. In the annual book it appears as part of the broader 220 kV Koshi corridor work needed to collect and move eastern hill generation. # Summary The Dhungesanghu-Basantapur 220/132 kV corridor is an eastern Koshi-corridor grid buildout asset. The page records substation capacities and annual-book evidence for the Dhungesanghu and Basantapur works within the broader Koshi Corridor programme. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 The appendix under-construction list names Dhungesanghu (132/33 kV, 30 MVA) and Basantapur (220/132 + 132/33 kV, 230 MVA) as active substation works under the Koshi Corridor 220 kV transmission line program. # Key Facts Substation | Capacity | ------------|---------:| Dhungesanghu | 30 MVA | Basantapur | 230 MVA | # Why It Matters The corridor is one of the enabling eastern-grid assets that sit behind arun-3-adjacent evacuation logic, even if it is not the final cross-border line itself. It is also part of the wider “collect before export” architecture summarized later in nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 and structurally linked to inaruwa-purnea-interconnection. # Limitations & Controversies The page is strongest on annual-book evidence for substation works and corridor context. It does not yet provide a complete line alignment, final commissioning history, current loading, or a separate verification of how each asset now operates within the Koshi Corridor. # See also inaruwa-purnea-interconnection arun-3 nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 stranded-generation

pages.title: Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project
pages.excerpt: A proposed 670 MW storage scheme with a current design and appraisal trail, but no verified financial close or construction start.
pages.body_text: Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project Figure 6.3-20 River Longitudinal Profile of the Dudh Koshi River Project area of Dudhkoshi Storage # Summary A proposed 670 MW storage reservoir scheme straddling Okhaldhunga, Khotang and Solukhumbu in the eastern koshi-basin. The February 2026 AIIB and DKJVCL materials describe a 600 MW underground main powerhouse and a 70 MW dam-toe ecological-flow powerhouse. The project is in pre-construction development and market sounding: AIIB financing is proposed, not approved or effective, and no current primary source establishes a firm construction start or commercial-operation date. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 670 MW current design basis; 635 MW retained as a historical variant | Status | Pre-construction / market sounding; financing proposed | River | Dudh Koshi (koshi-basin) | Districts | Okhaldhunga, Khotang, Solukhumbu | ## Engineering Dudhkoshi's current published design pairs a 220 m dam with an underground main powerhouse (600 MW) and a dam-toe ecological-flow powerhouse (70 MW). The current AIIB project summary and 2026 market-sounding teaser do not establish the previously listed 200 MW pumped-storage component, so that figure has been removed from the structured specification record pending a primary design source. The project's safeguard work explicitly includes sediment, slope, seismic, biodiversity and glof-risk assessment. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | 220 m current basis | Main powerhouse | 600 MW (underground) | Dam-toe powerhouse | 70 MW (ecological flow) | Underground powerhouse | Yes | Type | Storage | ## Storage The published project record uses approximately 1,581 MCM of total storage. That figure remains in the structured registry, but the current AIIB summary does not publish every reservoir parameter; detailed design documents should remain the authority for gross, live and operating storage. Compare the scale with kulekhani-cascade and the 140 MW tanahu-hydropower project under construction. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 1,581 MCM | ## Output The current structured design record uses approximately 3,377 GWh of annual energy and 1,252 GWh of dry-season energy. Dispatch and revenue outcomes remain design assumptions until the operating rule curve, PPA and final financing documents are disclosed. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 3,377 GWh | Dry-season design energy | 1,252 GWh | ## Financial AIIB lists USD 200 million of proposed sovereign financing and names ADB as lead co-financier. This is only part of the project's estimated capital requirement and must not be described as financial close, approval, effectiveness or disbursement. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total cost | ~USD 2.2 billion | Owner | NEA | Lead co-financier | ADB | AIIB amount | USD 200 million proposed | ## Schedule The project remains before financing approval and construction. Earlier planning dates for a 2027 start and 2031 operation are retained as historical targets only; the current primary project summaries do not establish them as firm milestones. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Construction start | Not established in current primary source | Commercial operation | Not established in current primary source | # Current Status and Performance Provenance As of 10 July 2026: proposed / pre-construction. The project has a current design basis, market-sounding material and proposed multilateral financing, but appraisal, full financing, safeguard completion, procurement and construction commencement remain separate pending milestones. Dimension | Current position | Evidence date | ---|---|---| Design | 600 MW main + 70 MW dam-toe powerhouse; 220 m dam | February 2026 | Financing | ADB lead co-financier; USD 200 million AIIB financing proposed | February 2026 | Safeguards | Category A / high risk; ESIA, resettlement, Indigenous Peoples, biodiversity and dam-safety instruments under preparation or review | February 2026 | Procurement | Market-sounding teaser issued | 2 February 2026 | Construction | Not started | 10 July 2026 verification | # Recent Updates Date | Update | Source | ---|---|---| 5 Feb 2026 | AIIB published the proposed-project summary and financing envelope | AIIB project summary | 2 Feb 2026 | DKJVCL issued the current market-sounding teaser | Development teaser | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Current evidence | ---|---|---| Full financing is not approved or effective | Financial close and major works procurement | AIIB lists only USD 200 million as proposed financing | Category A safeguard instruments remain under preparation or review | Appraisal and financing approval | AIIB project summary | Final design-basis reconciliation | Stable public specification record | 635 MW and 670 MW figures remain in historical materials | # Significance Dudhkoshi matters on three documented axes: 1. Scale. 670 MW of proposed reservoir generation in a system where the entire current storage fleet is 106 MW (kulekhani-cascade) and the only storage actually under construction is 140 MW (tanahu-hydropower). Dudhkoshi alone would roughly match the combined 2025 hydropower fleet of Nepal on energy volume and materially change the dry-season firm-power portfolio if built. 2. Seasonal storage. The reservoir and 1,252 GWh dry-season design figure make the project relevant to seasonal-mismatch without requiring the unsupported pumped-storage claim. 3. Safeguard-intensive design. The project is being scoped with landscape stabilization and sediment management built in — a response to Nepal's sediment-as-design-constraint reality and to the fact that the upper Dudh Koshi routinely receives GLOF pulses from the Everest region (see glof-risk). Compare Dudhkoshi (670 MW, storage, proposed multilateral financing) to arun-3 (900 MW, peaking RoR, SJVN, export-first). Both are in the Koshi basin, but they occupy different delivery stages and have different operating purposes. # Limitations & Controversies Four-decade gestation. The original feasibility was ADB-supported in the 1980s. Land acquisition restarted only in 2021. A project that has been "about to be built" for 40 years carries a credibility tax that any new timeline must earn against. Displacement footprint. AIIB's preliminary summary reports about 3,300 affected households and approximately 290 households expected to be physically and economically displaced. The transmission line and access-road impacts were still being assessed at publication, so these figures are not a final project-wide resettlement total. GLOF exposure. The 2024 Thame Valley GLOF traveled down the Dudh Koshi mainstem. A 220 m dam on a GLOF-exposed river demands a design flood that correctly accounts for cascading lake outburst scenarios, not a stationary climatology. How that design flood is set — and how conservative the spillway margin is — is the safety-critical question for the entire project. Financing status. AIIB sovereign financing is proposed, not approved, effective or disbursed. The disclosed USD 200 million amount also covers only part of the estimated project cost. # Official Visual References The new DKJVCL project material is a stronger visual source than the old bridge photos currently sitting in the top strip. The two most useful figure pages in the 2026 development teaser are the detailed dam-site layout and the basin study-area map. General layout of the Dudhkoshi dam site from the 2026 development teaser. Study-area and catchments map from the same teaser. Source: Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project Development Teaser (PDF) # Related storage-deficit — what Dudhkoshi would begin to address koshi-basin — the basin context glof-risk — the 2024 Thame Valley GLOF traveled down the Dudh Koshi river tanahu-hydropower firm-power sediment-as-design-constraint # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Cross-Border View With Projects data-map-inventory # Sources aiib-dudhkoshi-project-2026 dudhkoshi-nea-proposal-2024 nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.title: Gandaki Basin
pages.excerpt: The Gandaki (Narayani) basin is Nepal's central major river system, draining ~32,148 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Kali Gandaki, Marsyangdi, Budhi Gandaki, Trishuli, Seti, Madi, and East Rapti. The Kali Gandaki gorge between Annapurna and Dhaulagiri drops >5,500 verti
pages.body_text: Gandaki Basin # Summary The Gandaki (Narayani) basin is Nepal's central major river system, draining ~32,148 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Kali Gandaki, Marsyangdi, Budhi Gandaki, Trishuli, Seti, Madi, and East Rapti. The Kali Gandaki gorge between Annapurna and Dhaulagiri drops >5,500 vertical meters — by some measures the world's deepest. This is Nepal's most developed hydropower corridor. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Area in Nepal | 32,148 km² | Average discharge (border) | 1,952 m³/s (~61.6 BCM/yr) | Monsoon share | 74–80% | Peak-to-dry ratio | 22–30:1 | Gross hydropower potential | 19,803 MW (27.3% of national total) | # Hydropower Significance The most mature "buildable" basin. Hosts Nepal's early landmark projects — Kali Gandaki A (144 MW), Middle Marsyangdi (70 MW), and the kulekhani-cascade (on a tributary). The corridor benefited from road access (Prithvi and Siddhartha highways) and historical institutional familiarity. The proposed budhigandaki (1,200 MW) would be the basin's first major storage project and a system-shaping intervention for nepal-energy-profile. # Constraints sediment-as-design-constraint — the Kali Gandaki A plant is the definitive case study for turbine erosion. Suspended sediment spikes from 20 ppm (dry) to 50,000 ppm (monsoon). 65 million tonnes/year pass the dam site. More developed does not mean fully tapped. Significant untapped tributary potential remains. # Downstream Significance The Gandak system irrigates ~1.5–2 million ha in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh. The Gandak Treaty (1959) gave Nepal only 15 MW from a major barrage — one of the most cited examples of treaty asymmetry. See hydro-geopolitics. # Limitations & Controversies Sediment as design constraint. The Kali Gandaki A plant is the definitive case study for turbine erosion. Suspended sediment spikes from 20 ppm (dry) to 50,000 ppm (monsoon), with 65 million tonnes/year passing the dam site. Abrasive silt is a first-order design constraint across the basin, not just an implementation detail after head and flow are set. Treaty asymmetry. The Gandak Treaty (1959) gave Nepal only 15 MW from a major barrage — one of the most cited examples of treaty inequity in South Asian water governance. Future projects in this basin carry the memory of that history. Most developed does not mean fully tapped. Road access and institutional familiarity have concentrated development on the main stem and larger tributaries. Significant untapped potential remains on smaller tributaries, but the financing and grid-access gaps that blocked them historically persist. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.body_text: Gorakhpur–New Butwal 400 kV Interconnection # Summary Nepal's second major 400 kV cross-border link, under construction between New Butwal and Gorakhpur. POWERGRID's FY 2024/25 annual report records a 50:50 NEA–POWERGRID joint venture for the Indian portion. The Nepal and India sections, terminal works and the domestic New Butwal evacuation path must be monitored separately; a project-wide target year is not proof that all components are ready. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status | Under construction | Nepal terminal | New Butwal (Rupandehi) | India terminal | Gorakhpur (Uttar Pradesh) | Length | ~130 km (~18 km Nepal + ~112 km India) | Indian-side owner | Butwal-Gorakhpur Cross Border Power Transmission Limited (50:50 NEA–POWERGRID JV) | Nepal-side owner | nea | Commissioning | No firm current project-wide date established | Interconnection ID | | # Current Status As of 10 July 2026: under construction. The segment record separates the two countries and treats synchronized testing and New Butwal's domestic-grid connection as explicit dependencies. Segment | Status | Evidence date | Dependency | ---|---|---|---| New Butwal–Nepal/India border | Under construction | Verified 10 Jul 2026 | New Butwal terminal and domestic evacuation readiness | Nepal/India border–Gorakhpur | Under construction | POWERGRID FY 2024/25 | Synchronized Nepal-side completion and cross-border testing | # Recent Updates Date | Update | Source | ---|---|---| 31 Mar 2025 | POWERGRID recorded the 50:50 implementing JV and its paid-up capital | POWERGRID FY 2024/25 annual report | 31 Jul 2025 | The stated 22-month PMC period for the Indian portion elapsed; no public completion outcome is established by the reviewed POWERGRID records | POWERGRID FY 2023/24 annual report | 2 Jun 2023 | India and Nepal jointly carried out the groundbreaking | Embassy of India record | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Monitoring requirement | ---|---|---| Nepal and India segment schedules may diverge | Synchronized commissioning | Country- and package-level progress evidence | New Butwal terminal and domestic evacuation readiness | Transfer of cross-border capacity into Nepal's grid | Integrated testing and energisation record | Current trading and transmission-charge arrangements are not documented in this dossier | Commercial use | Applicable approved agreements and regulatory orders | # Significance Redundancy for the eastern link. Full N-1 cross-border security for the first time once both operate in parallel. Western evacuation. Opens a direct export door for gandaki-basin and karnali-basin generation — which has historically had no outlet matching its latent capacity. MCA corridor payoff. The US-funded mca-central-400 spine has little export value without this link — the two projects are schedule-linked in NEA's integrated resource plan. # Limitations & Controversies Schedule history. Public target dates have moved. The monitoring record therefore requires dated segment evidence instead of carrying the latest announced year forward as a firm date. Nepal-side readiness. New Butwal substation 400 kV bays await final MCA corridor completion; misalignment of the two projects could strand capacity on either side. Tariff mechanism. Cross-border trading charges for this link have not yet been fully negotiated under the 2021 cross-border guidelines. # See also mca-central-400 — the Nepal-side upstream corridor dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — the link it is meant to complement claim-transmission-immediate-blocker hydro-geopolitics # Sources powergrid-gorakhpur-butwal-fy2024-25 nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25

pages.title: Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV Corridor
pages.excerpt: The 220 kV east–west spine across central Nepal, running through the Hetauda → Bharatpur → Bardaghat load corridor. This is the line that carried Nepal's grid before the 400 kV era — and still carries the majority of Terai distribution load.
pages.body_text: Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV Corridor # Summary The 220 kV east–west spine across central Nepal, running through the Hetauda → Bharatpur → Bardaghat load corridor. This is the line that carried Nepal's grid before the 400 kV era — and still carries the majority of Terai distribution load. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 220 kV (double circuit) | Status | Operational | Length basis | 146.5 route-km / 293.0 circuit-km | Owner | nea | Terminals | Hetauda (Makwanpur) · Bharatpur (Chitwan) · Bardaghat (Nawalparasi) | Corridor ID | | # Map Interpretation The connected transmission layer now represents this corridor as two source-controlled features: Hetauda-New Bharatpur and New Bharatpur-Bardaghat. This replaced the older over-selected RPGCL extraction, which mixed adjacent 220 kV fragments into the HBB corridor. Current validation result: 2 features, 0 inferred connectors, 0 remaining endpoint gaps, and 143.365 km traced length against a 146.5 route-km basis. Public decision: default-visible, caveated. # Significance Load-centre spine. Serves the Bharatpur–Hetauda–Butwal urban belt, Nepal's second-largest consumption cluster after the Kathmandu Valley. Redundancy for 400 kV. During HDDI outages this corridor provides a lower-voltage fallback for east–west flow, at reduced capacity. Tie-in for western generation. Connects Marsyangdi-basin and Kali Gandaki-basin output to the central grid before the mca-central-400 fully commissions. # Limitations & Controversies Legacy capacity. 220 kV thermal limits constrain the amount of surplus generation the corridor can absorb; during monsoon peak, IPPs in the west are partly curtailed despite availability. Substation bottlenecks. Bharatpur's bus configuration has been flagged as a weak link in NEA's 2024 reliability review. Geometry precision remains caveated. The public route is now coherent and source-bounded, but the Bharatpur-Bardaghat portion is still a corridor-level SIA trace rather than a tower-by-tower alignment. # See also mca-central-400 — the 400 kV reinforcement dana-kushma-butwal-corridor — the 220 kV it links with in the west hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone

pages.title: Hetauda–Dhalkebar–Inaruwa 400 kV Backbone
pages.excerpt: Nepal's first domestic 400 kV backbone is operational east of Dhalkebar, while July 2026 NEA notices establish continued construction activity—not commissioning—on the Hetauda–Dhalkebar section.
pages.body_text: Hetauda–Dhalkebar–Inaruwa 400 kV Backbone 220 kV Substation at Dhalkebar # Summary Nepal's first major domestic 400 kV backbone, represented as two segments with different delivery states. Dhalkebar–Inaruwa is operational; Hetauda–Dhalkebar remains under construction. Describing the entire corridor simply as "operational" would overstate the current east–west transfer path to the dhalkebar-muzaffarpur gateway. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status | Partially operational: Dhalkebar-Inaruwa operational; Hetauda-Dhalkebar still under construction | Total spine length | ~288 km route basis | Owner | nea (Nepal Electricity Authority) | Key substations | Hetauda · Dhalkebar · Inaruwa | Segment status | Hetauda-Dhalkebar: under construction · Dhalkebar-Inaruwa: operational since June 2024 | Financing | ADB, KfW, World Bank (segment-wise) | Pane of operation | Central / Eastern Terai belt | Corridor ID | | # Current Status Evidence checked through 19 July 2026: partially operational. The corridor's status is stored by segment in , while the map uses document-bounded corridor geometry rather than a tower-by-tower engineering alignment. Segment | Status | Status date/basis | Principal dependency | ---|---|---|---| Hetauda–Dhalkebar | Under construction; commissioning not verified | NEA maintenance notices dated 3 and 5 Jul 2026 document conductor stringing | Current completion, remaining works and energisation are not stated in the notices | Dhalkebar–Inaruwa | Operating | June 2024 / NEA FY 2024/25 reporting | Completion of the western segment for a continuous backbone | # Recent Updates Date | Update | ---|---| FY 2024/25 | NEA reporting distinguishes the operating eastern section from the unfinished Hetauda–Dhalkebar section | 3–5 Jul 2026 | NEA operational notices document local shutdowns for conductor-stringing work on the Hetauda–Dhalkebar section | 19 Jul 2026 | Public NEA surfaces rechecked; construction activity is established, but completion and energisation remain unverified | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Evidence basis | ---|---|---| Remaining Hetauda–Dhalkebar works and right-of-way resolution | Continuous 400 kV operation across the full backbone | world-bank-hddi-rap and nea-hddi-construction-notices-july-2026 | # Map Interpretation In the connected transmission layer, HDDI is represented as two World Bank RAP-controlled corridor features: Hetauda-Dhalkebar and Dhalkebar-Inaruwa. The RPGCL overview fragments remain available in the raw audit/source layer, but they no longer drive the public connected network because they made the corridor read too straight and materially short. Public decision: default-visible, caveated. The current validation result has 0 inferred connectors, 0 remaining gaps, and a -1.22% length delta against the current 288 route-km basis. The geometry is still a document-grounded corridor trace, not a tower-by-tower alignment. # Significance First 400 kV domestic backbone. The operational Dhalkebar-Inaruwa section and the partly complete Hetauda-Dhalkebar section are the core east-west transfer path behind Nepal's export-readiness story. Aggregation point for IPP clusters. Evacuates the khimti-dhalkebar-corridor, Sunkoshi, Tamakoshi and (once online) arun-3 blocks toward India. Decouples load centres. Before HDDI, the Kathmandu Valley and the eastern Terai were weakly linked; HDDI re-wrote the grid topology. Mixed construction and operating state. Dhalkebar-Inaruwa is operational, while Hetauda-Dhalkebar remains in the build queue. Treating the whole backbone as operational would overstate current transfer readiness. # Limitations & Controversies Concentrated transfer dependency. Until parallel 400 kV paths are commissioned, outages or unfinished sections constrain domestic transfer and export routing. See claim-transmission-immediate-blocker. Thermal margin tightens as generation grows. NEA has flagged loading rates approaching design limits during the 2024 monsoon peak; mca-central-400 cannot arrive soon enough. N-1 reliability not fully certified. Sub-station-level redundancy at Dhalkebar is the subject of ongoing reinforcement projects. Map precision caveat. The public trace is now source-bounded and length consistent, but it is still not a tower-level engineering alignment. A future pass should replace it only if NEA or a lender publishes alignment sheets or tower coordinates. Current milestone caveat. NEA's FY 2024/25 report provides a July 2025 construction snapshot. July 2026 outage notices confirm later stringing work, but neither source establishes a current remaining-tower count or commissioning. # See also mca-central-400 — the parallel 400 kV spine dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — the border link HDDI feeds inaruwa-purnea-interconnection — future secondary export route off HDDI claim-transmission-immediate-blocker nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 # Sources world-bank-hddi-rap nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-hddi-construction-notices-july-2026

pages.title: Inaruwa–Purnea 400 kV Cross-Border Interconnection
pages.excerpt: The planned third 400 kV Nepal–India link, critical to evacuating the arun-3 export block (900 MW) and later upper-karnali-tier eastern generation. Currently in implementation-setup phase — the route exists on paper and in the bilateral MoU record, but construction has not begun.
pages.body_text: Inaruwa–Purnea 400 kV Interconnection # Summary The planned third 400 kV Nepal–India link, critical to evacuating the arun-3 export block (900 MW) and later upper-karnali-tier eastern generation. Currently in implementation-setup phase — the route exists on paper and in the bilateral MoU record, but construction has not begun. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status | Implementation setup | Nepal terminal | Inaruwa substation (Sunsari) — eastern terminus of hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone | India terminal | Purnea (Bihar) | Length | ~160 km total (≈50 km Nepal, ≈110 km India) | Primary purpose | Evacuation of arun-3 to the Indian grid | Status driver | Tied to arun-3 COD — originally 2023, now 2027+ | Interconnection ID | | # Significance Arun-3 depends on it. SJVN's 900 MW arun-3 was approved under an export-first model. Without this line, its generation cannot reach the Indian market at rated capacity — a direct instance of stranded-generation. Third 400 kV cross-border. Combined with dhalkebar-muzaffarpur and gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection, it would give Nepal three east/central/west 400 kV export paths — the first real geographic redundancy. Koshi basin anchor. Establishes the first 400 kV link serving the koshi-basin directly, opening the door to future eastern storage (e.g. dudhkoshi-storage). # Limitations & Controversies Schedule tied to Arun-3. Each slip in Arun-3 construction pushes the cross-border line as well — and vice versa. Environmental route. Alignment through Sunsari and Saptari districts still contested in local consultations. Indian-side approvals. Bihar state government concurrence and CEA tariff framework are the remaining gating items. # See also arun-3 — the project this line is built for hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone — upstream feeder from Inaruwa koshi-basin stranded-generation

pages.title: India — Energy Relationship with Nepal
pages.excerpt: Energy Balance (GWh) in FY 2076/77 (2019/20)
pages.body_text: India — Energy Relationship with Nepal Energy Balance (GWh) in FY 2076/77 (2019/20) # Summary India is the decisive external actor in Nepal's hydropower future. Not just as a neighbor, but as the main practical export market, balancing supplier in dry periods, transit state for Bangladesh sales, and counterpart in major treaty-linked water and power projects. # India's Multiple Roles Role | Mechanism | ------|-----------| Primary buyer | Only viable large-scale export market for Nepali electricity | Dry-season supplier | Nepal imports 400–500 MW daily in winter at NPR 11.50–16/unit | Approval gatekeeper | Indian regulatory approval required for cross-border trade | Transit state | Bangladesh electricity sales route through Indian grid | Treaty counterpart | Koshi (1954), Gandak (1959), Mahakali (1996) treaties | Investment filter | India blocks Chinese equity/EPC projects from cross-border export market | # Treaty History Treaty | Year | What Nepal Got | What India Got | --------|------|---------------|----------------| Koshi | 1954/1966 | Flood control (shared); INR 19,200/yr rent | Barrage on Nepali soil; irrigation rights | Gandak | 1959 | 15 MW | Irrigation over ~50x Nepal's allocation | Mahakali | 1996 | 50% of pancheshwar output | 50% of output + flood control + irrigation | Net result | | 15 MW received after 70 years of treaties | Significant irrigation and flood infrastructure | # The China Factor India views Nepal strictly as its strategic sphere of influence. It has explicitly blocked purchase of electricity from Nepali projects with Chinese equity or Chinese EPC contractors, forcing Nepali developers to align with Indian interests for market access. See india-cbte-2018. # Bangladesh Diversification Bangladesh entered as a buyer (FY 2024/25: NPR 266.7 million initial export). But the route depends on Indian transit, Indian approval, and Indian grid. Bangladesh diversifies the buyer set more than it diversifies the corridor and political dependence structure. # Limitations & Controversies Asymmetric treaty benefits. After 70 years of treaties (Koshi 1954, Gandak 1959, Mahakali 1996), Nepal has received 15 MW of firm capacity — a fraction of the irrigation and flood-control infrastructure India has built on Nepali soil. The structural imbalance in what each side values and extracts remains unresolved. Market concentration risk. India is the only viable large-scale export market, the dry-season supplier, the transit state for Bangladesh sales, and the approval gatekeeper for cross-border trade. This multi-role dependence creates a single-point-of-exposure that diversification to Bangladesh cannot materially reduce. China factor as dependency amplifier. India's explicit blocking of Chinese-equity/EPC projects from the cross-border market forces Nepali developers to align with Indian interests for market access, narrowing the developer pool and potentially inflating costs. # Related hydro-geopolitics — the analytical frame seasonal-arbitrage-trap — the trade dynamic pancheshwar — the stalled mega-project bhutan-hydropower-model — the comparison case

pages.excerpt: The Kabeli 132 kV corridor is an eastern Nepal branch network around the Soyak-Godak-Amarpur/Phidim area. It is represented as a branch corridor because the recovered NEA Kabeli IEE describes a bifurcated route rather than a single linear line.
pages.body_text: Kabeli / Godak-Soyak-Amarpur 132 kV Corridor The Kabeli 132 kV corridor is an eastern Nepal branch network around the Soyak-Godak-Amarpur/Phidim area. It is represented as a branch corridor because the recovered NEA Kabeli IEE describes a bifurcated route rather than a single linear line. # Summary The Kabeli / Godak-Soyak-Amarpur 132 kV corridor is a source-supported branch network in eastern Nepal. The page tracks the corridor as a bifurcated 132 kV system rather than a single forced line, based on the NEA Kabeli IEE route description. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV | Status | Under construction | Corridor ID | | Public map features | , , | Source basis | NEA Kabeli IEE pages 25-27 | Official route length | 83.74 km | Traced network length | 94.112 km | Validation delta | +12.39% | # Map Interpretation The connected network keeps Kabeli as a branch system: a southern trunk up to Soyak, one arm toward Godak, and one arm toward Phidim/Amarpur. The branch ends are not artificially connected to one another. This matters for reader trust. A single forced line would look cleaner, but it would misrepresent the project structure. # Limitations & Controversies Public decision: default-visible, caveated. The branch topology is source-supported and has no remaining endpoint gaps. The caveat is route precision: the current manual trace is still a document-grounded reconstruction, not a digitized alignment sheet. The highest-value improvement is to digitize the branch geometry more carefully from the Kabeli IEE route figures while preserving the trunk, Godak branch, and Amarpur/Phidim branch as separate network features. # See also data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network claim-transmission-immediate-blocker nepal-transmission-landscape-2025

pages.title: Kali Gandaki A
pages.excerpt: Nepal's largest operating power plant of any kind (144 MW), the Kali Gandaki A run-of-river scheme at Mirmi has anchored the national grid since 2002. It is Nepali-owned (NEA), ADB/JBIC-financed, and a useful foil to the newer India-developed export projects: it shows what a mult
pages.body_text: Kali Gandaki A # Summary Nepal's largest operating power plant of any kind (144 MW), the Kali Gandaki A run-of-river scheme at Mirmi has anchored the national grid since 2002. It is Nepali-owned (NEA), ADB/JBIC-financed, and a useful foil to the newer India-developed export projects: it shows what a multilaterally-funded, domestically-dispatched fleet backbone looks like — and also what two decades of wear do to one. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 144 MW | Status | Operating since 2002 | River | Kali Gandaki at Mirmi (gandaki-basin) | District | Palpa / Syangja | ## Engineering Three Toshiba Francis units in an above-ground powerhouse fed by a diversion dam with pondage. At 115 m gross head, Kali Gandaki A is a medium-head RoR design — less dramatic than upper-tamakoshi at 822 m, but with pondage that smooths daily load in a way pure RoR plants cannot. The pondage is not storage; it does not shift energy between seasons. See run-of-river-hydropower. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Units | 3 × 48 MW | Turbine type | Francis (Toshiba) | Gross head | 115 m | Type | Run-of-river with pondage | Owner / Operator | nea | ## Output The project was designed for ~860 GWh/yr but has averaged closer to 592 GWh — a ~30% shortfall that the ADB's own performance evaluation attributes to sedimentation, variable hydrology, and aging electromechanical equipment. This design-energy gap is a real-world demonstration of the principle in claim-mw-not-equal-value. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 860 GWh | Actual avg output | ~592 GWh | ## Financial Built at USD 354.8 million with ADB and JBIC financing, Kali Gandaki A was for two decades Nepal's single largest plant — the reference case for multilaterally-financed domestic hydropower. Compare with upper-tamakoshi (NPR 87 billion, domestic) and chameliya-hydropower (USD 226 million for 30 MW, 11-year build) for the cost-efficiency spectrum. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Construction cost | USD 354.8 million | Lead financier | ADB + JBIC | # Significance Kali Gandaki A still matters out of proportion to its size. At 144 MW it is only about 4% of Nepal's 2025 installed fleet, but it was for two decades the single largest plant on the grid — and in most years it produced more firm, dispatchable energy than any other asset NEA operates. It remains the reference point when discussing what a Nepali-utility-run, multilaterally-financed project can look like on the buildability spectrum. Compare kali-gandaki-a to two neighbours. upper-tamakoshi (456 MW, 2021) is larger, newer and also Nepali-developed, but pure RoR without pondage. arun-3 (900 MW, under construction) will be nameplate-bigger but peaking-design and India-dispatched. Kali Gandaki A sits between them in era and design philosophy — shared ADB lineage with Tanahu, NEA ownership like Upper Tamakoshi, and RoR-with-pondage shape that smooths evening load. # Limitations & Controversies The design-energy gap. The project was designed for roughly 860 GWh/year but has averaged closer to 592 GWh — ~30% below design. The ADB's own performance evaluation flagged sedimentation, variable hydrology and aging electromechanical equipment as factors. That gap is a real-world reminder that Nepal's nameplate capacity is not the same as its delivered energy, a distinction central to firm-power and seasonal-mismatch analysis. Rehabilitation overhang. In 2024 NEA floated a tender for design and supervision consultants to rehabilitate all three units. Any rehab of a fleet anchor plant introduces real derating risk during outage windows — exactly when the dry-season storage-deficit bites hardest. Timing the rehab around Nepal's import / export contracts with India is a non-trivial coordination problem. Pondage vs storage. Kali Gandaki A is not a reservoir project. The pondage it does have smooths daily load, not seasonal, so when monsoon flows fall off in January–May, Kali Gandaki A's contribution falls with them. Nepal's structural answer to that problem still sits in pages like dudhkoshi-storage, tanahu-hydropower and budhigandaki — not here. # See also gandaki-basin upper-tamakoshi run-of-river-hydropower firm-power nea # Sources kali-gandaki-a-adb-evaluation nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 nea-transmission-annual-book-2077

pages.title: Kali Gandaki Kowan
pages.excerpt: Kali Gandaki-Kowan is a 400 MW hydropower project under construction on the Kali Gandaki River — one of the largest projects in Nepal's active construction pipeline.
pages.body_text: Kali Gandaki-Kowan Kali Gandaki-Kowan is a 400 MW hydropower project under construction on the Kali Gandaki River — one of the largest projects in Nepal's active construction pipeline. # Summary Kali Gandaki-Kowan is tracked as a 400 MW under-construction hydropower project on the Kali Gandaki River. The page situates it in the Gandaki basin and frames its main analytical questions around evacuation capacity, construction scale, and project-delivery risk. # Kali Gandaki Basin The Kali Gandaki is one of Nepal's three major river systems, draining the region between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna — the deepest gorge in the world. The river's steep gradient and substantial dry-season baseflow (fed by glacial and snow melt) make it one of Nepal's most attractive hydropower corridors. Existing projects in the basin include Kali Gandaki A (144 MW, operating), Upper Modi A, and multiple projects across the Marsyangdi and Seti tributaries. # Transmission Context A 400 MW project requires significant transmission infrastructure for power evacuation. The Kali Gandaki corridor is served by the Dana-Kushma-Butwal 220 kV corridor and connects into the national east-west backbone. However, evacuation capacity at this scale remains a binding constraint — projects in the Kali Gandaki and Marsyangdi valleys compete for limited transmission slots toward the Butwal and Kathmandu load centers. See claim-transmission-immediate-blocker. # Construction Risk at Scale Projects in this capacity range face proportionally higher execution risk. The Kali Gandaki valley's complex geology, combined with the logistical challenges of moving heavy equipment through narrow mountain roads, has historically pushed build costs well above the NPR 200 million/MW mark for comparable large projects. Whether Kali Gandaki-Kowan can achieve competitive per-MW costs will determine whether it becomes a debt-burdened asset or a genuinely viable generator. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 400 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Kali Gandaki (gandaki-basin) | District | Mustang | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page is currently strongest on basin context, capacity, and broad transmission/buildability concerns. It does not yet verify final project cost, financing, detailed design, construction progress, COD target, environmental/social risk, or dedicated evacuation arrangements from project-level source documents. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources kali-gandaki-a-adb-evaluation

pages.title: Karnali Basin
pages.excerpt: The Karnali basin is Nepal's western major river system and the largest by area at ~43,153 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Bheri, West Seti, Humla Karnali, Mugu Karnali, and Tila. The Karnali feeds the Ghaghara, which contributes ~40% of the Ganges' baseflow at Varanasi
pages.body_text: Karnali Basin # Summary The Karnali basin is Nepal's western major river system and the largest by area at ~43,153 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Bheri, West Seti, Humla Karnali, Mugu Karnali, and Tila. The Karnali feeds the Ghaghara, which contributes ~40% of the Ganges' baseflow at Varanasi. This is Nepal's most dramatically underused basin — essentially zero large-scale hydropower despite having the best sites. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Area in Nepal | 43,153 km² | Average discharge (border) | 1,256 m³/s (~39.6 BCM/yr) | Monsoon share | 65–72% | Peak-to-dry ratio | 15–20:1 (best stability) | Gross hydropower potential | 20,385 MW (28.1% of national total) | # Why It Matters Most The Karnali has the best dry-season flow stability of any major Nepali system (lowest peak-to-dry ratio at 15–20:1 vs 25–50:1 for Koshi). WECS calls it the basin with the highest hydropower potential. It is the most obvious strategic priority for future development. # Why It Remains Undeveloped Remoteness — western Nepal has historically had fewer roads, less political attention, and less financing reach Transmission gap — the grid west of Butwal relies on legacy 132 kV lines incapable of handling large generation Political neglect — eastern-centric development patterns systematically disadvantaged the west The proposed karnali-chisapani (10,800 MW) alone would transform Nepal's energy posture, but it remains conceptual # Climate Projections CMIP6 modeling projects the Karnali will experience 3–23% decrease in winter/spring discharge by end of century, alongside 18–51% increase in monsoon/post-monsoon discharge. Temporal concentration of water will become even more extreme. See peak-water. A useful basin-specific warning from ICIMOD: over 1981–2012, average precipitation in the Karnali study basin trended downward by 4.91 mm/year, yet discharge stayed broadly constant over the observed record. That is exactly the kind of rainfall-flow decoupling that makes annual averages misleading for energy planning. # Limitations & Controversies Remoteness and infrastructure gap. Western Nepal has historically had fewer roads, less political attention, and less financing reach than the central and eastern corridors. The grid west of Butwal relies on legacy 132 kV lines incapable of handling large generation, creating a chicken-and-egg problem: no transmission, no projects; no projects, no transmission justification. Political neglect. Eastern-centric development patterns have systematically disadvantaged the west. Every national hydropower master plan since the 1960s has identified Karnali as a priority; none has funded the pre-feasibility or transmission backbone to make it actionable. Climate uncertainty. CMIP6 projects a 3–23% decrease in winter/spring discharge by end of century, alongside 18–51% increase in monsoon/post-monsoon discharge. The basin's current advantage — the best dry-season stability in Nepal — may erode, making long-lead-time investments riskier. Karnali Chisapani remains conceptual. At 10,800 MW, the basin's signature project has no DPR, no timeline, and no institutional champion. Four decades of appearing in master plans without advancing is a credibility tax on the entire basin. # Downstream Significance The Karnali/Ghaghara system serves ~2–3 million ha in UP and connects to Bangladesh's Ganges flow. See ganges-contribution. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.title: Karnali Chisapani Project
pages.excerpt: The largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal at 10,800 MW — an order of magnitude beyond anything operating or under construction. Located on the karnali-basin main stem near the Chisapani gorge in the western Terai, this is the project that would transform Nepal
pages.body_text: Karnali Chisapani Project # Summary The largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal at 10,800 MW — an order of magnitude beyond anything operating or under construction. Located on the karnali-basin main stem near the Chisapani gorge in the western Terai, this is the project that would transform Nepal into one of Asia's major power producers. It is also the most purely conceptual project in the wiki: no DPR, no timeline, and no single institution driving it forward. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 10,800 MW | Status | Conceptual | River | Karnali main stem (karnali-basin) | ## Engineering A proposed ~270 m dam on the Karnali main stem — the largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal. The design concept envisions a storage dam that would impound the Karnali's monsoon flow and release it through the dry season, providing both power generation and downstream regulation. But no detailed engineering design exists; the 10,800 MW figure is a planning estimate from basin potential studies, not a turbine-by-turbine layout. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | ~270 m | Dam type | Conceptual (likely rockfill or RCC) | Type | Storage | ## Storage The wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment describes a valley-shape paradox that constrains Karnali Chisapani's effective storage: despite the enormous dam height, the steep Karnali valley walls mean that only 16.2 of the total 28.2 BCM can be actively regulated. The remaining 12 BCM is dead storage — water sitting below the lowest outlet level, trapped by topography. This is a geological constraint, not a design choice, and it means the project's flood-control and irrigation-regulation value is structurally capped regardless of dam height. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 28,200 MCM | Effective storage | 16,200 MCM | Dead storage (valley-shape constraint) | ~12,000 MCM | ## Output At 10,800 MW, Karnali Chisapani would be one of the world's largest single hydropower installations — comparable to Brazil's Belo Monte (11,233 MW) and exceeding China's Xiluodu (13,860 MW, though that is a cascade). But the project has no design energy estimate — a sign of just how conceptual it remains. For comparison: Belo Monte generates ~39,500 GWh/yr; a 10,800 MW storage plant on the Karnali could theoretically produce 35,000–50,000 GWh/yr depending on head and flow regime. The output benefits (flood control for downstream India, irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara system, and massive storage-deficit relief) are strategic promises, not bankable numbers. ## Financial No cost estimate exists at the conceptual stage, but a back-of-envelope calculation is sobering. At a conservative USD 1.2 million/MW for a storage dam of this scale (Three Gorges came in at ~USD 1,000/kW in 1990s dollars; large Himalayan storage runs higher), the total construction cost could reach USD 13 billion — roughly one-third of Nepal's annual GDP. Even a fraction of that would require co-investment at a scale Nepal has never attempted. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Estimated cost (rough) | USD 10–15 billion | Nepal's annual GDP (FY 2024/25) | ~USD 45 billion | Financing requirement | Bilateral / multilateral consortium essential | Primary buyer | India (no other market can absorb 10,800 MW) | ## Schedule No timeline exists. The project has never progressed beyond basin-level reconnaissance studies. See buildability and hydro-geopolitics. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Current stage | Reconnaissance / basin study only | DPR | Not initiated | Treaty framework | None | Earliest conceivable COD | 2040s (optimistic) | # Limitations & Controversies Scale far exceeds Nepal's fiscal capacity. At an estimated USD 10–15 billion (roughly one-third of annual GDP), the project requires co-investment at a scale Nepal has never attempted. Even a fractional commitment would strain sovereign balance sheets. No institutional champion. Unlike Budhigandaki (Budhigandaki Company Limited), Dudhkoshi (NEA/AIIB), or Arun-3 (SJVN India), Karnali Chisapani has no developer, no lead financier, and no project office. It exists only in basin-scale assessments. Valley-shape dead-storage constraint. Despite a ~270 m dam height, steep Karnali valley walls mean ~12,000 MCM of the 28,200 MCM total is dead storage below the lowest outlet level. This caps flood-control and irrigation-regulation value regardless of dam height. Bilateral dependency with no treaty framework. The project requires India as co-investor and primary buyer (no other market can absorb 10,800 MW), but no bilateral treaty or joint project entity exists. The Pancheshwar precedent — 30 years, zero output — does not inspire confidence. Displacement at unprecedented scale. A 270 m dam on the Karnali main stem would displace tens of thousands across multiple districts. Nepal's largest displacement to date (Budhigandaki, ~8,117 households) is domestic; a binational resettlement plan has no precedent. # Historical Context Karnali Chisapani has been a fixture of Nepal's hydropower imagination since at least the 1960s, when early basin surveys identified the Chisapani gorge as a potential mega-dam site. The project appears in every generation of Nepal's hydropower master planning — from Hari Man Shrestha's seminal 1966 PhD thesis through the 1990s basin studies to the World Bank's Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment. But it has never moved beyond the conceptual stage because the question has never been whether it can be built — the question is who builds it and who buys the power. The pattern is instructive: every time Nepal's hydropower ambition resets (post-1990 democracy, post-Maoist conflict, post-2015 constitution), Karnali Chisapani reappears as the aspirational endpoint. The gap between recurring aspiration and zero progress is itself a data point for buildability — a reminder that megaprojects require more than good topography. # Regional Comparison Project | Country | Capacity | Dam height | Status | ---------|---------|----------|-----------|--------| Karnali Chisapani | Nepal | 10,800 MW | ~270 m | Conceptual | Belo Monte | Brazil | 11,233 MW | Run-of-river | Operating (2019) | Three Gorges | China | 22,500 MW | 181 m | Operating (2012) | Itaipu | Brazil/Paraguay | 14,000 MW | 196 m | Operating (1984) | Grand Inga | DRC | 40,000+ MW | Various | Stalled (conceptual) | Xiluodu | China | 13,860 MW | 285.5 m | Operating (2014) | pancheshwar | Nepal/India | 6,480 MW | 315 m | Stalled (30 yrs) | Karnali Chisapani belongs in the same conversation as Grand Inga: a technically viable mega-site that cannot advance without a governance and financing architecture that does not yet exist. Itaipu required a bilateral treaty between Brazil and Paraguay in 1973; construction started in 1975 and took 9 years. The comparison suggests that the engineering timeline is the easy part — the political timeline is the constraint. # Downstream Bilateral Context The Karnali River becomes the Ghaghara River in India, joining the Ganges system in Uttar Pradesh. The Ghaghara is the largest tributary of the Ganges by discharge, and its monsoon floods are a recurring disaster in eastern UP and Bihar. A 16 BCM effective storage reservoir at Chisapani could regulate approximately 15–20% of Ghaghara wet-season flow, converting destructive flood peaks into dry-season irrigation releases. The bilateral calculus is asymmetric in ways that have blocked progress: Nepal's benefit: 10,800 MW of generation, massive export revenue, domestic dry-season firming, national prestige India's benefit: flood control (valued in billions of avoided damages), irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara command area, a large block of clean energy at the border The valuation problem: India can get flood-control benefits from domestic dams on the Ghaghara downstream without a treaty; Nepal cannot capture those benefits unilaterally without India as co-investor and offtaker. This is the same asymmetric valuation that has stalled pancheshwar. # Why It Remains Conceptual 1. Scale of investment far exceeds Nepal's fiscal capacity. Total cost could reach USD 10–15 billion — at minimum 4–6x the cost of Nepal's most expensive project to date (Budhigandaki at ~USD 2.77 billion). 2. Requires India as co-investor and primary buyer. No other market can absorb 10,800 MW. India's domestic hydropower ambitions (Arunachal Pradesh, Bhutan joint ventures) compete for the same political and financial bandwidth. 3. Downstream bilateral politics. Water sharing, flood-control valuation, and irrigation benefit allocation are unresolved at the conceptual level. The Pancheshwar precedent (30 years, zero output) does not inspire confidence. 4. Environmental and social displacement at unprecedented scale. A 270 m dam on the Karnali main stem would displace tens of thousands of people across multiple districts (Kailali, Bardiya, Surkhet, Achham). The reservoir would flood significant agricultural land in the Terai. 5. No institutional champion. Unlike Budhigandaki (Budhigandaki Company Limited), Dudhkoshi (NEA/AIIB), or Arun-3 (SJVN India), Karnali Chisapani has no developer, no lead financier, and no project office. 6. Pre-feasibility has never been funded. The project has never received the USD 10–20 million that a serious pre-feasibility study would require. It exists only in basin-scale assessments. # What Pre-Feasibility Would Require To move from concept to credible candidate, Karnali Chisapani would need: A bilateral agreement-in-principle with India establishing a joint project structure (treaty, not MOU — the Pancheshwar lesson) A pre-feasibility study funded by a multilateral institution (World Bank, ADB, or AIIB) covering geotechnical investigation, hydrological modelling, environmental and social baseline, and preliminary economic analysis A displacement and resettlement framework that accounts for the project's unprecedented footprint A power purchase framework with India that covers export from a plant of this scale — the existing cross-border PPAs (Arun-3, Upper Karnali) are for projects under 1,000 MW; 10,800 MW is a different order of commercial commitment A transmission corridor plan — the existing Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur 400 kV cross-border line is rated for ~1,000 MW; Karnali Chisapani would need a dedicated high-capacity interconnector, possibly HVDC # Significance If ever realized, Karnali Chisapani would transform Nepal's energy position from regional exporter to Asian power producer. It would provide massive storage-deficit relief, flood control for downstream India, and irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara system. But the project also illustrates the valley-shape paradox from the wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment: despite the enormous dam, steep valley walls constrain effective storage to roughly half the total volume. The dead storage is a permanent reminder that topography, not ambition, sets the ceiling. More broadly, Karnali Chisapani is the limiting case for Nepal's hydropower strategy. If pancheshwar tests whether bilateral governance can deliver a 6,480 MW project, Karnali Chisapani tests whether the governance architecture at all can reach an order of magnitude beyond that. The answer, so far, is no. # Related karnali-basin — the river system pancheshwar — the only project in a comparable bilateral/governance class budhigandaki — the largest domestically-controlled storage advancing hydro-geopolitics — the analytical frame buildability — why megaprojects stall storage-deficit — what this project would address at scale Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory # Sources wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.title: Karnali Solar Energy Project
headings: 1. It is the first formal NEA–AEPC co-delivery structure at scale.
2. It validates solar + BESS economics at the remote site
3. It prepares the grid-edge integration question
pages.excerpt: A programme line referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/25 (Distribution / Customer Service Directorate) covering off-grid solar plants with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in Karnali, with operation and maintenance support from NEA. The programme is emerging as Nepal'
pages.body_text: Karnali Solar Energy Project A programme line referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/25 (Distribution / Customer Service Directorate) covering off-grid solar plants with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in Karnali, with operation and maintenance support from NEA. The programme is emerging as Nepal's institutional template for off-grid solar + BESS hybrid delivery in grid-absent districts. # Summary The Karnali Solar Energy Project is an off-grid solar plus BESS programme line referenced in NEA FY 2024/25. The page tracks it as an emerging NEA/AEPC-style remote-energy delivery template for grid-absent Karnali districts. # What the project is Location: Karnali Province — the grid-weakest and resource-strongest off-grid zone in Nepal (Dolpa, Humla, Mugu, Jumla, Kalikot, Jajarkot, Rukum, Surkhet, Salyan, Dailekh). Configuration: Multi-site, each site ~50 kWp – 1 MWp solar + BESS (4–8 hour). Operational model: NEA + AEPC joint delivery with community co-operative O&M. Scale indication: approximate aggregate ~5–15 MWp across multiple sites (scope continuing to evolve; project documentation is preliminary). Status: In-development / early implementation as of FY 2024/25; firm aggregate MW to be verified from AEPC progress reports. # Why this programme matters Three things that make Karnali Solar the institutional template rather than just another remote project: ## 1. It is the first formal NEA–AEPC co-delivery structure at scale. Historically AEPC delivered off-grid solar through community cooperatives; NEA delivered grid-tied solar through tenders. Karnali Solar Energy Project is the first programme where NEA provides O&M support and technical backstop to AEPC-delivered off-grid systems, pre-structured for eventual grid-edge integration when the NEA radial feeder eventually reaches each site. ## 2. It validates solar + BESS economics at the remote site Diesel generation in remote Karnali sites costs NPR 60–90/kWh (delivered fuel + logistics + wear). Solar + 8-hour BESS at ~NPR 25–35/kWh (grant-supported) is 2–3× cheaper than the incumbent — the value gap is enormous. This is the highest-leverage per-kWh solar in Nepal, by far. ## 3. It prepares the grid-edge integration question As NEA's grid finally reaches former off-grid villages (~8.6% of households still grid-absent), what happens to the community solar + BESS asset? Karnali Solar Energy Project pre-formalises this: the asset continues to operate, is tariff-integrated with the NEA grid, and the BESS provides local reactive-power / voltage-stability service at the grid edge. Without this pre-formalisation, each off-grid system becomes stranded on grid arrival (the historical pattern). # Site-by-site data Preliminary publication from NEA FY 2024/25 references the programme at aggregate level; per-site details (exact location, MWp, BESS hours, developer, community partner) require cross-reference with AEPC monitoring reports. # Relevance to project Anchors the rooftop-minigrid-offgrid track for Karnali specifically Evidence for claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-coalition politics in action Operational template for solar + BESS economics beyond data-solar-hydro-lcoe's utility frame Institutional precedent for the AEPC–NEA integration protocol argued in aepc # Limitations & Controversies Exact site list, MWp per site, BESS specification, developer / community partner Cumulative CAPEX / CAPEX per kWp FY 2024/25 generation + diesel-displacement data AEPC monitoring report for the programme # Related aepc nea-solar rooftop-minigrid-offgrid karnali-basin — geographic context data-rooftop-shs-deployment — the Karnali SHS deployment footprint this programme builds on

pages.title: Kataiya–Kushaha 132 kV Cross-Border Interconnection
pages.excerpt: The oldest Nepal–India interconnection still in operation — the historic first link that defined the Nepal–India power trade template. Originally energised in 1971 at 33 kV, upgraded to 132 kV, it has been through five decades of bilateral tariff and exchange-rate politics.
pages.body_text: Kataiya–Kushaha 132 kV Interconnection The oldest Nepal–India interconnection still in operation — the historic first link that defined the Nepal–India power trade template. Originally energised in 1971 at 33 kV, upgraded to 132 kV, it has been through five decades of bilateral tariff and exchange-rate politics. # Summary The Kataiya-Kushaha 132 kV interconnection is the oldest operating Nepal-India grid link. The page tracks its historic role as the first Nepal-India interconnection and its continued eastern Terai import function. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV (originally 33 kV) | Status | Operational (since 1971) | Nepal terminal | Kushaha (Sunsari) | India terminal | Kataiya (Bihar) | Historic role | First Nepal–India grid tie | Direction | Predominantly imports into eastern Nepal | Interconnection ID | | # Significance Origin point of the Nepal–India grid relationship. Every later interconnection inherits contractual and technical conventions established here. Eastern Terai import backbone. Still the principal import route for dry-season supply to Saptari–Siraha–Sunsari, where domestic eastern generation is thin. Legacy accounting reference. Many of the bilateral power trade arrangements (e.g. the Radhika energy exchange protocol) were framed around this single link. # Limitations & Controversies Legacy voltage. 132 kV thermal capacity is small relative to the region's modern load. During load growth spikes it has required load shedding or emergency procurement. Planned upgrade path unclear. Discussions to convert or parallel with a 220 kV link have not progressed beyond feasibility notes. # See also india-energy-relationship dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — the successor 400 kV era hydro-geopolitics

The page records the programme as presented in the FY 2019/20 annual book, including ceremonial and cable-laying evidence. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 The annual book shows the program both as a ceremonial milestone on the opening pages and again in the project-management chapter, where cable-laying works in Chabahil are presented as part of the Kathmandu Valley distribution enhancement package. # Why It Matters It is one of the clearest examples of NEA trying to modernize the urban grid, not just add generation or long-distance transmission. It links directly to nea's distribution-reliability mandate and to the broader network-upgrade frame captured in nepal-transmission-landscape-2025. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is based on annual-book evidence of the programme and does not provide a full package-by-package implementation record. Coverage area, completion status, outage impact, cost, contractor performance, and current operational benefits need newer distribution-project records before detailed evaluation. # See also nea nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-domestic-demand
