The Desanding Basin Collapse — Commissioning Catastrophe
Financial Position — Constrained by Legacy Costs
pages.excerpt: 52.4 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap district. Originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented project, completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission dispute. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined).
pages.body_text: Likhu-4 52.4 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap district. Originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented project, completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission dispute. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined). # Summary Likhu-4 is a 52.4 MW operating run-of-river hydropower project on the Likhu Khola in Ramechhap district. It was originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented plant and was completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission wheeling-charge dispute. The page tracks it as a regulatory case study and stranded-generation recovery example using the current CARE Nepal and JICA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 52.4 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Ramechhap | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (CARE Nepal / DoED data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | November 2021 | Developer | Green Ventures Ltd (GVL) | Primary equity | Triveni Group + Bhilwara Energy (India) | Original design | 120 MW export-oriented | Current design | 52.4 MW domestic grid | PPA | Standard NEA domestic PPA | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BB | Contractor (civil) | SSNR Projects (India) | Evacuation | New Khimti substation → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and auto-generated spec table list Likhu-4 as "Under construction." The plant commissioned in November 2021. The narrative follows CARE Nepal credit rating data and DoED registries. # From Export Megaproject to Domestic Afterthought — A Regulatory Case Study Likhu-4 was originally conceived as a 120 MW export-oriented hydropower project, intended to wheel power directly to India across the Dhalkebar– Muzaffarpur cross-border interconnector. A dispute over cross-border transmission wheeling charges — the tariff India would charge for conveying Nepali-generated power across its grid to Indian buyers — caused Green Ventures Ltd (GVL) to abandon the export model entirely. The project was completely redesigned and downscaled to 52.4 MW to cater exclusively to the domestic grid via a standard PPA with NEA. This represents a 57% capacity reduction from original design — a regulatory-risk write-down that no developer voluntarily accepts unless the alternative (persisting with the export model) was financially non-viable. The Likhu-4 redesign is Nepal's clearest documented example of cross-border transmission policy directly determining project scale. The wheeling dispute with India did not kill the project — a 52.4 MW plant was still viable. But it killed two-thirds of it. Every other proposed export project in Nepal's pipeline (Upper Karnali, West Seti, Arun-3 free-power component, 28,500 MW target with 15,000 MW for export) faces the same wheeling charge risk, and Likhu-4 is the only completed project that has already absorbed it. See buildability and stranded-generation. # The Desanding Basin Collapse — Commissioning Catastrophe In May 2021, on the eve of production testing, a wall of Likhu-4's desanding basin suffered a catastrophic structural collapse. The developer publicly blamed the Indian civil contractor, SSNR Projects, alleging construction defects. A desanding basin failure at a RoR plant on a Himalayan sediment-loaded river is among the most consequential possible civil-engineering failures. The basin is the first line of defence protecting the headrace tunnel and turbines from abrasive sediment. A structural collapse on the eve of commissioning meant the plant could not operate safely — sediment-laden water entering the headrace would destroy the Francis turbine runners within weeks. The incident delayed full commissioning and required emergency repairs. The event remains one of Nepal's best-documented examples of how construction-phase quality failures at the contractor interface convert directly into revenue loss — and how the limited-recourse SPV structure concentrates that loss on equity while debt continues to capitalise interest. The plant eventually commissioned in November 2021, but the delayed revenue and repair costs pushed GVL's capital structure deeper into leverage territory. # Financial Position — Constrained by Legacy Costs Green Ventures currently carries a CARE-NP BB rating — two notches below investment grade and below both Likhu-2 (BBB-) and Likhu-1 (BB+). The rating is constrained by: 1. High capital costs — the redesign from 120 MW to 52.4 MW did not fully recapture sunk engineering and licensing expenditure from the export-design phase 2. Commissioning delay — the six-month delay from the desanding basin collapse meant six months of capitalized interest without revenue 3. Independent developer structure — unlike the Dugar-controlled plants (Likhu-1, Likhu-2, Likhu Khola A) which benefit from shared management and cross-SPV expertise, GVL operates as a standalone entity The BB rating, while below the cascade average, is not a default warning — it reflects the margin pressure of a project that absorbed extraordinary regulatory and construction-phase costs before generating a single kWh. Unlike the Dugar-controlled cascade plants, Likhu-4 has no UAE FDI component. The equity is held by Triveni Group (Nepal) and Bhilwara Energy (India) — making Likhu-4 the only Likhu cascade plant with Indian equity exposure. Indian EPC contractor failures (SSNR) combined with Indian policy disputes (wheeling charges) affecting an Indian-invested project is a concentration pattern that would concern any project finance credit committee. # Transmission — Same Corridor, Different Story Like the rest of the cascade, Likhu-4 evacuates through New Khimti. Following the late-2023 200 MVA transformer upgrade, Likhu-4 was among the first cascade plants to receive CEA export approval for Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur wheeling into the Indian day-ahead market — a remarkable reversal for a project that abandoned export at the design stage. The transmission infrastructure that did not exist when the original 120 MW export model was conceived now exists, and Likhu-4 benefits from it at 52.4 MW. This is not a vindication of the Indian wheeling-charge regime. It is evidence that cross-border transmission policy evolves faster than a RoR hydro project can be redesigned and built. A project conceived for one regulatory environment commissions into a different one. Likhu-4 is the case study. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on regulatory-history and credit-rating context. It does not independently verify the desanding basin failure root cause, contractor liability adjudication, current month-by-month operating performance, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The redesign from 120 MW to 52.4 MW means some original-design data no longer reflects the built asset. # See also buildability — regulatory risk as a design-determining constraint stranded-generation — when the grid cannot receive what the plant generates q-design-discharge — Likhu-4's generation data in context koshi-basin — basin context for the Likhu Khola system khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV backbone the cascade depends on arun-3 — the India-developed export archetype Likhu-4's original design was modelled on

pages.excerpt: The Likhu Khola is a hydropower-rich tributary in the koshi-basin, straddling Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The Likhu system has attracted significant IPP investment with multiple generation-licence projects across the upper and lower reaches.
pages.body_text: Likhu Cascade The Likhu Khola is a hydropower-rich tributary in the koshi-basin, straddling Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The Likhu system has attracted significant IPP investment with multiple generation-licence projects across the upper and lower reaches. # Summary The Likhu Cascade is a 213 MW cluster of four run-of-river hydropower plants on the Likhu Khola in the Koshi basin, spanning Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The page tracks the cascade as a single-corridor generation cluster with shared transmission infrastructure and mixed developer equity, using the current wiki source set. # Plants in the Cascade Plant | Capacity (MW) | Status | District | -------|--------------|--------|----------| likhu-1 | 77.0 | Under construction | Solukhumbu | likhu-2 | 55.0 | Under construction | Solukhumbu | likhu-khola-a | 29.04 | Operating | Solukhumbu | likhu-4 | 52.4 | Under construction | Ramechhap | lower-likhu | 28.1 | Under construction | Ramechhap | Nupche Likhu HEP | 57.5 | Survey | Ramechhap | Total | ~299 | | | [!note] Likhu-3 does not appear in the current MoE/DoED registry. The numbering (1, 2, 4) reflects the registry's actual naming — Likhu-3 may have been a planned designation that was never licensed, or the gap reflects the staggered licensing history of the corridor. # Corridor Context The upper Likhu projects (1, 2, Likhu Khola A) cluster in the Solukhumbu highlands, while Likhu-4, Lower Likhu, and Nupche Likhu sit further downstream in Ramechhap. The Likhu is a tributary of the Sun Koshi, and its projects share transmission corridors with the broader Khimti-Tamakoshi system via khimti-dhalkebar-corridor. # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on aggregate registry context and corridor-level narrative. It does not independently verify individual plant construction status, commissioning dates, current generation, or financing terms beyond the existing source set. Plant-level details should be checked against the respective entity pages and their source links before detailed use. The aggregate capacity figure includes projects at varying stages of development. # See also likhu-1 likhu-2 likhu-4 likhu-khola-a lower-likhu koshi-basin

pages.title: Likhu Khola 'A'

Cascade Position — Smallest, but Structurally Identical
pages.excerpt: 29.04 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu district. The smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213.44 MW combined across 4 plants) and the first MV Dugar project to commission.
pages.body_text: Likhu Khola 'A' 29.04 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu district. The smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213.44 MW combined across 4 plants) and the first MV Dugar project to commission. # Summary Likhu Khola A is a 29.04 MW operating run-of-river hydropower project on the Likhu Khola in Solukhumbu district. It is the smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade and the first MV Dugar–Mogha Energy project to commission, in February 2022. The page tracks it as a cascade-financial benchmark with a two-tier PPA structure, using the current CARE Nepal credit-rating source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 51 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Specifications (CARE Nepal / DoED data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | February 8, 2022 | Developer | Numbur Himalaya Hydropower Limited | Primary equity | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy DMCC (UAE, ~7% FDI) | Project cost | NPR 5,996 million (~NPR 206M/MW) | Debt / equity | 75:25 | PPA structure | 24.2 MW take-or-pay (135.68 GWh/yr), 4.84 MW take-and-pay | Financing consortium | Laxmi Bank (lead), Siddhartha Bank (co-lead), Century Commercial Bank, Citizens Bank, Bank of Kathmandu | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BBB- (reaffirmed March 2025) | PBILDT margins | 82–91% | Evacuation | New Khimti substation → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Likhu Khola A as "Under construction" at 51 MW. The plant commissioned on February 8, 2022 at a confirmed capacity of 29.04 MW. The narrative follows CARE Nepal credit rating data and developer operational disclosures. # The Finishing Line — First to Commission Likhu Khola A was the first MV Dugar project to reach the finish line, commissioning on February 8, 2022 — nearly 18 months before likhu-2 (July 2023) and over two years before likhu-1 (April 2024). For a conglomerate simultaneously developing three generation assets in the same river basin, getting the smallest project operational first was strategically essential: it established the developer's creditworthiness with lenders, demonstrated construction capability to the regulator, and generated early cash flow to support the larger builds. At NPR 5,996 million (~NPR 206M/MW), Likhu Khola A's capital cost sits in line with Nepal's post-2015 private IPP benchmark. The 75:25 debt-equity ratio is lower than the cascade's other Dugar-controlled plants (likhu-1 at 80:20, likhu-2 at 78:22), reflecting the conservative leverage typical of first-mover projects in an unproven basin. # The MV Dugar FDI Model Likhu Khola A shares the cascade's defining equity architecture: the MV Dugar Group (a Nepali conglomerate with interests in banking, insurance, automotive trading, and infrastructure) paired with Mogha Energy DMCC, a UAE-based investment firm. Mogha Energy holds a confirmed ~7% institutional promoter stake alongside Dugar family majority holdings. This FDI model — a domestic group clustering multiple projects under shared foreign capital through separate SPVs — is a departure from Nepal's traditional single-project domestic bank consortium structure. For the UAE investors, the cluster offers risk diversification: three projects (77 + 55 + 29 = 161 MW cumulative under Dugar control) share the same basin, corridor, and regulatory regime, but operate as legally distinct entities with independent PPAs and debt. Butwal Power Company (BPC) holds no equity in Likhu Khola A. BPC's involvement in the Likhu basin is exclusively technical — its subsidiary HCEL provided engineering consultancy and construction supervision, generating consulting revenue, not generation revenue. # PPA Structure — Partial Curtailment Exposure Likhu Khola A's PPA has a distinctive two-tier structure. Of the 29.04 MW installed capacity, only 24.2 MW (83.4%) is contracted on strict take-or-pay terms, yielding 135.68 GWh/year with no NEA curtailment risk. The remaining 4.84 MW (16.6%) was built targeting future uncontracted take-and-pay off-take, exposed to NEA dispatch discretion. This contrasts with likhu-1, where 80% is take-or-pay, and likhu-2, where 75% is take-or-pay. Likhu Khola A sits between the two on curtailment protection: better than Likhu-2's 25% exposure, below Likhu-1's 20%. # Financial Performance CARE Ratings Nepal reaffirmed the project's bank facilities at CARE-NP BBB- in March 2025, supported by: PBILDT margins averaging 82% to 91% — strong operating cash generation Improving debt coverage ratios as the project seasons past its commissioning ramp-up Revenue stability from the high take-or-pay share (83.4%) The BBB- rating places Likhu Khola A in the same CARE tier as likhu-2 (BBB- Is), above likhu-4 (BB). The rating reflects the project's conservative leverage structure and diversified lending consortium (5 banks), mitigated by the single-corridor transmission risk shared by the entire cascade. # Cascade Position — Smallest, but Structurally Identical At 29.04 MW, Likhu Khola A is dwarfed by likhu-1 (77 MW), likhu-2 (55 MW), and likhu-4 (52.4 MW) in capacity terms. But it shares the cascade's structural vulnerabilities: Hydrological interdependence: as an upstream plant in the Likhu system, its tailwater discharge affects downstream operators. Emergency shutdowns or desilting operations at Likhu Khola A alter inflow parameters for lower cascade plants — a cascade externality that no standalone PPA accounts for. Single corridor dependency: all four cascade plants evacuate through the New Khimti substation into the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV line. The same 100 MVA transformer that bottlenecked likhu-2 at 60% PLF in FY 2023/24 constrained the entire cascade. The late-2023 upgrade to 300 MVA resolved the immediate crisis, but a single substation failure returns all four plants to stranded-generation status. See buildability and stranded-generation. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on credit-rating and PPA-structure context from CARE Nepal disclosures. It does not independently verify final design parameters, construction-phase quality records, current operating performance month-by-month, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because it pairs large carryover storage with meaningful dry-season output, making it more relevant to system value than many larger wet-season-heavy projects. # Summary Lower Badigad is a 380.3 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Gandaki basin. It is pinned in the storage shortlist for its large carryover storage (995.9 MCM total, 505.5 MCM effective) and meaningful dry-season output (354.7 GWh, 26.0% dry share). The page tracks it as a planning-layer storage comparator using the current JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 380.3 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Gandaki (gandaki-basin) | Annual energy | 1366.0 GWh | Dry-season energy | 354.7 GWh | Dry share | 26.0% | Total storage | 995.9 MCM | Effective storage | 505.5 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 995.9 MCM | Effective storage | 505.5 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1366.0 GWh | Dry-season energy | 354.7 GWh | Dry-season share | 26.0 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Lower Badigad is one of the stronger Gandaki storage candidates in the shortlist: 995.9 MCM total storage, 505.5 MCM effective storage, and 354.7 GWh of dry-season energy. Its dry share is lower than Nalsyau Gad or Dudhkoshi, but the reservoir scale is large enough that it remains important for seasonal regulation. Its strategic role is also geographic. The Gandaki basin is already a central hydropower corridor, and storage in that basin has a different grid value than remote far-western storage. Lower Badigad belongs in the wiki because it is a credible comparator to tanahu-hydropower, kali-gandaki-a, and other Gandaki assets. # Status And Timing Lower Badigad is a planning candidate from the JICA/NEA storage material, not an under-construction project. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Lower Badigad STO in the 2031-2035 window. Treat that as a planning horizon rather than a confirmed construction-start date. The next evidence to watch is whether the project advances from storage-master-plan candidate to a named developer, updated feasibility package, environmental assessment, financing plan, and grid-connection commitment. # Map Interpretation The map marker is a river-aligned project reference. It is appropriate for comparing storage candidates and basin leverage, but not for property-level impact analysis. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on master-plan and shortlist context. pages.title: Lower Solu Hydropower Project
pages.excerpt: Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in the Solukhumbu district — part of the Dudh Koshi river system that includes the benchmark Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) project.
pages.body_text: Lower Solu Hydropower Project Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in the Solukhumbu district — part of the Dudh Koshi river system that includes the benchmark Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) project. # Summary Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Solu Khola in Solukhumbu district, part of the Dudh Koshi river system. It enters a corridor with an established capital-efficiency benchmark set by Sahas Urja's 86 MW Solu Khola project. The page tracks it as a build-cost-discipline case study using the current ICRA/Sahas Urja source set. # Solu Corridor The Solu Khola / Dudh Koshi river system in Solukhumbu has emerged as a significant eastern Nepal hydropower corridor. Sahas Urja's 86 MW Solu Khola project (commissioned March 2023) demonstrated that with disciplined capital deployment — achieving NPR 172–175 million/MW vs. industry averages exceeding NPR 200–250 million/MW — projects in this corridor can generate strong financial returns even under the standard NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA framework. Lower Solu, at a comparable 82 MW, enters a corridor with an established benchmark and transmission infrastructure shaped by its predecessor. # The Sahas Urja Benchmark The success of Sahas Urja creates both opportunity and pressure for Lower Solu: Opportunity: Transmission infrastructure exists, river hydrology data is available, and the financing community has a positive reference point in the same valley Pressure: Sahas Urja's NPR 172–175 million/MW build cost, 69% PLF, and NPR 900M+ annual profit set a high bar that investors will compare against # Build Cost Discipline The single most important variable determining Lower Solu's financial outcome is construction cost per MW. In the fixed-tariff regime where every MW-hour sells at the same regulated rate regardless of how much it cost to build, capital efficiency is the only lever for profitability. Sahas Urja proved that ~NPR 173M/MW is achievable in this corridor; projects that drift toward NPR 250M/MW or beyond will struggle to achieve positive equity returns. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 82 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Solu Khola | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability sahas-urja-benchmark-icra-2026 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on corridor-benchmark and capital-efficiency context. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost per MW, commissioning date, financing closure, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The Sahas Urja benchmark creates comparative pressure, but Lower Solu's actual cost and performance will require project-level verification before detailed financial analysis. # Sources sahas-urja-benchmark-icra-2026

pages.excerpt: Madhya Bhotekoshi (Middle Bhotekoshi) is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is one of the key capacity additions in the Bhote Koshi corridor, an area that has seen repeated geological setbacks includi
pages.body_text: Madhya Bhotekoshi Madhya Bhotekoshi (Middle Bhotekoshi) is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is one of the key capacity additions in the Bhote Koshi corridor, an area that has seen repeated geological setbacks including landslides and glacial lake outburst floods. # Summary Madhya Bhotekoshi is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is part of the Chilime Hydropower Company Limited expansion strategy and one of three Chilime-promoted projects forming a ~256 MW cluster in the Trishuli–Bhote Koshi system. The page tracks it as a geologically exposed corridor build using the current NEA and sector-analysis source set. # Chilime Group Strategy Madhya Bhotekoshi is part of the Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) expansion strategy. After Chilime's own 22.1 MW plant established a highly profitable operational track record, CHCL used its internal accruals and brand equity to spin off downstream subsidiaries — Rasuwagadhi (111 MW), Sanjen (42.5 MW), and Madhya Bhotekoshi (102 MW) — effectively bypassing the terminal BOOT-model cliff where assets must be handed over to the state. This holding company model is the mechanism through which Nepal's most successful hydro entity perpetuates itself. # Bhote Koshi Corridor Risk The Bhote Koshi valley is one of Nepal's most geologically active river corridors. Projects in this stretch — including the original Bhote Koshi project, Upper Bhotekoshi (45 MW, operating), Madhya Bhotekoshi, and Rasuwagadhi — face elevated construction risk from landslides, flash floods, and seismic activity. Madhya Bhotekoshi's construction timeline and cost profile must be understood within this risk context. # Significance At 102 MW, Madhya Bhotekoshi represents a significant block of capacity in the under-construction pipeline. Along with Rasuwagadhi downstream and Sanjen in the adjacent valley, it forms a ~256 MW cluster of Chilime-promoted projects that will shape water allocation and transmission planning in the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi system. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 102 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Bhote koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Sindhupalchok | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability chilime sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on corporate-strategy and corridor-risk context. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost, commissioning date, financing closure, or geological event probability beyond the existing source set. The Bhote Koshi valley's landslide, flash-flood, and seismic risks are documented at the corridor level but not quantified for this specific project site. # Sources sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026

pages.title: Madhya Marsyangdi
headings: The Marsyangdi Cascade — 170 MW in One Valley
The Contrast That Matters — Design vs Actual
Renewal Cycle — A Younger Plant with a Different Problem
pages.excerpt: Madhya Marsyangdi (Middle Marsyangdi) is a 70 MW operating hydropower project on the Marsyangdi River — one of Nepal's established generation assets with a multi-decade operational track record.
pages.body_text: Madhya Marsyangdi Madhya Marsyangdi (Middle Marsyangdi) is a 70 MW operating hydropower project on the Marsyangdi River — one of Nepal's established generation assets with a multi-decade operational track record. # Summary Madhya Marsyangdi is a 70 MW peaking run-of-river hydropower project operating on the Marsyangdi River in Lamjung district, Gandaki Province. Commissioned in December 2008, it is the middle anchor of the ~170 MW Marsyangdi cascade and recorded 107.6% of design generation in FY 2081/82. The page tracks it as an operating-plant performance benchmark using the current NEA annual report source set. # Marsyangdi Cascade Madhya Marsyangdi sits in the middle of one of Nepal's most productive hydropower corridors. The Marsyangdi River, a tributary of the Trishuli/Narayani system in the Gandaki basin, hosts a cascade of projects: Upper Marsyangdi A (50 MW), Madhya Marsyangdi (70 MW), and Marsyangdi Besi (50 MW, under construction). This ~170 MW cumulative capacity makes the Marsyangdi cascade a significant block of the national generation portfolio. # Operating History As an operating plant, Madhya Marsyangdi provides a different lens from the pre-COD and under-construction projects that dominate the pipeline: actual generation data, real maintenance costs, and historical PLF performance under the standard PPA framework. Operating projects reveal whether the financial models in IPO prospectuses materialize in practice — and at what cost. # Transmission The Marsyangdi valley's generation feeds into the national grid via the Marsyangdi corridor infrastructure, connecting to the east-west backbone. The Upper Marsyangdi 220 kV line provides the key evacuation route for this cascade. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 70 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Marsyangdi (gandaki-basin) | District | Lamjung | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Middle Marsyangdi (MMHPS) is a 70 MW peaking run-of-river plant in Lamjung District, Gandaki Province — the middle anchor of the 170 MW Marsyangdi cascade. Commissioned in December 2008, it diverts flow from the Marsyangdi River originating in glacier-fed Tilicho Lake and can reserve flow for up to five hours of peaking, even during low discharge. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Peaking run-of-river (PROR) | Units | Francis | Commissioning | December 2008 | Peaking capacity | 5 hours | Design generation | 398 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 427.9 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 107.6% | Year-over-year change | −3% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 7,091.1 GWh | District | Lamjung, Gandaki Province | In FY 2081/82, MMHPS completed overhaul of Unit 2, restored desander basins in-house, rebuilt spillway chute no. 1 with M60 concrete and steel lining, and installed a digital governor panel, 110V battery bank, and RTU for real-time Load Dispatch Centre communication. # The Marsyangdi Cascade — 170 MW in One Valley MMHPS sits between Upper Marsyangdi A (50 MW, operating, upstream) and Marsyangdi Besi (50 MW, under construction, downstream) — a cumulative 170 MW in the Marsyangdi valley of the Gandaki basin. This is one of Nepal's most concentrated generation corridors. The Marsyangdi River, a glacier-fed tributary of the Narayani system, provides more reliable base flow than the monsoon-dominated rain-fed tributaries where most private IPPs are located. The cascade's cumulative water use is increasingly significant as Marsyangdi Besi approaches commissioning. Environmental flow requirements and sediment management decisions at Upper Marsyangdi A directly affect MMHPS and the downstream plant. The Marsyangdi corridor connects to the national grid via the Upper Marsyangdi 220 kV transmission line, feeding the east-west backbone. # The Contrast That Matters — Design vs Actual MMHPS's 107.6% of design generation (427.9 GWh against 398 GWh) is the highest performance ratio in the NEA large-plant fleet. Compare: Plant | MW | Design (GWh) | FY 2081/82 (GWh) | % of Design | ---|---|---|---|---| Middle Marsyangdi | 70 | 398 | 427.9 | 107.6% | Kali Gandaki A | 144 | 842 | 863.5 | 102.5% | Marsyangdi | 69 | 462.5 | 451.8 | 97.0% | Chameliya | 30 | 184.2 | 142.4 | 77.3% | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60 | 489.8 | 356.0 | 72.7% | The divergence at the bottom of the table is q-design-discharge in action: the plants that underperform by 20–30% are the ones whose design hydrology assumptions were too aggressive. MMHPS's opposite result suggests the Tilicho-fed Marsyangdi basin has more reliable baseflow than the monsoonal rain-fed catchments where design overestimation is endemic — or that the 2008-era design hydrological study was appropriately conservative. This is the structural pattern the chilime page documents at 22 MW: conservative Q-design (Q65+) in a snow/glacier-fed basin produces actual generation above contracted energy. MMHPS demonstrates the same mechanism at 70 MW — and at three times the scale. See q-design-discharge for the full generation performance comparison across the RoR fleet. # Renewal Cycle — A Younger Plant with a Different Problem At 16 years post-commissioning, MMHPS is entering the phase where routine overhauls begin to graduate toward major rehabilitation. The FY 2081/82 work scope — Unit 2 overhaul, desander basin restoration, spillway chute rebuild with M60 concrete and epoxy coating — is heavier maintenance than the plant would have required in its first decade. The digital governor panel and RTU installation signals a shift from mechanical to digital control, the modernization trajectory that aging plants like kali-gandaki-a are now facing at greater cost and outage risk. MMHPS's relatively young age means this transition can be done incrementally rather than as an emergency rehab — but it also means it is a test case for what that incremental path looks like. Every NEA plant eventually follows it. # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on NEA annual-report and cascade-level context. It does not independently verify long-term maintenance cost trends, remaining useful life estimates, environmental flow compliance, or sediment-management records beyond the existing source set. FY 2081/82 generation data is a single-year snapshot; multi-year performance trends would require additional verification. The renewal-cycle discussion is forward-looking and not yet grounded in completed rehabilitation data. # See also gandaki-basin — the Marsyangdi feeds the Narayani / Gandaki system q-design-discharge — why MMHPS's 107.6% is a structural signal chilime — the same pattern at smaller scale (conservative Q + glacier-fed) marsyangdi — downstream PROR plant (69 MW, commissioned 1989) run-of-river-hydropower seasonal-mismatch — even 107.6% doesn't fix the monsoon-drought cycle

pages.title: Mahakali Basin
pages.excerpt: The Mahakali river forms Nepal's far-western border with India. It is a transboundary basin with far smaller current development than the three major eastern systems. The basin's significance is primarily geopolitical — it is the site of the pancheshwar multipurpose project and t
pages.body_text: Mahakali Basin # Summary The Mahakali river forms Nepal's far-western border with India. It is a transboundary basin with far smaller current development than the three major eastern systems. The basin's significance is primarily geopolitical — it is the site of the pancheshwar multipurpose project and the subject of the 1996 Mahakali Treaty. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Average discharge | ~600 m³/s | Monsoon share | ~73% | Lakes in basin (Nepal side) | 16 | # Hydropower Significance The Mahakali Treaty (1996) entitles Nepal to 50% of pancheshwar's output (6,480 MW total, or ~3,240 MW for Nepal). After 28+ years, Nepal has received zero megawatts from this treaty. See hydro-geopolitics. The Mahakali already supports irrigation via the Mahakali irrigation system on the Indian side. # Limitations & Controversies Zero megawatts after 28+ years. The Mahakali Treaty (1996) entitles Nepal to 50% of pancheshwar's output (~3,240 MW). After nearly three decades, Nepal has received zero megawatts. This is one of the most instructive cases of treaty promise without implementation in South Asia. Data scarcity. Average discharge (~600 m³/s), monsoon share (~73%), and lake count (16) are the only basin-scale figures in public sources. No detailed hydropower potential study, no sediment load data, and no climate projection specific to the Mahakali appear in the cited WECS basin plan. Geopolitical concentration. The basin's significance is almost entirely tied to the Nepal-India bilateral relationship. Unlike the Koshi, Gandaki, or Karnali basins — which host multiple projects and diverse financing — the Mahakali has one project (Pancheshwar) and one treaty. The basin cannot be analyzed independently of bilateral politics. No current operating large hydropower. Unlike the other three major basins, the Mahakali has no operating plant above a few megawatts. The basin is entirely prospective, with no operational data to ground planning assumptions. # Strategic Notes The basin is less about sheer resource volume and more about the diplomatic relationship with India. The failure of Pancheshwar to materialize is one of the strongest examples of how hydro-geopolitics shapes — and stalls — Nepal's energy future. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.body_text: Main Load Dispatch Centre NEA's main system-operations node in Kathmandu, paired in the annual book with the Emergency Control Center at Hetauda as the backup facility for national grid dispatch and contingency management. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 72 describes the main LDC in Kathmandu as the primary operating center and the Hetauda ECC building as the backup center for transmission system control during emergencies. # Summary The Main Load Dispatch Centre is NEA's primary system-operations node in Kathmandu, paired with the Emergency Control Center at Hetauda as the backup facility for national grid dispatch and contingency management. The page tracks it as a system-operations entity using the NEA transmission annual book source set. # Why It Matters The dispatch center is the operational layer behind every corridor page: hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone, dhalkebar-muzaffarpur, and the rest only matter if NEA can actually control them as one system. It is one of the clearest institutional links between nea as owner and the real-time grid described in nepal-transmission-landscape-2025. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on institutional context from a single NEA annual-book snapshot (FY 2019/20). It does not independently verify current operational status, staffing, real-time control capability, SCADA/EMS system details, or backup-facility readiness beyond the existing source set. This is not an official GIS alignment. pages.title: Marsyangdi
headings: Why Marsyangdi Matters — The Aging Fleet Benchmark
pages.excerpt: Figure 6.3-16 River Longitudinal Profile of the Marsyangdi River
pages.body_text: Marsyangdi Figure 6.3-16 River Longitudinal Profile of the Marsyangdi River Unit No.1 overhauling works Monthly seasonal variation of last three fiscal years Wet vs Dry Season Generation of last three fiscal years Comparison: % of designed vs % of Target (FY 2081/82) Marsyangdi - Kathmandu 220 kV Transmission Line Construction of Shade at Phulbari Ghat, River bank protection at Gaidakot, Nawalpur Radial Gates 2 and 3 # Summary 69 MW · operating · on the Marsyangdi · in Gorkha district. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 69 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Marsyangdi (gandaki-basin) | District | Gorkha | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Marsyangdi is a peaking run-of-river plant — 4 hours of daily peaking capacity from 69 MW of installed generation across three Francis units. Commissioned in 1989, it has now operated for 36 years and accumulated over 15,000 GWh of lifetime generation. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Peaking run-of-river (PROR) | Units | 3 × Francis | Commissioning | 1989 | Design generation | 462.5 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 451.8 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 97% | FY 2081/82 vs target | 97% | Year-over-year change | +1.28% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 15,046.929 GWh | District | Tanahun (not Gorkha — see correction note) | [!warning] Registry data correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list the district as Gorkha. The NEA's own FY 2024/25 report places Marsyangdi in Tanahun district, Gandaki Province. The map data reflects the registry. The narrative here follows the NEA source. This fiscal year, Marsyangdi completed overhaul of Unit No. 2 and maintained key infrastructure including radial gates, desander basin floating boom, and gantry crane wire rope. Repairs were also performed on the hook block, shaft seal, and sliding ring of Unit No. 3. # Why Marsyangdi Matters — The Aging Fleet Benchmark Marsyangdi is one of only a handful of NEA operating plants that actually hits its design numbers. At 97% of design generation (451.8 GWh against 462.5 GWh), it dramatically outperforms the median private IPP — where, as documented in q-design-discharge, zero of 100+ projects in a recent Urja Khabar audit exceeded 80% of contracted energy. This makes Marsyangdi a critical reference point. If a 36-year-old NEA plant with 1980s turbine technology can achieve 97% of its design energy, the design-energy gap at newer private IPPs cannot be explained by hydrology alone. Something else — Q-design optimism, build-quality shortcuts, commissioning-phase derating, or the PPA structure itself — is driving the performance divergence. See q-design-discharge and claim-mw-not-equal-value. The seasonal generation charts visible in the NEA FY 2024/25 report images above confirm the pattern: even a plant that achieves 97% annually still undergoes the classic RoR seasonal collapse — monsoon surplus tapering to a fraction of nameplate in January–February. Marsyangdi cannot escape seasonal-mismatch, regardless of its design-performance discipline. # Rehabilitation on the Horizon At 36 years old, Marsyangdi is the second-oldest large NEA plant still in regular service (after Trishuli, commissioned 1967). The Unit 2 overhaul completed this fiscal year is routine — but the plant approaches an age where major rehabilitation becomes a binary question: invest in full electromechanical replacement or accept progressive derating. The parallel is kali-gandaki-a (144 MW, commissioned 2002), where NEA floated a rehabilitation tender in 2024 to replace all three turbine runners after 22 years. Marsyangdi, at nearly double that age on the turbines, faces a larger decision. Every rehab of a fleet anchor plant introduces outage risk during dry season — precisely when the storage-deficit exposure peaks. The overhaul data from FY 2081/82 is an early signal: the maintenance scope is expanding. Radial gates, desander basin components, gantry crane wire rope, shaft seals — these are not routine wear items. They are the visible surface of an aging electromechanical fleet that NEA's capital budget will eventually need to confront at scale. # Limitations & Controversies Aging fleet anchor. At 36 years, Marsyangdi is the second-oldest large NEA plant still in regular service. The Unit 2 overhaul completed in FY 2081/82 is routine, but the plant approaches an age where full electromechanical replacement becomes a binary decision. Every rehab introduces outage risk during dry season — precisely when storage-deficit exposure peaks. Registry data error. The Ministry of Energy registry lists the district as Gorkha; the NEA FY 2024/25 report places Marsyangdi in Tanahun. The map data currently reflects the registry; this remains a reconciliation item. This kind of slug-location mismatch is a recurring data-quality issue across NEA's multi-source reporting. Non-replicable performance context. Marsyangdi's 97% of design energy is exceptional against the private IPP baseline, but it was built as an NEA plant in the 1980s with conservative Q-design, pre-climate-shift hydrology, and sovereign financing. The conditions that produced this performance are not replicable for modern private IPPs operating under the current PPA regime. Cannot escape seasonal mismatch. Even at 97% annual performance, Marsyangdi undergoes the classic RoR seasonal collapse — monsoon surplus tapering to a fraction of nameplate in January–February. The plant is a benchmark for design discipline, not a solution to seasonal-mismatch. # See also kali-gandaki-a — the next aging fleet anchor, now entering rehab q-design-discharge — why Marsyangdi's 97% is striking against the IPP baseline seasonal-mismatch — the structural problem even a well-run RoR cannot solve claim-mw-not-equal-value — nameplate vs delivered energy gandaki-basin — basin context; the Marsyangdi cascade feeds the Narayani run-of-river-hydropower

pages.title: MCA Central 400 kV Corridor (Lapsiphedi–Ratmate–Hetauda–Damauli–Butwal)
pages.excerpt: The second 400 kV spine Nepal is building — the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Nepal) compact's headline infrastructure, running from Lapsiphedi (Kathmandu Valley ring) through Ratmate, Hetauda, Damauli and terminating at New Butwal, where it feeds the gorakhpur-butwal-interco
pages.body_text: MCA Central 400 kV Corridor # Summary The second 400 kV spine Nepal is building — the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Nepal) compact's headline infrastructure, running from Lapsiphedi (Kathmandu Valley ring) through Ratmate, Hetauda, Damauli and terminating at New Butwal, where it feeds the gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection. When complete, this corridor ends the single-point-of-failure problem on the eastern backbone. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status | Under construction (partial energisation 2025) | Route-length basis | 308.65 route-km | Circuit-length basis | 617.3 circuit-km | Owner | nea (construction by MCA-Nepal contractors) | Terminal substations | Lapsiphedi · Ratmate · Hetauda · Damauli · New Butwal | Financing | US MCC grant (~US$500M corridor share) + Government of Nepal | Target full commissioning | 2026–2027 | Corridor ID | | # Map Interpretation The connected transmission layer now uses a source-aware MCA atlas trace rather than the older RPGCL overview fragments. It is modeled as five project segments: Lapsiphedi-Ratmate, Ratmate-New Hetauda, Ratmate-New Damauli, New Damauli-New Butwal, and New Butwal-India border. Public decision: default-visible, high confidence. Validation shows 5 atlas-derived features, no inferred connectors, no endpoint gaps, and a -1.32% delta against the 308.65 route-km compact basis. # Significance Second 400 kV spine. Parallels hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone via an entirely different geographic axis (Kathmandu → Western Terai), providing real N-1 redundancy for the first time. Gateway to the second cross-border link. Terminates at New Butwal, the Nepal end of gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection. Evacuates the western IPP cluster. Picks up output from the Marsyangdi and Kali Gandaki basins that has historically been trapped behind legacy 132 kV — partially solving claim-transmission-immediate-blocker for the west. Symbolic role. First large US-funded infrastructure grant in Nepal; its progress is read as a proxy for Nepal's willingness to diversify foreign partners beyond India and China. # Limitations & Controversies Right-of-way disputes. Sections through Nuwakot and Kavre saw protracted community opposition over tower siting and compensation. Partial commissioning ≠ full rating. Early 2025 energisation covers the Ratmate–Hetauda link only; the full end-to-end 400 kV transfer capability awaits terminal substation completion at Damauli and New Butwal. Dependent on cross-border terminal. Full value is unlocked only when gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection also commissions. Atlas trace, not tower survey. The public geometry is route-grade for map and topology use, with sheet-level provenance, but it should not be read as a cadastral tower alignment. # See also hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone — the existing backbone it parallels gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection — the border link it feeds dana-kushma-butwal-corridor — the 220 kV it relieves claim-transmission-immediate-blocker

pages.title: Middle Tamor
headings: The Stranded Asset — Transmission Before Generation
pages.excerpt: 73 MW · under construction · on the Tamor River · in Taplejung district. A Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of evacuation infrastructure in Nepal's easternmost Koshi basin development corridor.
pages.body_text: Middle Tamor 73 MW · under construction · on the Tamor River · in Taplejung district. A Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of evacuation infrastructure in Nepal's easternmost Koshi basin development corridor. # Summary Middle Tamor is a 73 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Tamor River in Taplejung district, Koshi basin. It is a Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of the Dhunge-Sanghu substation and Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV evacuation line. The page tracks it as a stranded-generation case study using the NEA licence and Urja Khabar/MoEWRI source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 54 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Tamor (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Taplejung | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 urja-khabar-generation-audit # Specifications (NEA Licence / MoEWRI data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Sanima Middle Tamor Hydropower Ltd (Sanima Group; formerly Tamor Sanima Energy Pvt. Ltd.) | Capacity | 73 MW (73,000 kW — confirmed from NEA generation licence table and Urja Khabar MoEWRI data) | Status | Under construction — stranded pending Dhunge-Sanghu Substation completion | River | Tamor River, Taplejung district, Koshi basin (eastern Nepal) | Generation licence | 2073.09.26 (approx December 2016) | Loan | NPR 7.3 billion (per NEA licence table) | Evacuation | Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV line (127 towers, first circuit strung by April 2024) | Substation | Dhungesanghu substation commissioned July 6, 2025 | [!warning] Registry capacity discrepancy. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Middle Tamor at 54 MW. Both the NEA generation licence table (73,000 kW) and the Urja Khabar/MoEWRI data confirm that the licensed and built capacity is 73 MW. The 54 MW figure likely reflects earlier survey-stage estimates. The narrative follows the NEA licence and MoEWRI confirmed data. # The Stranded Asset — Transmission Before Generation Middle Tamor is explicitly named in the Urja Khabar/MoEWRI report as one of 18 Nepali hydropower projects whose financial viability has been crippled by state-side transmission failures. The wording is stark: "Stranded pending the completion of the Dhunge-Sanghu Substation." The Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV transmission line was built specifically to evacuate Middle Tamor's 73 MW. Its 127 towers were erected across eastern Nepal's difficult terrain, and the first circuit was strung by April 2024. The Dhungesanghu substation was finally commissioned on July 6, 2025. But the project had already been waiting for years — generation capacity approved, financed, and built before the evacuation infrastructure that would make it useful. This is the classic Nepal hydropower timing failure that the buildability and stranded-generation pages document: private developers mobilise capital and construction on schedule, only to discover that the public-sector transmission backbone — promised in the same licensing window — is years behind. The financiers who underwrote NPR 7.3 billion in project debt did not underwrite the Nepal Electricity Authority's substation construction programme. # The Tamor Basin — Eastern Frontier The Tamor River drains the eastern flank of the Koshi basin, rising near the Kanchenjunga massif and flowing south through Taplejung district before joining the Sun Koshi to form the Sapta Koshi. Unlike the crowded Tamakoshi, Khimti, and Likhu corridors to the west — where multiple IPPs compete for the same transmission capacity — the Tamor basin is relatively undeveloped. Middle Tamor is one of the first large projects in the basin. Its 73 MW places it at a scale comparable to likhu-2 (55 MW) and likhu-1 (77 MW), but without the benefit of shared corridor infrastructure or the clustering advantages that the MV Dugar Group exploited in the Likhu Cascade. The Tamor's isolation cuts both ways: fewer competing offtakers on the line, but no neighbouring plants to share the political and financial burden of pushing transmission through. # Sanima Group — Portfolio Developer Sanima Middle Tamor Hydropower Ltd (formerly Tamor Sanima Energy Pvt. Ltd.) is the project SPV, backed by the Sanima Group — one of Nepal's largest private hydropower developers. Sanima's growing portfolio includes sanima-mai (22 MW), which has published Q40 design discharge data used in the q-design-discharge analysis. The group's strategy mirrors the cluster-development approach seen elsewhere in Nepali private hydro: establish a track record with a smaller project (Sanima Mai), then scale to larger capacity in a new basin (Middle Tamor). The corporate continuity — same developer, same financing relationships, same regulatory experience — reduces execution risk. But it does not solve the transmission problem. Sanima can build a power station; it cannot build a substation on land it does not own, using a budget it does not control. # The Transmission Problem The Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV line that will evacuate Middle Tamor's generation is a single-circuit corridor through eastern Nepal's steepest topography. 127 towers crossing landslide-prone terrain create single-point failure risks that the Likhu Cascade's khimti-dhalkebar-corridor also faces — but with less redundancy and no neighbouring plants to share the outage costs. For the full structural analysis of how transmission planning failures create systemic IPP risk, see buildability. For the growing inventory of projects that commissioned into a grid that could not take their power, see stranded-generation. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on licence and stranded-generation context from NEA and MoEWRI disclosures. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost, commissioning date, financing closure, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The 54 MW vs 73 MW registry discrepancy is noted but not resolved. Hydrological and transmission risk is documented at the corridor level but not quantified for this specific project site. # See also sanima-mai — 22 MW Sanima Group operating asset with Q40 data q-design-discharge — design discharge methodology and Sanima Mai data buildability — transmission planning failure as structural IPP risk stranded-generation — the grid evacuation bottleneck problem koshi-basin — basin context and eastern Nepal corridor geography

pages.body_text: Mithila Solar PV Electric Project (Eco Power, 10 MWp) Early-round IPP utility solar plant developed by Eco Power Development Company Pvt. Ltd., commissioned ~2021 in Dhanusha district, Madhesh Province. The largest single Phase I IPP plant by MWp. # Summary Mithila Solar is a 10 MWp operating utility solar plant in Dhanusha district, Madhesh Province, developed by Eco Power Development Company Pvt. Ltd. Commissioned circa 2021, it is the largest single Phase I IPP solar plant and a grid-adjacent Terai siting archetype. The page tracks it as a Phase I operational benchmark using the NEA annual report source set. # Specifications Item | Value | ---|---| Capacity | 10.0 MWp | Location | Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province | Owner / Developer | Eco Power Development Company Pvt. Ltd. | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | B2 — Eastern Terai / Madhesh | Interconnection | Dhanusha 33 kV | Commissioning | ~2021 | PPA tariff | Phase I round (~NPR 8/kWh blended) | Site elevation | ~80 m | Expected annual generation | ~16 GWh/yr | Status | Operating | # Why it matters Mithila Solar's siting is the clearest Phase I validation of the grid-adjacent Terai siting archetype later encoded in the nea-960mw-solar-tender: Mithila / Janakpur is the heart of Nepal's densest 132 kV grid cluster (hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone). Dhanusha has Zone B2 GHI of ~4.9–5.1 kWh/m²/day — among the best Terai solar resource. Flat agricultural terrain with <2° slope. Proximity (within ~70 km) to the Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur 400 kV cross-border interconnection (dhalkebar-muzaffarpur). Mithila Solar is the pattern match for dozens of 960 MW tender awards in Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, and Bara; its operational track record is the evidence base IPPs used when bidding the Phase IV tender at near-LCOE prices. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on programme and siting-context from NEA annual report evidence. It does not independently verify exact commissioning date, current monthly generation, availability, degradation rate, land tenure details, or O&M arrangements beyond the existing source set. The ~16 GWh/yr expected generation figure is a planning estimate, not a verified operational output. Phase I PPA tariff is approximate. # Related nea-solar butwal-solar-ridi-8-5mwp, bishnu-priya-nawalparasi — Phase I cohort hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone — grid backbone dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — adjacent cross-border data-solar-fleet-inventory

pages.body_text: Mugu Karnali Storage HEP At a proposed 1,902 MW, Mugu Karnali is one of Nepal's largest storage projects in feasibility development. VUCL's official project page publishes a detailed current design basis; NEA Engineering Company describes the feasibility work as ongoing. Neither source establishes construction commencement, financial close or a firm commissioning date. # Summary Mugu Karnali Storage HEP is a proposed 1,902 MW conventional storage project in the Karnali basin. The current primary project page does not describe it as pumped storage. It gives eight Francis units and 6,291.8 GWh of annual design energy, correcting the earlier wiki values of ten units and 5,883 GWh. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 1,902 MW | Status | Pre-construction / feasibility under review | River | Karnali (karnali-basin) | District | Mugu (registry primary); Bajura referenced in early materials | Province | Karnali Pradesh | ## Engineering VUCL publishes a 283 m dam, 793.45 m³/s design discharge, eight 242.67 MW Francis units, 4,843.2 MCM of total storage and 2,238.95 MCM of live storage. NEA Engineering publishes a 276 m gross-head figure. These remain feasibility-stage design parameters rather than final construction quantities. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Units | 8 × 242.67 MW Francis | Gross head | 276 m | Dam height | 283 m | Design discharge | 793.45 m³/s | Total / live storage | 4,843.2 / 2,238.95 MCM | Type | Storage | ## Output VUCL publishes 6,291.8 GWh of annual design energy, split into 2,415 GWh dry-season and 3,876.8 GWh wet-season energy. These are design outputs, not an operating forecast. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 6,291.8 GWh | Dry-season design energy | 2,415 GWh | ## Governance VUCL is the licensed state-owned developer and NEA Engineering Company is the design consultant in the current official record. Public EOI and PPP reporting should be logged as dated procurement events; expressions of interest do not establish a selected partner, ownership control or financing close. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited (VUCL) | Design consultant | NEA Engineering Company Limited | Development model | PPP proposals reported; final partner not established | ## Financial VUCL publishes a base-2024 project cost described as "46,000 Crore" and a 75:25 debt/equity assumption. The currency and cost basis must be verified from the feasibility report before conversion into USD or cost-per-MW comparisons, so the wiki does not publish a converted total. ## Schedule VUCL describes a ten-year implementation duration. The current source set does not establish a firm construction-start or commissioning year. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Construction start | Not established | Commercial operation | Not established | Published duration | 10 years | # Current Status As of 10 July 2026: pre-construction, with feasibility material under expert review and a separate 271.5 MW re-regulating-dam application visible in the current DoED register. Dimension | Current position | Evidence | ---|---|---| Design | 1,902 MW storage; eight units; 6,291.8 GWh | VUCL project page | Feasibility | Ongoing / under expert review | NEA Engineering current project and annual-report material | Cascade | Separate 271.5 MW re-regulating-dam application | DoED application register | Construction | Not started | 10 Jul 2026 verification | # Recent Updates Date | Update | ---|---| 2 Jul 2026 | Current DoED register verified the separate re-regulating-dam application | 10 Jul 2026 | Wiki specification record reconciled to the current VUCL design page | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Required evidence | ---|---|---| Feasibility basis remains under review | Final design and investment decision | Approved feasibility report | Main project, re-regulating dam and overlapping licence boundaries are not reconciled in one public record | Stable cascade and licence definition | DoED/VUCL boundary decision | Evacuation, financing and partner selection are not established | Construction readiness | Approved transmission and financing package | # Top-Capacity Comparison Mugu Karnali belongs to a small class of projects that individually exceed Nepal's entire current operating fleet: Project | MW | Type | Status | Developer | ---------|-----|------|--------|-----------| Mugu Karnali | 1,902 | Storage | Feasibility / pre-construction | VUCL | budhigandaki | 1,200 | Storage | Pre-construction | Budhigandaki Co. Ltd. | arun-3 | 900 | Peaking RoR | Under construction | SJVN (India) | upper-karnali | 900 | RoR | Stalled (18 yrs) | GMR (India) | karnali-chisapani | 10,800 | Storage | Conceptual | None | pancheshwar | 6,720 | Storage / multipurpose | Stalled before final DPR | Bilateral (Nepal/India) | Mugu Karnali is distinguished by its scale and published seasonal storage parameters. The current primary page does not establish pumped storage capability. # Significance Mugu Karnali is relevant to long-horizon storage-deficit and firm-power analysis because its current design combines 1,902 MW with 2,415 GWh of dry-season energy. Its scale also makes transmission, financing, reservoir operation and the downstream cascade part of the project definition rather than secondary details. None of that design value should be counted as available capacity while feasibility and investment decisions remain pending. # Limitations & Controversies Horizon risk. A ten-year implementation duration and the absence of a firm start date place the project outside near-term capacity planning. Transmission gap. The official design includes an approximately 40 km, 400 kV double-circuit connection to the proposed Regil/Rengil hub. The downstream grid path and capacity needed to move 1,902 MW are not yet established in the project dossier; without them the asset would face stranded-generation risk. Feasibility depth. Published capacity, head, storage and energy figures remain subject to the approved feasibility and detailed design. Partner and financing uncertainty. Expressions of interest and PPP reporting do not establish selected ownership, financing or reservoir dispatch control. Competing Karnali priorities. The Karnali basin has multiple large projects competing for limited development and transmission bandwidth: upper-karnali (900 MW, stalled), phukot-karnali (426 MW, survey), nalsyau-gad (410 MW, survey), karnali-chisapani (10,800 MW, conceptual). Mugu Karnali must compete for developer attention, financing, and — critically — transmission capacity with projects at varying stages of readiness. # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit upper-karnali west-seti arun-3 hydro-geopolitics seasonal-mismatch stranded-generation solar-hydro-complementarity bangladesh-trade-route data-map-inventory # Sources vucl-mugu-karnali-project mugu-karnali-feasibility-2025
