2. Off-grid solar + BESS at these sites has extraordinary kWh-value.
3. It is the long-dated solar export corridor.
pages.excerpt: Not a project, an entity classification of the geographic zone with Nepal's best solar resource. Covers the trans-Himalayan rain-shadow valleys of Mustang, Dolpa, upper Manang, upper Humla, Mugu (upper), and parts of Jumla — a band of high-elevation (2,500–4,500 m) valleys shield
pages.body_text: Mustang / Trans-Himalayan High-Altitude Solar Zone Not a project, an entity classification of the geographic zone with Nepal's best solar resource. Covers the trans-Himalayan rain-shadow valleys of Mustang, Dolpa, upper Manang, upper Humla, Mugu (upper), and parts of Jumla — a band of high-elevation (2,500–4,500 m) valleys shielded from the monsoon by the Greater Himalaya. This zone has world-class GHI and DNI (5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day, 6.0–6.8 kWh/m²/day respectively) with ~260–290 clear-sky days per year. It is also, for the foreseeable future, the hardest solar zone in Nepal to monetise because of grid distance, low local demand, and terrain-induced transmission costs. # Summary Mustang / Trans-Himalayan High-Altitude Solar Zone is a geographic entity classification covering the trans-Himalayan rain-shadow valleys of Mustang, Dolpa, upper Manang, upper Humla, and Mugu — Nepal's best solar resource zone by GHI and DNI. The page tracks it as a resource-zone archetype using the WB ESMAP, Global Solar Atlas, and AEPC source set. # Resource characteristics Parameter | Value | ---|---| Mean GHI | 5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day | Mean DNI | 6.0–6.8 kWh/m²/day | Clear-sky days / year | 260–290 (among highest in Nepal) | Monsoon GHI penalty | 5–15% (rain-shadow intact) | Winter GHI (Dec–Feb) | 5.2–5.8 kWh/m²/day — highest in Nepal | Elevation | 2,500–4,500 m | Ambient temperature | Cool; module efficiency ~3–5% better than Terai | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | A | Comparative reference | Ladakh, Atacama, Tibetan Plateau | # Representative districts and sites District | Representative site | Elevation | GHI | Notes | ---|---|---:|---:|---| Mustang | Jomsom | 2,730 | ~6.0 | ESMAP pyranometer station | Mustang | Upper Mustang (Lo Manthang) | 3,850 | ~6.3 | Trekking-dependent demand | Dolpa | Dunai, Dho Tarap | 2,090–4,050 | 5.9–6.4 | Remote, low demand | Upper Manang | Manang village | 3,540 | ~6.1 | Seasonal demand | Upper Humla | Simikot area | 2,960 | ~6.0 | Grid-absent | Mugu (upper) | Gamgadhi area | 2,080–3,500 | 5.8–6.2 | Grid-absent | # Why the zone is strategically interesting Three genuine reasons, despite the grid-distance challenge: ## 1. It is the only Nepal zone where winter is the best solar month. Winter clear-sky days are more numerous than summer clear-sky days here (summer can have valley-mist + high-altitude storms; winter is cloudless). The complementarity argument in solar-hydro-complementarity is strongest here: Zone A in winter generates ~110% of its April peak, exactly when Nepal's hydro fleet is at its weakest. ## 2. Off-grid solar + BESS at these sites has extraordinary kWh-value. Incumbent energy source is mostly: (a) no electricity at all, (b) diesel generation at NPR 60–90/kWh, (c) firewood for heating and cooking. Displacing (b) makes Zone A solar the highest-value per-kWh energy investment in Nepal — 10–15× the utility-tariff-equivalent value. ## 3. It is the long-dated solar export corridor. The ratmate-rasuwagadhi-kerung-400kv line, if completed, opens a trans-Himalayan interconnection to Tibet. Zone A solar, transmitted northward, becomes relevant to China's western-grid imports. This is a 15–20 year story, not a near-term strategy; the page treats long-dated Zone A solar optionality as conditional on conservation-compatible land zoning. # Near-term constraints Grid distance: Nearest 132 kV substation is typically 100–200 km away. Terrain multiplies per-km transmission cost 3–5×. Local demand: Mustang's total population ~14,000; Dolpa's ~37,000. Grid-scale off-take is absent. Land tenure: Much of upper Mustang and Dolpa is inside Annapurna Conservation Area and Shey Phoksundo National Park. Utility-scale ground-mount is largely excluded. Access: Road connectivity seasonal; airlift-only sites in winter. Construction: Cold-climate installation window is April–October only. # What Zone A is for, realistically In order of near-term deployability: 1. Off-grid + BESS for remote institutional and community sites — the karnali-solar-energy-project template, extended to Mustang and Dolpa. 2. Diesel-displacement at trekking lodges and research stations — 5–50 kWp each, high unit economics. 3. Pilot research sites for high-altitude PV degradation / snow-load / bifacial performance — valuable to global solar R&D, underrated in Nepal. 4. Long-dated grid export optionality via trans-Himalayan interconnection. Utility-scale GW-class solar in Mustang is not a 2030 project. It is a 2040 project and the value is in preserving the land zoning and interconnection optionality now. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on resource-assessment and zoning context from satellite and pyranometer sources. It does not independently verify site-grade coordinates, parcel-level land availability, conservation-area boundary precision, or current grid-distance measurements beyond the existing source set. Utility-scale GW-class deployment is characterised as a 2040 option, not a near-term project. Representative district and site data are indicative, not exhaustive. # Related solar-resource-geography-nepal — zone framework data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — numerical tables karnali-solar-energy-project — template programme rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — track this zone lives in ratmate-rasuwagadhi-kerung-400kv — long-dated interconnection wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the measurement source global-solar-atlas-nepal — the satellite cross-reference

pages.title: Nalsyau Gad
headings: Shortlist Context: How Nalsyau Gad Compares
pages.excerpt: Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA promising-storage set used by this wiki. It is pinned in both data-layer-storage-shortlist and data-layer-priority-watchlist because it contributes the kind of dry-season
pages.body_text: Nalsyau Gad Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA promising-storage set used by this wiki. It is pinned in both data-layer-storage-shortlist and data-layer-priority-watchlist because it contributes the kind of dry-season energy Nepal's run-of-river-heavy system is missing. # Summary Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA shortlist used by this wiki, with 581.8 GWh dry-season energy (41.4% dry share). It is pinned in both the storage shortlist and priority watchlist. The page tracks it as a dry-season portfolio option using the JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 410 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Karnali (karnali-basin) | Annual energy | 1406.1 GWh | Dry-season energy | 581.8 GWh | Dry share | 41.4% | Total storage | 419.6 MCM | Effective storage | 296.3 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 419.6 MCM | Effective storage | 296.3 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1406.1 GWh | Dry-season energy | 581.8 GWh | Dry-season share | 41.4 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Nalsyau Gad's value is not just its 410 MW nameplate. The JICA/NEA storage-screening figures give it 581.8 GWh of dry-season energy, equal to 41.4% of annual energy. That is the strongest dry-energy output in the promising-storage shortlist and one of the few project records that directly addresses the storage-deficit rather than only adding wet-season energy. ## Shortlist Context: How Nalsyau Gad Compares Among the JICA promising-storage candidates in the wiki, Nalsyau Gad occupies a unique position — highest dry-energy share by a significant margin: Project | MW | Annual (GWh) | Dry (GWh) | Dry Share | Effective Storage (MCM) | ---------|-----|-------------|-----------|-----------|--------------------------| Nalsyau Gad | 410 | 1,406.1 | 581.8 | 41.4% | 296.3 | Kokhajor-1 | 112 | 278.9 | 94.1 | 33.7% | 166.1 | Madi | 200 | 621.1 | 170.7 | 27.5% | 235.1 | Naumure (W. Rapti) | 245 | 1,157.5 | 309.9 | 26.8% | 580.0 | Lower Badigad | 380 | 1,366.0 | 354.7 | 26.0% | 505.5 | Chera-1 | 149 | 563.2 | 120.6 | 21.4% | 141.1 | Andhi Khola | 180 | 648.7 | 137.1 | 21.1% | 238.7 | Lower Jhimruk | 143 | 454.7 | 94.4 | 20.8% | 211.6 | Sun Koshi No.3 | 536 | 1,883.6 | 335.9 | 17.8% | 555.0 | What makes the 41.4% figure significant is that it approaches the dry-share range of seasonal-storage projects with much larger reservoirs. kulekhani-cascade achieves ~50% dry share with only 106 MW. budhigandaki projects 42% at 1,200 MW with 3,300 MCM of total storage. Nalsyau Gad is delivering comparable dry-energy concentration with less than one-tenth the reservoir volume of Budhigandaki and at a capacity point that is commercially viable for domestic financing. This is why it appears in the priority watchlist despite being survey-stage. A project can be strategically important before it is construction-ready if it changes the dry-season balance, especially in a system where kulekhani-cascade is still the only operating seasonal-storage anchor and tanahu-hydropower is the only large storage project in active construction. ## Reservoir Economics Nalsyau Gad's 296.3 MCM effective storage on 410 MW yields a storage-to-capacity ratio of 0.72 MCM/MW — lower than Naumure (2.37 MCM/MW) or Sun Koshi No.3 (1.04 MCM/MW), but the project achieves its high dry share through a different mechanism: favourable basin hydrology in the upper Karnali catchment rather than sheer reservoir volume. The Karnali basin receives reliable monsoon precipitation and has a less flashy dry-season recession than eastern basins like the Koshi, meaning a moderate storage volume can achieve proportionally more dry-season firming. This hydrological advantage is partly why the Karnali basin dominates the JICA shortlist: 6 of the 9 candidates (Nalsyau Gad, Lower Badigad, Naumure, Madi, Andhi Khola, Chera-1) are Karnali-basin projects. The basin's flow regime is intrinsically more storage-friendly. # Status And Timing Nalsyau Gad should be read as a planning / promising-storage candidate, not a confirmed near-term build. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Nalsyau Gad STO in the 2031-2035 project window. That is a planning sequence, not a construction contract. Near-term milestones that would need to occur: Feasibility study update — the JICA IPSDP provides screening-level data; a bankable feasibility study is the next technical gate Developer assignment — currently no developer is designated (unlike Dudhkoshi/NEA or Tanahu/NEA). VUCL (Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited) is the most likely candidate given its mandate for Karnali-basin storage (mugu-karnali-storage, phukot-karnali) Environmental and social screening — the Nalsyau Gad catchment requires baseline data on resettlement footprint, downstream water-use impacts, and biodiversity Financing structure — whether this follows the NEA/AIIB sovereign model (Dudhkoshi), the VUCL/PPP model (Mugu Karnali), or a new structure Transmission evacuation — routing from the upper Karnali catchment into the western hill grid and ultimately to the 400 kV backbone. See nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 # Transmission & Grid Integration Nalsyau Gad's location in the upper Karnali catchment presents a transmission challenge. The western Karnali region has limited 220 kV connectivity; the nearest 400 kV infrastructure is the proposed Karnali corridor. A 410 MW storage plant in this location would require: A dedicated 220 kV transmission line from the powerhouse to the nearest substation Integration with the planned Karnali basin transmission backbone (linked to upper-karnali and mugu-karnali-storage evacuation plans) Possibly a collector substation serving multiple Karnali storage projects (Nalsyau Gad, Lower Badigad, and Madi are all in the same general catchment) The transmission constraint is not a deal-breaker — 410 MW is within the range of standard 220 kV double-circuit capacity — but it adds a material cost component that the JICA screening-level cost estimates may not fully capture. Transmission costs for western hill storage are consistently higher per km than eastern corridor equivalents. # Geological & Site Character The Nalsyau Gad site is in the upper reaches of the Nalsyau Gad river — a Karnali tributary draining the southern flank of the Saipal Himal range in far-western Nepal. The JICA screening identifies the site as having suitable dam-axis topography for a storage reservoir with ~420 MCM total capacity, suggesting a relatively wide valley section upstream of a constriction — the classic storage-dam site geometry. Key geological considerations include: Himalayan foothill geology — sedimentary and metamorphic rock formations typical of the Lesser Himalayan zone, with potential for weak interbedded shales Seismic zone 4+ — within the active Himalayan deformation front Sediment load — the Nalsyau Gad drains steep terrain; sediment management in the reservoir design will be critical for maintaining active storage volume over the project life. See sediment-as-design-constraint GLOF exposure — lower than the Dudh Koshi or Arun basins, but the upper Karnali has glacially-fed tributaries that require assessment # Limitations & Controversies Survey-stage data only. The JICA IPSDP figures are screening-level, not bankable. A full feasibility study could shift capacity, energy, or storage numbers materially. No developer assigned. Unlike Dudhkoshi (NEA), Tanahu (NEA), or Mugu Karnali (VUCL), Nalsyau Gad has no institutional sponsor moving it forward. Transmission cost uncertainty. The western hill grid is less developed than the eastern and central corridors. Evacuation from a remote Karnali tributary adds cost. Competing Karnali priorities. The Karnali basin has multiple storage candidates vying for limited development bandwidth: Mugu Karnali (1,902 MW, pre-construction), Phukot Karnali (426 MW, survey), Upper Karnali (900 MW, stalled), Karnali Chisapani (10,800 MW, conceptual). Nalsyau Gad must compete for developer attention, financing, and transmission capacity with larger projects. Downstream water-use impacts. The Nalsyau Gad feeds the Karnali main stem; flow alteration could affect downstream ecosystems and, potentially, cross-border flows into India's Ghaghara system. See hydro-geopolitics. # Map Interpretation The map marker is a river-aligned project reference derived from the registry/project point. It is suitable for basin-level and corridor-level comparison, but it should not be treated as a final dam-axis coordinate. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit firm-power data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist data-layer-priority-watchlist mugu-karnali-storage — the largest Karnali storage project sediment-as-design-constraint nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-map-inventory

pages.title: Naumure (W. Rapti)
pages.excerpt: Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because its effective storage is unusually large for its installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin.
pages.body_text: Naumure (W. Rapti) Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because its effective storage is unusually large for its installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin. # Summary Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin (Karnali basin). It is pinned in the storage shortlist for its unusually large effective storage (580 MCM) relative to installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin. The page tracks it as a planning-layer storage comparator using the JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 245 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | West Rapti (karnali-basin) | Annual energy | 1157.5 GWh | Dry-season energy | 309.9 GWh | Dry share | 26.8% | Total storage | 1021.0 MCM | Effective storage | 580.0 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 1021.0 MCM | Effective storage | 580.0 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1157.5 GWh | Dry-season energy | 309.9 GWh | Dry-season share | 26.8 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Naumure is not the largest storage candidate by MW, but it is one of the most interesting by reservoir function: 1,021 MCM total storage, 580 MCM effective storage, and 309.9 GWh of dry-season energy. That combination makes it important to the wiki's argument that Nepal's deficit is about timing and controlled water, not only installed capacity. The project also matters because the West Rapti is not usually the headline basin in Nepal hydropower discussions. Including Naumure keeps the storage conversation from collapsing into only Karnali, Koshi, and Gandaki mega-projects. # Status And Timing Naumure should be read as a planning candidate. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Naumure STO in the 2036-2040 window. There is no confirmed construction start in the current wiki evidence set. The key open questions are scheme selection, interaction with other West Rapti candidates, environmental and downstream water-use implications, financing, and whether the project becomes a power-only scheme or a broader multipurpose water-storage project. # Map Interpretation The map marker uses a named West Rapti / Rapti River anchor near Dang. It is a basin-level reference for map reading, not a final project-coordinate claim. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on master-plan and shortlist context. It does not independently verify feasibility-study details, environmental and social assessment, financing plan, grid-connection commitment, or construction timeline beyond the existing source set. The IPSDP milestone window (2036–2040) is a planning horizon, not a confirmed construction-start date. The layout conflict with Lower Jhimruk in the current design set means the project should not be counted naively alongside it. Map markers are basin-level references, not final site coordinates. # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit firm-power data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist

[!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 54 describes the Nawalpur substation as a 132/33 kV, 63 MVA node with additional 33 kV double-circuit line works to feed the local load area. # Why It Matters This is the kind of mid-voltage reinforcement asset that sits between the headline 220/400 kV corridors and the distribution-level service outcome. It adds detail to the broader story of nea trying to convert bulk power growth into local reliability improvements. # Limitations & Controversies The page is based on the FY 2019/20 NEA annual-book description and does not establish the current construction status, final equipment configuration, commissioning date, or measured reliability effect after completion. # See also nea nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-domestic-demand

pages.title: NEA 960 MW National Solar Tender
headings: Why this tender matters (beyond the MW)
1. It establishes the price floor for Nepal solar.
4. It is the test case for [[agrivoltaics-and-land]].
pages.excerpt: The single largest solar procurement event in Nepal's history. A national-scale competitive-bid tender launched 2024 for 960 MWp of utility-scale grid-tied solar PV across Nepal, awarded to 63 projects from multiple IPPs. PPA signing and financial closure staged over FY 2025/26 a
pages.body_text: NEA 960 MW National Solar Tender # Summary The single largest solar procurement event in Nepal's history. A national-scale competitive-bid tender launched 2024 for 960 MWp of utility-scale grid-tied solar PV across Nepal, awarded to 63 projects from multiple IPPs. PPA signing and financial closure staged over FY 2025/26 and FY 2026/27; if ~70% of awards reach COD, Nepal's operating utility solar expands ~5× over the current fleet by FY 2028/29. The tender that represents the institutional bet that Nepal's solar scaling can be delivered through competitive IPP PPAs — not donor-funded NEA self-build, not off-grid AEPC programmes. # Key Facts Item | Value | ---|---| Total capacity tendered | 960 MWp | Number of projects selected | 63 | Typical project size | 5–25 MWp | Geographic distribution | Terai-dominant (Madhesh + Lumbini + Sudurpaschim + Koshi provinces) | Procurement model | Tariff-based competitive bidding | Tariff range (awarded) | NPR 4.99–5.54/kWh (NEA corrected LoI) ≈ $0.037–$0.041 | PPA tenor | 25 years, standard NEA PPA structure | Grid integration study | Cumulative Grid Impact Study completed FY 2024/25 under wb-grid-solar-ee-project TA line | Expected PPA closures | FY 2025/26–2026/27 | Expected first CODs | FY 2026/27 | Expected full portfolio COD | FY 2028/29 (if ~70% conversion rate) | # Tender structure by province (approximate) Province | MW in tender (approx.) | Notes | ---|---|---:| Madhesh (Bara, Parsa, Rautahat, Sarlahi, Dhanusha) | ~350–400 | Densest Terai grid; most bids received | Lumbini (Nawalparasi, Rupandehi, Kapilvastu, Banke) | ~200–250 | Hetauda-Bharatpur-Bardaghat corridor access | Sudurpaschim (Kailali, Kanchanpur) | ~80–120 | Far-west Terai | Koshi (Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari, Saptari) | ~150–200 | Eastern backbone | Bagmati (Makwanpur, Chitwan) | ~30–60 | Central, smaller allocations | Gandaki + Karnali (limited) | ~20–40 | Hydro co-location and resource-zone pockets | Total | ~960 | | The geographic weighting toward Terai provinces reflects the solar-resource-geography-nepal grid-adjacency priority — most awards sit within 10 km of existing 132 or 220 kV substations on the hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone and dana-kushma-butwal-corridor. # Why this tender matters (beyond the MW) Four reasons: ## 1. It establishes the price floor for Nepal solar. The awarded tariff range (4.99–5.54 NPR/kWh) is the first portfolio-scale solar price discovery in Nepal. Earlier rounds (Phase I at 8.40, Phase III around the 6.40 band) were single-digit-count project awards; 960 MW with 63 awards is the first price point that reflects actual competitive equilibrium. The tariff is a current benchmark for comparing future project evaluations against older 2017-era numbers. ## 2. It validates the market. 63 IPPs winning awards implies a functional pipeline of developers, advisors, local EPC firms, and debt financiers. The Nepal solar market was single-digit-developer-deep before this tender; it is now dozens-of-developer-deep. This matters more than the physical MW — a market of depth 1 cannot scale; a market of depth 60 can. ## 3. It stress-tests the institutional fit. The tender has four binding constraints: land acquisition (Terai agricultural politics), grid integration (penetration levels, forecast management), financial close (local-currency long-tenor debt), PPA discipline (NEA single-buyer liability). If the tender's 70%+ of awards reach COD on the FY 2026–28 schedule, the model works; if conversion falls below 50%, each of these four binding constraints becomes a programme-level fix. ## 4. It is the test case for agrivoltaics-and-land. The first awarded projects will surface which land-acquisition model works at scale. If pure-purchase / fee-simple conversion dominates and succeeds, agrivoltaics is merely an add-on. If land-acquisition delays kill > 30% of awards, agrivoltaic lease templates become a programme-level requirement for the next tender round. # Tariff context The tender tariff sits at the crossover point between solar and hydro (solar-lcoe-crossover): Benchmark | Price (NPR/kWh) | ---|---:| 960 MW tender awarded (capacity-weighted) | ~5.43 | NEA small RoR hydro PPA (blended) | 6.20 | NEA PRoR hydro PPA (blended) | 6.80 | NEA time-weighted-value of solar | ~4.80 | NEA time-weighted-value of small RoR | ~7.00 | Each MW in this tender is already materially cheaper than equivalent small RoR hydro on a blended basis and ~30% cheaper on a time-weighted basis. This is the tariff point that claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro stands on. # Limitations & Controversies Land acquisition delays. Terai agricultural land politics may stall >30% of awards if fee-simple purchase becomes contentious. Agrivoltaic lease templates are not yet in tender documents. Grid integration at scale. Cumulative Grid Impact Study completed, but actual penetration levels and forecast management at 960 MW+ are untested in Nepal's grid. Financial close risk. Local-currency long-tenor debt availability remains partial; FX risk persists for imported components. PPA settlement delays. NEA single-buyer liability creates counterparty risk; standard PPA mechanisms (escrow, performance guarantees) are untested at this portfolio scale. Weather and monsoon COD delays. Grid-extension coordination and schedule discipline are developer-by-developer variables. Tariff-crash political backlash risk. The transparent bidding process mitigates this, but a future tariff revision or policy reversal could chill investor confidence. # Implementation risks and watch items Risk | Mitigation | Status | ---|---|---| Land-acquisition delays on fee-simple conversion | Lease templates, agrivoltaic structures | Not yet in tender docs | Grid-integration penetration issues | Completed Grid Impact Study + future BESS requirements | First pass complete | Local-currency long-tenor debt availability | Nepal Rastra Bank policy; donor blending | Partial; FX risk persists | PPA settlement delays from NEA | Escrow accounts; performance guarantees | Standard PPA mechanisms | Weather / monsoon COD delays | Schedule discipline, grid-extension coordination | Developer-by-developer | Tariff-crash political backlash | Transparent bidding + price disclosure | Tender ran transparently | # Related nea-solar — programme parent nea-solar-loi-2024 — corrected row-level LoI award source nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — programme context solar-lcoe-crossover — the price story this tender anchors data-solar-fleet-inventory — the fleet this tender expands data-solar-hydro-lcoe — the numerical crossover agrivoltaics-and-land — the next-round institutional enhancement hybrid-siting-logic — the siting logic this tender operationalises claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro, claim-solar-terai-only-short-cycle-build — the tracked claims this tender evidences # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 wb-grid-solar-ee-project nea-solar-loi-2024

pages.excerpt: The utility-scale grid-tied solar programme operated by Nepal Electricity Authority. Sits inside NEA as a distinct programme line that has grown from a single 25 MWp NEA-EPC plant (Bidur/Trishuli, 2022) to a ~1.1 GWp pipeline as of FY 2024/25.
pages.body_text: NEA Solar Programme # Summary The utility-scale grid-tied solar programme operated by Nepal Electricity Authority. Sits inside NEA as a distinct programme line that has grown from a single 25 MWp NEA-EPC plant (Bidur/Trishuli, 2022) to a ~1.1 GWp pipeline as of FY 2024/25. # Programme evolution Phase | Years | Character | Key output | ---|---|---|---:| Pre-programme | 2010–2015 | Isolated small pilots | <1 MWp demonstration sites | Phase I — first IPP auctions | 2016–2018 | 5-developer competitive bid | 24 MWp awarded, 3 plants commissioned 2019–20 | Phase II — NEA self-build | 2019–2022 | WB Grid Solar & EE Project | 25 MWp Bidur/Trishuli commissioned 2022 | Phase III — IPP rounds | 2023–2024 | Competitive-bid IPP PPAs | 170 MWp PPAs signed (8 plants) | Phase IV — the 960 MW tender | 2024–2025 | National-scale IPP portfolio | 960 MWp awarded (63 projects) (nea-960mw-solar-tender) | Phase V (emerging) | 2025– | Hybrid / floating / grid-impact | Reservoir floating PV, grid-impact studies, ~585 MW additional study-stage | # Key Facts (FY 2024/25) Operating utility-scale solar: 141.74 MWp across 25 DoED-listed plants (all grid-tied; NEA-owned + IPP-owned combined) NEA-owned share: ~24.36 MWp (Bidur/Trishuli / Devighat blocks) IPP / public-utility-owned share: ~117.38 MWp (commissioned under early IPP rounds and institutional utility plants) PPA-signed, pre-COD: 170 MWp (8 plants, FY 2024/25 signings) Tender-awarded, pre-PPA: 960 MWp (63 projects from 2024/25 tender) Under grid-impact study, beyond 960 MW: ~585 MWp Annual PV generation (FY 2024/25): ~220 GWh (CF ~18%) # Tariff structure NEA's tariff-based competitive bidding framework for utility solar: Phase I (2016–18): NPR 7.30–8.40/kWh, single-round competitive Phase III (2023–24): NPR 5.94–6.50/kWh, competitive bidding with ceiling Phase IV (960 MW, 2024–25): NPR 4.99–5.54/kWh, national tender with province-balanced allocation See data-solar-hydro-lcoe for the full time-series and solar-lcoe-crossover for the cross-over narrative. # Programme organizational structure NEA's utility solar programme is scattered across several NEA directorates — a structural weakness: Generation Directorate — NEA-owned plant operation (Bidur/Trishuli) Project Management Directorate — tender design, PPA negotiation Transmission Directorate — grid-impact studies and interconnection Distribution Directorate — net-metering for rooftop Engineering Services Department / NEC — EPC supervision No single dedicated "solar cell" exists at senior-management level. The 960 MW tender exposed coordination friction across these five lines; a consolidated Renewable Energy Directorate is the obvious institutional fix. # Major utility plants under the programme Plant | Capacity (MWp) | Status | Owner | Notes | ---|---:|---|---|---| Bidur / Trishuli | 25.00 | Operating (2022) | NEA | bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp | Butwal Solar | 8.50 | Operating (2020) | Ridi HP Development | butwal-solar-ridi-8-5mwp | Mithila Solar PV | 10.00 | Operating (2021) | Eco Power Development | mithila-solar-dhanusha-10mwp | Bishnu Priya Solar Farm | ~0.96 | Operating (2018) | Surya Power Company | bishnu-priya-nawalparasi | Khungri solar award | 50 | LoI-awarded / pre-PPA | Rapti Urja Pvt. Ltd. | khungri-solar-hybrid-50mw | Karnali Solar Energy Project | ~10 (pilot) | Planned/implementation | NEA / AEPC hybrid | karnali-solar-energy-project | 960 MW tender portfolio | 960 (63 projects) | PPA in progress | Various IPPs | nea-960mw-solar-tender | Other small IPP plants (~17 plants) | ~90 (combined) | Operating | Various IPPs | From Phase I + III rounds | # Institutional challenges ## 1. Land acquisition is the new bottleneck Phase I–III plants were small enough (0.5–25 MWp) that land was project-specific. Phase IV (960 MW) triggers the land-at-scale question that agrivoltaics-and-land addresses. NEA does not have a land-programme office; this function needs to move to a new body or to AEPC. ## 2. Grid integration at 1+ GW solar The cumulative grid impact study NEA completed under Phase IV anticipates 4–6% instantaneous-penetration events by 2027 when 960 MW is partially commissioned. Forecast management, BESS requirements, and reactive-power compensation remain pre-commissioning design dependencies. ## 3. PPA exposure balance NEA's PPA liability has grown to NPR 77.1B annual electricity purchase cost (see nea). Solar PPAs are adding ~NPR 6–8B/year to this. The single-buyer model (nepal-power-trade-schemes) plus fixed-price solar PPAs creates a structural interest-rate-sensitive liability that needs transparent treatment. ## 4. Talent depth NEA's solar engineering depth is thin; the Grid Solar & EE Project invested in training but the talent base for an additional 1 GW programme is a 3–5 year capacity-build, not a tender-cycle fix. # Limitations & Controversies No dedicated solar directorate. The programme is scattered across five NEA directorates (Generation, Project Management, Transmission, Distribution, Engineering Services). The 960 MW tender exposed coordination friction; a consolidated Renewable Energy Directorate does not yet exist. Land acquisition at scale untested. Phase IV (960 MW) triggers land-at-scale questions that NEA has no office to answer. Fee-simple purchase in the Terai is politically contentious; agrivoltaic lease templates are not yet in tender documents. Grid integration at 1+ GW untested. The cumulative grid impact study anticipates 4–6% instantaneous-penetration events by 2027. Forecast management, BESS requirements, and reactive-power compensation remain pre-commissioning design dependencies. PPA liability exposure growing. Solar PPAs add ~NPR 6–8B/year to NEA's NPR 77.1B annual electricity purchase cost. The single-buyer model plus fixed-price solar PPAs creates a structural interest-rate-sensitive liability. Talent depth gap. NEA's solar engineering capacity is thin for a 1 GW+ programme. The Grid Solar & EE Project invested in training, but the talent base for portfolio-scale solar is a 3–5 year build, not a tender-cycle fix. # Related nea — the parent institution nea-960mw-solar-tender — the defining programme bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp — the flagship wb-grid-solar-ee-project — the financing anchor for Phase II data-solar-fleet-inventory — the full portfolio solar-lcoe-crossover — the tariff trajectory hybrid-siting-logic — the direction Phase V should take

pages.title: Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA)
pages.excerpt: Figure 2.1-2 NEA Organization Chart (as of September 2022)
pages.body_text: Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Figure 2.1-2 NEA Organization Chart (as of September 2022) Timeline of Hydropower Development by NEA # Summary Nepal's central electricity institution. Simultaneously serves as primary generator, monopsony buyer, and sole grid operator — a combination that creates structural conflicts of interest. # Roles Role | Description | ------|-------------| Generator | Operates NEA-owned plants (Kulekhani, Kali Gandaki A, etc.) | Single buyer | Purchases all IPP output through long-term PPAs | Grid operator | Runs the Integrated Nepal Power System (INPS) | System planner | Coordinates dispatch via Load Dispatch Center | # Key Facts NEA and subsidiaries: ~36% of installed hydro; IPPs: ~64% Total system loss: 12.26% (FY 2024/25) Eliminated scheduled load shedding in 2018 76% of firms still reported regular outages in 2022 National grid coverage: 97.6% (FY 2024/25). NEA consumer-category shares should not be read as household access rates. # Financial Health (FY 2024/25) Metric | FY 2023/24 | FY 2024/25 | Change | --------|-----------|-----------|--------| Profit before tax (NPR B) | 14.46 | 9.06 | −37.3% | Revenue from electricity sales (NPR B) | — | 125.27 | +8.46% | Total income (NPR B) | — | 138.87 | — | Total operating expenses (NPR B) | — | 97.79 | +10.15% | Electricity purchase cost (NPR B) | — | 77.10 | +11.73% | Total assets (NPR B) | — | 684.91 | +6.2% | Forex losses (NPR B) | — | ~2.50 | (yen appreciation) | May 2025 white paper (new MD Hitendra Dev Shakya) contested the previous management's claimed NPR 8B profit, revealing a NPR 5.26B loss and total liabilities of NPR 385 billion (including NPR 171.4B in long-term foreign loans under government guarantee). The discrepancy between the audited profit and the white-paper loss figure reflects different accounting treatments and periods — but signals that NEA's true fiscal position is worse than public-facing reports suggest. Debt Service Coverage Ratio: 2.27 (above 1.2 minimum — still comfortable) Return on Historic PPE: 4.50% (below 6% requirement) Debt-Equity Ratio: 47.59:52.41 # Institutional Issues Frequently dominates policy landscape, leaving the Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) sidelined Generation licensing not coordinated with transmission line planning Inter-agency disputes over EIAs, land acquisition, and forest clearance delay projects The single-buyer model limits market flexibility and creates PPA liability risk PPA liability exposure is growing: electricity purchase costs rose 11.73% in one year to NPR 77.1B, while export prices (the revenue relief valve) are falling — creating a structural squeeze between obligated payments to IPPs and realized market income Leadership instability: MD changeover (Ghising to Shakya, April 2025) resulted in dueling public narratives about NEA's financial health # Limitations & Controversies Financial reporting ambiguity. The May 2025 white paper by new MD Hitendra Dev Shakya revealed a NPR 5.26B loss and NPR 385 billion in total liabilities, contradicting the previous management's claimed NPR 8B profit. The discrepancy signals that NEA's true fiscal position may be worse than public-facing reports suggest. Leadership instability. The April 2025 MD changeover (Ghising to Shakya) produced dueling public narratives about financial health, creating policy uncertainty and complicating long-term planning. Structural conflict of interest. NEA simultaneously serves as primary generator, monopsony buyer, and sole grid operator — a combination that limits market flexibility, sidelines the Electricity Regulatory Commission, and creates concentrated PPA liability risk. Growing PPA liability squeeze. Electricity purchase costs rose 11.73% in one year to NPR 77.1B, while export prices (the revenue relief valve) are falling — creating a structural squeeze between obligated payments to IPPs and realized market income. # Related stranded-generation — NEA's grid cannot absorb what generators produce seasonal-arbitrage-trap — NEA manages the import/export trade that produces value loss india-energy-relationship — NEA is the counterpart for cross-border commercial arrangements

pages.body_text: Nepal Energy Profile # Summary Energy-specific profile of Nepal for electricity-system context. # System Snapshot (FY 2024/25) Metric | Value | --------|-------| DoED operating registry | 3,791.874 MW (Apr 10, 2026, 189 plants >1 MW) | Separate DoED sub-MW list | 15.197 MW across 19 plants (last updated Jul 7, 2025; not the same cut-off date) | NEA annual report figure | 3,591.262 MW total / 3,389.912 MW hydro (FY 2024/25 cut-off) | Hydro share | 94.4% of the FY 2024/25 installed mix | Fleet type | >90% run-of-river-hydropower | Storage capacity | 106 MW (kulekhani-cascade) | System peak demand | 2,901 MW (Jul 1, 2025) | National peak demand | 2,409 MW | Monsoon surplus | ~850 MW exported during peak production | Per-capita electricity use | 370–465 kWh/yr | Grid electricity share of final energy | 7.23% (FY 2079/80) — up from 4.96% (FY 2078/79). See data-final-energy-mix | Net trade position | Seasonal exporter (since 2023); FY 2024/25 net exports: 699 GWh | Export revenue | NPR 17.46B (India + Bangladesh) | Approved export capacity | 941 MW (400 MW bilateral + 540 MW IEX) | Transmission | 5,742 circuit-km at 66 kV+; 8,867 MVA substations | System losses | 12.26% total system loss (NEA FY 2024/25) | Cross-border transfer capacity | ~1,141 MW approved | Grid coverage | 97.6% national grid coverage (NEA FY 2024/25) | Sep 2024 flood damage | 11 operational projects, 600+ MW affected | [!warning] Supreme Court Hydropower Halt In early 2025, Nepal's Supreme Court ordered a halt to development activities — including hydropower — within all protected areas. The ruling covers 12 national parks, 6 conservation areas, 1 hunting reserve, 1 wildlife reserve, and 13 buffer zones. IPPAN / sector estimates reported through NEFPORT put the affected exposure at 267 hydropower projects totaling 19,736 MW. This is a significant new constraint on the "developable potential" claim, but the project/MW count is an industry estimate, not a Supreme Court table. # The Core Paradox Nepal has crossed from chronic shortage into seasonal surplus. It now exports electricity in the monsoon and still imports in the dry season. The country has more electricity than it can sell and less than it needs — at the same time, every year. See seasonal-mismatch. # Reliability Transition The country is far better off than during the classic shortage era, but that recent success can be overstated if the timeline is forgotten: Scheduled load shedding ended in 2018. Before that, outages lasted up to 14 hours/day between 2007 and 2017. World Bank NIETTP project documents estimate the macroeconomic cost of that era at roughly 7% of GDP per year. That history matters because today's system should be read as a transition from shortage to fragile seasonal surplus, not as a finished reliability story. # Energy Beyond Electricity Nepal's broader energy system is not electricity-centered. Biomass still dominates. In the FY 2079/80 WECS balance, residential use was 60.75% of final energy, grid electricity 7.23% (up from 4.96% the prior year — a real jump driven by +21.2% electricity consumption against −41.5% coal and −16.1% petroleum). Hydro's share of total final energy is about 6.8%. Nepal's electricity story is more advanced than its total energy transition. Full cross-tab at data-final-energy-mix; strategic frame at energy-substitution-pathway and domestic-led-hydro-strategy. # Limitations & Controversies Data reconciliation gaps. NEA reports 3,591.262 MW total / 3,389.912 MW hydro (FY 2024/25); the DoED operating registry lists 3,791.874 MW. The discrepancy (~200 MW) reflects different cut-off dates, sub-MW plant inclusion rules, and NEA vs DoED accounting boundaries. System-scale claims are source-dependent unless the source boundary is stated explicitly. Supreme Court protected-area halt. The early 2025 ruling halting development in all protected areas could affect 267 projects totaling 19,736 MW under the current IPPAN / sector estimate. This is a live constraint on "developable potential" claims that existing capacity figures do not yet reflect; the number should be attributed as industry exposure framing, not court quantification. Fragile seasonal surplus. The transition from chronic shortage to seasonal surplus is recent (since 2023). The system still imports 400–500 MW daily in winter. Framing Nepal as "energy sufficient" ignores the dry-season dependency. Per-capita electricity use is low. At 370–465 kWh/yr, Nepal's per-capita consumption is a fraction of regional peers. NEA's 97.6% grid-coverage figure measures reach, not consumption intensity. # Related data-fleet-composition — fleet breakdown data-trade-time-series — import/export trajectory data-potential-pyramid — from 83,000 MW to 3,591 MW installed data-map-inventory — merged map, layer, and figure catalog nea — the institutional center

headings: Nepal–India Electricity Transmission and Trade Project (NIETTP)
pages.excerpt: NIETTP is a World Bank-backed transmission and trade program linking Nepal-India exchange-capacity expansion with domestic 220/400 kV reinforcement works.
pages.body_text: Nepal–India Electricity Transmission and Trade Project (NIETTP) # Summary NIETTP is a World Bank-backed transmission and trade program linking Nepal-India exchange-capacity expansion with domestic 220/400 kV reinforcement works. 400 kV Tower at Koshi River The World Bank-backed program that bundled Nepal's first large cross-border-capacity push with domestic reinforcement works. In the annual book's 2020 framing, NIETTP is the umbrella program linking the cross-border-exchange objective to both hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone and the hetauda-bharatpur-bardaghat-corridor reinforcement works. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 66 describes NIETTP as a World Bank-funded project intended to establish roughly 1,000 MW of Nepal–India high-voltage exchange capacity while also executing the Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV line and associated substations. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Program type | Transmission and trade program | Core objective | Increase Nepal–India exchange capacity and improve reliability | Funding | World Bank | Linked assets in 2020 book | HDDI 400 kV works; Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV works | Framing | Cross-border trade + domestic reinforcement in one package | # Why It Matters NIETTP is the programmatic bridge between domestic grid hardening and the export-opening logic that later runs through dhalkebar-muzaffarpur and india-energy-relationship. It shows that Nepal's cross-border story was never just a border-wire story. The domestic substations and 220/400 kV reinforcements were part of the same reliability package. # Limitations & Controversies This page summarizes NIETTP from NEA annual-book framing and does not independently reconcile each linked asset's latest completion status, financing closeout, commissioning history, or realized transfer capacity. # See also dhalkebar-muzaffarpur india-energy-relationship hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone hetauda-bharatpur-bardaghat-corridor

pages.title: Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project
headings: The DPR: What WAPCOS Drafted in 2016
pages.excerpt: A proposed bi-national multipurpose project on the Mahakali/Sharda border river. The current official Nepal project description gives 6,720 MW for the full scheme: 6,480 MW at the high dam plus 240 MW at the Rupali Gad re-regulating dam, with 12,333 GWh of average annual energy.
pages.body_text: Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project # Summary A proposed bi-national multipurpose project on the Mahakali/Sharda border river. The current official Nepal project description gives 6,720 MW for the full scheme: 6,480 MW at the high dam plus 240 MW at the Rupali Gad re-regulating dam, with 12,333 GWh of average annual energy. The Mahakali Treaty was signed in 1996, but the 2016 WAPCOS draft DPR has not become a mutually accepted final DPR and construction has not started. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 6,720 MW total: 6,480 MW high dam + 240 MW re-regulating dam | Status | Stalled — 30 years, zero construction | Treaty basis | Mahakali Treaty (1996) | DPR | Drafted by India's WAPCOS (2016, unapproved) | River | Mahakali / Sharda (mahakali-basin) | ## Engineering At 315 m, the proposed rockfill dam on the Mahakali River would be among the world's largest of its type — taller than the Nurek Dam (300 m, Tajikistan) and comparable in scale to the Rogun Dam (335 m, under construction). The site is in the Mahakali gorge near the Nepal-India border, with the dam axis straddling the international boundary. The published concept uses two equal underground powerhouses, one on each bank, providing 3,240 MW per country at the high dam. The official Nepal project page describes six 540 MW Francis units on each side. An 83 m Rupali Gad re-regulating dam adds 240 MW and moderates downstream flow variation from peaking operation. But the engineering question is not whether the dam can be built — it is whether the bilateral governance structure can deliver it. 30 years after the Mahakali Treaty was signed, Nepal has received zero megawatts. This is the definitive case for buildability as a political construct, not an engineering one. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | 315 m | Dam type | Rockfill | Powerhouses | Two underground powerhouses, 3,240 MW each | Units (high dam concept) | 12 × 540 MW total | Re-regulating component | Rupali Gad, 240 MW | Type | Storage / Multipurpose | ## Storage & Output Pancheshwar's multipurpose design means three outputs share the same reservoir: 1. Power generation (6,720 MW full scheme, with equal high-dam powerhouse capacity on each bank) 2. Irrigation regulation for downstream Uttar Pradesh and Nepal's far-western Terai — valued differently by each side 3. Flood control — the Mahakali/Sharda is a monsoon flood source for the Ghaghara-Ganges system The official Nepal project description gives 12,333 GWh of average annual energy for the full scheme and 6.56 billion m³ of live storage at the high dam. These are published project parameters, not evidence of an approved final DPR or construction readiness. Parameter | Value | ---|---| Average annual energy | 12,333 GWh | High-dam live storage | 6,560 MCM | ## Financial The current official source set does not establish an approved project cost, financing plan, sovereign guarantees or financial close. Cost and benefit-allocation estimates in older commentary should be treated as dated proposals until the final DPR and bilateral decisions are published. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Approved project cost | Not established | Financing close | Not achieved | Benefit allocation | Bilateral issues remain unresolved | ## Schedule The Mahakali Treaty was signed in 1996. The DPR was drafted by India's WAPCOS in 2016 and remains unapproved — now a decade in ministerial limbo. This is not a construction delay; this is a governance delay at the most fundamental level. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Treaty signed | 1996 | DPR drafted | 2016 (WAPCOS, India) | DPR approved | No (as of 2026) | Construction start | No date | Time since treaty (no output) | 30 years | # Current Status As of 10 July 2026: stalled before an agreed final DPR. India's Ministry of Jal Shakti records that WAPCOS submitted the draft final DPR in November 2016 and that finalisation remains underway because contentious issues are unresolved. Dimension | Current position | Evidence | ---|---|---| Treaty basis | Mahakali Treaty, 1996 | Official India project page | Technical concept | 6,720 MW full scheme; 12,333 GWh annual energy | Official Nepal project description | DPR | Draft final submitted November 2016; mutually accepted final DPR unresolved | Ministry of Jal Shakti project page | Construction | Not started | 10 Jul 2026 verification | # Recent Updates The current official websites continue to publish project, disclosure and institutional material, but no source reviewed for this update establishes final DPR approval or construction commencement. # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Responsible forum | ---|---|---| No mutually accepted final DPR | Investment approval, procurement and construction | Pancheshwar Development Authority and both governments | Bilateral technical and benefit-allocation issues remain open | Final project configuration and financing | Joint water-resources institutions | Financing commitments are not established | Financial close | Both governments / project authority | # Limitations & Controversies Final DPR unresolved. The 2016 draft remains the central evidence gap. Technical figures may change until a mutually accepted final DPR is published. Benefit allocation unresolved. Official India material explicitly records contentious bilateral issues but does not provide a current, agreed allocation protocol in the source set used here. Social and environmental evidence is incomplete. Displacement, resettlement, biodiversity, downstream-flow and cumulative-impact totals should not be treated as current without the final assessment documents. Seismic and dam-safety requirements are material. A 315 m Himalayan rockfill dam requires current project-specific design and review evidence; regional hazard descriptions are not a substitute. Financing unresolved. No approved cost and financing package is established in the current official record. # The DPR: What WAPCOS Drafted in 2016 The Detailed Project Report drafted by India's WAPCOS in 2016 is the most important unapproved document in Nepal-India hydropower relations. Key technical elements reported in public summaries include: Dam axis: near the Pancheshwar gorge, with the dam body straddling the international boundary Installed capacity: 6,720 MW full scheme (6,480 MW high dam plus 240 MW re-regulating dam) Annual energy: 12,333 GWh on the current official Nepal project page High-dam live storage: 6.56 billion m³ on the current official Nepal project page Irrigation: command area in both Nepal's far-western Terai and India's Uttar Pradesh Flood control: downstream regulation for the Sharda-Ghaghara system The DPR's unapproved status means none of these figures are bankable. Until the Joint Expert Group finalizes and both cabinets approve the report, procurement cannot begin. # The Benefit-Sharing Impasse Official India material states that contentious bilateral issues prevent final DPR agreement. Public commentary commonly identifies irrigation, regulated-water and other non-power benefits among those issues, but the current wiki source set does not establish a mutually agreed valuation or allocation formula. Precise negotiating positions should be linked to joint minutes before being presented as current. ## Parallel stalls Pancheshwar is not unique — several Nepal-India joint projects are stuck on similar valuation questions: Saptakoshi High Dam: JTE meetings stalled; 17th JTE was October 2023 Sunkoshi Storage: similar bilateral design and benefit-sharing stalemates Naumure (West Rapti): not yet bilateral but downstream impacts with India are foreseeable The pattern is systemic: India-Nepal water cooperation lacks a standardized framework for valuing and sharing non-electricity benefits. Every project becomes a standalone negotiation, and every standalone negotiation stalls on the same question. # International Comparison: Itaipu Parameter | Itaipu (Brazil/Paraguay) | Pancheshwar (Nepal/India) | -----------|--------------------------|---------------------------| Treaty signed | 1973 | 1996 | Construction start | 1975 | Not started | COD | 1984 | No date | Treaty-to-COD | 11 years | 30+ years and counting | Capacity | 14,000 MW | 6,720 MW full scheme | Dam type | Concrete gravity/buttress | Rockfill | Dam height | 196 m | 315 m | Benefit split | 50/50 (power — Paraguay sells excess to Brazil) | 50/50 (power) / unresolved (non-power) | Governance | Itaipu Binacional (single entity) | Pancheshwar Development Authority; final DPR unresolved | Financing | Brazilian guarantee + export revenue | Unresolved | The Itaipu comparison is instructive: the treaty created a single binational entity (Itaipu Binacional) with clear governance, Brazil guaranteed the debt (80% of the cost), and Paraguay's excess power was purchased by Brazil at a defined price. Pancheshwar has none of these. The critical difference is governance architecture. Itaipu showed that a single joint entity with clear commercial mandate can deliver. Pancheshwar shows that a treaty without an implementing entity, without financing commitments, and without a mechanism for valuing non-power benefits cannot. # Displacement & Social Impact The reservoir and associated infrastructure would affect communities on both sides of the border. The current source set used for this update does not contain an approved, consolidated resettlement plan or a final cross-border affected-household total. Historical estimates should be retained only with their document date and assessment boundary. # Seismic & Environmental Risk The Himalayan setting makes seismic loading, slope stability, sediment, spillway design and downstream-flow change material assessment topics for a 315 m rockfill dam. The current page does not assign a project hazard class or quantify those impacts because the governing final DPR, dam-safety review and environmental documents are not in the source set. # Unresolved Milestones The evidence trail supports three pending milestones without prescribing how the two governments should resolve them: 1. A mutually accepted final DPR. 2. A documented agreement on outstanding bilateral technical and benefit-allocation issues. 3. An approved cost, financing and implementation package capable of supporting procurement and construction. # Significance Pancheshwar is the ultimate case study for hydro-geopolitics. It shows how bilateral treaty structures, domestic politics on both sides, the difficulty of valuing non-electricity benefits, and the absence of a single executing entity can prevent even the most strategically obvious projects from materializing. The comparison with budhigandaki — a 1,200 MW domestically-controlled storage project that is actually advancing — supports the domestic-led-hydro-strategy thesis: projects that Nepal can control unilaterally are slow, but projects that require bilateral consensus may be impossible. # Related mahakali-basin — the river india-energy-relationship — the bilateral context hydro-geopolitics — the analytical frame budhigandaki — the domestically-controlled storage counterpoint karnali-chisapani — the other mega-project in the same governance class domestic-led-hydro-strategy — the policy thesis Pancheshwar supports buildability — why governance matters as much as engineering Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory # Sources pancheshwar-official-project-record national-water-plan-nepal wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment

pages.title: Phukot Karnali
pages.excerpt: Phukot Karnali is a 426-480 MW Karnali basin peaking run-of-river project promoted by VUCL and currently treated in the wiki as a survey-stage, pre-construction project.
pages.body_text: Phukot Karnali # Summary Phukot Karnali is a 426-480 MW Karnali basin peaking run-of-river project promoted by VUCL and currently treated in the wiki as a survey-stage, pre-construction project. Phukot Karnali is a 426-480 MW peaking run-of-river project on the Karnali in Kalikot district, promoted by Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited. It is pinned in both the data-layer-priority-watchlist and data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects because it is one of the few large Karnali projects with a stronger document-backed project-area anchor, a state developer, and a plausible place in Nepal's 2030s buildout sequence. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 426 MW | Status | Survey / study | Registry licence | Survey | River | Karnali (karnali-basin) | District | Kalikot | Province | Karnali Pradesh | Promoter | Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited | ## Engineering Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Units | 6 | Unit capacity | 79 MW | Turbine type | Francis | Underground powerhouse | yes | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | PROR | ## Governance Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Phukot is a medium-large Karnali project, not a mega-reservoir like mugu-karnali-storage. That makes it strategically different: it is big enough to matter for the western generation stack, but small enough that its buildability, access, and evacuation questions are less extreme than the very largest Karnali schemes. VUCL's project-status material describes a project in Kalikot using Karnali River flow, feeding the integrated power system at the proposed Regil grid substation. The same status document lists a 474 MW main underground powerhouse, six 79 MW Francis units, an additional 6 MW environmental-release powerhouse, a 400 kV double-circuit evacuation line of about 2.3 km to Regil, and an estimated construction duration of about five years once full construction starts. The wiki keeps the registry value of 426 MW in the generated spec table because that is the value carried through the DoED-linked project dataset. The wider project literature often uses 480 MW or 474+6 MW. That discrepancy is not a contradiction in the map; it is a sign that the page is combining registry, VUCL, and planning-source views of the same project. # Status And Timing As of the current wiki evidence set, Phukot should be read as pre-construction / survey-stage, not an operating or under-construction plant. A 2025 news item reported renewed ministerial direction to take Karnali projects forward with NHPC collaboration, but the stronger planning anchor for this wiki is the IPSDP milestone ladder, which places Phukot Karnali in the 2031-2035 project window. The practical read is: Question | Current Read | ----------|--------------| Is construction visibly underway? | Not confirmed by the sources used here. | Is there a construction-duration estimate? | Yes: VUCL status material estimates about five years for construction. | Is there a dated planning window? | Yes: IPSDP groups Phukot Karnali in 2031-2035. | What has to be watched next? | Development-vehicle clarity with NHPC/VUCL, generation licence status, financing, PPA/offtake, Regil grid hub readiness, and land/environmental approvals. | # Map Interpretation The map point is based on an official project-area center from the VUCL status report and is already close to the mapped Karnali reach. That makes it more defensible than a plain registry coordinate, but it still should not be treated as a final dam-axis coordinate. The project includes a dam, underground powerhouse, tunnel system, and grid connection; the marker is a project reference, not a detailed engineering layout. # Limitations & Controversies Phukot's main risk is not the absence of hydropower resource. The Karnali flow is the reason the project exists. The binding questions are delivery questions: who finances it, whether NHPC participation becomes a final investment structure, whether the Regil evacuation path advances on time, and whether the five-year construction estimate survives detailed contracting. It also matters for the claim-mw-not-equal-value argument. A 426-480 MW Karnali project can be valuable, but its value depends on dispatch timing, dry-season contribution, grid absorption, and export or domestic offtake arrangements. Capacity alone does not settle the case. # Registry note Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset VUCL PKHEP status report and current project registry VUCL project-status PDF: Phukot Karnali Project Status # See also karnali-basin stranded-generation buildability data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-priority-watchlist data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects

pages.title: Rasuwagadhi
pages.excerpt: Rasuwagadhi is a 111 MW Bhote Koshi run-of-river project in Rasuwa, developed within the Chilime/NEA subsidiary structure. NEA Engineering records commercial commissioning in January 2025, severe flood damage in July 2025 and partial generation returning in December 2025 while lo
pages.body_text: Rasuwagadhi # Summary Rasuwagadhi is a 111 MW Bhote Koshi run-of-river project in Rasuwa, developed within the Chilime/NEA subsidiary structure. NEA Engineering records commercial commissioning in January 2025, severe flood damage in July 2025 and partial generation returning in December 2025 while longer-term rehabilitation planning continued. # Ownership & Structure Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company Limited is an NEA subsidiary, structurally nested under Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL). Chilime holds a 33% stake, while the NEA directly holds 18%, keeping the project within the state umbrella. As a Chilime subsidiary, Rasuwagadhi benefits from CHCL's institutional brand — but unlike its parent, it does not enjoy the anomalous "Regular/Excess" tariff architecture. # PPA & Financial Model Rasuwagadhi's PPA was signed in November 2011 under the standardized IPP tariff structure of NPR 4.80/kWh (wet season) and NPR 8.40/kWh (dry season), with a 3% annual escalation cap for eight years. By 2011, regulatory pressure from private IPPs had forced the NEA to subject even its own subsidiary ventures to the same commercial tariff schedule as independent developers. There is no evidence of renegotiation to elevate these rates. The project raised NPR 66 crore through a local/staff IPO in 2018. Unlike Chilime (which IPO'd after 7 years of profitable operations), Rasuwagadhi's shares were sold while the project was still under construction. # Commissioning, Flood Damage & Restoration The project entered commercial operation in January 2025. On 8 July 2025, rapid discharge from a supraglacial lake on the Purepu Glacier produced a destructive flood through the Lende/Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridor. NDRRMA's first situation report recorded three hydropower plants among the affected infrastructure while the detailed causal and damage investigations were still under way. See ndrrma-rasuwa-glacial-flood-sitrep-2025. NEA Engineering records severe damage at Rasuwagadhi to civil structures, hydromechanical equipment and electromechanical systems, followed by suspension of generation. Its FY 2081/82 report says one unit returned to partial generation on 6 December 2025 and two units generated under available dry-season discharge from 25 December. The report does not establish final rehabilitation completion or later operating status. See nea-engineering-annual-report-2081-82. # Geopolitical Position Located near Nepal's northern border with Tibet in Rasuwa district, Rasuwagadhi sits in a corridor that includes the Kerung border crossing — an increasingly strategic trade and infrastructure point between Nepal and China. This geographic positioning gives the project significance beyond its 111 MW capacity. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 111 MW | Status | Commercially commissioned January 2025; partial generation restored by December 2025 | Registry licence | Generation | River | Bhote koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | Commercial operation | January 2025 | Flood interruption | 8 July 2025 | # Limitations & Controversies The page has a verified commissioning month and a dated partial-restoration record, but it does not establish final rehabilitation completion, current unit availability, the final flood-loss amount, post-restoration generation, the post-delay cost position or any revised tariff treatment. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability chilime glof-risk nea-engineering-annual-report-2081-82 ndrrma-rasuwa-glacial-flood-sitrep-2025 ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 # Sources nea-engineering-annual-report-2081-82 ndrrma-rasuwa-glacial-flood-sitrep-2025 ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026

pages.body_text: Ratmate–Rasuwagadhi–Kerung 400 kV Transmission Line # Summary Ratmate-Rasuwagadhi-Kerung is a proposed 400 kV Nepal-China interconnection concept linking Ratmate to the Rasuwagadhi/Kerung border axis. Nepal's planned first grid interconnection with China in the annual-book 2020 planning frame. The project is both a power-trade idea and a geopolitical signal: a proposed 400 kV route from the Ratmate side of the Nepal grid to the Rasuwagadhi/Kerung border axis. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 65 says the Ratmate–Rasuwagadhi–Kerung line was being advanced as Nepal's first power-grid interconnection with China, with a planned ~70 km 400 kV double-circuit line from the Rasuwagadhi border point to Ratmate and a power-exchange substation at Ratmate. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Counterparty direction | China / Tibet Autonomous Region | Status in 2020 book | Detail survey and feasibility stage | Nepal endpoint | Ratmate | Border axis | Rasuwagadhi–Kerung | # Why It Matters This is the clearest 2020-era public example of Nepal trying to widen its grid geopolitics beyond the India-only transmission frame. Even as a survey-stage line, it belongs with rasuwagadhi and hydro-geopolitics because the point of the project was energy-security optionality, not just another domestic corridor. # Limitations & Controversies The available page evidence establishes the 2020 planning frame, route concept, and survey/feasibility status; it does not confirm a final alignment, implementation agreement, financing, construction start, or operating exchange arrangement with China. # See also rasuwagadhi hydro-geopolitics mca-central-400 nepal-transmission-landscape-2025

pages.title: Sahas Urja — Solu Khola (Dudh Koshi) Hydroelectric Project
headings: Sahas Urja Limited — Solu Khola (Dudh Koshi) Hydroelectric Project
Why Sahas Urja Matters to This Wiki
pages.excerpt: 86 MW run-of-river hydropower project on the Solu Khola, a tributary of the Dudh Koshi, in Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province. Nepal's most-cited private IPP success story — and the project that shows the standard PPA rate is only viable at exceptional scale.
pages.body_text: Sahas Urja Limited — Solu Khola (Dudh Koshi) Hydroelectric Project # Summary 86 MW run-of-river hydropower project on the Solu Khola, a tributary of the Dudh Koshi, in Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province. Nepal's most-cited private IPP success story — and the project that shows the standard PPA rate is only viable at exceptional scale. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 86 MW | Status | Operating | River | Solu Khola (tributary of Dudh Koshi) | District | Solukhumbu, Koshi Province | Entity type | Private IPP | Incorporated | February 2014 (private limited), converted to public limited September 2014 | ## Output Sahas Urja's Q41 design parameter is more aggressive than the DoED 2018 Q45 mandate — the developers accepted higher dry-season underutilization risk in exchange for maximizing monsoon energy capture. As documented in q-design-discharge, this is a calculated bet that only works at scale. The 19.28% dry-season energy mix produces ~100 GWh of premium-priced winter generation, enough absolute volume to carry the project's debt load despite the wet-season rate. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 520.20 GWh | Dry-season energy | 100.27 GWh | Dry-season share | 19.28 % | Plant load factor | 69.05 % | Q-design | Q41 | Type | Run-of-River | COD | March 1, 2023 | ## Financial Sahas Urja operates on the identical NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA rate as every other private RoR IPP of its era. Its strong financial performance — NPR 2.648 billion revenue, NPR 902 million net profit in FY2023/24 — does not establish that the rate is broadly adequate; it shows the rate is only viable at exceptional scale and cost discipline. The median 10–30 MW IPP cannot replicate these economics. For a detailed breakdown, see the PPA Structure and Financial Performance sections below. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| PPA rate (wet) | NPR 4.80/kWh | PPA rate (dry) | NPR 8.40/kWh | Debt/equity | 76/24 | Build cost | NPR 172–175 million/MW | ## Governance Him Prasad Pathak, the founder-chairman, is a central figure in Nepal's energy landscape — a Secretary and Executive Committee member of IPPAN, giving him direct lobbying access to MoEWRI, ERC, and NEA. His acquisition of a 51% controlling stake in Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki PRoR) for ~NPR 2 billion extends the Sahas Urja playbook to a new scale. See the Promoters and Institutional Connections section for the full institutional mapping. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Sahas Urja Limited | Lead financier | Nepal Investment Bank (10-bank consortium) | # PPA Structure PPA signed: February 25, 2015 with NEA (take-or-pay) Wet season rate: NPR 4.80/kWh Dry season rate: NPR 8.40/kWh Escalation: 3% annually for 8 years, contingent on meeting RCOD milestones Sahas Urja retained all 8 escalation tranches by achieving on-time commissioning. Many peer IPPs lose escalation rights due to construction delays. Contracted annual energy: 520.20 GWh (Dry: 100.27 GWh / Wet: 419.93 GWh = 19.28% dry mix) Source: Sahas Urja Progress Report W010; ICRA Nepal. # Financial Performance (FY2023/24) Metric | Value | ---|---| Total revenue | NPR 2.648 billion | Net profit | NPR 902.33 million (114.66% YoY increase) | Gross profit margin | 95.54% | Net profit margin | 23.61% (after interest) | Interest expense | NPR 805.9 million (down from NPR 1.165 billion prior year) | Plant Load Factor | 69.05% | Generation performance | 87–89% of contracted energy in initial full operating years | Build cost (final) | NPR 172–175 million/MW (vs initial budget NPR 138M/MW, vs industry average NPR 200–300M/MW) | Financing | 76% debt, 10-bank consortium led by Nepal Investment Bank | Source: ICRA Nepal B.119 (April 2026); ClickMandu financial reporting; Himalayan Capital analysis. The company's 114.66% profit growth was driven fundamentally by interest cost reduction — base rates fell between FY2022/23 and FY2023/24, dropping interest expense from NPR 1.165 billion to NPR 805.9 million. This shows that even the sector's strongest IPP remains heavily leveraged to macroeconomic rate cycles, not just hydrological performance. # Why Sahas Urja Matters to This Wiki Sahas Urja is Nepal's most-cited private IPP success story. It operates on the identical NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA rate as every other private run-of-river IPP of its era. Its strong financial performance does not establish that the standard IPP rate is broadly adequate; it indicates the opposite: the rate is only viable at exceptional scale and cost discipline that the overwhelming majority of Nepal's hydro project pipeline cannot replicate. The median Nepal IPP is 10–30 MW. At that scale and at industry-average build costs of NPR 200–300 million/MW, the NPR 4.80/8.40 rate does not generate sufficient revenue to service debt and cover operating costs — as documented across the generation performance data in q-design-discharge and the debt service analysis in upper-tamakoshi. Sahas Urja's success is structural arbitrage: it captured the same fixed tariff as smaller projects but with a cost base and generation volume that made the math work. It is not a replicable model. At NPR 172–175 million/MW build cost on 86 MW, it achieved a capital efficiency that a 15 MW project on a remote tributary cannot match regardless of management quality. The single most important financial mechanic: Sahas Urja's 86 MW scale means that its 19.28% dry energy mix still yields 100 GWh of premium-priced (NPR 8.40/kWh) dry-season generation — enough absolute volume to cover fixed costs and debt service even if the remaining 80% of generation is sold at the depressed NPR 4.80 wet rate. A 15 MW IPP with the same 19% dry mix generates only ~17 GWh of dry-season revenue — insufficient to carry its debt load. See ppa-pricing for the full rate comparison table and nea-triple-authority for the institutional framework. # Promoters and Institutional Connections Chairman: Him Prasad Pathak Managing Director: Sushil Thapa Directors: Mukti Ram Pandey, Mahendra Kumar Giri Him Prasad Pathak is a central figure in Nepal's energy landscape. He began with the modest 5 MW Upper Hugdi Khola project before scaling to the 86 MW Solu Khola. He serves as a Secretary and Executive Committee member of IPPAN (Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal), giving him direct lobbying access to MoEWRI, ERC, and NEA. Pathak orchestrated Sahas Urja's acquisition of a 51% controlling stake in Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki PRoR project) for approximately NPR 2 billion. He subsequently secured an NPR 52.5 billion consortium loan from 10 commercial banks for the Budhi Gandaki project — one of the largest private syndications in Nepal's history. Source: Sahas Urja corporate disclosures; ICRA Nepal; Annapurna Express; ShareSansar. Political connections: The company states no political affiliations. Independent verification of promoter PEP (Politically Exposed Person) status is not possible — the SEBON IPO prospectus exists but is in non-machine-readable scanned PDF format, frustrating automated accountability tracking. Local share distribution to 8,000+ promoters including 2,900 project-affected locals required coordination with local political structures — a documented pattern per the IFC local shares report. [UNVERIFIED: political affiliation verification beyond IFC pattern documentation.] # Limitations & Controversies Non-replicable economics. Sahas Urja's financial performance does not establish that the standard NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA rate is broadly adequate. It points in the opposite direction: the rate is only viable at exceptional scale (86 MW) and cost discipline (NPR 172–175M/MW) that the median 10–30 MW IPP cannot replicate. Interest-rate leverage. The 114.66% profit growth in FY2023/24 was driven by interest cost reduction, not operational improvement. Even the sector's strongest IPP remains heavily leveraged to macroeconomic rate cycles. Aggressive Q41 design. The Q41 design parameter accepts higher dry-season underutilization risk than the DoED Q45 mandate. This is a calculated bet that only works at scale; smaller projects with the same design would face worse dry-season revenue shortfalls. Political connection opacity. Promoter PEP status is not independently verifiable. The SEBON IPO prospectus exists only in non-machine-readable scanned PDF format, frustrating automated accountability tracking. # Sources icra-nepal-surveillance-a996-b119 sahas-urja-progress-report-w010 clickmandu-financial-reporting himalayan-capital-analysis # See also ppa-pricing — the rate comparison table placing Sahas Urja in context nea-triple-authority — the institutional framework governing PPA enforcement q-design-discharge — why Sahas Urja's 87–89% contracted generation performance is exceptional upper-tamakoshi — the NEA subsidiary comparison case chilime — the subsidiary with the favorable billing architecture
