pages.excerpt: Sanjen Khola is a 78 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in Rasuwa and part of the same Sanjen valley development context as the smaller Sanjen project.
pages.body_text: Sanjen Khola # Summary Sanjen Khola is a 78 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in Rasuwa and part of the same Sanjen valley development context as the smaller Sanjen project. Sanjen Khola is a 78 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Sanjen Khola in Rasuwa district. At nearly double the capacity of the adjacent Sanjen project (42.5 MW), it is the larger of the two Sanjen River developments. # Sanjen Cluster The Sanjen River valley in Rasuwa hosts two closely-related projects: Sanjen (42.5 MW, Chilime subsidiary) and Sanjen Khola (78 MW). Together, they represent ~120 MW of capacity from a relatively small catchment, raising questions about optimized water use, cumulative environmental impact, and whether both projects can simultaneously achieve their contracted energy yields from the same river system. # Development Context Both Sanjen projects benefit from the Chilime-Trishuli transmission corridor infrastructure that connects Rasuwa district generation to the national grid. The corridor's capacity to evacuate the combined output of Chilime (22.1 MW), Sanjen, Sanjen Khola, Rasuwagadhi (111 MW), and other projects in the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi system is a binding operational constraint — not just an abstract planning concern. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 78 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Sanjen | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page is based on annual-report and registry context and does not verify final commissioning timing, current construction percentage, dry-season energy performance, or cumulative environmental effects across the Sanjen River projects. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25

pages.title: Sanjen
pages.excerpt: Sanjen is a 42.5 MW run-of-river project in Rasuwa developed within the Chilime subsidiary network and treated here as under construction.
pages.body_text: Sanjen # Summary Sanjen is a 42.5 MW run-of-river project in Rasuwa developed within the Chilime subsidiary network and treated here as under construction. Sanjen is a 42.5 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Sanjen River in Rasuwa district, promoted as part of the Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) subsidiary network. # Subsidiary Structure Sanjen Hydropower Company is one of three major subsidiaries spun off by CHCL to expand its generation portfolio beyond the original 22.1 MW Chilime plant. The holding company model — where a profitable legacy asset incubates and partially finances downstream projects — is the mechanism that has allowed CHCL to dominate Nepal's hydro-market narrative. Sanjen, Rasuwagadhi (111 MW), and Madhya Bhotekoshi (102 MW) together form a ~256 MW pipeline under the CHCL umbrella. # PPA Context Like Rasuwagadhi, Sanjen operates under the standard IPP tariff architecture of NPR 4.80/kWh (wet) and NPR 8.40/kWh (dry), not the preferential "Regular/Excess" billing system enjoyed by its parent company Chilime. This means Sanjen faces the same revenue structure as private IPPs despite its state-backing, and its financial viability depends on cost control and construction execution rather than bespoke tariff advantages. # Rasuwa District Context Sanjen and the nearby Sanjen Khola (78 MW) project are located in Rasuwa district, north of the Trishuli valley. This area has seen concentrated hydropower development driven by proximity to the Chilime-Trishuli transmission corridor and the Kathmandu load center. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 42.5 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Sanjen | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page describes Sanjen from subsidiary, PPA, and registry context, but does not independently confirm latest COD, current physical progress, cost escalation, or realized operating performance. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability chilime sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 # Sources sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026

The Solu Corridor Tingla-Mirchaiya 132 kV line evacuates generation from the Solu/Okhaldhunga area south toward Mirchaiya. It is operational, but the public route geometry is still lower-confidence than the main 220 kV and 400 kV corridors because the current trace is reconstructed from NEA narrative and anchor points rather than an alignment atlas. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV | Status | Operational | Corridor ID | | Public map feature | | Source basis | NEA Transmission Annual Book 2077 pages 47-52 | Official route length | 90.0 km route basis | Traced network length | 78.844 km | Validation delta | -12.40% | # Map Interpretation The map trace is a corridor-level reconstruction from the source-stated Mirchaiya and Tingla terminals, the Maruwa/Katari reroute context, and the municipal corridor through Okhaldhunga. It should be read as a faithful directional corridor, not as final engineering alignment. # Confidence Public decision: default-visible with explicit QA warning. The line is important and operational, so it remains visible. The warning exists because the geometry is low-confidence and because NEA sources appear to mix route-km and circuit-km: the older yearbook describes a 90 km route, while later inventory-style reporting lists 180 km, likely double-circuit conductor accounting. # Limitations & Controversies This corridor needs a true route-grade IEE/RAP/alignment source before it can be promoted. pages.excerpt: Sun Koshi No.3 is a 536 MW Koshi basin storage candidate with large reservoir volume and a 2031-2035 planning-window placement in the current IPSDP milestone layer.
pages.body_text: Sun Koshi No.3 # Summary Sun Koshi No.3 is a 536 MW Koshi basin storage candidate with large reservoir volume and a 2031-2035 planning-window placement in the current IPSDP milestone layer. Sun Koshi No.3 is a 536 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Koshi basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because it combines large reservoir scale with meaningful dry-season output in Nepal's eastern-central hydro corridor. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 536 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Koshi (koshi-basin) | Annual energy | 1883.6 GWh | Dry-season energy | 335.9 GWh | Dry share | 17.8% | Total storage | 1220.0 MCM | Effective storage | 555.0 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 1220.0 MCM | Effective storage | 555.0 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1883.6 GWh | Dry-season energy | 335.9 GWh | Dry-season share | 17.8 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Sun Koshi No.3 has 1,220 MCM total storage, 555 MCM effective storage, and 335.9 GWh of dry-season energy in the storage-shortlist table. Its dry share, 17.8%, is lower than Nalsyau Gad, Dudhkoshi, or Kokhajor-1, so the case for the project rests more on total reservoir block and basin position than on dry-share efficiency. This makes it a useful comparator for dudhkoshi-storage. Both are Koshi-basin storage candidates, but they occupy different strategic roles: Dudhkoshi is the stronger quantified dry-season block, while Sun Koshi No.3 is a large east-central storage option with different location and transmission implications. # Status And Timing Sun Koshi No.3 is a planning candidate, not an active construction project in the current wiki evidence set. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Sunkoshi 3 STO in the 2031-2035 window. Watch for updated feasibility, developer structure, environmental approvals, financing, and how the project is treated in relation to downstream river regulation and cross-border hydrology concerns. # Map Interpretation The current map marker is a river anchor. Use it for basin and strategic comparison, not for final dam-axis or reservoir-boundary analysis. # Limitations & Controversies The page treats Sun Koshi No.3 as a planning candidate and does not confirm updated feasibility design, developer structure, financing, environmental approvals, dam-axis coordinates, or reservoir-boundary impacts. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # See also koshi-basin storage-deficit firm-power dudhkoshi-storage data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist

pages.body_text: Super Madi # Summary Super Madi is a 44 MW Madi Khola run-of-river project under construction in Kaski district, separate from the upstream Upper Madi project. Super Madi is a 44 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Madi Khola in Kaski district, Gandaki Province. [!note] Disambiguation "Super" is the official tier designation in the Nepal DoED/MoE registry — distinct from "Upper". On the same Madi Khola, upper-madi (25 MW) is an upstream operating plant, while Super Madi (44 MW) is a larger downstream project under construction. These are separate assets with different promoters and PPAs. # Significance At 44 MW, Super Madi is a mid-sized project by Nepal's under-construction standards, but noteworthy for its location in the Madi River system — a tributary of the Seti Gandaki/Narayani system in western Nepal's hydropower-rich Gandaki basin. The Madi Khola valley in Kaski has seen successive rounds of hydropower development, with multiple projects operating or under construction in close proximity. # Context Super Madi sits within the broader Gandaki basin development landscape, where projects must navigate the interactions between upstream-downstream water use, environmental flow requirements, and the transmission infrastructure needed to evacuate power from relatively remote valleys into the national grid. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 44 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Madi Khola (gandaki-basin) | District | Kaski | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page distinguishes the asset and its basin context, but it does not verify current construction progress, commissioning schedule, final offtake arrangements, or cumulative flow and environmental constraints in the Madi Khola valley. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25

pages.title: Super Trishuli
pages.excerpt: Super Trishuli is a 100 MW under-construction run-of-river project in the Trishuli cascade and is distinct from the Upper Trishuli project tiers.
pages.body_text: Super Trishuli # Summary Super Trishuli is a 100 MW under-construction run-of-river project in the Trishuli cascade and is distinct from the Upper Trishuli project tiers. Super Trishuli is a 100 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Trishuli River — the largest project in the Trishuli cascade's current development pipeline. [!note] Disambiguation "Super" is the official Nepal DoED/MoE registry tier — distinct from "Upper". The Trishuli corridor hosts multiple named tiers: upper-trishuli-3a (60 MW), upper-trishuli-3b (37 MW), upper-trishuli-1 (216 MW), trishuli (Devighat), and Super Trishuli (100 MW). Each is a separate asset with its own promoter, PPA, and status. See trishuli-cascade for the corridor overview. # Trishuli System The Trishuli River is Nepal's most heavily developed hydropower corridor, benefiting from proximity to Kathmandu's load center and established transmission infrastructure. The cascade includes multiple projects at various stages: the original Trishuli Devighat plant, Upper Trishuli 3A (60 MW, NEA-owned, operating), Upper Trishuli 3B (37 MW, subsidiary, under construction), and Super Trishuli (100 MW). Together, these projects extract significant energy from the Trishuli's flow, but also concentrate risk — geological events, sediment surges, or flow alterations from upstream projects cascade through the entire system. # PPA Structure As a private/IPP project, Super Trishuli operates under the standard tariff framework of NPR 4.80/kWh (wet) and NPR 8.40/kWh (dry) with 3% annual escalations over eight years. At 100 MW of run-of-river capacity in the Trishuli's seasonal flow regime, the project's financial model is heavily dependent on achieving competitive build costs and maximizing the dry-season energy share. # Industry Context The 100 MW mark represents a significant threshold: projects at this scale are large enough to require complex syndicated financing but not large enough to command the bespoke PPA terms that have been applied to mega-projects like Upper Karnali or West Seti. Super Trishuli sits at the intersection of Nepal's standard IPP model and the challenges of scaling that model to triple-digit capacities. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 100 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Gorkha | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page frames Super Trishuli within the Trishuli cascade and standard IPP model, but does not independently confirm latest construction progress, COD, project cost, hydrological energy split, or downstream coordination arrangements. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25

pages.title: Tamakoshi V
headings: The Cascade Model — Paired with Upper Tamakoshi
pages.excerpt: Tamakoshi V is a downstream cascade project of Upper Tamakoshi, developed as an under-construction NEA-linked asset with revised capacity figures across registry and NEA/JICA sources.
pages.body_text: Tamakoshi V # Summary Tamakoshi V is a downstream cascade project of Upper Tamakoshi, developed as an under-construction NEA-linked asset with revised capacity figures across registry and NEA/JICA sources. 99.8 MW · under construction · on the Tama Koshi · in Dolakha district. A cascade project of upper-tamakoshi (456 MW), designed to operate in tandem with Nepal's largest power plant. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 87 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Tama Koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Dolakha | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (NEA / JICA IPSDP data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | Current capacity | 99.8 MW (revised from earlier 87 MW plan) | Developer | Tamakoshi Jalvidyut Company Limited (TKJVCL) | Financing | Employers Provident Fund (EPF) | Construction progress | 15.34% (as of FY 2024/25) | Design discharge | 66 m³/s | Catchment area | 2,153 km² | Headrace tunnel | 8.2 km | Cascade position | Downstream of upper-tamakoshi (456 MW PROR) | Location | Bigu Rural Municipality, Dolakha District | RCOD (target) | 2025/2026 per JICA IPSDP | [!note] Capacity revision. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Tamakoshi V at 87 MW — the originally surveyed capacity. NEA and JICA IPSDP narrative sections confirm the project is now developed at 99.8 MW. The NEA licence table records 94.8 MW (94,800 kW) as an interim licence figure. This narrative follows the 99.8 MW confirmed development capacity. # The Cascade Model — Paired with Upper Tamakoshi Tamakoshi V is the first cascade project explicitly designed to operate in tandem with upper-tamakoshi. At 99.8 MW, it captures energy from the tailwater discharge of the 456 MW PROR powerhouse upstream — effectively extracting additional generation from the same Tama Koshi water that has already passed through Upper Tamakoshi's turbines. This cascade pairing is structurally significant for three reasons: 1. Hydrological efficiency: Instead of spilling Upper Tamakoshi's tailwater, Tamakoshi V captures it for secondary generation. This is the same cascade principle as the kulekhani-cascade, but at 10× the scale. 2. Shared transmission: Tamakoshi V plugs into the same New Khimti → Khimti-Dhalkebar 220/400 kV evacuation corridor that Upper Tamakoshi depends on. The corridor's 400 kV GIS building and transformer banks at New Khimti were designed with this combined load in mind. 3. Operational interdependence: Any curtailment, maintenance shutdown, or flood closure at Upper Tamakoshi immediately zeroes Tamakoshi V's inflow. The downstream plant is not an independent asset — it is a rider on the upstream plant's operational schedule. This interdependence is not captured in standalone PPA terms. # The EPF Financing Model Tamakoshi V is financed by Nepal's Employers Provident Fund (EPF) — the country's largest pension fund. This marks a departure from the commercial bank consortium model that dominates private IPP financing. The EPF model carries distinct structural implications: Long-term liability matching: EPF's pension obligations span decades, making its capital well-suited to infrastructure with long depreciation schedules. Commercial banks struggle with the 15-year tenors typical of hydro lending. Lower cost of capital: As a mandatory social security institution, EPF can deploy capital at rates below commercial lending — reducing the project's DSCR pressure relative to commercially-financed IPPs of equivalent scale. Public accountability: EPF's investment decisions are ultimately answerable to Nepal's workforce. The financial performance of Tamakoshi V will directly affect millions of pension accounts — a political dimension absent from private bank consortiums. Precedent value: If Tamakoshi V succeeds under EPF financing, it establishes a template for domestic institutional capital to fund Nepal's hydropower pipeline without the currency risk and short tenors of international project finance. # The NEA Subsidiary Ecosystem Tamakoshi Jalvidyut Company Limited (TKJVCL) sits within the same NEA subsidiary architecture that produced upper-tamakoshi (via UKHLL), but with a distinct developer entity and financing source. The relationship: Project | Capacity | Developer | Financing | Status | ---|---|---|---|---| upper-tamakoshi | 456 MW | Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Ltd. (UKHLL) | Consortium (NEA + EPF + NTC + others) | Operating (2021) | Tamakoshi V | 99.8 MW | Tamakoshi Jalvidyut Company Ltd. (TKJVCL) | EPF | Under construction | tamakoshi-3 | 650 MW | TBI Holding Co. Ltd. | — | Survey | The Tama Koshi basin in Dolakha now carries three NEA-linked projects at different delivery stages — from the operating 456 MW anchor to the 650 MW survey-stage aspirational — with Tamakoshi V as the bridge asset connecting current operations to future basin expansion. # Construction Status As of the NEA FY 2024/25 annual report, Tamakoshi V has reached 15.34% construction progress. Key milestones: Contractor's camp near headworks and powerhouse area completed Bunker near headworks area completed Batching and crusher plant installed and operational Road access from Singati Bazar (near Upper Tamakoshi) established The project's RCOD target under the JICA IPSDP milestone ladder is 2025/2026, though current progress suggests a realistic completion window beyond that date. The NEA annual report lists Tamakoshi V alongside Trishuli 3B (37 MW), Rolwaling (22 MW), and Upper Modi (60 MW) as NEA-linked projects "in different stages of construction." # Transmission and Corridor Risk Tamakoshi V shares the Tama Koshi transmission corridor with the largest concentration of generation capacity in Nepal. The New Khimti substation — originally sized for Upper Tamakoshi (456 MW) — now serves the entire Likhu cascade (213 MW) plus Tamakoshi V (99.8 MW), for a combined corridor load exceeding 768 MW. The 200 MVA auto-transformer upgrade completed in late 2023 (which resolved likhu-2's stranded generation crisis) was a necessary but not sufficient fix. As Tamakoshi V approaches COD, the corridor will face renewed capacity pressure — and the cascade interdependence with Upper Tamakoshi means any upstream NEA dispatch decision directly determines Tamakoshi V's revenue. # Cascade Interdependence and Risk The tandem operation model — Tamakoshi V catching Upper Tamakoshi's tailwater — is hydrologically elegant but operationally fragile: Upstream curtailment: If NLDC curtails Upper Tamakoshi for grid stability, Tamakoshi V's inflow drops to zero. The downstream PPA contains no compensation mechanism for upstream operational decisions by the same NEA that signs both contracts. Flood exposure: The September 2024 flood that shut Upper Tamakoshi for 88 days (reducing generation to 67% of design) would have zeroed Tamakoshi V for the same period. Unlike chilime's snow-fed buffer, the Tama Koshi is a high-discharge monsoon system with extreme seasonal volatility. Single corridor dependency: A transformer failure at New Khimti strands both plants simultaneously — 555.8 MW of combined NEA-subsidiary generation offline in a single event. See buildability and stranded-generation. # Limitations & Controversies The page reconciles multiple public capacity figures but still depends on source snapshots for progress, RCOD, corridor loading, and cascade-operation risk; it does not replace updated project-company disclosures, lender reporting, or dispatch data. # See also upper-tamakoshi — upstream 456 MW anchor plant tamakoshi-3 — 650 MW survey-stage project in the same basin koshi-basin — basin context buildability — transmission planning and corridor risk stranded-generation — the evacuation bottleneck problem q-design-discharge — design discharge and contracted energy khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — shared 220/400 kV backbone likhu-2 — same corridor, stranded generation precedent

pages.title: Tamor Storage
pages.excerpt: Tamor Storage is a 200 MW survey-stage storage hydropower project on the Tamor River in eastern Nepal.
pages.body_text: Tamor Storage # Summary Tamor Storage is a 200 MW survey-stage storage hydropower project on the Tamor River in eastern Nepal. Tamor Storage is a proposed 200 MW storage hydropower project on the Tamor River in eastern Nepal, currently at the survey/study stage. # Storage Value Storage hydropower is the critical missing piece in Nepal's generation portfolio. Run-of-river projects dominate the fleet — they produce abundant energy during the monsoon but collapse during the dry season when system demand peaks. See storage-deficit and seasonal-mismatch. Tamor Storage, at 200 MW with a reservoir, would provide firm, dispatchable capacity to the eastern grid — the kind of generation that can be scheduled to meet evening peak demand in the dry winter months. This is fundamentally different from the run-of-river model where output is at the mercy of seasonal hydrology. # Development Hurdles Storage projects in Nepal face three compounding challenges: 1. Geology: Dam sites in the young, seismically active Himalaya require extensive investigation 2. Resettlement: Reservoirs displace communities, creating political and social costs that run-of-river projects avoid 3. Financing: Storage projects have higher capital costs and longer construction timelines, requiring a PPA framework that compensates firm capacity — not just energy (kWh) The ERC's 2026 directive on reservoir-based power plants attempts to address this by transitioning large projects to a cost-plus determination model, explicitly allowing developers to factor in loan interest, depreciation, and foreign exchange risk. See nea-triple-authority. # System Context In a system increasingly saturated with monsoon-heavy run-of-river generation, Tamor Storage's value lies not in its annual energy contribution but in its seasonal firmness. A 200 MW reservoir that can deliver into the dry-season evening peak would have outsized system value compared to a 200 MW run-of-river project that adds to the monsoon surplus. See firm-power and solar-hydro-complementarity for the integrated portfolio argument. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 200 MW | Status | Survey / study | Registry licence | Survey | River | Tamor (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Panchthar | Province | Province No 1 | # Limitations & Controversies The page describes the project from registry and IPSDP context and does not confirm a final dam design, reservoir boundary, resettlement footprint, financing model, tariff treatment, or construction timeline. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower storage-deficit firm-power # Sources moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025

pages.title: Tanahu Hydropower Project
pages.excerpt: A 140 MW storage-type reservoir scheme on the Seti River and the most advanced large reservoir project under construction in Nepal. The NEA FY 2024/25 baseline reported about 67% physical progress; a later April 2026 public update reported roughly 75%. ADB's current project recor
pages.body_text: Tanahu Hydropower Project # Summary A 140 MW storage-type reservoir scheme on the Seti River and the most advanced large reservoir project under construction in Nepal. The NEA FY 2024/25 baseline reported about 67% physical progress; a later April 2026 public update reported roughly 75%. ADB's current project record also exposes audited financial statements, contract utilisation and environmental and social monitoring, allowing progress to be tracked by package rather than by a single headline percentage. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 140 MW | Status | Under construction — ~67% NEA FY 2024/25 baseline; ~75% April 2026 public update | River | Seti (gandaki-basin) | District | Tanahu | ## Engineering A 140 m RCC dam with an underground powerhouse — the only large dam-and-reservoir project actually in active construction in Nepal. Tanahu is proof-of-concept: if it completes, dudhkoshi-storage and budhigandaki become easier to finance because the conversation no longer begins "Nepal has never built a large reservoir since 1982." Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | 140 m | Dam type | RCC | Underground powerhouse | Yes | Type | Storage | Owner | nea | ## Governance ADB-financed, NEA-owned, and shadowed by two Accountability Mechanism complaints (2024 and 2025) over land and buffer-zone compensation. The complaints flag untitled-land registration, free prior informed consent, and demarcation issues. See buildability. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Lead financier | Asian Development Bank | Developer | NEA | ## Schedule Roughly 67% complete in the NEA FY 2024/25 reporting baseline, with a later public progress update placing it around 75% in April 2026. The ADB record shows that the original loan closing dates were revised to 30 June 2026; package milestones and commissioning evidence should be used instead of extrapolating a completion date from the headline percentage. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Completion | ~67% in NEA FY 2024/25; ~75% in Apr 2026 public update | # Current Status As of 10 July 2026: under construction. The ADB project remains active and publishes financial, procurement and safeguard records. The wiki does not treat the April 2026 percentage as proof of commissioning or infer a commercial-operation date from it. Dimension | Current position | Evidence | ---|---|---| Physical delivery | Major packages under construction; roughly 75% in the April public update | tanahu-progress-2026 | Finance | Active ADB project; FY 2024/25 audited project statements disclosed January 2026 | ADB project documents | Safeguards | Ninth Panel of Experts report disclosed April 2026 | ADB project documents | Operation | Not commissioned | Project monitoring record | # Recent Updates Date | Update | ---|---| Apr 2026 | ADB disclosed the ninth environmental and social Panel of Experts report | Apr 2026 | Public progress update placed overall physical progress at approximately 75% | Jan 2026 | ADB disclosed audited project financial statements for FY 2024/25 | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Monitoring basis | ---|---|---| Remaining package and integration works | Commissioning | Package-level construction record | Land, compensation and environmental-management issues | Completion with safeguard compliance | Current ADB monitoring and Panel of Experts reports | Schedule slippage beyond earlier loan dates | Reliable commercial-operation forecast | Revised ADB timetable | # Significance Tanahu matters less for its nameplate 140 MW and more as proof of concept — is Nepal capable of delivering a large reservoir project at all, on a reasonable timeline, with multilateral financing? Until Tanahu commissions, the only operating storage plant in the country is kulekhani-cascade (106 MW). Tanahu will nearly triple the storage fleet on day one. The strategic implication cascades upward. If Tanahu completes, dudhkoshi-storage (670 MW) and budhigandaki (1200 MW) become easier to finance: the next multilateral conversation no longer begins "Nepal has never actually built a large reservoir since 1982." If Tanahu fails — especially on the social-compliance dimension the Accountability Mechanism is reviewing — future large storage proposals will carry that memory as a risk premium. Compare Tanahu (140 MW, reservoir, ADB, domestic) to arun-3 (900 MW, peaking RoR, SJVN-India, export-oriented). Both are under construction but solve different problems: Tanahu addresses dry-season firm-power for Nepal; Arun-3 adds monsoon export capacity to India. Nepal's structural energy problem is the former, not the latter. # Limitations & Controversies Social-compliance complaints. The 2024 and 2025 Accountability Mechanism filings are the visible surface of a harder question: can a large reservoir in the middle hills be executed with buffer-zone demarcation, untitled-land registration, and free prior informed consent done properly? Current complaints flag all three. ADB accepted the 2025 complaint for eligibility review in April. Schedule discipline. Roughly 67% physical progress after ~10 years of construction is slower than comparable multilateral-financed projects elsewhere; a later April 2026 public update put progress around 75%. Each additional year compounds NEA's dry-season firm-power exposure, since the entire medium-term planning rationale for Tanahu depends on it arriving before the seasonal-mismatch pressure peaks. Not a basin-scale answer. Even at full output, Tanahu cannot close the dry-season gap on its own. It is one node in a portfolio that would need Dudh Koshi Storage, Budhi Gandaki or similar scale to operate alongside. Framing Tanahu as "the storage solution" sets up disappointment; framing it as "the first storage receipt" sets up a reasonable expectation. # Official Visual References Tanahu's current public photo trail is still messy from a reuse and licensing standpoint, but the project overview deck circulated by Tanahu Hydropower Limited in 2016 does include two official visuals that are materially better than generic Seti River scenery. Project location map from the THL overview deck. General layout slide from the same deck. Source: An Overview of Tanahu Hydropower Project (PDF) # Related storage-deficit — what Tanahu begins to address buildability — Tanahu's progress suggests storage is difficult but not impossible kulekhani-cascade — the only current storage asset firm-power dudhkoshi-storage budhigandaki # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Cross-Border View With Projects data-map-inventory # Sources adb-tanahu-project-documents-2026 tanahu-adb-status-2025 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 nea-transmission-annual-book-2077

[!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 45 states that Tingla substation (132/33 kV, 30 MVA) was commissioned on Bhadra 07, 2076, and identifies it as part of the Solu Corridor 132 kV transmission line project. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132/33 kV | Capacity | 30 MVA | Status in 2020 book | Commissioned | Corridor | Solu Corridor 132 kV | Upstream line noted | Mirchaiya–Tingla 132 kV double circuit, ~90 km | # Why It Matters Tingla is a concrete example of the smaller corridor substations that had to exist before generation in eastern hill basins could actually reach the grid. It belongs in the same “transmission before value” story as claim-transmission-immediate-blocker and the later nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 synthesis. # Limitations & Controversies The page confirms the annual-book commissioning record and basic rating, but it does not establish current transformer loading, bay configuration, outage history, or subsequent upgrades after the 2020 source snapshot. # See also solu sahas-urja claim-transmission-immediate-blocker nepal-transmission-landscape-2025

pages.title: Trishuli Cascade
pages.excerpt: Trishuli Cascade is a corridor overview page for operating, under-construction, and survey-stage hydropower projects along the Trishuli River.
pages.body_text: Trishuli Cascade # Summary Trishuli Cascade is a corridor overview page for operating, under-construction, and survey-stage hydropower projects along the Trishuli River. The Trishuli River is Nepal's most heavily developed hydropower corridor, benefiting from proximity to Kathmandu's load center and well-established transmission infrastructure. Starting from the original 1967 Trishuli plant, the corridor has accumulated layers of development across different licensing eras, sponsors, and ownership models (NEA-owned, subsidiary, and private IPP). # Plants in the Cascade Plant | Capacity (MW) | Status | Ownership | -------|--------------|--------|-----------| Upper Trishuli-I Cascade HEP | 24.6 | Survey | — | upper-trishuli-1 | 216 | Under construction | IPP | upper-trishuli-3a | 60 | Under construction | NEA | upper-trishuli-3b | 37 | Under construction | Subsidiary (Trishuli Jal Vidyut Co.) | trishuli-galchhi | 75 | Under construction | IPP | super-trishuli | 100 | Under construction | IPP | trishuli (Devighat) | 24 | Operating | NEA | Trishuli Khola | 4.4 | Survey | — | Total | ~540.6 | | | # Corridor Significance The Trishuli-Gandaki corridor is the backbone of central Nepal's generation. Projects in this corridor supply directly to Kathmandu's load center via the shortest transmission paths in the country. The corridor road (Pasang Lhamu Highway / Prithvi Highway) provides construction access, and the established marsyangdi-upper-220 and trishuli-galchhi transmission infrastructure provides evacuation. A persistent analytical challenge: upper-trishuli-3b (37 MW, subsidiary) is frequently conflated with upper-trishuli-3a (60 MW, NEA-owned) — they are separate assets with different promoters and PPAs on adjacent reaches of the Trishuli. # Concentration Risk The corridor's density concentrates systemic risk: geological events, sediment surges, or flow alterations from upstream projects cascade through the entire system. The September 2024 floods demonstrated how a single extreme event can affect multiple plants simultaneously. # Related Corridors The Trishuli River is a tributary of the Narayani/Gandaki system (see gandaki-basin). The adjacent Bhote Koshi corridor (rasuwagadhi, madhya-bhotekoshi, upper-bhotekoshi) shares transmission infrastructure and Chilime-group sponsorship patterns with several Trishuli projects via the chilime-trishuli-220kv-transmission-line. # Limitations & Controversies The cascade table combines projects at different evidence levels and status stages, so it should be treated as a corridor orientation page rather than a reconciled hydrology, licensing, or cumulative-impact assessment. # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # See also upper-trishuli-3a upper-trishuli-3b — frequently confused with 3A upper-trishuli-1 super-trishuli trishuli trishuli-galchhi gandaki-basin chilime-trishuli-220kv-transmission-line

pages.title: Trishuli Galchhi
headings: The Trishuli Corridor — Nepal's Densest River
Low-Head Design — a Different Engineering Profile
pages.excerpt: Trishuli Galchhi is a 75 MW under-construction low-head run-of-river project on the Trishuli River in Nuwakot, developed by Siddhakali Power within Api Power's portfolio.
pages.body_text: Trishuli Galchhi # Summary Trishuli Galchhi is a 75 MW under-construction low-head run-of-river project on the Trishuli River in Nuwakot, developed by Siddhakali Power within Api Power's portfolio. 75 MW · generation licence recorded · on the Trishuli River · in Nuwakot district. Construction status is tracked separately from the regulatory licence. Nepal's densest river corridor, less than two hours from Kathmandu. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 75 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Nuwakot | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 doed-licensing-directive-2075 # Specifications (Developer / regulatory data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river, low-head | Developer | Siddhakali Power Ltd (~80% Api Power Company Ltd subsidiary) | Generating units | 2 × 44 MW (likely Kaplan turbines) | Gross head | ~58.5 m (net ~49–60 m) | Design discharge | 176 m³/s | Dam | 24.5 m barrage, 8 × 12 m radial gates | Headrace tunnel | 8.15 km | Contract energy | ~430 GWh/yr | Project cost | NPR 14.40 billion | Debt / equity | ~70:30 | Financing consortium | Laxmi Bank (lead) | PPA | 30-year, signed June 2, 2016 | PPA rates | NPR 4.80/kWh (wet) / NPR 8.40/kWh (dry) | PPA terms | 80% take-or-pay, 3% × 8yr escalation | RCOD (PPA) | May 2020 | ICRA Grade | 4 (Api Power, 2016) | CARE-NP issuer rating | B- (Api Power, 2022) | # The Trishuli Corridor — Nepal's Densest River Trishuli Galchhi sits on the single most hydropower-dense river in Nepal. From the original 24 MW trishuli plant (1967) to the 216 MW upper-trishuli-1 upstream, the Trishuli corridor now hosts roughly 540 MW of cumulative capacity across generation-licensed, under-construction, and operating projects — including upper-trishuli-3a (60 MW), upper-trishuli-3b (37 MW), and multiple smaller plants. See trishuli-cascade for the full corridor profile. The corridor's defining advantage is proximity: the Kathmandu load center is under 50 km away, meaning minimal transmission losses and no dependence on the Khimti–Dhalkebar trunk that bottlenecks eastern-basin projects. Trishuli Galchhi's location in Nuwakot district, directly abutting the Kathmandu Valley's northern edge, makes it one of the most strategically sited projects in the pipeline. # Low-Head Design — a Different Engineering Profile At 58.5 m gross head with Kaplan turbines and 176 m³/s design discharge, Trishuli Galchhi represents a fundamentally different engineering philosophy from the high-head Pelton plants that dominate Nepal's private IPP pipeline. What low-head means for this project: High unit flow, low head. Unlike a 400 m-head Pelton project that funnels a small jet of water through a narrow penstock, Trishuli Galchhi must move 176 m³/s of water through a large-diameter 8.15 km headrace tunnel. Civil works are proportionally larger — the intake, desilting basin, tunnel diameter, and powerhouse tailrace all scale with discharge volume, not head. Run-of-river in the truest sense. A 24.5 m barrage dam with 8 × 12 m radial gates operates as a river-level diversion — no significant storage, no reservoir pondage beyond diurnal regulation. The plant's output tracks river flow almost in real time, making it more exposed to seasonal hydrology than plants with small pondage or peaking reservoirs. Lower cost per MW — in theory. At ~NPR 14.40 billion (NPR 192M/MW), the capital cost per megawatt is at the lower end of the benchmark range. Low-head plants trade expensive steel penstocks and surge shafts for large concrete volumes and extensive tunnel systems. The 70:30 debt-equity ratio reflects a conventional consortium structure where lower per-MW cost keeps absolute equity commitments manageable. Kaplan turbines for the 2 × 44 MW units are the correct choice for the head range: double-regulated (adjustable runner blades and wicket gates) to maintain efficiency across fluctuating river flows. This is technically sound but adds mechanical complexity and maintenance cost compared to simple Pelton runners. # Api Power's Portfolio Play Trishuli Galchhi is not a standalone project but part of Api Power Company Ltd's broader portfolio buildout. Through the Siddhakali Power Ltd SPV (~80% Api Power equity), the project sits alongside other Api Power assets including Upper Naugarh Gad (8 MW). The CARE-NP B- issuer rating assigned to Api Power in 2022 tells the portfolio story. A B- rating — four notches below investment grade — reflects significant financial stress at the holding-company level: Multiple concurrent under-construction exposures across the portfolio strain developer equity commitments. A developer simultaneously funding several SPVs faces disproportionate liquidity pressure during construction delays (which Trishuli Galchhi has experienced). Concentrated river risk. Api Power's portfolio is geographically concentrated, exposing its aggregate revenue to the same hydrological and regulatory corridor dynamics. The ICRA Grade 4 from 2016 pre-dated the financial stress and is now six years stale — it predates the portfolio's construction-phase accumulations and the 2019–2023 interest rate cycle that strained leveraged IPP developers across Nepal. The Laxmi Bank-led consortium financing structure is conventional by Nepali IPP standards, but the developer's credit profile matters more for construction-phase lenders than for operational-phase debt service. If construction delays compress rainy-season generation before the loan repayment clock starts, the project's economics tighten immediately. # Construction Delay Risk The original PPA filing set RCOD at May 2020 — a date that has clearly passed without commissioning. Six years from projected completion with no public progress reports suggests at least a 4–5 year delay, consistent with patterns at dozens of Nepali IPP projects that encountered post-2015 earthquake reconstruction costs, COVID-era construction interruptions, COVID-era supply chain disruptions, and the protracted equity-raising timeline typical of lower-credit developers. No recent progress reports or construction milestone disclosures have been found for Trishuli Galchhi. The absence of contractor information, verified completion percentages, or an updated commissioning target in the public record is itself a data point: projects nearing COD tend to produce disclosure, while projects stuck in mid-construction tend to produce silence. # Cascade Context — Sharing the Trishuli Trishuli Galchhi shares the river with some of Nepal's most prominent projects: Upstream: upper-trishuli-1 (216 MW) is the cascade's dominant project, with a different developer consortium (Korea South-East Power, Nepal Water & Energy Development Company) and a far more complex engineering profile. Parallel and downstream: upper-trishuli-3a (60 MW) and upper-trishuli-3b (37 MW) operate in the same reach, with interlinked hydrology. Downstream: The original trishuli plant (24 MW, 1967) is Nepal's second-oldest operating hydropower asset and remains in service under NEA operation — a living piece of Nepal's hydropower history at the bottom of the cascade. Unlike the Likhu cascade (trishuli-cascade), the Trishuli corridor is not dominated by a single developer or lending group. It is a competitive corridor with multiple developers, multiple contractor groups, and varying technical approaches — from high-head tunnels (Upper Trishuli-1) to low-head barrages (Trishuli Galchhi) to medium-head plants (3A/3B). This diversity is a strength in normal operations but a coordination challenge during extreme hydrological events where upstream gates affect downstream head. # Limitations & Controversies The page draws together developer, rating, PPA, and registry context, but public progress disclosures are limited; current construction percentage, revised COD, contractor status, and updated financing position remain unverified here. # See also trishuli-cascade — corridor overview and cumulative capacity context upper-trishuli-1 — upstream 216 MW cascade leader upper-trishuli-3a — 60 MW project in the same reach upper-trishuli-3b — 37 MW project in the same reach trishuli — 1967 original plant, 24 MW NEA-operated pioneer gandaki-basin — basin context

pages.title: Trishuli
headings: The Heritage Plant — 58 Years and Counting
60% of Design — The Fleeting Rehab Benefit
pages.excerpt: Repair of generator side covers during overhauling Stator of unit-2 during overhauling
pages.body_text: Trishuli Repair of generator side covers during overhauling Stator of unit-2 during overhauling Samundratar 132/33 kV Substation # Summary 24 MW · operating · on the Trishuli · in Nuwakot district. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 24 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Nuwakot | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Trishuli is Nepal's oldest operating hydropower plant, commissioned in 1967 with Indian government funding. Originally 21 MW (7 × 3 MW units), it was rehabilitated in 1995 to 24 MW with six 3.5 MW Francis units and one 3 MW standby unit. As a peaking run-of-river plant on the Trishuli River in Nuwakot, it has anchored the Kathmandu Valley grid for nearly six decades. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Peaking run-of-river (PROR) | Original capacity (1967) | 21 MW (7 × 3 MW) | Current capacity (post-1995 rehab) | 24 MW (6 × 3.5 MW + 1 × 3 MW standby) | Peaking capacity | 21 MWh | Design generation | 163 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 97.7 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 60.0% | FY 2081/82 vs target | 81% | Year-over-year change | −17% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 6,031.9 GWh | District | Nuwakot, Bagmati Province | In FY 2081/82, Trishuli completed significant rehabilitation work: a 10 MVA (66/11 kV) and an 18 MVA (6.6/66 kV) transformer were installed, tested, and commissioned. A 6.6 kV, 3000A switchgear and a 400V, 300A LT AC panel were also commissioned. The auto guide vane closing system was modernized and redesigned across all units for improved overspeed protection — a critical safety upgrade for a plant running 1960s turbine hardware. Powerhouse maintenance covered rotor shaft work on Unit 1, bearing repairs on Units 2, 5, and 6, MIV repair on Unit 2, and oil cooler installation on Unit 1. # The Heritage Plant — 58 Years and Counting Trishuli was commissioned when Nepal's grid barely existed. At 21 MW, it was the first major power source serving Kathmandu — and for years, it was the grid. Over 58 years, it has accumulated 6,031.9 GWh of lifetime generation, roughly a third of kali-gandaki-a's lifetime output from one-sixth the capacity, purely because it has been running for 35 more years. The 1995 rehabilitation — from 21 to 24 MW — was Nepal's first major hydropower upgrade. The current rehabilitation program (transformers, switchgear, digital governors, overspeed protection) is the second round. At 58 years, the question is not whether Trishuli needs another rehab but whether the electromechanical core — turbine runners, generator windings, penstock integrity — can sustain another upgrade cycle or whether the plant is approaching end of economic life. This is the aging-fleet extreme case. Every rehabilitation argument applied to kali-gandaki-a (22 years old) and marsyangdi (36 years old) applies to Trishuli at nearly triple the age. The plant that Nepal's grid was built around is also the plant that demonstrates, more starkly than any other, what Himalayan hydro looks like at 60 — and whether another round of rehab is technically possible, financially justified, or a signal that NEA needs a replacement strategy for its oldest assets. # 60% of Design — The Fleeting Rehab Benefit Trishuli's 60% design-performance ratio is the lowest in the NEA fleet. At 97.7 GWh from a 163 GWh design, the rehab that raised capacity from 21 to 24 MW in 1995 did not prevent progressive output decline. The 17% year-over-year drop (FY 2080/81 to 2081/82) suggests the decline is continuing. This is the structural problem: a 60% PLF at 24 MW compares unfavorably with even the private IPP median. The current rehab — new transformers, digital switchgear, modernized overspeed protection — addresses electrical and control infrastructure but does not touch the hydraulic core: turbine runners, guide vanes, penstock lining, intake structure. Those are the components where 58 years of sediment-laden Himalayan river flow accumulates surface wear and geometric erosion. The parallel is chameliya-hydropower: a plant built at extreme cost that underperforms due to engineering failures. Trishuli is the inverse — a plant built at low cost for its era that is now underperforming due to decades of normal wear. Both end up in the same place: a generation asset that delivers substantially below what the nameplate promises. See claim-mw-not-equal-value. # Limitations & Controversies Aging-fleet extreme case. At 58 years, Trishuli is Nepal's oldest operating hydropower plant. The 1995 rehabilitation raised capacity from 21 to 24 MW, but FY 2081/82 generation was only 60% of design (97.7 GWh vs 163 GWh). The current rehab addresses electrical infrastructure but not the hydraulic core — turbine runners, guide vanes, penstock lining — where 58 years of sediment-laden Himalayan flow accumulates wear. End-of-economic-life uncertainty. The question is not whether Trishuli needs another rehab but whether the electromechanical core can sustain another upgrade cycle. At some point, replacement becomes cheaper than continued rehabilitation, but no public replacement strategy exists. Progressive output decline. The 17% year-over-year drop (FY 2080/81 to 2081/82) suggests the decline is continuing. Even after rehab, Trishuli's 60% PLF is the lowest in the NEA fleet and compares unfavorably with the private IPP median. Rehab does not address hydraulic wear. New transformers, switchgear, and digital governors improve reliability and safety but do not restore the turbine hydraulic efficiency lost to decades of sediment abrasion. This is a fundamental limitation of electrical-only rehabilitation on aging Himalayan plants. # See also kali-gandaki-a — the next plant in the aging-fleet trajectory marsyangdi — 36-year-old fleet anchor, approaching its own rehab decision chameliya-hydropower — the construction-failure counterpoint claim-mw-not-equal-value — nameplate vs delivered energy buildability — execution risk across the project lifecycle gandaki-basin — basin context; the Trishuli feeds the Narayani run-of-river-hydropower

pages.excerpt: Udipur-Damauli-Bharatpur 220 kV Reinforcement is represented in the map as a RAP-backed Udipur-Markichowk-Bharatpur corridor trace for lower Marsyangdi evacuation.
pages.body_text: Udipur-Damauli-Bharatpur 220 kV Reinforcement # Summary Udipur-Damauli-Bharatpur 220 kV Reinforcement is represented in the map as a RAP-backed Udipur-Markichowk-Bharatpur corridor trace for lower Marsyangdi evacuation. The Udipur-Damauli-Bharatpur 220 kV reinforcement is the lower Marsyangdi evacuation route from the Udipur area toward Bharatpur/Aptari. In the map it is represented as the source-backed Udipur-Markichowk-Bharatpur line because that is the route basis stated in the recovered NEA Marsyangdi RAP. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 220 kV | Status | Under construction | Corridor ID | | Public map feature | | Source basis | NEA Marsyangdi RAP pages 22-24 | Official route length | 64.45 km | Traced network length | 65.311 km | Validation delta | +1.34% | # Map Interpretation This corridor is now represented by a single RAP-backed trace in the connected transmission layer. It replaces the older RPGCL overview extraction, which showed the same corridor as many disconnected fragments. The trace should be read as a corridor-level alignment, not a tower-by-tower engineering route. The RAP text gives 64.45 route-km, while the project map labels the same Udipur-Markichowk-Bharatpur line as 67 km. The current map trace falls inside that source envelope. # Confidence Public decision: default-visible, high confidence. The confidence comes from three checks: the route is backed by a project RAP, the public feature has no inferred connectors, and the traced length is within 2% of the RAP route-length basis. # Limitations & Controversies Khudi-Udipur is not forced into this corridor. It should remain a separate scope item unless a route-grade source confirms that it belongs in this segment rather than in the upper Marsyangdi package. # See also marsyangdi-upper-220 mca-central-400 data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network claim-transmission-immediate-blocker

pages.body_text: Upper Arun Hydroelectric Project ERT survey at IkhuwaKhola HPP (IKHPP) Core Drilling at JawaTila # Summary Upper Arun is a 1,063.36 MW peaking run-of-river hydropower project in Bhotkhola Rural Municipality, Sankhuwasabha, promoted through Upper Arun Hydro-Electric Limited, an NEA subsidiary. The project has moved beyond the older FY 2019/20 study-stage description: UAHEL now publishes current project parameters, including rated discharge, rated head, average annual energy, a 400 kV evacuation link to Haitar, and a target schedule that enters construction in 2026 and reaches completion in December 2032. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Across book pages 113–116, NEA frames Upper Arun as a priority project with access-road work, feasibility optimization, project-location mapping, and draft engineering preparation still underway. [!cite] uahel-upper-arun-project UAHEL lists Upper Arun as 1,063.36 MW including a 2.36 MW eco-flow plant, with average annual energy of 4,518 GWh excluding eco-flow generation and year-round minimum peaking of 697 MW for six hours daily at Q95 inflow. # Specifications Field | Value | ---|---| Project type | Peaking run-of-river | Location | Bhotkhola Rural Municipality, Sankhuwasabha District, Koshi Province | Installed capacity | 1,063.36 MW, including 2.36 MW eco-flow plant | Rated discharge | 235.44 m3/s | Rated head | 508.26 m | Average annual energy | 4,518 GWh, excluding 18 GWh from eco-flow turbine | Minimum peaking | 697 MW for six hours daily at Q95 inflow | Main generation units | Six Pelton turbines | Evacuation plan | 5.8 km 400 kV double-circuit line to Haitar substation | Target construction entry | 2026 | Target completion | December 2032 | # Why It Matters Upper Arun is a good example of how long the pipeline is between identifying a large Himalayan project and reaching bankable execution. It belongs with arun-3 and nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 because any future Upper Arun build would need both project delivery and corridor evacuation to line up. Its peaking design makes it materially different from ordinary run-of-river MW in the Arun basin, though this does not remove financing, access-road, environmental, and evacuation risks. # Limitations & Controversies Preparation-stage schedule. UAHEL publishes a target construction start in 2026 and target completion in December 2032, but those are project targets rather than evidence of financial closure, PPA execution, or construction commencement. Corridor dependency. Any future Upper Arun build would need both project delivery and corridor evacuation to line up with arun-3 infrastructure and the nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 backbone. The project cannot advance independently of these larger system decisions. Developer-source boundary. The current specifications come from UAHEL's own project page. They should be cross-checked against NEA annual reports, DoED license records, lender documents, and environmental approvals before being treated as final bankable parameters. # See also arun-3 nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 nea # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 uahel-upper-arun-project

pages.body_text: Upper Bhotekoshi # Summary Upper Bhotekoshi is a 45 MW operating Bhote Koshi run-of-river project used in the wiki as a high-confidence operating marker in the priority-watchlist layer. Upper Bhotekoshi is a 45 MW operating project on the Bhote Koshi in Sindhupalchok. It is pinned in the data-layer-priority-watchlist not because it is large, but because it is a useful reality-check marker: an existing high-gradient Koshi-basin plant where the river valley, operating status, and project geography are legible. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 45 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Bhote Koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Sindhupalchok | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Why It Matters Upper Bhotekoshi is part of the operating hydro fleet that grounds the wiki's map layers in real assets rather than only future projects. It shows the classic Himalayan run-of-river logic: steep relief, compact valley geometry, and generation that depends on river flow rather than large seasonal storage. Its watchlist role is methodological. When the map displays dozens of survey-stage records, Upper Bhotekoshi is one of the markers that helps calibrate what an operating point looks like in the source data. # Status And Timing The project is already operating. There is no construction-start or finish-date issue to track in this layer context. The relevant updates are operational performance, outage history, flood/sediment exposure, and how Bhote Koshi valley generation connects into the eastern grid. # Map Interpretation The marker is an operating-project registry point near the mapped river and is labeled as a higher-confidence site point in the priority-watchlist layer. # Limitations & Controversies The page confirms operating status and map role but does not provide a full outage history, sediment/flood exposure record, annual generation series, ownership history, or detailed evacuation-connection assessment. # Registry note Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # See also koshi-basin run-of-river-hydropower stranded-generation data-layer-priority-watchlist

pages.title: Upper Karnali
headings: The GMR Saga: Timeline of an Unbuilt Project
pages.excerpt: A 900 MW export-oriented project with a revised partner structure but no verified financial close, disbursement or construction start.
pages.body_text: Upper Karnali # Summary A 900 MW run-of-river scheme on the Karnali, awarded to GMR in 2008 and still at an early, pre-construction stage. The project has a revised partner structure but no verified achieved financial close, disbursement or construction commencement. A June 2026 ICRA rationale records GMR 34%, SJVN 34%, IREDA 5% and NEA 27%, while continuing to describe the project as being at a very early stage of development. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 900 MW | Status | Stalled / pre-construction; financial close not verified | River | Karnali (karnali-basin) | Districts | Surkhet, Dailekh, Achham | Province | Karnali Pradesh | Licence awarded | 2008, via international competitive bidding | ## Engineering Upper Karnali is a run-of-river diversion scheme on the Karnali main stem — the same engineering archetype as arun-3 but in the western Karnali basin. At 900 MW, it would be the second-largest RoR plant in Nepal after Arun-3. The project's engineering challenge is not the head or flow regime (the Karnali has reliable hydrology) but the transmission distance: 900 MW from the mid-Karnali to the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur export corridor requires a new 400 kV transmission spine through western Nepal. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-River | Annual design energy | 3,466 GWh | Planned export share | ~88% | ## Output Design annual energy is reported at approximately 3,466 GWh, with a large export orientation. Public statements have cited several possible Bangladesh volumes, but the wiki has not verified an executed, bankable offtake agreement and the approvals needed to wheel that electricity through India. The Bangladesh component makes Upper Karnali the test case for Nepal's "second neighbour" trade strategy — but no PPA has yet closed. The Bangladesh figures have shifted repeatedly: 250 MW, 300 MW, 500 MW, and 200 MW have all been quoted at different moments between 2017 and 2025. A moving target is not a market — it is a signal that the tri-nation transmission architecture (Nepal → India → Bangladesh) remains unresolved. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 3,466 GWh | Planned export share | ~88% | India export | Primary target (no firm PPA) | Bangladesh export | Multiple quantities announced; bankable executed PPA not verified | ## Governance The current reported ownership structure is GMR 34%, SJVN 34%, IREDA 5% and NEA 27%. Ownership participation is not equivalent to financing approval, financial close or funds disbursed. See hydro-geopolitics. The 2008 international competitive bidding awarded the project to GMR under a Project Development Agreement (PDA) — a bilateral contract between the Government of Nepal and the developer that gave GMR exclusive development rights with defined milestones. GMR failed to meet the financial closure deadline; the government extended it repeatedly. Each extension eroded the credibility of the PDA model: if deadlines are routinely extended, they are not deadlines. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | GMR Upper Karnali Hydropower Limited | Reported ownership (Jun 2026) | GMR 34% · SJVN 34% · IREDA 5% · NEA 27% | Concession type | PDA (international competitive bidding, 2008) | Original financial close deadline | ~2014 (extended repeatedly) | ## Schedule Eighteen years have passed since the 2008 award without construction commencement. The project should be monitored through evidence of financial close, offtake, land and access readiness, notice to proceed and physical works—not through deadline-extension announcements. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Licence awarded | 2008 | Financial closure | Not achieved (as of 2026) | Completion | ~0% | Construction | Not started | # Current Status and Performance Provenance As of 10 July 2026: stalled / pre-construction. The partner structure has changed, but the current primary evidence does not show financial close, lender disbursement or a construction notice to proceed. Dimension | Current position | Evidence date | ---|---|---| Ownership | GMR 34%, SJVN 34%, IREDA 5%, NEA 27% | 29 Jun 2026 | Financial close | Not verified | 29 Jun 2026 | Construction | Very early development stage; physical works not established | 29 Jun 2026 | Offtake | Prospective export arrangements; bankable status not verified | 10 Jul 2026 review | # Recent Updates Date | Update | Source | ---|---|---| 29 Jun 2026 | ICRA recorded the current proposed ownership split and described the project as very early stage | ICRA rating rationale | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Verification rule | ---|---|---| Achieved financial close and disbursement are not evidenced | Notice to proceed and major construction | Require lender or project-company closing disclosure | Bankable power offtake is not evidenced | Revenue certainty and financing | Require executed PPA and applicable approvals | Export evacuation remains a critical dependency | Delivery of contracted electricity | Require committed project-to-market transmission path | # The GMR Saga: Timeline of an Unbuilt Project Year | Event | ------|-------| 2008 | GMR wins international competitive bidding for 900 MW Upper Karnali; PDA signed with Government of Nepal | 2008–2014 | GMR undertakes survey and feasibility studies; financial closure targeted for ~2014 | 2014 | High-level committee raises concerns about downstream irrigation impacts on India's Ganga system; objection stalls progress | 2015–2017 | PDA deadlines extended; GMR begins discussions with Bangladesh for export PPA | 2017 | Bangladesh PPA announced — initially 500 MW, later adjusted to 250–300 MW range | 2018–2020 | Further PDA extensions; financial closure repeatedly deferred | 2020–2022 | COVID-19 disruptions; project enters "force majeure" discussions | 2023–2024 | Supreme Court of Nepal intervenes: rules that open-ended PDA extensions are not permissible; grants only 186-day allowance for time lost under court's own interim orders | 2025 | SJVN and IREDA join equity stack alongside GMR; NEA takes a stake | 2026 | ICRA records revised ownership participation while describing the project as very early stage | The dated record shows repeated attempts to resolve a linked financing, offtake, transmission and deadline problem. The revised ownership may change the sponsor base, but it does not itself prove that any of those milestones has closed. # The Supreme Court Intervention The Supreme Court's ruling is significant beyond Upper Karnali. By limiting extensions to 186 days (for time lost under the court's own interim orders), the court signaled that the PDA-extension cycle — where projects are awarded, deadlines are missed, extensions are granted, and nothing is built — is not legally sustainable. This has implications for: Other stalled PDAs: west-seti (750 MW, NHPC), arun-3 (already executing, less relevant) Future licensing: the Investment Board Nepal's PDA framework may need tighter milestone enforcement Investor confidence: the ruling cuts both ways — it disciplines developers to meet deadlines, but also makes Nepal a riskier jurisdiction if deadlines are seen as infeasible # The Bangladesh Question Upper Karnali's Bangladesh PPA has been "live" since 2017 but has never closed. The underlying problem is not the commercial terms — Bangladesh needs power and Nepal has it — but the transmission architecture. Exporting from Nepal to Bangladesh requires wheeling power through India's grid, which requires: 1. A Nepal-India cross-border transmission agreement (Upper Karnali → Muzaffarpur or equivalent) 2. An India-Bangladesh cross-border transmission agreement (existing Baharampur–Bheramara link, 1,000 MW, operational since 2013) 3. A tri-nation wheeling agreement (Nepal → India → Bangladesh) — no precedent exists at this scale The India-Bangladesh link exists, but the Nepal-India link for Upper Karnali does not. Until the 400 kV Karnali corridor is built from the project site to the Indian border, the Bangladesh PPA is a promise without a delivery mechanism. See nepal-transmission-landscape-2025. # Significance Upper Karnali is the twin case to arun-3 — same licence era, similar capacity, same India-developer / export-first model — but with the opposite outcome. Arun-3 is at 74% physical progress; Upper Karnali has been at "about to reach financial closure" for a decade. Reading the two projects together is how you understand the variance in Nepal's India-developed export class: the contract is not the product, execution is. The project also marks how hydro-geopolitics has widened in Nepal's hydropower conversation. The original export target was India, while successive Bangladesh proposals make Upper Karnali a test case for tri-nation energy trade whose bankable arrangements remain unverified. The revised ownership brings Indian state-owned entities and NEA into the project company alongside GMR. The monitored distinction is that equity participation is not the same milestone as committed project debt or financial close. # Comparison: Arun-3 vs Upper Karnali Parameter | Arun-3 | Upper Karnali | -----------|--------|---------------| Licence awarded | 2008 | 2008 | Capacity | 900 MW | 900 MW | Developer | SJVN (India, state-owned) | GMR (India, private) | Status | Under construction; progress must be read with its evidence date | Not started | COD | Target has moved; verify against current SJVN disclosure | No verified date | Financial closure | Achieved | Not achieved | Export PPA | India (firm) | None (India uncertain, Bangladesh unclosed) | Transmission | Dedicated evacuation line under delivery with the project | Project-to-market corridor not committed in the current record | Years to construction | ~10 | 18+ and counting | The comparison isolates the variables: same basin (Koshi vs Karnali), same era (2008), same model (PDA, export-first). The difference is developer — SJVN is a state-owned Indian utility with sovereign backing and a balance sheet that can absorb construction risk; GMR is a private conglomerate whose energy portfolio shifted substantially after 2008. See buildability for why developer identity matters more than project design. # Limitations & Controversies Eighteen years without a turbine. The 2008 licence award predates the current nea grid code in some dimensions; deadlines have been extended repeatedly. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled against open-ended extensions, granting only a 186-day allowance for time lost under its own interim orders — a signal that the judiciary no longer accepts the PDA-extension cycle as routine. Bangladesh transmission dependency. Even if a final PPA closes, the 200–500 MW export to Bangladesh depends on a Nepal–India–Bangladesh transmission corridor that is still under development. Upper Karnali's export model contains an unresolved infrastructure prerequisite that is not on its balance sheet but is on its critical path. The India-Bangladesh Baharampur–Bheramara link exists, but the Nepal-India segment does not. Downstream irrigation overhang. A 2014 high-level committee raised concerns about impacts on downstream irrigation in India's Ganga system. That objection was never fully resolved, only procedurally managed, and resurfaces in each PDA extension debate. The concern is structural: 900 MW of Karnali diversion reduces flow in the Ghaghara, which is a major irrigation source for Uttar Pradesh. GMR Group's execution posture. Unlike SJVN, GMR is a private Indian conglomerate whose project pipeline has shifted substantially since 2008. GMR's energy portfolio now includes domestic Indian thermal and renewable projects, airport infrastructure, and highways — hydropower in Nepal is one of many competing capital allocations. Whether GMR remains the right primary sponsor — now that SJVN and IREDA are in the equity stack — is an open strategic question that Nepal has not formally asked. Transmission gap. The 400 kV Karnali corridor from the project site to the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur export point does not exist. Building it requires coordinated investment from Nepal and India across some of Nepal's most rugged terrain. Until this corridor is committed, Upper Karnali is stranded-generation. # Official Visual Source Gap Upper Karnali is still unusually thin on stable public document figures. The Investment Board Nepal project and factsheet pages remain visible in search indexes, but the live page and factsheet download currently resolve to 404s, while the active GMR project page exposes basic project text without a reusable layout plate or site figure. This page avoids generic valley scenery in both the top strip and body until a durable brochure, E&S disclosure, or layout PDF is recovered from the official source stack. Tracked official references: Investment Board Nepal project page Investment Board Nepal factsheet page GMR Upper Karnali project page # See also karnali-basin arun-3 hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation run-of-river-hydropower mugu-karnali-storage nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 buildability data-map-inventory # Sources icra-upper-karnali-2026 upper-karnali-official-records-2022-2026 upper-karnali-pda-record jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.title: Upper Marsyangdi A
headings: Why the Upstream Plant Matters to the Cascade
pages.excerpt: Upper Marsyangdi A is a 50 MW operating run-of-river plant on the Marsyangdi River in Lamjung District — the upstream anchor of the 170 MW Marsyangdi cascade. Developed by Sinohydro-Sagarmatha Power Company (a Sino-Nepali joint venture), the plant signed its PPA in 2010 and commi
pages.body_text: Upper Marsyangdi A # Summary Upper Marsyangdi A is a 50 MW operating run-of-river plant on the Marsyangdi River in Lamjung District — the upstream anchor of the 170 MW Marsyangdi cascade. Developed by Sinohydro-Sagarmatha Power Company (a Sino-Nepali joint venture), the plant signed its PPA in 2010 and commissioned around 2016–2017, making it one of the earlier private IPP projects on the Marsyangdi system. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 50 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Marsyangdi (gandaki-basin) | District | Lamjung | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Specifications (NEA IPP Registry) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Sinohydro-Sagarmatha Power Company (P) Ltd. | PPA date | ~2010 (BS 2067) | RCOD | ~2017 (BS 2073) | Type | Run-of-river (private IPP) | Cascade position | Upstream of madhya-marsyangdi (70 MW) and Marsyangdi Besi (50 MW, under construction) | District | Lamjung, Gandaki Province | # The Marsyangdi Cascade — Upstream Anchor Upper Marsyangdi A sits at the head of one of Nepal's most productive hydropower corridors. The Marsyangdi River, originating in the Annapurna massif near Manang, hosts three projects in sequence: Plant | MW | Status | Position | ---|---|---|---| Upper Marsyangdi A | 50 | Operating | Upstream | madhya-marsyangdi | 70 | Operating | Middle | Marsyangdi Besi | 50 | Under construction | Downstream | Total | 170 | | | As the uppermost project, Upper Marsyangdi A's operations — particularly sediment management at its intake and flow diversion through the headrace — directly affect water quality and discharge timing for the downstream plants. This is the cascade dependency that Nepal's hydropower planning rarely accounts for in project-level PPA economics: the upstream plant's design discharge determines how much the downstream plant receives, and the downstream PPA cannot charge back for upstream externalities. # Learning Curve Asset Upper Marsyangdi A serves as a benchmark for the cost and performance assumptions embedded in newer Marsyangdi developments. Because it commissioned approximately 7–8 years before Marsyangdi Besi (the downstream under-construction plant), its operational history should inform the financial models used to justify the downstream project. Key questions a full analysis would answer: 1. Build cost vs budget. The Sinohydro-Sagarmatha joint venture used a Chinese contractor model. The actual cost per MW — and how it compared with the NPR 200–300 million/MW industry-average range at the time — would calibrate the cost assumptions for Marsyangdi Besi. 2. PLF vs contracted energy. Madhya Marsyangdi achieves 107.6% of design from the same river system. If Upper Marsyangdi A performs similarly, the Marsyangdi basin may be systematically under-designed relative to actual hydrology — the chilime pattern at cascade scale. 3. Maintenance cost trajectory. As the plant approaches 10 years of operation, the maintenance cost curve — routine overhauls, sediment wear on turbine runners, desander basin cleaning frequency — becomes a real dataset for predicting lifecycle costs on the same river. 4. Sediment management. Upstream plants on steep Himalayan tributaries handle the highest sediment loads. How Upper Marsyangdi A manages its intake desander — and what passes through to the headrace — determines turbine wear at both this plant and Madhya Marsyangdi downstream. The NEA annual reports cover NEA-owned plants in detail but do not publish private IPP generation data. Upper Marsyangdi A's actual performance data would need to come from the developer's annual reports, ICRA Nepal surveillance ratings, or the DoED generation monitoring database. # Why the Upstream Plant Matters to the Cascade When Upper Marsyangdi A diverts river flow through its headrace tunnel, it reduces the flow available to Madhya Marsyangdi's intake downstream. If the upstream plant's design discharge is close to the river's dry-season flow — and both plants are running at full peaking capacity — the downstream plant may face water scarcity in low-flow months. This is a regulatory problem, not just an engineering one: Nepal's water allocation framework does not cascade-bind PPA obligations, so the downstream developer has no contractual remedy against reduced inflow from upstream operations. This makes Upper Marsyangdi A a case study in why the Marsyangdi basin — and Nepal's cascade-heavy river systems generally — needs integrated water accounting rather than project-level licensing. See gandaki-basin and seasonal-mismatch. # Limitations & Controversies Regulatory gap in cascade water allocation. Nepal's water allocation framework does not cascade-bind PPA obligations. When Upper Marsyangdi A diverts river flow through its headrace, the downstream plant (madhya-marsyangdi) has no contractual remedy against reduced dry-season inflow — a problem the current licensing structure does not address. Opaque operational data. NEA annual reports cover NEA-owned plants in detail but do not publish private IPP generation data. Upper Marsyangdi A's actual performance — PLF, maintenance cost trajectory, and sediment wear rates — is not publicly available, limiting its usefulness as a benchmark for downstream projects. Sediment management externality. As the uppermost plant in the cascade, Upper Marsyangdi A's intake desander performance and headrace sediment passage directly affect turbine wear at Madhya Marsyangdi downstream. This operational interdependence is not priced or regulated across project boundaries. # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # See also madhya-marsyangdi — the downstream 70 MW plant, operating at 107.6% of design gandaki-basin — the Marsyangdi feeds the Narayani / Gandaki system run-of-river-hydropower chilime — the conservative-design overperformance pattern, at smaller scale seasonal-mismatch — the structural limitation even well-performing RoR cannot fix
