pages.title: Upper Tamakoshi
headings: FY 2081/82 — Climate Event, Not Structural Failure
The Rolwaling Diversion — Current Delivery Status Unverified
pages.excerpt: A 456 MW operating peaking run-of-river project tracked through company disclosures, with financial recovery and expansion milestones kept separate.
pages.body_text: Upper Tamakoshi Permanent Camp Facility Overall Project Layout # Summary Nepal's largest operating hydropower plant at 456 MW. Located on the Tama Koshi River in Dolakha district. Commissioned in 2021. # Current Status and Performance Provenance As of 10 July 2026: operating. UTKHPL published combined annual reports for FY 2079/80 and 2080/81 in April 2026 and its FY 2082/83 third-quarter financial report in May 2026. Those company disclosures are the current evidence base for operations, debt, insurance recovery and shareholder monitoring; older research compilations should not be treated as the final word when a newer filing differs. Dimension | Current position | Evidence | ---|---|---| Delivery | Operating; 456 MW | Structured project registry and UTKHPL disclosures | Financial reporting | Third-quarter FY 2082/83 report published | 13 May 2026 | Annual reporting | FY 2079/80 and FY 2080/81 annual reports published | 6 Apr 2026 | Expansion | Rolwaling diversion milestone and contribution require current project-company verification | Monitoring gap | # Recent Updates Date | Update | Source | ---|---|---| 13 May 2026 | FY 2082/83 third-quarter financial report published | UTKHPL project updates | 6 Apr 2026 | Sixteenth and seventeenth annual reports published | UTKHPL annual reports | # Active Blockers Blocker | Prevents | Current handling | ---|---|---| Financial recovery and insurance/debt reconciliation remain filing-dependent | A stable forward financial assessment | Update from company and rating disclosures, not secondary summaries | Rolwaling diversion schedule, cost and incremental energy lack a current milestone record in the wiki | Reliable expansion forecast | Keep the milestone explicitly unverified until a primary update is ingested | [!warning] Evidence boundary. The detailed generation and financial sections below were assembled from audited accounts, rating material and research compilations with different reporting cut-offs. Where those figures conflict with the April–May 2026 company filings, the newer primary filing should control and the discrepancy should be logged rather than silently averaged. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 456 MW | Status | Operating | River | Tama Koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Dolakha | ## Engineering With 822 m of gross head — among the highest in Nepal — Upper Tamakoshi concentrates one of the steepest river drops in the country through tunnels and penstocks to an underground powerhouse. This is the engineering archetype of Nepal's dominant hydro form: high-head diversion with no significant dam. See run-of-river-hydropower. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Gross head | 822 m | Headrace tunnel | 7.2 km | Underground powerhouse | Yes | Type | Run-of-River | ## Output Upper Tamakoshi's 2,281 GWh/yr design energy and 65% plant load factor set the benchmark for Nepal's RoR fleet. But actual generation has tracked below contracted levels — water flow in Spring 2023 collapsed to 45.12% of historical hydrological expectations, an example of the gap between design hydrology and operational reality explored in q-design-discharge. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 2,281 GWh | Plant load factor | 65 % | ## Financial Built at NPR 87–89 billion (~NPR 196 million/MW), financed with an effective 88:12 debt-to-equity ratio at COD (original 75:25 model was overwhelmed by NPR ~14 billion in Interest During Construction). First-year PPA at NPR 3.74/kWh wet and NPR 6.96/kWh dry — among the lowest tariffs in the sector. The structural gap between these rates and the project's debt service is the core of the nea-triple-authority problem. See the Financial Performance section below for the detailed breakdown. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| PPA rate (wet) | NPR 3.74/kWh | PPA rate (dry) | NPR 6.96/kWh | Debt/equity | 75/25 | ## Schedule Commissioned in 2021 after roughly seven years of construction, Upper Tamakoshi was the plant that broke Nepal's load-shedding era. Compare with chameliya-hydropower — a 30 MW project that took 11 years — for a case study in execution risk. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Commercial operation | 2021 | Completion | 100 % | # Generation Performance (FY 2079/80 – 2081/82) Three years of actual dispatch data now confirm that Upper Tamakoshi's turbines and hydrology are broadly performing as designed — the financial crisis is a balance-sheet problem, not an engineering one. Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh) | Actual (GWh) | % of Contracted | Context | ---|---|---|---|---| FY 2079/80 | 2,281 | 1,945.83 | 85.3% | First stable operating year | FY 2080/81 | 2,281 | 2,058.36 | 90.2% | Peak production — best year to date | FY 2081/82 | 2,281 | 1,529.07 | 67.0% | 88-day forced shutdown (Sep 2024 flood) | Source: UKHLL audited accounts; NEA Annual Report FY 2081/82; ICRA Nepal credit assessments. [!important] Previous generation estimate corrected. Earlier versions of this page estimated FY 2079/80 generation at ~1,340 GWh (~59% of contracted), back-calculated from revenue. The correct figure from actual dispatch data is 1,945.83 GWh (85.3%) — substantially higher. The financial distress argument is correspondingly stronger, not weaker: the plant hit 90% of contracted energy in FY 2080/81 and still posted a net loss. This is not a generation problem; it is a structural tariff problem. ## FY 2080/81 — The Analytical Pivot The 90.2% generation in FY 2080/81 is the single most important data point in understanding Upper Tamakoshi. A run-of-river plant achieving 90% of contracted energy is performing exceptionally well by any regional standard. The Tamakoshi basin hydrology was accurately mapped; the Q-design discharge (66 m³/s) reflects real river behaviour under normal conditions. This result kills one version of the Upper Tamakoshi story — that it is a victim of hydrological forecasting error or q-design-discharge optimism. It is not. The turbines spin as designed when the river flows as modelled. What it shows instead is that the financial distress is structurally inevitable even at near-peak generation. At 2,058 GWh and NPR 3.74/6.96 blended tariff, maximum gross revenue is approximately NPR 9.3–9.5 billion. Interest expense alone (~NPR 6.7 billion) consumes over 70% of that ceiling. Principal amortization takes most of the remainder. The company cannot break even at its contracted tariff even when the river cooperates. ## FY 2081/82 — Climate Event, Not Structural Failure In late September 2024 (Ashwin 2081), post-monsoon flooding caused catastrophic damage to the plant's surface civil structures: Left and right desander ponds severely compromised (critical for removing abrasive silt before water enters the Pelton turbines) Underground box culverts damaged Surface control rooms affected A critical 220 kV transmission tower destroyed, cutting grid evacuation Electricity generation was entirely suspended for 88 days. Partial operations resumed in mid-January 2025 using only the repaired left desander pond — engineers accepted suboptimal single-desander operation rather than wait 45 more days for full reconstruction, knowing the financial cost of continued downtime. Physical damage was assessed at approximately NPR 1.79 billion. Business interruption losses reached approximately NPR 1.43 billion. Total insurance claim submitted: NPR 2.0 billion — but the NPR 1.43 billion in business interruption losses are largely unrecoverable because the insurance policy's Loss of Profit (LOP) coverage explicitly excludes transmission infrastructure failures, and the destroyed 220 kV tower that cut grid evacuation was classified as a transmission asset rather than a generation asset. [!warning] Insurance claim NOT settled. As of May 2026, the NPR 2.0 billion claim remains submitted but unpaid. The gap between total losses (NPR 3.22B) and the claim amount (NPR 2.0B) reflects the transmission exclusion. Domestic insurers lack settlement authority — the risk was ceded to international reinsurers who have deployed independent loss adjusters contesting coverage under "maintenance period defects" and "foreign debris" clauses. Until the claim is paid, UKHLL lacks the capital to fully rehabilitate the desander basins. See glof-risk and buildability. Full dual-desander operations were not restored until mid-2025. # Significance Upper Tamakoshi is the plant that broke Nepal's load-shedding era. At 456 MW, it represents ~16% of total installed hydro capacity and was the foundation of Nepal becoming a net power exporter in FY 2024/25 (NPR 17.47 billion in cross-border trade revenue). It is also the archetype of Nepal's dominant engineering form: high-head diversion with no significant dam. The river drops 822 meters naturally; the engineering concentrates it through tunnels and penstocks to an underground powerhouse with six 76 MW Pelton turbines. But the plant that ended load-shedding is now formally insolvent. Both facts are true simultaneously — and together they define the central tension in Nepal's energy sector. # Financial Performance ## The Structural Mathematics of Default Upper Tamakoshi was financed at what was modelled as a 75:25 debt-to-equity ratio. By commissioning in August 2021 — after an 11-year construction period interrupted by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, border blockades, and COVID-19 — capitalized Interest During Construction (IDC) had swelled the debt burden to the point where the effective leverage ratio at COD was 88:12. The project was almost entirely debt-funded at the moment it started generating revenue. Metric | FY 2079/80 | FY 2080/81 | FY 2081/82 | ---|---|---|---| Actual generation | 1,945.83 GWh | 2,058.36 GWh | 1,529.07 GWh | Total revenue | ~NPR 8.68 billion | ~NPR 9.3–9.5 billion | ~NPR 6.9 billion | Interest expense | ~NPR 6.68 billion | Insufficient coverage | Insufficient coverage | Net profit/(loss) | ~NPR (2.52) billion | ~NPR (1.39) billion | ~NPR (2.57) billion | Accumulated losses | — | — | NPR 12.18 billion | Total debt | ~NPR 78.6 billion | ~NPR 78.6 billion | Default | DSCR | [!warning] Current construction status is unverified. UTKHPL's FY 2080/81 annual statements describe the 22 MW Rolwaling project as under construction, with an EPC contract awarded and a PPA application in process. The May 2026 quarterly statement reports NPR 2.103 billion of Rolwaling capital work in progress, but gives no package-progress percentage, stop/restart date or commissioning schedule. Those disclosures do not support the former claim that work was completely halted or that construction sites were blockaded. No current delivery status should be inferred from the accounting balance alone. The dry-season energy matters disproportionately: at NPR 6.96/kWh versus NPR 3.74/kWh, an extra 212 GWh skewed toward the dry season could add NPR 1.2–1.5 billion in annual revenue. Whether that is sufficient to bring DSCR above 1.0x depends on the debt restructuring terms that accompany any resolution. # Limitations & Controversies Structural default at near-peak generation. UKHLL was downgraded to ICRA D (Default) in FY 2081/82 despite achieving 90.2% of contracted energy in FY 2080/81. The crisis is a tariff-debt mismatch, not an engineering failure. See nea-triple-authority and ppa-pricing for the structural analysis. September 2024 flood damage. 88-day forced shutdown, NPR 1.79 billion physical damage, NPR 1.43 billion business interruption. Insurance claim of NPR 2.0 billion remains unsettled as of May 2026 due to transmission-exclusion clauses. See Financial Performance section above for full detail. Rolwaling delivery status unverified. The latest company filing in the wiki reports capital work in progress but no package milestone, stop/restart date or commissioning schedule. Cascading systemic risk. Default forces domestic banks (EPF, CIT, commercial banks) to reclassify loans as NPAs; hardens hydropower insurance market; signals to foreign investors that current risk-allocation framework may be uninvestable for mega-projects. # Structural implication The gap between revenue and debt service at Upper Tamakoshi is not a commissioning-phase issue that will resolve with time. At its current PPA rate — which is among the lowest in the sector — the project's revenue cannot cover its interest, let alone principal. To break even by year 15, estimates suggest it would require an effective tariff roughly 2–3 times higher than current levels. See ppa-pricing. Upper Tamakoshi is the most prominent case of the structural dynamic explored in nea-triple-authority: NEA as regulator set the tariff framework; NEA as majority shareholder (41%) participated in the equity structure that got diluted; NEA as sole off-taker buys at rates that cannot service the debt. Three different roles, one institution, zero mechanism for the commercial interest to override the regulatory one. The PPA tariff (NPR 3.74/6.96) was set in an era when the project's capital structure was modelled at 75:25. By commissioning, it was 88:12. The tariff was never adjusted. The entire cost escalation — IDC, earthquake repairs, contractor delays — was absorbed by the balance sheet. The off-taker's obligation was unchanged. # Broader systemic implications The ICRA default downgrade to D has cascading effects: Domestic banking system. UKHLL's debt is held by EPF, CIT, Rastriya Beema Sansthan, Nepal Telecom, and domestic commercial banks. A D rating forces these institutions to reclassify their UKHLL loans as non-performing assets (NPAs), eroding their own profitability and threatening yield distributions to ordinary Nepalese whose retirement savings sit in the EPF and CIT. Future project financing. If Nepal's flagship 456 MW project — backed by the state utility, staffed by NEA's engineers, and celebrated as a triumph of domestic financing — cannot service its debt, commercial banks will demand higher equity contributions, punitive rates, or refuse syndication on future IPP mega-projects entirely. Insurance market. The NPR 2–3 billion insurance claim hardened Nepal's hydropower insurance market. Future projects face higher premiums against a PPA structure that provides no pass-through for increased OPEX. Every rupee of premium increase deepens the cash-flow deficit that already threatens DSCR. Export ambitions. Nepal's export targets require hundreds of billions in fresh capital. UKHLL's default signals to both domestic and foreign investors that the current risk-allocation framework — developer bears 100% of geological, hydrological, and construction delay risk at a non-escalating monopsony tariff — is uninvestable for complex mega-projects. # Related run-of-river-hydropower — the architecture Upper Tamakoshi exemplifies q-design-discharge — why generation falls short of contracted energy nea-triple-authority — the institutional conflict at the root of the tariff problem ppa-pricing — the tariff structure that cannot service the debt glof-risk — the flood hazard that triggered the 2024 shutdown buildability — execution risk in Nepal's hydro sector kulekhani-cascade — Nepal's only operational storage, for contrast tanahu-hydropower — another Nepali-developed project with different financing # Sources utkhpl-disclosures-2026 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 ukhl-financials-generation-fy2079-82

pages.title: Upper Tamor
pages.excerpt: Upper Tamor is a 285 MW under-construction Tamor River hydropower project in eastern Nepal and one of the larger private/IPP projects in the current pipeline.
pages.body_text: Upper Tamor # Summary Upper Tamor is a 285 MW under-construction Tamor River hydropower project in eastern Nepal and one of the larger private/IPP projects in the current pipeline. Upper Tamor is a 285 MW hydropower project under construction on the Tamor River in eastern Nepal — one of the largest private/IPP projects in the under-construction pipeline. # Tamor Basin Significance The Tamor River is a major tributary of the Koshi system, draining the eastern Himalayan slopes of the Kanchenjunga massif. Unlike the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors closer to Kathmandu, the Tamor basin has historically seen less hydropower development due to its distance from load centers and transmission constraints. Upper Tamor, at 285 MW, represents a step-change in eastern Nepal's generation capacity. # Development Context The Tamor River system has attracted attention for both run-of-river and storage development potential. Upper Tamor sits alongside Tamor Storage (200 MW, survey stage) in the project pipeline. Together, these projects would fundamentally reshape the eastern grid — but also require significant transmission investment to evacuate power from the Tamor valley to the national backbone. # Financing Challenge At 285 MW, Upper Tamor's capital requirements place it in the top tier of Nepali private hydro projects. The project's financial viability will depend on achieving competitive build costs, managing construction risk in a relatively remote location, and securing transmission evacuation — all within the standard NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA framework. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 285 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Tamor (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Taplejung | Province | Province No 1 | # Limitations & Controversies The page frames Upper Tamor's scale, basin position, and financing challenge, but does not verify current construction progress, final COD, project cost, dry-season energy share, or transmission evacuation readiness. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025

It is pinned in the data-layer-priority-watchlist because it sits in the central-north Trishuli corridor, where hydropower value depends directly on evacuation capacity into the Kathmandu and wider national grid. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 216 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Why It Matters Upper Trishuli-1 is not a top-10 capacity project, but it is strategically important because of location. Trishuli projects sit close to the country's central load geography and to transmission corridors that matter immediately for domestic reliability. A 216 MW project in this corridor can be more system-relevant than a larger but remote survey marker if it reaches commissioning and evacuates cleanly. The project also helps explain why the priority watchlist is not just a biggest-MW layer. Upper Trishuli-1 is included for corridor and buildout relevance. # Status And Timing The generated spec classifies the project as under construction / generation licence. The IPSDP milestone ladder places Upper Trishuli-1 in the ~2025 project bucket, alongside other near-term projects such as Rasuwagadhi, Sanjen, Upper Trishuli 3B, Madhya Bhotekoshi, and Arun 3. The practical watch items are physical progress, commissioning schedule, grid-connection readiness, and whether output is constrained by the central transmission network. # Map Interpretation The marker is a river-aligned project reference derived from the registry point. pages.title: Upper Trishuli 3A
headings: The 73% Problem — Why Design Energy Fails Here
The Flood Event — Climate-Resilience in Real Time
pages.excerpt: Upper Trishuli 3A is a 60 MW operating NEA run-of-river plant on the Trishuli, with NEA generation data showing performance below its high design-energy assumption.
pages.body_text: Upper Trishuli 3A # Summary Upper Trishuli 3A is a 60 MW operating NEA run-of-river plant on the Trishuli, with NEA generation data showing performance below its high design-energy assumption. Lifting of upper bracket during overhauling 60 MW · operating · on the Trishuli · in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 60 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Upper Trishuli 3A is NEA's second-largest plant by annual design energy (489.76 GWh) despite only 60 MW of installed capacity — a reflection of the Trishuli River's high and relatively stable discharge. Two 30 MW vertical Francis units operate at 70% probability of exceedance as a pure run-of-river plant (not peaking RoR — it runs on whatever the river provides). Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river (ROR) | Units | 2 × 30 MW Francis | PE design basis | 70% POE | Design generation | 489.76 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 356 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 72.7% | FY 2081/82 vs target | 78% | Year-over-year change | −17% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 2,391.5 GWh | Districts | Rasuwa and Nuwakot, Bagmati Province | [!warning] Status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list the plant as "Under construction (Generation licence)." The NEA's FY 2024/25 report covers it as an operating station with multi-year generation data, cumulative lifetime output, completed overhauls, and operational incident reporting. The plant is operating. The registry status is stale. For the first time in FY 2081/82, NEA's in-house maintenance team overhauled both Units 1 and 2 — a significant operational milestone that included repairs to draft tube gates, inlet valves, and head covers. Radial gates received major maintenance with seal, plate, and rail bar replacements. SCADA systems and communication links were restored with sensor and PLC upgrades, and pre-monsoon civil works included concrete repairs and gabion spur construction near the tailrace. # The 73% Problem — Why Design Energy Fails Here At 72.7% of design generation, Upper Trishuli 3A has the lowest design-performance ratio in NEA's large-plant fleet alongside Chameliya (77.3%). Compare: Plant | MW | % of Design (FY 2081/82) | Type | ---|---|---|---| Middle Marsyangdi | 70 | 107.6% | PROR, glacier-fed | Kali Gandaki A | 144 | 102.5% | PROR with pondage | Marsyangdi | 69 | 97.0% | PROR | Chameliya | 30 | 77.3% | PROR, major construction failure | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60 | 72.7% | ROR, high-design-energy | The 489.76 GWh design figure is aggressive for a 60 MW plant — it implies a plant load factor of ~93%, which would place it among the highest PLFs in the global hydro fleet. At 356 GWh actual, the PLF is ~68% — still respectable for a RoR plant but dramatically below the design assumption. This is the q-design-discharge problem at NEA scale. A plant built on 70% POE hydrology with a 93% PLF design has almost no margin for actual seasonal variability. The 17% year-over-year decline (FY 2080/81 to 2081/82) suggests the hydrology assumption was tested and failed. # The Flood Event — Climate-Resilience in Real Time On the morning of 2081/03/24 at approximately 4:30 AM, a sudden flood caused by intense rainfall in the upper catchment sent uncontrolled water and debris into the dam premises. Because there was no early warning system, several key structures were affected before operators could respond. Damage summary: Diversion Radial Gate-1: ~1.5 m of lower gate skin plate detached; control panel and hydraulic unit submerged Gates 2, 3, and 4: structurally intact but currently inoperative due to damaged hydraulic systems Gate-2's pressure unit submerged; Gate-3's hydraulic cylinder broken Stoplog gantry crane and lifting mechanism damaged Control building, piers, staff quarters, and operating platforms impacted by debris and silt deposition Gate operating panels, motors, and sensors submerged No human casualties were reported. But the event is a real-world test of what Nepal's RoR fleet faces as rainfall intensity increases in the Himalayan catchment. The missing early warning system — flagged in the NEA's own incident report — is the operational gap that climate-resilient design would need to close across the fleet. See glof-risk and buildability for the broader infrastructure-resilience context. # Significance — NEA's Highest-Design-Energy RoR Asset Upper Trishuli 3A's design energy (489.76 GWh from 60 MW) reflects what the Trishuli River basin can deliver: reliable, year-round baseflow from a catchment that drains the Langtang-Helambu massif. At 356 GWh actual, it still delivers more energy per MW than any other NEA RoR plant — a function of basin hydrology, not engineering superiority. But the plant also shows that no RoR asset, regardless of basin quality, can guarantee its design energy. The 489.76 GWh target is the high-end assumption; 356 GWh is reality. The gap between them is the structural reason Nepal's RoR-heavy fleet cannot close the seasonal-mismatch without storage — even in its best basins. # Limitations & Controversies The page corrects stale registry status using NEA operating data, but its analysis is still bounded by the FY 2024/25 annual-report snapshot and does not include a full hydrology series, post-flood recovery data, or independent engineering review of the early-warning gap. # See also q-design-discharge — why 72.7% of design is a structural signal seasonal-mismatch — the system problem even a well-sited RoR cannot fix buildability — how flood events test infrastructure resilience glof-risk — the broader hazard context for Himalayan RoR headworks gandaki-basin — basin context; the Trishuli feeds the Narayani run-of-river-hydropower

pages.title: Upper Trishuli 3B
pages.excerpt: Upper Trishuli 3B is a 37 MW under-construction Trishuli cascade project developed through a subsidiary company and distinct from NEA-owned Upper Trishuli 3A.
pages.body_text: Upper Trishuli 3B # Summary Upper Trishuli 3B is a 37 MW under-construction Trishuli cascade project developed through a subsidiary company and distinct from NEA-owned Upper Trishuli 3A. Upper Trishuli 3B is a 37 MW run-of-river hydropower project in the Trishuli cascade, developed under Trishuli Jal Vidyut Company Limited — a subsidiary corporate model distinct from the NEA's directly-owned Trishuli assets. # Distinction from Trishuli 3A A persistent confusion in sector research conflates Upper Trishuli 3B (37 MW) with Upper Trishuli 3A (60 MW). The distinction is critical: Trishuli 3A (60 MW) is wholly owned, constructed, and operated directly by the NEA as an internal Generation Directorate asset. It has no commercial PPA — electricity is dispatched via internal transfer pricing based on cost of generation. Trishuli 3B (37 MW) is developed under a subsidiary corporate model and holds a standard commercial PPA at NPR 4.80/kWh (wet) and NPR 8.40/kWh (dry), consistent with the prevailing IPP tariff schedule. # Trishuli Cascade Dynamics Upper Trishuli 3B is part of the larger Trishuli River cascade that includes multiple projects at different stages — from the operating Trishuli Devighat plant to the NEA-owned Upper Trishuli 3A (60 MW), the subsidiary Trishuli 3B (37 MW), and Super Trishuli (100 MW, under construction). The cascade's cumulative impact on Trishuli River flows, sediment transport, and downstream water availability makes coordination across entity boundaries important for system-level planning. # Build Cost Context Industry analysis notes that projects in the Trishuli corridor, including Upper Trishuli 3B, have faced build costs exceeding NPR 200–250 million per MW — significantly above the NPR 172–175 million/MW benchmark set by optimal projects like Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW). # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 37 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Trishuli (gandaki-basin) | District | Rasuwa | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page resolves the 3A/3B distinction and PPA context, but does not verify the latest construction percentage, COD, cost escalation, or hydrological coordination with adjacent Trishuli cascade assets. # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 # Sources ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026

pages.body_text: Uttarganga Storage Hydropower Project # Summary Uttarganga is an 828 MW survey-stage storage hydropower project in Baglung and one of the largest storage records in the top-capacity layer. Uttarganga is an 828 MW storage hydropower project in Baglung promoted by NEA. It is pinned in the data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects layer because it is the fourth-largest capacity marker in the display set and one of the few top-10 records that is explicitly a storage project. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 828 MW | Status | Survey / study | Registry licence | Survey | River | Uttar Ganga | District | Baglung | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | Promoter | Nepal Electricity Authority | # Why It Matters Uttarganga matters because it combines two properties that rarely overlap in Nepal's project stack: very large capacity and storage. Most top-10 capacity markers are survey-stage run-of-river or peaking run-of-river concepts. Uttarganga is a direct part of the storage-deficit question. Its location in Gandaki Province also makes it a counterweight to the Karnali-heavy top-10 list. If it advanced, it would strengthen the western-central storage portfolio rather than adding another remote Karnali mainstem marker. # Status And Timing The current map layer treats Uttarganga as survey / study stage. NEA annual-book material provides official visual references for the project site and proposed reservoir area, but the wiki evidence set does not confirm physical construction. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Uttarganga STO in the 2031-2035 project window. That is the best planning-window anchor currently in the wiki. # Map Interpretation The marker is a river-aligned project reference derived from the registry point. Use it for strategic comparison, not for final dam-axis or reservoir-boundary analysis. # Limitations & Controversies The page documents Uttarganga as a storage candidate with official visual references, but does not establish final dam design, reservoir boundary, resettlement footprint, financing, tariff structure, construction start, or current environmental-approval status. # Registry note Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset # Public Visual Availability The official annual-book record described in nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 includes project-site and proposed-reservoir visuals. Those project-specific visual assets are not bundled with this public wiki release, so this page does not reproduce them. # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # See also buildability storage-deficit data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects

pages.body_text: Water and Energy Commission Secretariat (WECS) # Summary WECS is Nepal's government planning body for water and energy, and its basin plans, hydropower-potential assessments, and energy balances are core sources for this wiki. Nepal's government planning body for water and energy. Produces the authoritative basin plans, potential assessments, and energy balances that form the data backbone of this research. # Key Publications wecs-river-basin-plan-2024 — Basin-level discharge, seasonal profiles, strategic planning wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 — Revised national hydropower potential (72,544 MW gross / 32,680 MW techno-economic) wecs-energy-synopsis-2024 — Full energy balance showing grid electricity as only 4.96% of final energy # Role in Sector WECS handles theoretical planning while nea handles operational execution. The Department of Electricity Development (DoED) manages licensing between them. This fragmented institutional structure is part of the governance weakness identified across the evidence base. # Limitations & Controversies This page is an institutional orientation page, not a full governance history of WECS; it does not independently assess mandate changes, staffing, budget authority, publication delays, or how WECS recommendations are implemented by operating agencies. # Related nepal-energy-profile — the system WECS plans for hydropower-potential-categories — WECS provides the definitive numbers

pages.title: West Seti Hydroelectric Project
pages.excerpt: Figure 6.3-2 River Longitudinal Profile of the West Seti River
pages.body_text: West Seti Hydroelectric Project Figure 6.3-2 River Longitudinal Profile of the West Seti River # Summary A long-stalled reservoir storage project in Sudurpashchim Province — the most prominent example of how Chinese withdrawal and project handoff have shaped Nepal's hydro-geopolitics. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 750 MW | Status | Stalled — Chinese withdrawal 2018, NHPC takeover 2022, EIA hearings 2025 | River | Seti River (karnali-basin) | Districts | Bajhang / Baitadi / Doti / Dadeldhura | Province | Sudurpashchim | ## Engineering A 195 m concrete-faced rockfill dam (CFRD), 433 m long — the largest dam design in far-west Nepal. The project's political trajectory overshadows its engineering: conceived in the 1980s, awarded to China Three Gorges Corporation (2012), abandoned by CTG (2018), transferred to India's NHPC (2022). CTG's withdrawal was not purely technical — the commercial terms and geopolitical signaling (Indian sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure near the border) were likely decisive. See hydro-geopolitics. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | 195 m | Dam type | Concrete-face Rockfill | Dam length | 433 m | Type | Storage | ## Governance West Seti, alongside budhigandaki's history of Chinese-then-domestic pivots, represents a pattern: Chinese entities engage with Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. India then steps in — but progress remains slow. The net result is decades lost on projects that would directly address storage-deficit. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | NHPC Limited (India, since 2022) | Previous developer | China Three Gorges Corporation (2012–2018) | ## Schedule No construction timeline. NHPC is conducting EIA public hearings and updating the detailed project report as of late 2025. An associated project — SR-6 (450 MW) — has been proposed. Neither has a committed construction start. See buildability. # Limitations & Controversies Four decades of modality changes with zero construction. Conceived in the 1980s, held by SMEC for 17 years, awarded to CTG (2012), abandoned (2018), transferred to NHPC (2022), and still in EIA hearings as of late 2025. Each handoff resets the timeline. Chinese withdrawal pattern. CTG's 2018 withdrawal — citing geological issues, altitude, and resettlement — fits a broader pattern where Chinese entities engage Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. The net result is decades lost on storage that would directly address storage-deficit. No committed construction timeline. NHPC is updating the DPR and conducting EIA hearings, but no construction start has been announced. The associated SR-6 project (450 MW) is similarly undated. Geopolitical sensitivity. India's sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure near the border contributed to CTG's unfavorable operating environment. The NHPC takeover resolves the China problem but does not resolve the engineering, resettlement, or financing challenges. # Timeline of Stalling Year | Event | ------|-------| ~1980s | Project conceived | 2001–2011 | SMEC (Australia) held license; 17 years, limited progress | 2012 | Awarded to China Three Gorges Corporation (CTG) | 2018 (Sep) | CTG withdrew — cited geological issues, high altitude, resettlement difficulty. Rejected Nepal's proposal to reduce capacity from 750 to 620 MW | 2022 (Sep) | Transferred to India's NHPC Limited | 2025 (Oct) | Public hearings begun for Environmental Impact Assessment | # Current Status (as of late 2025) NHPC (India) is conducting EIA public hearings across affected areas Detailed project report is being updated An associated project — SR-6 (450 MW) — has been proposed below the confluence of Seti River and Budhiganga, in Doti/Achham districts, with a 207 m dam and potential 652 MW capacity No construction timeline announced # Why China Left CTG's withdrawal was not purely technical. The project illustrates the limits of Chinese hydropower engagement in Nepal: 1. Geological and altitude risk — genuine engineering concerns in far-west Nepal 2. Resettlement complexity — Nepal lacked a clear R&R framework 3. Commercial terms — Nepal proposed PPA payment in USD (unusual for Nepal), and CTG rejected a capacity reduction 4. Geopolitical signaling — India's sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure in border-adjacent areas created an unfavorable operating environment # Significance West Seti, alongside budhigandaki's history of Chinese-then-domestic pivots, represents a pattern: Chinese entities engage with Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. India then steps in (NHPC for West Seti, domestic for Budhigandaki) — but progress remains slow. The net result is decades lost on storage projects that would directly address storage-deficit. # Related hydro-geopolitics — the China-India triangulation storage-deficit — what West Seti would help solve budhigandaki — parallel trajectory of Chinese withdrawal, domestic/Indian pivot pancheshwar — another stalled storage mega-project, for different reasons # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.body_text: Western Nepal 132 kV Backbone # Summary Western Nepal 132 kV Backbone is the operational 132 kV Terai-side grid chain represented in the map to show western grid reach beyond Butwal. The operational 132 kV Terai-side grid chain that carries the map west of Butwal: Butwal-Shivapur-Lamahi-Kohalpur, Kohalpur-Bhurigaun-Lamki, and Lamki-Pahalwanpur-Attariya-Mahendranagar. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV | Status | Operational | Length basis | 404.89 route-km / 809.78 circuit-km | Source geometry | RPGCL 2021 official geospatial vector map | Status/length basis | NEA FY 2024/25 existing high-voltage line inventory | Corridor ID | | # Map Interpretation This corridor is now in the major transmission network because otherwise western Nepal looks emptier than it is. It is not a 400 kV export spine or a 220 kV bulk-transfer corridor; it is the operational 132 kV backbone that keeps Lumbini, Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, and Kanchanpur connected across the west. Current validation result: 3 features, 0 inferred connectors, 0 remaining endpoint gaps, and 418.149 km traced length against a 404.89 route-km basis. Public decision: default-visible, caveated. # Limitations & Controversies The route is source-backed but national-scale. It comes from RPGCL vector linework and NEA inventory control, not a tower-by-tower alignment sheet. It should be read as the western grid-reach backbone, with lighter visual weight than 220/400 kV lines. # See also data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network chameliya-attariya-132 kohalpur-surkhet-dailekh-132 dana-kushma-butwal-corridor gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection

pages.title: Availability-Declaration Penalties
pages.excerpt: A source-bounded explanation of reported availability-declaration deductions in Nepal's hydropower PPAs; signed contracts, enforcement ledgers and adjudicated outcomes remain unavailable.
pages.body_text: Availability-Declaration Penalties # Summary Availability-declaration penalties are reported contractual deductions that can apply when a hydropower producer delivers less energy than a declared or contracted threshold. The current wiki evidence is secondary PPA analysis. Signed PPAs, project-level deduction records and adjudicated outcomes remain missing. # Simple Explanation A generator forecasts how much electricity it expects to supply. Some contracts may permit a deduction when actual delivery falls below the applicable threshold. To determine whether a deduction was valid in a particular case, a reader needs that project's signed contract, dispatch and outage records, invoice calculation and any appeal outcome. # Reported Standard-Contract Mechanism nea-standard-ppa-clauses and ad-penalty-clause-research report the following formula from secondary analysis of standard wording: Compensation = [0.80 × min(Monthly Contract Energy, Availability Declaration) − (Actual Delivered + Scheduled Outage + Forced Outage + Force Majeure Energy)] × Purchase Rate This formula has not been checked against a representative set of signed project PPAs. It must not be treated as proof that every negotiated contract contains identical wording or that the provision was enforced in a particular way. # Curtailment Exposure The secondary analysis reports no explicit curtailment carve-out in the standard wording it reviewed. That identifies a potential contractual exposure when an off-taker dispatch instruction reduces delivery. It does not establish that every signed PPA lacks relief, that a penalty was imposed after a curtailment instruction, or that a dispute was resolved against a generator. # Barahi Evidence Status Legacy pages described barahi-hydropower as an audited case. The primary audited filing, fiscal year, signed PPA and regulatory or adjudication record are not present. The case is a research lead and must not be used as evidence of a confirmed deduction or legal outcome. # Evidence Needed A representative sample of signed PPAs and amendments. Project-level availability declarations, dispatch instructions, accepted energy, outage reasons and invoice calculations. Penalty ledgers showing amounts assessed, waived, disputed and recovered. ERC, arbitration or court decisions with the applicable contract version. A primary company filing for any named project case. No sector-wide penalty percentage or revenue effect is supported by the current corpus. # Common Misunderstandings A reported formula is not an enforcement record. Contract wording and actual deductions are different evidence questions. Low generation does not prove an AD penalty. Hydrology, outages, maintenance, transmission and dispatch can all affect delivery. A structural conflict risk does not establish a particular legal outcome. See nea-triple-authority. Barahi is not currently a verified case. The primary evidence trail is missing. # Related nea-triple-authority intervention-nea-structural-separation barahi-hydropower q-design-discharge

pages.title: Agrivoltaics and Land
headings: What agrivoltaics is, in Nepal-specific terms
Why it is the politically survivable path
pages.excerpt: Agrivoltaics — dual-use of land for crop production and solar PV generation — is the politically survivable path for scaling Terai utility solar beyond the ~2 GW that fee-simple land purchases can support. Nepal's binding constraint on the next 5–10 GW of solar is land, not techn
pages.body_text: Agrivoltaics and Land # Summary Agrivoltaics — dual-use of land for crop production and solar PV generation — is the politically survivable path for scaling Terai utility solar beyond the ~2 GW that fee-simple land purchases can support. Nepal's binding constraint on the next 5–10 GW of solar is land, not technology or capital. # Simple Explanation Building 5 GW of solar needs ~12,500 hectares of flat, grid-adjacent land. Nepal has only ~5,000–15,000 hectares of publicly owned or non-permanently-cultivated land that fits. After that, solar must either buy farmland from smallholders — politically explosive — or share the land with agriculture. Agrivoltaics means raising solar panels high enough that farmers can still grow crops underneath, sharing both land and revenue. # Common Misunderstandings "Agrivoltaics is a nice-to-have bonus." In Nepal's Terai, it is the only politically survivable configuration for multi-gigawatt ground-mount solar. "Every solar site must be agrivoltaic." Government-owned parcels, degraded land, hydro co-location sites, and industrial-zone-adjacent land remain first-choice options for the first 1.5–2 GW. "Agrivoltaics is capex-free." High-canopy configurations cost ~1.3–1.5× standard ground-mount; the capex multiplier is real and must be priced into tariffs. Module costs have collapsed, grid costs are middling, LCOE is already below small hydro (solar-lcoe-crossover). The binding constraint on the next 5–10 GW of Nepal solar is neither technology nor money. It is land. Specifically, it is the politics of converting Terai agricultural land into ground-mounted solar at the scale the grid can absorb. This page argues that agrivoltaics is not a "nice to have" framing for Nepal; it is the only politically survivable at-scale configuration for Terai utility solar, and explains why. # The land arithmetic Utility-scale ground-mount solar needs ~2.5 ha per MWp at typical Nepal spacing (row-to-row, tilt, O&M lanes). Building 5 GW on fee-simple purchased land requires ~12,500 ha — roughly 0.6% of Nepal's total cultivated area, but concentrated in a narrow belt: Terai agricultural land: ~1.4 million ha Within 10 km of a 132+ kV substation in Terai: ~220,000 ha Non-forest, non-protected, slope < 3%, within that belt: ~160,000 ha Of which, publicly-owned (sarkari) or non-permanently-cultivated: ~5,000–15,000 ha (estimates vary; no single cadastral register) So the fee-simple, non-agricultural, grid-adjacent land available for 5 GW of Terai solar is roughly the land needed for 2–6 GW. Nothing past that is buildable without either (a) buying agricultural land from smallholders, or (b) finding a way to share the land with agriculture. Option (a) is a political non-starter at that scale. Nepal's hydropower-era displacement politics (Upper Tamakoshi, Budhigandaki, Pancheshwar) has produced a sensitised Terai farming public, distrustful of large land conversions, with active civil society and elected representation. Fee-simple conversion of rice paddy to PV modules — at the ten-district Terai scale — produces a food-security / landlessness fight that a government elected with an agricultural base cannot win and should not try. Option (b) is agrivoltaics. # What agrivoltaics is, in Nepal-specific terms The generic agrivoltaic definition — dual-use of land for crop production and PV generation, through elevated or spaced modules — covers a range of configurations: Configuration | Module height | Crop compatibility | Yield interaction | Capex multiplier | ---|---|---|---|---:| Low-mount vegetable rotation | 0.8–1.2 m | Leafy greens, onion, garlic, turmeric, shade-tolerant veg | +5 to −10% crop yield under partial shade | 1.0–1.1× | High-canopy rice / wheat | 3.0–4.5 m | Rice, wheat, maize (partial-shade-tolerant varieties) | −10 to −25% crop yield; tractor access preserved | 1.35–1.55× | Animal-grazing (agri-PV) | 1.2–1.8 m with fencing | Goat / sheep grazing under; moderates heat | Forage gains; livestock welfare up | 1.05–1.15× | Tree / plantation (orchard-PV) | 2.5–4.0 m | Mango, litchi, guava, banana | Microclimate benefit; water saving | 1.2–1.4× | Pond-edge / irrigation canal | 1.5–3.0 m over canal | Fish / aquaculture below | Reduces evaporation from canals | 1.1–1.3× | Two of these configurations fit Nepal's Terai farming calendar especially well: Leafy greens + low-mount PV on the 6-month paddy-to-fallow rotation. Paddy in monsoon (when PV yield is lowest anyway), leafy greens Oct–May under the modules (when PV yield is highest and the crop benefits from shade in the pre-monsoon heat). Ideal match. High-canopy PV over rice + wheat double-crop. Higher capex but preserves the dominant Terai land-use pattern; yield penalty of 10–20% on rice is offset by a PV revenue-share of NPR 40,000–80,000 per ropani per year, a 4–10× uplift on smallholder cash income. The economics of this are not marginal. # Why it is the politically survivable path A solar project structured as: 25-year lease (not purchase) of 1–5 ha from each participating smallholder, with a right of return at lease-end. Revenue share of a defined percentage of PPA receipts, indexed to inflation. Preserved agricultural use under / between modules, with the farmer as the agricultural tenant. Shared community-scale services — rural electrification credit, pump irrigation at cost, cold-storage co-development. …has a fundamentally different political valence than "buy the land for a solar farm." It resembles a successful cooperative more than a land grab. It mirrors the structure that made India's Gujarat and Maharashtra agrivoltaic deployments land-lightly, while the pure-purchase models in Rajasthan and Karnataka have had recurring land-conflict problems. It is also the structure most compatible with Nepal's cooperative-heavy rural economy (aepc-renewable-framework) and with the farmers' cooperative (krishak sahakari) networks that already operate at the 10–500-household scale across Terai. # What this concept is not saying Not that every Terai solar site must be agrivoltaic. Government-owned sarkari parcels, degraded / alkali land, oxbow scrub, industrial-zone-adjacent land, and hydro-co-location sites (hybrid-siting-logic) remain the first choice where available — perhaps the first 1.5–2 GW. Not that agrivoltaics automatically solves all politics. It changes the coalition, but requires specific contract drafting (lease-not-sale, revenue-share, return rights) that Nepal does not yet have template law for. Not that it is capex-free. The ~1.3–1.5× capex multiplier on high-canopy configurations is real and must be priced into tariffs. At current module prices, the agrivoltaic LCOE is still well below hydro PPA (solar-lcoe-crossover). # Structural conditions for scaling Scaling agrivoltaics to national significance requires four institutional conditions that are not yet in place: 1. A lease-template framework for 20–25 year solar leases on agricultural land, separating usufruct transfer from fee-simple conversion. Absent this, every agrivoltaic site is negotiated one-off, which constrains scaling. 2. An agrivoltaic tariff adder — NPR 0.30–0.50/kWh uplift for dual-use configurations, conditional on post-build crop verification. This would offset the capex multiplier. 3. A recognised agricultural-technical standard for minimum module height, row spacing, and crop-light requirements — Nepal currently has none. 4. A VGF / green-finance channel for the incremental capex — the eib-rural-solar-phase2 and wb-grid-solar-ee-project are the most natural hosts, but neither currently prices an agrivoltaic multiplier. Absent these four conditions, Terai utility solar hits the land wall at roughly 2 GW and stalls. With them, the same physical resource becomes a 10–15 GW build-out path that takes nothing out of food production, and actively raises smallholder cash income. See intervention-transmission-completion and claim-solar-terai-only-short-cycle-build for the policy implications. # Related solar-resource-geography-nepal — why Terai is the zone that matters here hybrid-siting-logic — the first ~2 GW without triggering the land fight solar-lcoe-crossover — why the capex multiplier is absorbable rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the complementary non-ground-mount story nea-960mw-solar-tender — the first portfolio-scale test claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the tracked claim this page operationalises

pages.title: Bay Of Bengal Terminal
pages.excerpt: This marker is the terminal reach of the generated route-to-ocean trace.
pages.body_text: Bay Of Bengal Terminal # Summary This marker is the terminal reach of the generated route-to-ocean trace. # Simple Explanation It is the map point that says: the Nepal-origin downstream route does not stop at the Indian plains. It continues through the lower delta system until it reaches the Bay of Bengal. # Why It Matters It gives the map a complete endpoint. Without it, the downstream river story visually stops in the plains or delta, even though the strategic route continues through the lower Padma-Meghna system to the sea. # How To Read The Marker Use it as the end of the strategic route trace, not as a detailed coastal or tidal model. # Caveat The terminal point comes from the HydroRIVERS route trace. It does not represent all distributaries, estuarine channels, or coastal sediment dynamics. # Common Misunderstandings It is not a coastal model. The point marks the route endpoint, not tides, ports, erosion, or delta morphology. It is not a claim that Nepal controls downstream outcomes. It only completes the visual trace from Himalayan basins to the sea. It is not a precise distributary selection. The lower delta contains many channels; this marker is a strategic route endpoint. # Related data-layer-nepal-origin-ocean-routes padma-meghna-delta lower-delta-bay-interface how-to-read-geopolitics-map

pages.title: Bihar Ganges Trunk Zone
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone marks the shared Ganges corridor where separate Nepal-linked routes become one downstream political geography.
pages.body_text: Bihar Ganges Trunk Zone # Summary This dependency zone marks the shared Ganges corridor where separate Nepal-linked routes become one downstream political geography. # Simple Explanation Several Nepal-origin river routes start as separate Himalayan basin stories. By the Bihar Ganges trunk, they have entered a shared lower-basin corridor, so the map shifts from individual tributaries to a common downstream zone. # Why It Matters The map needs this zone because users can otherwise over-focus on individual tributaries. By the Bihar Ganges trunk, Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali/Ghaghara, and Mahakali/Sharda routes are part of a broader lower-basin story. # How To Read The Zone Use it as the bridge between the upstream route merges and the ganges-padma-transition. It is where individual Nepal-linked routes become a shared downstream trunk. # Caveat The polygon is a broad context zone. It is not a model of flow shares, river operations, or local water allocation. # Common Misunderstandings The zone is not a hydrological allocation model. It does not estimate how much water comes from each Nepal-linked basin. It is not a legal or administrative boundary. It is a strategic map layer for reading downstream dependency. It does not collapse all tributaries into one story upstream. The merge matters downstream; basin-specific constraints still matter in Nepal. # Related kosi-ganges-merge gandak-ganges-merge ghaghara-ganges-merge ganges-padma-transition ganges-contribution

pages.title: Buildability
pages.excerpt: Buildability is the first-order filter on Nepal’s hydropower future: a project is not “good” because a desk study assigns a large MW number—it is good if the entire delivery package remains credible after geology, hydraulics, hazards, and grid realities are stressed.
pages.body_text: Buildability # Summary Buildability is the first-order filter on Nepal’s hydropower future: a project is not “good” because a desk study assigns a large MW number—it is good if the entire delivery package remains credible after geology, hydraulics, hazards, and grid realities are stressed. # Simple Explanation Buildability asks: can this project actually be built and operated, given Nepal's mountains, earthquakes, sediment, and thin construction market? A project that looks good on paper may fail because the tunnel collapses, the turbines wear out in months from silt, or the transmission line to evacuate the power never gets built. # What buildability actually tests A serious buildability review chains interdependent risks: Geology and underground works — tunneling and cavern stability under high cover, fault zones, and variable rock mass ratings. Sediment and abrasion — turbine technology, wear life, and maintenance cycles are not O&M trivia when concentrations swing orders of magnitude seasonally (see sediment-as-design-constraint). Hydraulic transients and flood/GLOF exposure — hazard tolerance and intake resilience. Evacuation — generation without stranded-generation-grade transmission is incomplete infrastructure. See the likhu-2: four private IPPs totaling 213 MW commissioned into a New Khimti substation sized for half their output, stranding ~40% of contracted generation in FY 2023/24 until a 200 MVA transformer upgrade restored the corridor. Execution realism — contractor capacity, local logistics winter, and financing covenants that survive delay. See chameliya-hydropower (11-year build, $7.5M/MW, headrace tunnel collapse) and upper-trishuli-3a (2024 flood destroyed gates and control room, 88-day outage at upper-tamakoshi). # Strategic implication The planning-relevant metric is therefore system value — incremental dependable energy, loss factors, curtailment risk, and delivered cost — rather than headline megawatts. That reframing connects naturally to storage-deficit (seasonal re-timing is worthless if the dam never reaches COD) and to basin-scale complexity in karnali-basin megaproject corridors. Megaprojects such as budhigandaki are instructive case files: the controversy is not only "how big," but whether the integrated package of reservoir, tunnels, communities, and finance can survive the decades-long path to operation. At the opposite scale, marsyangdi (69 MW, 36 years old) demonstrates that aging units approaching overhaul age carry a different buildability risk. khimti-i (60 MW, 1996) proves what an early-generation negotiated PPA can deliver, while likhu-4 (120→52 MW redesign after India wheeling dispute) shows buildability includes the regulatory environment the project commissions into. # Common Misunderstandings "Licensed = buildable" — many licensed projects stall for years due to financing, geology, or grid constraints. A license is a permit, not a construction guarantee. "Buildability is just engineering" — it includes social acceptance, financing, regulatory environment, and market access. "Big projects are inherently better" — megaprojects concentrate risk; a portfolio of smaller, buildable projects may deliver more system value. # Related sediment-as-design-constraint — the turbine-wear dimension stranded-generation — when buildable generation cannot be monetized storage-deficit — re-timing is worthless if the dam never reaches COD karnali-basin — basin-scale megaproject complexity budhigandaki — the largest buildability test case claim-governance-binding — institutional failures as binding constraint # Sources wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 adb-hydropower-growth-nepal wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022

pages.title: Consumption Trajectory Outlook
headings: The Consumption Story in One Sentence
Risk Factors — What Could Slow or Accelerate Growth
What the Data Cannot Yet Answer
pages.excerpt: What Nepal's electricity consumption growth trajectory implies for the country's energy strategy — the import-displacement opportunity, the growth risks, and the metric that determines whether the hydro build-out succeeds or fails on its own terms.
pages.body_text: Consumption Trajectory Outlook # Summary What Nepal's electricity consumption growth trajectory implies for the country's energy strategy — the import-displacement opportunity, the growth risks, and the metric that determines whether the hydro build-out succeeds or fails on its own terms. This page synthesizes data-domestic-demand, data-industrial-electricity-consumers, data-agricultural-energy-consumption, and data-consumption-geographic-distribution into a forward view. The companion supply-side analysis is twenty-year-strategy. # Simple Explanation Nepal is using much more electricity than it did a few years ago, but electricity is still a small share of total energy use. The concept asks whether new hydropower will be absorbed by domestic cooking, transport, industry, and agriculture, or whether weak domestic demand leaves Nepal dependent on low-value seasonal exports. # The Consumption Story in One Sentence Nepal's electricity consumption has grown ~55% in four years (from ~7,277 GWh to 11,288 GWh), but electricity is still only 7.23% of total final energy and 0.5% of households cook with it — meaning the growth runway is measured in decades, not years. # Current State — Electricity Consumption (FY 2024/25) Segment | GWh | Growth (4yr CAGR) | Electricity Penetration in Segment | ---------|------:|------:|------:| Residential | ~4,742 | ~10.8% | 5.0% of residential energy | Industrial | ~4,136 | ~10.1% | 11.6% of industrial energy (FY 2079/80) | Commercial | ~879 | ~14.5% | 9.9% of commercial energy (FY 2079/80) | Construction/Mining | ~591 | — | 55.5% of sector energy — already majority-electric | Agriculture | ~315 | — | 22.5% of agricultural energy | Transport | ~25 | — | 0.05% — essentially zero | Other (streetlight, irrigation, temp) | ~620 | ~17.8% | — | Total electricity | ~11,288 | ~11.6% | 7.23% of total final energy | \ Estimated from WECS sector share applied to FY 2024/25 total # The Consumption Growth Model Per-capita electricity consumption is 465 kWh/yr and growing ~10% annually. At this rate: Year | Per-capita (kWh) | Implied total (GWh) | Context | ------|------:|------:|---------| FY 2024/25 | 465 | 11,288 | Current | ~2029 | ~750 | ~18,000 | Nepal reaches current India per-capita | ~2034 | ~1,200 | ~28,800 | Reaches lower-middle-income norm | ~2040 | ~2,000 | ~48,000 | Reaches middle-income norm | This trajectory is not a forecast — it's a sense-check. At 10% annual demand growth, domestic consumption alone would absorb roughly the output of the planned hydro pipeline (see data-potential-pyramid) without needing massive export growth. But sustaining 10% demand growth requires the substitution pathway in energy-substitution-pathway to actually happen — cooking electrification, industrial fuel-switching, and EV uptake. # The Import Displacement Ledger The single most powerful number in the consumption profile is the gap between what Nepal currently imports (fossil fuels) and what it could displace with domestic electricity: Fuel | Total Consumption (TJ) | Import Cost (NPR Bill./yr, est.) | Displaceable by Electricity? | Electricity Equivalent (GWh) | ------|------:|------:|------:|------:| Diesel (all sectors) | 49,728 | ~120 | Yes — transport, ag pumps, gensets | ~13,800 | LPG (all sectors) | 23,677 | ~55 | Yes — induction cooking | ~6,600 | Petrol (all sectors) | 21,932 | ~75 | Partial — EV passenger vehicles | ~6,100 | Coal (industrial) | 34,016 | ~40 | Partial — electric kilns, hydrogen | ~9,400 | ATF / jet fuel | 6,191 | ~20 | No — aviation | — | Total displaceable | ~129,353 | ~290 | | ~35,900 GWh | [!finding] Total displacement opportunity is ~3× current electricity consumption If Nepal electrified all technically-displaceable fossil fuel consumption, it would need ~35,900 GWh of additional electricity — roughly triple the current 11,288 GWh. This is the domestic demand ceiling that the domestic-led-hydro-strategy is designed to capture. ## Displacement already underway EV passenger vehicles: >70% of new passenger vehicle imports in FY 2024/25 were EVs, driven by tax differentials Electric cooking: NEA FY 2024/25 report explicitly flags government policy to encourage electric cooking, transportation, and industry Industrial switching: diesel genset → grid connection is happening as reliability improves ## Displacement not yet started Brick kilns: ~1,500+ coal-burning kilns, essentially zero electric kilns deployed Freight transport: diesel trucks and buses, no material electrification Cement clinker: coal-fired, hydrogen co-firing still in concept stage (see green-hydrogen-nepal) LPG-to-induction cooking at scale: 0.5% household penetration, needs appliance cost reduction and reliability improvements # Risk Factors — What Could Slow or Accelerate Growth ## Upside risks (faster consumption growth) Factor | Mechanism | Magnitude | --------|-----------|-----------| LPG subsidy removal / rebalancing | Shift households from LPG to induction cooking | +50–75 PJ (~14,000–21,000 GWh) potential | Industrial policy for ferroalloys | Attract electro-intensive industry with cheap reliable power | +500–2,000 GWh per major plant | EV adoption beyond passenger vehicles | Electric buses, two-wheelers, three-wheelers | +500–1,500 GWh by 2030 | Data centres / ICT expansion | Nepal's competitive advantage — cheap green power + English-speaking workforce | +200–500 GWh | Cold chain build-out | Refrigerated transport and storage for agriculture | +500–1,000 GWh | ## Downside risks (slower consumption growth) Factor | Mechanism | Magnitude | --------|-----------|-----------| Manufacturing decline continues | Manufacturing already fell from 7.3% to 5.7% of GDP | −200–500 GWh vs trend | Grid reliability stalls | If outages persist, firms stay on diesel, households don't buy induction cookers | −300–800 GWh vs potential | Fuelwood inertia | Cultural preference + zero cash cost keeps biomass dominant in cooking | −100–200 PJ cooking load | Tariff distortion | If industrial tariffs don't reflect the true cost advantage over diesel, fuel-switching economics erode | −100–300 GWh | Migration / depopulation | Rural areas lose electricity consumers faster than urban gains | −100–200 GWh | # The Metric That Determines Success From energy-substitution-pathway: Biomass + fossil share of Nepal's final energy consumption. Today ~92.8%. A serious transition by 2040 should bring it below 70%, implying ~25–30 PJ of net displacement per year. Applied to 2025-2030 specifically, the intermediate targets are: Metric | Current (FY 2024/25) | 2030 Target | Status | --------|------:|------:|--------| Electricity share of final energy | 7.23% (FY 2079/80) | 12–15% | On track if 10% demand CAGR holds | Electric cooking penetration | 0.5% | 5–10% | Requires active policy push | EV share of new vehicle sales | >70% (passenger only) | >90% (all light vehicles) | Ahead on passenger, behind on freight | Industrial electricity share | 11.6% (FY 2079/80) | 18–22% | Requires grid reliability + industrial policy | Per-capita electricity | 465 kWh | 800–1,000 kWh | On track | Diesel displaced in agriculture | ~0 (currently rising) | 20–30% of ag diesel | Requires tubewell electrification programme | # The Export Surplus Question If domestic consumption grows at 10% CAGR and generation grows at roughly the same pace (the IPSDP pipeline implies ~12,000-15,000 MW installed by 2035), the net export profile depends on which grows faster: Scenario | Demand CAGR | Supply CAGR | 2030 Net Export (GWh) | Character | ----------|------:|------:|------:|-----------| Demand-led | 12% | 10% | ~500–1,500 | Imports still needed in winter | Balanced | 10% | 10% | ~2,000–3,500 | Monsoon exports, winter imports | Supply-led | 8% | 12% | ~5,000–7,000 | Large monsoon surplus, seasonal trade deepens | The current trajectory (~11.6% demand growth, ~10% supply growth) most closely resembles the "Demand-led" scenario — if it sustains. The key variable is whether the demand-side policies (cooking electrification, EV uptake, industrial switching) materialize at the same pace as the supply-side pipeline (22 projects commissioned in FY 2024/25 alone). The nightmare scenario is the "Supply-led" one: large monsoon surplus with weak domestic demand → exports at low spot prices while winter imports at high peak rates persist → the seasonal-arbitrage-trap institutionalizes. # What the Data Cannot Yet Answer 1. Hourly consumption by consumer category — we know the evening peak shape but not which sectors drive it (residential cooking + lighting probably dominates). Without this, the storage + demand-side management sizing is approximate. 2. Actual industrial sub-sector GWh — the estimates in data-industrial-electricity-consumers are indicative. NEA has this data but does not publish it. 3. Captive generation inventory — how much diesel generation capacity exists behind industrial meters, and how much is actually dispatched, is unmeasured. This is the hidden consumption layer. 4. Province-level sectoral splits — we have provincial totals but not the domestic/industrial/commercial breakdown within each province. 5. Price elasticity of demand — how sensitive is each consumer category to tariff changes? Essential for demand-side policy design but unresearched for Nepal. # Common Misunderstandings Fast electricity-demand growth does not mean the whole energy system is electrified. Electricity is still a small share of final energy consumption. Export surplus is not automatically a sign of success. It can reflect weak domestic absorption, especially if monsoon exports coexist with winter imports. Per-capita electricity growth is not the same as fuel substitution. The transition test is whether biomass, LPG, diesel, petrol, and coal are actually displaced. # Related data-domestic-demand — the core electricity demand data data-industrial-electricity-consumers — industrial sub-sector profile data-agricultural-energy-consumption — agricultural energy and diesel displacement data-consumption-geographic-distribution — where consumption is geographically data-final-energy-mix — the total-energy denominator energy-substitution-pathway — the strategic framework for displacement domestic-led-hydro-strategy — why domestic load matters more than exports twenty-year-strategy — the supply-side counterpart seasonal-arbitrage-trap — what happens if demand lags supply unresolved-questions — data gaps this page inherits

pages.title: Domestic-Led Hydro Strategy
headings: Why domestic demand is not a small story
The constraint is not "can Nepal export?" — it can
pages.excerpt: Domestic-led hydro strategy means planning Nepal's power system around its own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus rather than defining the investment program around export markets. Hydropower remains central, but solar complementarity,
pages.body_text: Domestic-Led Hydro Strategy # Summary Domestic-led hydro strategy means planning Nepal's power system around its own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus rather than defining the investment program around export markets. Hydropower remains central, but solar complementarity, BESS, and demand shaping now belong inside the strategy. # Simple Explanation Nepal could build dams mainly to sell electricity to India. A "domestic-led" strategy says: build dams (and solar) mainly to power Nepali homes, factories, and transport first. Sell any leftover electricity abroad. The sequencing matters because domestic demand creates jobs and tax revenue that exports alone do not. # Common Misunderstandings "Domestic-led means anti-export." It does not. Exports are valuable; the strategy says they should follow domestic need, not lead it. "Nepal lacks enough domestic demand." Per-capita electricity use is ~370–465 kWh/year — 5–7× below middle-income norms — indicating large headroom for efficient demand growth. "Domestic-led is only about hydro." The better operational phrase is domestic-led power strategy with a hydro backbone: solar, BESS, and demand shaping are integral. Domestic-led hydro means planning the power system around Nepal's own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus, not to define the investment program. After the solar audit, the better operational phrase is domestic-led power strategy with a hydro backbone: hydropower remains central, but solar-hydro-complementarity, BESS, and demand shaping now belong inside the strategy rather than beside it. # The consensus across analytical lines Across multiple research threads in this project, the core strategic recommendation converges: Nepal should pursue domestic-led hydro with export support, not export-led hydro with domestic leftovers. The distinction is not anti-export; it is about sequencing and the objective function. Exports are valuable when they absorb genuine surplus at acceptable prices; they are costly when they institutionalize the seasonal-arbitrage-trap — cheap monsoon sales and expensive winter imports on the same national balance sheet. Recent trade and demand evidence frames the current failure plainly: "The system is getting better at monetizing surplus, but it still pays a winter scarcity tax, and it has not yet built enough domestic electrification depth to turn hydropower into broad-based wealth." # Why domestic demand is not a small story nepal-energy-profile makes clear that "low consumption" is better read as headroom than as lack of need. Per-capita electricity use is ~370–465 kWh/year — roughly 5–7x below a middle-income norm of 2,000–3,000 kWh/year. Electricity's share of final energy is small (7.23% in FY 2079/80, up from 4.96% the year before — see data-final-energy-mix) — so electrification of cooking, heat, mobility, and process heat is a multi-decade demand builder. The specific sinks to target, ranked by volume, are worked out in energy-substitution-pathway. The sectoral breakdown (FY 2020/21, NEA) reveals a critical structure (see data-domestic-demand): Residential: 43% of electricity sales (~3,138 GWh) Industrial: 39% of electricity sales (~2,816 GWh) — nearly as large despite being a tiny fraction of customer count Industry is already the second-biggest user and the highest-leverage expansion target The electric cooking gap is the most dramatic underdevelopment: fewer than ~1% of Nepal's households use electricity for cooking. Biomass and imported LPG dominate. This is not a preference story — it is a reliability and appliance-access story. Shifting even 20–30% of cooking loads to electricity would create large, distributed, flexible domestic demand that simultaneously absorbs monsoon surplus and cuts the LPG import bill. Industrialization, urbanization, and replacement of costly fossil inputs add concurrent load. Highest-value uses include displacing captive diesel, electrifying cooking and transport, and feeding manufacturing where reliability converts kWh into jobs and tax base. The current fuel-displacement model in energy-substitution-pathway supports a fuel-specific domestic value premium rather than a single headline ratio: roughly 2.1-2.6× export value for LPG cooking and 4.3-6.6× for diesel mechanical displacement, with biomass value depending heavily on whether health and time externalities are counted. # The constraint is not "can Nepal export?" — it can Nepal is improving its exchange-linked value capture: the IEX price spread flipped positive in 2023-24 (Nepal sold at ₹5.61/kWh, bought at ₹4.43/kWh). But the whole-system average was still negative (sold Rs 8.72/unit, bought Rs 9.17/unit) because structural winter imports at peak-hour rates wash out the monsoon gains. The hard constraint is "whether Nepal can build domestic demand and system efficiency fast enough that exports become a high-value optimization layer, not the primary story." # Exports as complement, not compass india-energy-relationship will remain decisive for corridors, approvals, and timing. bhutan-hydropower-model is often invoked as a managed export reference — useful less as a blueprint to copy than as a reminder that host-country load and fiscal design shaped outcomes. Nepal's geography and politics differ, but the lesson holds: contracts and domestic anchors matter as much as megawatts. # Links to supply-side innovation When surplus is structural in the monsoon, domestic absorption can be engineered — not only through wires but through electrolysis and ammonia. green-hydrogen-nepal is the most ambitious demand-creation path: it turns seasonal glut into chemical industry and food security inputs instead of low-priced spill. Solar adds a second supply-side innovation: it lets Nepal build dry-season daytime energy on a short cycle while reservoir hydro moves slowly through buildability and finance constraints. The domestic strategy should therefore treat nea-960mw-solar-tender as a bridge, not a distraction: solar buys time for storage hydro, and storage hydro makes solar useful after sunset. # Related data-domestic-demand — demand distribution data, cooking gap, load profile seasonal-arbitrage-trap — the cost of not building domestic demand stranded-generation — monsoon surplus that domestic load could absorb green-hydrogen-nepal — industrial-scale demand from surplus solar-in-the-master-narrative — how solar changes the strategy without replacing hydro claim-solar-terai-only-short-cycle-build — why solar is the short-cycle bridge twenty-year-strategy — how demand-building fits the phased strategy

pages.title: Eastern UP Ghaghara-Gandak Belt
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone gives context for the western and central Nepal-linked routes entering the agricultural plains of eastern Uttar Pradesh.
pages.body_text: Eastern UP Ghaghara-Gandak Belt # Summary This dependency zone gives context for the western and central Nepal-linked routes entering the agricultural plains of eastern Uttar Pradesh. # Simple Explanation It is a downstream context area on the map. The point is not that Nepal manages this region, but that river timing from Nepal-linked basins eventually passes into a densely used agricultural plain where floods, dry-season water, and settlement exposure matter. # Why It Matters The zone is included because the Ghaghara and Gandak routes connect Nepal-linked basin timing to dense agricultural and settlement geography. It is a downstream exposure area, not a water-control area. # How To Read The Zone Read it with ghaghara-ganges-merge, gandak-ganges-merge, and data-layer-future-regulation-scenario. The question is how future upstream storage and river timing could matter in a region already sensitive to floods and seasonal water availability. # Caveat The polygon is broad and strategic. It is not an irrigation command boundary, crop raster, or flood-inundation model. # Common Misunderstandings This is not an irrigation map. It does not show canal command areas or crop water demand. It is not a flood forecast. It only marks a downstream exposure belt relevant to Nepal-linked river routes. It should not be read as control. The layer shows dependency geography, not upstream authority. # Related ghaghara-ganges-merge gandak-ganges-merge downstream-river-geopolitics how-to-read-geopolitics-map
