What this pathway implies for strategy
pages.excerpt: Energy substitution pathway names the specific question a hydro build-out must answer if it is to transform Nepal's energy system and not just its export ledger: which non-electric energy flows are being displaced, in what order, by what policy and infrastructure? Without this le
pages.body_text: Energy Substitution Pathway # Summary Energy substitution pathway names the specific question a hydro build-out must answer if it is to transform Nepal's energy system and not just its export ledger: which non-electric energy flows are being displaced, in what order, by what policy and infrastructure? Without this lens, "more hydro MW" and "more electricity consumption" can both rise while Nepal's overall energy system — dominated by fuelwood, coal, and imported petroleum — barely shifts. This is the strategic complement to domestic-led-hydro-strategy: where that page argues why domestic load matters more than exports, this one argues which specific loads to build. # Simple Explanation The substitution pathway is the bridge between electricity supply and actual energy transition. It asks which existing fuels Nepal stops burning when it adds clean electricity: fuelwood in kitchens, diesel in transport and pumps, LPG in cooking, or coal in industry. # Why the substitution frame exists The master-thesis treats hydropower as a conversion problem: turning hydrological advantage into firm, deliverable, financeable power. But even a perfectly converted fleet only creates kWh. Those kWh become welfare only when they displace something Nepal currently burns. From data-final-energy-mix, Nepal's FY 2079/80 final energy is: Biomass 68.7% (340 PJ) — overwhelmingly fuelwood in cooking Petroleum 19.4% (103 PJ) — diesel, petrol, LPG, ATF, all imported Electricity 7.23% (38.5 PJ) — 94% of it from hydro Coal 6.39% (34 PJ) — 99% of it burned in brick kilns and cement plants Other renewables (biogas, solar, µhydro, wind) 3.1% (16.5 PJ) Everything outside electricity is a candidate substitution target. Ranking them by physical magnitude yields a clear priority stack. # The three dominant sinks, ranked by volume ## Sink 1 — Fuelwood in residential cooking and heating (257 PJ) The single largest energy flow in Nepal. 48.3% of all final energy consumed. Affected population: essentially all of rural Nepal plus significant urban pockets. Substitute: electric induction cooking, heat-pump water heating, electric room heating in winter. Why it's hard: appliance cost, grid reliability (evening peak 18:30–19:25 is exactly cooking time), LPG subsidy currently undercuts electric cooking on marginal-cost terms. Why it's the biggest lever: displacing 20–30% of cooking load creates ~50–75 PJ of new electric demand — roughly doubling current electricity consumption. That is bigger than any plausible export contract. Connected wiki pages: data-domestic-demand (the Biomass + fossil share of Nepal's final energy consumption. Today that share is ~92.8% (68.7% biomass + 19.4% petroleum + 6.4% coal − small overlap). A serious transition by 2040 should bring that share below 70%, implying ~25–30 PJ of net biomass+fossil displacement per year. That in turn implies specific quantities of induction cookers deployed, kilns retrofitted, EVs sold, and industrial processes electrified — all measurable, all currently unmeasured at the system level. If Nepal builds 20,000 MW of hydro and the biomass+fossil share in 2040 is still 85%, the build-out has failed on its own terms. If Nepal builds only 10,000 MW but the share falls to 65%, the strategy has succeeded. # Common Misunderstandings More hydropower is not automatically substitution. New electricity must connect to a real end use that replaces biomass or fossil fuel. More domestic consumption is not automatically better. The quality of demand matters: displacing imported diesel or LPG has different value from adding low-value discretionary load. Exports and substitution are not interchangeable. A kWh exported earns revenue; a kWh used domestically can avoid imported-fuel spending and change the energy mix. # Related data-final-energy-mix — the underlying data domestic-led-hydro-strategy — the strategic envelope data-domestic-demand — sectoral electricity demand today green-hydrogen-nepal — the coal-displacement pathway twenty-year-strategy — phased implementation seasonal-arbitrage-trap — what happens if substitution is not built claim-mw-not-equal-value — the value-capture logic master-thesis — the overarching argument

pages.title: Environmental Flow Policy
pages.excerpt: The IPSDP executive summary treats environmental flow and protected-area restrictions as buildability constraints, not as side notes. In the SEA mitigation table on page 37, moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 says hydropower planning must evaluate and manage environmental flows and m
pages.body_text: Environmental Flow Policy # Summary The IPSDP executive summary treats environmental flow and protected-area restrictions as buildability constraints, not as side notes. In the SEA mitigation table on page 37, moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 says hydropower planning must evaluate and manage environmental flows and must respect statutory restrictions in protected areas. # Simple Explanation Environmental flow policy is the rule-of-thumb that a hydropower project cannot treat the whole river as available for diversion. Some flow must remain for downstream ecology, communities, legal requirements, and protected-area constraints. # What the IPSDP says directly Hydropower can alter downstream flow, habitat continuity, and river-wide flow patterns. Where adverse effects are expected, project planning should refer to the IFC Good Practice Handbook: Environmental Flows for Hydropower Projects (2018) and build an explicit E-flow management plan. For projects inside national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, hunting reserves, conservation areas, or buffer zones under Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act (2029/1973), prior permission is required. The same table says river modification and damming are not assumptions a developer can make inside protected areas; maintenance-flow and mitigation requirements remain in force. # Why this matters This is one of the clearest official signals in the current wiki that hydropower potential categories are not simply a matter of head and discharge. Protected-area law, river-ecology constraints, and mitigation hierarchy all cut directly into what is realistically developable. That makes this page a direct bridge between buildability, hydropower-potential-categories, and glof-risk: those concepts are all about why paper potential collapses when real-world constraints are applied. # Confidence boundary This page is limited to the policy and mitigation language stated in the IPSDP executive summary. It does not attempt to summarize Nepal's whole EIA or hydropower-permitting regime beyond what that table states. # Common Misunderstandings Environmental flow is not only an environmental side issue. It changes buildable energy, project design, and licensing risk. Protected-area restrictions are not captured by MW potential alone. A technically attractive site can still be constrained by law and mitigation requirements. This page is not a full legal guide. It summarizes the IPSDP signal, not the entire permitting regime. # Related buildability hydropower-potential-categories glof-risk moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025

pages.title: Firm Power
headings: Installed MW ≠ what you can count on in February
Potential pyramids are not firm-power statements
pages.excerpt: Firm power is dependable, year-round, dispatchable electrical capability under credible drought and system stress assumptions—not a branding label for “big projects,” and not interchangeable with installed megawatts, annual energy (GWh), or even average seasonal output.
pages.body_text: Firm Power # Summary Firm power is dependable, year-round, dispatchable electrical capability under credible drought and system stress assumptions—not a branding label for “big projects,” and not interchangeable with installed megawatts, annual energy (GWh), or even average seasonal output. # Simple Explanation Firm power is the electricity you can actually count on when the grid is under the most stress — not the nameplate capacity printed on a turbine, and not the annual total generation. It is the amount of power that would still be available during the driest, darkest, most constrained weeks of the year. # Installed MW ≠ what you can count on in February A plant can be “online” while being strategically irrelevant for reliability if its energy is concentrated in monsoon weeks when the grid is already long—or if its output is volatile within-day in ways that the transmission system cannot absorb. Conversely, a smaller reservoir or import contract may contribute more firm value than a large RoR string, depending on commit rights, hydrology, and dispatch rules. The right planning question is therefore not “how many MW?” but how much electricity is deliverable when the alternative is rationing, diesel, or blackout—and at what cost. # Potential pyramids are not firm-power statements National “potential” figures sit at the top of a reduction chain from theoretical resource to what is financeable and buildable; see hydropower-potential-categories and the tabulated reductions in data-potential-pyramid. Those layers measure energy opportunity, not contract-grade dependability. Firm power is the bottom of the stack in strategic terms: it is what you underwrite, what you trade, and what industrialization plans should assume in dry weeks. # Examples A 100 MW RoR plant may generate near 100 MW in August but only 30–40 MW in January — its firm power contribution is closer to the January number for planning purposes. kulekhani-i (60 MW reservoir storage) can release stored water in dry weeks, making it one of Nepal's few sources of true firm power despite its small size. # Analytical payoff Keeping firm distinct from big clarifies why winter deficits can persist even as installed capacity rises, why export discussions hinge on commitment windows not annual averages, and why system adequacy is a seasonal adequacy problem first. # Common Misunderstandings "Installed capacity = dependable capacity" — nameplate MW is a hardware label, not a reliability guarantee. "Annual energy (GWh) proves adequacy" — a system can have high annual energy while still failing in scarcity hours. "Firm power = base load" — firm power can be peaking capacity; the concept is about dependability, not run duration. See ONTOLOGY.md disallowed alias. # Related seasonal-mismatch — the problem firm power addresses run-of-river-hydropower — why RoR delivers less firm power than nameplate suggests storage-deficit — the physical gap in seasonal firming claim-mw-not-equal-value — the canonical claim about conflation of MW, energy, and firm power data-potential-pyramid — the reduction chain from theoretical to dependable hydropower-potential-categories — the definitions that matter for planning # Sources wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 wecs-hydropower-potential-2019

This marker helps readers follow the central Nepal river route as it becomes the Narayani/Gandak system and then joins the wider Ganges corridor. # Why It Matters Gandaki is a central Nepal route with strong irrigation and plains relevance downstream. It connects Nepal's river timing story to the Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh agricultural belt. # How To Read The Marker Use this point to understand the central route: Gandaki in Nepal, Narayani near the border, Gandak in the plains, and then the Ganges trunk. # Caveat The marker is approximate and interpretive. pages.title: Nepal's Contribution to the Ganges
headings: Western basins as part of the same puzzle
pages.excerpt: Nepal occupies about 13% of the Ganges basin area yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and 70–80% of dry-season flow. This hydrological asymmetry — small footprint, large leverage on timing — is the physical basis for Nepal's upstream role in South Asian water secur
pages.body_text: Nepal's Contribution to the Ganges # Summary Nepal occupies about 13% of the Ganges basin area yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and 70–80% of dry-season flow. This hydrological asymmetry — small footprint, large leverage on timing — is the physical basis for Nepal's upstream role in South Asian water security. # Simple Explanation Nepal is a small country in a huge river basin. But the rivers that start in Nepal's Himalayas feed almost half the Ganges' water — and even more of its dry-season flow. This means what Nepal does with its rivers (dams, storage, diversions) affects hundreds of millions of people downstream, mostly in India and Bangladesh. # Common Misunderstandings "Nepal's contribution is proportional to its land area." It is not. Nepal's Himalayan geography concentrates precipitation and meltwater into a small area, producing outsized downstream contributions. "High contribution means Nepal has unlimited bargaining power." Contribution creates leverage, but leverage without institutional capacity and enforceable agreements does not translate into durable benefit. "The 40%/70% figures are exact and current." They are historical estimates from the 2005 National Water Plan that predate recent climate shifts; the directional conclusion is robust but the exact percentages should be treated cautiously. Nepal occupies only about 13% of the Ganges basin area, yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and on the order of 70–80% of dry-season flow measured at Farakka-style accounting points in strategic basin literature. This hydrological asymmetry—small footprint, large leverage on timing—is the physical basis for Nepal’s upstream role in South Asian water security. # Underused abundance Nepal's problem is not that the basin is empty. In National Water Plan framing, the country has roughly 225 BCM of annual water availability but uses only about 15 BCM for economic and social purposes. The strategic issue is therefore conversion: storage, delivery, irrigation timing, and coordinated releases — not raw annual scarcity. # What the asymmetry implies downstream Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and—through the concatenated regime—Bangladesh are sensitive to Nepal-origin contributions for: Kharif and rabi irrigation scheduling (canal drafts depend on low-flow stability). Flood peaks shaped by transboundary storms and sediment pulses (see koshi-basin for the extreme case). Drought resilience when monsoon spatial correlation fails. Aggregated planning numbers in basin assessments commonly cite ~5–7 million hectares of irrigated agriculture and ~200–250 million people as significantly affected by Nepal-influenced flow regimes (definitions vary; treat as order-of-magnitude strategic scale, not a census). # Climate change raises the stakes If variability intensifies and low flows become less reliable while extreme events increase, the marginal value of upstream storage, forecasting, and coordinated releases rises. Nepal’s geography could translate into bargaining power—but only if institutional capacity converts hydrology into credible, enforceable cooperation. Today, the more common pattern is leverage without durable agreement: episodic crisis diplomacy rather than rules-based benefit sharing. # Geopolitics and national planning The strategic read is developed in parallel on hydro-geopolitics and india-energy-relationship: electrons and cubic meters are joint products in peoples’ minds even when markets separate them. Nepal’s National Water Plan discourse (see national-water-plan-nepal) is the domestic mirror—attempting to align IWRM, energy, and disaster risk under one national narrative. # Western basins as part of the same puzzle karnali-basin feeds the Ghaghara complex and therefore UP’s vast irrigated plains. Storage and diversion debates there are not “local” Nepali stories; they are subcontinental stories with Nepali headwaters at the center. # Analytical bottom line Nepal’s contribution to the Ganges is not proportional to its land share. That fact creates real upstream leverage—and also moral hazard if Nepal builds unilateral infrastructure that ignores downstream sensitivities. The research task is to map where cooperation creates surplus for both sides versus where zero-sum framing is unavoidable.

pages.title: Ganges-Padma Transition
pages.excerpt: This marker explains the naming and political transition where the lower Ganges route enters Bangladesh and becomes part of the Padma system.
pages.body_text: Ganges-Padma Transition # Summary This marker explains the naming and political transition where the lower Ganges route enters Bangladesh and becomes part of the Padma system. # Simple Explanation The same downstream route is read through different names and political geographies as it crosses from India into Bangladesh. This marker helps readers understand why a Nepal-origin river trace eventually becomes a Bangladesh delta story. # Why It Matters For Nepal's upstream story, this is where the downstream frame shifts from northern India plains politics into Bangladesh delta dependence. The same route that began as Himalayan basin geography becomes a lower-basin, dry-season, sediment, and delta-stability question. # How To Read The Marker Use it as a hinge between the Ganges trunk and the padma-meghna-delta. It helps readers understand why the Nepal-origin route-to-ocean layer crosses beyond India. # Caveat This marker is a strategic transition point. It does not resolve border hydrology, treaty allocations, or local distributary behavior. # Common Misunderstandings The transition marker is not a treaty claim. It identifies a map-reading shift, not allocation rights. It is not a precise distributary model. The Padma-Meghna delta has complex local channels beyond this marker. It does not mean Nepal determines Bangladesh outcomes. It shows how upstream basin geography connects to downstream dependency. # Related padma-meghna-delta padma-meghna-delta-dependency ganges-contribution bangladesh-trade-route

pages.title: Ghaghara-Ganges Merge
pages.excerpt: This marker explains the downstream handoff for the karnali-basin route. Nepal's Karnali becomes the Ghaghara system downstream and eventually joins the Ganges trunk.
pages.body_text: Ghaghara-Ganges Merge # Summary This marker explains the downstream handoff for the karnali-basin route. Nepal's Karnali becomes the Ghaghara system downstream and eventually joins the Ganges trunk. # Simple Explanation The Karnali basin is often discussed as a Nepal hydropower and storage frontier. This concept shows where that upstream story enters the downstream Ghaghara-Ganges corridor, where timing, flood, sediment, and dry-season release questions become regional. # Why It Matters Karnali is one of Nepal's most important future storage and hydropower basins. If large storage is eventually built, the downstream question is not only how much energy Nepal generates. It is how timing, flood attenuation, dry-season releases, and sediment behavior are perceived through the Ghaghara-Ganges corridor. # How To Read The Marker The marker connects karnali-basin and mahakali-sharda-handoff to the shared Ganges trunk. It is a map-reading handoff, not a hydrodynamic attribution point. # Caveat The marker does not say Nepal controls the Ghaghara or Ganges. It says Nepal-linked routes enter this downstream political geography. # Common Misunderstandings This is not a claim of control over the Ghaghara or Ganges. It is a downstream route marker. It does not prove any specific storage impact. It identifies where future regulation questions would become relevant. It is not a flow-share calculation. The marker supports map reading, not hydrological attribution. # Related karnali-basin eastern-up-ghaghara-gandak-belt bihar-ganges-trunk-zone data-layer-future-regulation-scenario

pages.body_text: GLOF Risk # Summary A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) is a sudden release of water from a glacier-related lake. The lake may sit on, beside or below a glacier and may be impounded by moraine, ice or bedrock. As the flood moves downstream it can entrain large volumes of sediment and debris, creating loads and channel changes that are poorly represented by ordinary river-flow records. # Simple Explanation Glaciers and their surrounding landforms can create lakes with changing water levels, outlets and natural barriers. A sudden breach, overtopping event or internal drainage failure can release water rapidly. The moving flood may then erode its channel, collect boulders and sediment, form temporary blockages and produce additional surges far downstream. # Why It Matters in Nepal Nepal's steep relief places settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower works and transmission assets along narrow river corridors below glacierised headwaters. Exposure is therefore not limited to infrastructure beside a lake. A project may instead be affected through flood-wave propagation, sediment bulking, channel avulsion, intake burial, scour or loss of access and monitoring systems. For hydropower planning, GLOF exposure connects physical hazard to buildability. Historical gauge records remain useful, but they do not by themselves describe every lake-breach or cascading-failure hydrograph. Project-level conclusions require site-specific lake, slope, sediment, routing and infrastructure-exposure studies. # Technical Explanation Glacial lakes have different geometries and drainage controls. Some are dammed by unconsolidated moraine or ice; others occupy bedrock depressions or form on a glacier surface. Triggers and release processes can include avalanche-generated displacement waves, overtopping, erosion of a moraine, drainage through or beneath ice, and cascading release from one lake into another. Downstream effects depend on more than the water initially stored in the lake. Steep gradients can accelerate the flow; erosion can add sediment and boulders; deposition can redirect the channel; and temporary ponding can create secondary surges. These processes link GLOF hazard to sediment-as-design-constraint and to the wider hydrological uncertainty described in claim-climate-harder-not-easier. # Documented Recent Examples ## 2024 — Thame Valley / Dudh Koshi The 16 August 2024 event was a documented two-lake cascade. A rock avalanche entered Upper Ngole Cho, generating a displacement wave and release that struck Lower Ngole Cho. The lower-lake breach was measured at about 21.6 m deep and 51 m wide; the resulting hyper-concentrated flow carried debris for more than 80 km and damaged the Khumbu hydropower intake and other infrastructure in Thame. These figures come from the later field and satellite investigation, not only the initial rapid assessment. See icimod-ndrrma-thame-glof-2024. ## 2025 — Rasuwa / Lende–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli On 8 July 2025, rapid discharge from a supraglacial lake on the Purepu Glacier sent a destructive flood through the transboundary Lende/Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridor. NDRRMA's first situation report recorded damage to the border bridge, dry port, road and three hydropower plants while noting that detailed causal and damage investigations were continuing. See ndrrma-rasuwa-glacial-flood-sitrep-2025. The 111 MW rasuwagadhi plant had entered commercial operation in January 2025. NEA Engineering records severe civil, hydromechanical and electromechanical damage, suspension of generation, one unit returning on 6 December and two-unit generation under available dry-season discharge from 25 December. See nea-engineering-annual-report-2081-82. # Common Misunderstandings "A GLOF is just a large monsoon flood." No. It originates from sudden release of a glacial lake and may develop a very different flood wave and sediment load. "Every destructive flood involving glacier ice is a GLOF." No. Ice avalanches, rock-ice avalanches, landslide-dam failures and other high-mountain processes can generate debris-rich floods without a glacial lake outburst. The initiating mechanism must be established before applying the label. "Only assets close to a glacier are exposed." No. Flood routing, erosion and sediment transport can carry impacts far downstream. "A GLOF label proves that climate change caused the individual event." No. Regional glacier and glacial-lake change can alter hazard conditions, but attribution of a particular trigger requires event-specific evidence. # Related buildability claim-climate-harder-not-easier dudhkoshi-storage koshi-basin peak-water rasuwagadhi sediment-as-design-constraint # Sources icimod-ndrrma-thame-glof-2024 — field and satellite reconstruction of the 2024 Thame event ndrrma-rasuwa-glacial-flood-sitrep-2025 — early government situation report for the 2025 Rasuwa flood nea-engineering-annual-report-2081-82 — Rasuwagadhi commissioning, damage and partial-restoration record icimod-hkh-glacier-change — regional glacier-change context icimod-koshi-sediment-threats — Koshi sediment and hazard context

pages.title: Green Hydrogen Nepal
headings: Why fertilizer is the natural first anchor
pages.excerpt: Green hydrogen in Nepal is best understood as a bridge technology between surplus monsoon electricity and hard-to-electrify domestic industry—not as a export commodity fantasy disconnected from grid physics. Electrolysis converts low-utilization wet-season kWh into storable molec
pages.body_text: Green Hydrogen Nepal # Summary Green hydrogen in Nepal is best understood as a bridge technology between surplus monsoon electricity and hard-to-electrify domestic industry—not as a export commodity fantasy disconnected from grid physics. Electrolysis converts low-utilization wet-season kWh into storable molecules (hydrogen, then ammonia or other carriers), reshaping the economics of seasonal-arbitrage-trap by absorbing energy when the system is long and delivering products when the economy needs them. # Simple Explanation Green hydrogen turns electricity into a fuel or industrial input. For Nepal, the useful idea is not exporting hydrogen for its own sake; it is using wet-season surplus electricity to make domestic products such as fertilizer, industrial heat, or ammonia that are hard to electrify directly. # Why fertilizer is the natural first anchor Nepal imports essentially all chemical fertilizer; food security and farm productivity are therefore foreign-exchange and supply-chain dependent. A domestic ammonia pathway—hydrogen → Haber-Bosch → urea/ammonium products—ties directly to sovereignty and base-load demand. Order-of-magnitude sector sketches in national roadmaps suggest a modern fertilizer complex can present hundreds of megawatts of baseload-class demand (commonly cited ~500 MW in policy-grade scenarios—exact sizing is plant-design specific). That scale matters: it is large enough to change dispatch rather than decorate it. # Cement and other industrial offtake Cement decarbonization is another hydrogen sink: replacing fossil fuel combustion in clinker/pyroprocessing with hydrogen or hybrid fuels stacks up large annual H₂ demand in national modeling discourse (illustrative national figures on the order of ~228,000 tonnes H₂/year implying ~2 GW of electrolysis capacity are used in roadmap arithmetic—treat as planning magnitude, not a signed FEED package). The point for domestic-led-hydro-strategy is structural: these are domestic value chains that pay for reliability differently than spot export. # Policy trajectory The Green Hydrogen Policy (2024) signals official intent to coordinate standards, pilots, incentives, and safety. The typical staged narrative runs pilots 2025–2027 toward industrial scale by ~2035, with cost projections in policy documents clustering around ~$2.15/kg by mid-2030s under favorable renewable input cost paths—again, a directional planning anchor. # Relationship to curtailment and surplus If new RoR continues to outpace demand and storage, stranded-generation risk rises: energy with nowhere to go at non-trivial variable cost. Electrolysis is one of the few scalable sinks that can ride renewable variability if system integration (oxygen use, water treatment, grid connection, industrial symbiosis) is solved. Detailed citations and program structure belong in green-hydrogen-roadmap-nepal. # Common Misunderstandings Green hydrogen is not a substitute for basic grid planning. It can absorb surplus only if transmission, industrial siting, and offtake are designed together. Export hydrogen is not the core Nepal use case in this wiki. Domestic fertilizer, cement, and industrial substitution are the stronger near-term frames. Roadmap-scale numbers are planning magnitudes. They should not be read as financed projects, signed PPAs, or committed industrial plants.

Why India And Bangladesh Marks Are Here
pages.excerpt: The geopolitics preset is not a Nepal-only map. It follows Nepal-linked rivers into the northern Indian plains, Bangladesh, and the Bay of Bengal because the political question is about downstream exposure, not just upstream origin.
pages.body_text: How To Read The Geopolitics Map # Summary The geopolitics preset is not a Nepal-only map. It follows Nepal-linked rivers into the northern Indian plains, Bangladesh, and the Bay of Bengal because the political question is about downstream exposure, not just upstream origin. # Simple Explanation Read the map as a route-and-exposure guide. It shows how rivers that begin in or pass through Nepal continue into downstream regions where timing, floods, sediment, dry-season flows, and future storage choices can become political. # Visual Grammar Read the layers in this order: Map mark | Meaning | ----------|---------| Nepal-linked basin polygons | Where Nepal sits inside the upstream basin geography. | Nepal rivers and downstream rivers | The main water routes from Nepal into the plains. | Ocean route | A strategic continuation through the Ganges/Padma/Meghna system to the Bay of Bengal. | Route notes | Merge, handoff, naming, and delta markers that explain the route. | Dependency zones | Broad downstream exposure areas for flood, dry-season, agricultural, population, sediment, and delta sensitivity. | Population anchors | City and delta points that help orient the human geography around the routes. | Flow regulation | Storage projects that could change timing, dry-season support, flood attenuation, sediment behavior, and cooperation risk. | # The Core Rule Do not read the downstream layers as water-control claims. They are exposure claims. The map does not say Nepal controls Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, or Bangladesh water security. It says Nepal-linked rivers pass through sensitive downstream geographies where timing, flood pulses, sediment, dry-season flow, and future storage decisions can matter politically. # How To Click Around Start with downstream-river-geopolitics. Then follow the route notes: 1. mahakali-sharda-handoff 2. ghaghara-ganges-merge 3. gandak-ganges-merge 4. kosi-ganges-merge 5. ganges-padma-transition 6. padma-meghna-delta 7. bay-of-bengal-terminal Then read the exposure zones: eastern-up-ghaghara-gandak-belt north-bihar-kosi-gandak-floodplain bihar-ganges-trunk-zone padma-meghna-delta-dependency lower-delta-bay-interface # Why India And Bangladesh Marks Are Here The downstream marks exist because Nepal's hydropower and storage choices are also timing choices. A run-of-river project mostly follows the hydrograph. A storage project can shift water across time, trap sediment, attenuate floods, or change the reliability of dry-season releases. That is why the map keeps data-layer-future-regulation-scenario visible with the downstream layers. The political value of storage is not just megawatts. It is the ability to regulate time. # Common Misunderstandings The map is not a claim of Nepalese control downstream. It shows exposure pathways, not authority. Dependency zones are not hydrological models. They are interpretive map layers for reading geography. Storage markers are not policy prescriptions. They show where timing regulation could matter if projects are built. # Related downstream-river-geopolitics ganges-contribution hydro-geopolitics data-layer-nepal-origin-ocean-routes data-layer-downstream-dependency-zones

pages.title: Hybrid Siting Logic
headings: Archetype 1 — Solar at existing hydropower sites ("hydro co-location")
pages.excerpt: Solar plants are not free-floating technology choices; they are three things co-located — a module field, a land parcel, and an interconnection. Cheap modules have collapsed the first; solar-lcoe-crossover. Land and interconnection are now the binding constraints on Nepal solar,
pages.body_text: Hybrid Siting Logic # Summary Solar plants are not free-floating technology choices; they are three things co-located — a module field, a land parcel, and an interconnection. Cheap modules have collapsed the first; solar-lcoe-crossover. Land and interconnection are now the binding constraints on Nepal solar, and the siting archetypes that minimise those two costs beat the ones that optimise GHI alone. This page frames the three siting archetypes — hydro co-location, substation-adjacent greenfield, floating PV on reservoirs — and argues that the first and third together will carry most of the political coalition for utility-scale solar in Nepal through 2035. # Simple Explanation Hybrid siting asks where solar can be built without paying twice for land, roads, grid access, and local acceptance. In Nepal, the best solar sites are often not the sunniest places; they are places where hydropower, reservoirs, substations, or existing rights-of-way already solve the expensive parts of a project. # Archetype 1 — Solar at existing hydropower sites ("hydro co-location") The cheapest MW Nepal can build, in the specific sense that almost every non-module cost is already paid. What's already there at a typical operating hydropower site: An access road (often 3–15 km of graded mountain road, the single most expensive item in hill-country solar). An interconnecting substation (11/33 → 132/220 kV). Spare evacuation headroom, especially in dry season when the hydro plant runs at 30–40% of monsoon output and the transformer / line is underused. A skilled O&M crew, security, and a fenced site. Water for panel cleaning. Permitting precedent with NEA, local government, forest department, and the community. What the solar build adds: 1–10 MWp of PV modules (1–8 ha of dry / desilted terrain adjacent to the powerhouse or along the headrace road). A combiner box, inverters, and a tap into the existing step-up transformer. ~NPR 40–60 million per MWp installed (vs ~NPR 70–90 million for greenfield) — a 35–40% capex reduction from land, road, and interconnection savings. Why it is also operationally elegant: The interconnection loading pattern is anti-phased with the hydro plant. In the dry-season afternoon, the hydropower plant under-utilizes its evacuation; the solar PV fills the spare capacity of the same substation. In the monsoon-day overlap, dispatch holds hydro pondage through midday and releases it in the evening peak (see solar-hydro-complementarity). Net transformer capacity utilization goes up, not down. Candidate sites with published feasibility or public tender interest: kulekhani-cascade — reservoir + three cascade plants; ~10–20 MWp ground + ~15–30 MWp floating potential. kali-gandaki-a — 144 MW NEA flagship; dam-adjacent flats suited to 25–40 MWp ground PV. khimti-i — 60 MW IPP; headrace-adjacent terraces, 10–15 MWp candidate. marsyangdi / madhya-marsyangdi — cascade co-location, 20–40 MWp combined. tanahu-hydropower — storage reservoir under construction; co-location should be designed in before impoundment. The 50 MW Khungri LoI award is a candidate to watch for this archetype, but the corrected NEA LoI establishes only a Rolpa IPP solar award anchored to the Khungri grid node. It should not be treated as a proven hydro-hybrid project until PPA, interconnection, or commissioning documents confirm shared hydro evacuation. # Archetype 2 — Substation-adjacent greenfield (Terai) The 960 MW NEA tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) and the next 2–3 GW of utility-scale solar will overwhelmingly be this archetype: 10–50 MWp ground-mount, 1–8 km from an existing 132 or 220 kV substation, on the Terai plain. Why it works: Highest 132 kV grid density in the country (hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone, dana-kushma-butwal-corridor). Flat terrain (<3° slope), lowest construction cost in Nepal. Proximity to load centres and to Indian-grid interconnections for future export. Water for panel cleaning (Terai is canal-irrigated). Why it is politically fragile: Terai is Nepal's prime agricultural land; fee-simple conversion to solar triggers food-security objections (agrivoltaics-and-land). Land acquisition — even at 2–5 ha per site — collides with fragmented tenure, smallholder resistance, and the memory of hydropower-era displacement. Non-agricultural alienable land (government-owned sarkari parcels, dried-out oxbows, public waste) is scarce and over-subscribed. The design move that makes it durable: do not buy land. Lease for 25 years with a revenue-share clause, anchor on agrivoltaic configuration, and bundle rural-electrification / pump-irrigation offtake into the PPA. The 960 MW tender is experimenting with variants of this; the next decade of Terai solar depends on whether that politics stabilises. # Archetype 3 — Floating PV on reservoirs The highest-leverage single lever in Nepal's solar portfolio, by an uncomfortable margin. What floating PV buys that ground-mount does not: No land acquisition — the reservoir exists; deploying on ~5–20% of its surface takes nothing out of agricultural rotation. Cooler panel operating temperature — ~2–5% yield uplift from evaporative cooling. Reduced reservoir evaporation — 30–50% evaporation reduction on covered surface; in a country with storage-deficit and a dry-season water-tight operating regime, this is not a side benefit, it is a water-system benefit sold separately. Shared interconnection — dam powerhouse already carries the 11/33 kV step-up and the substation. Floating PV taps in at the tail. Anti-algae — covered water bodies see fewer blooms; Kulekhani in particular has had sedimentation / eutrophication concerns that floating PV partially mitigates. Candidate reservoirs: Reservoir | Surface (ha) | 10% coverage (ha) | Nameplate (MWp) | Status | ---|---:|---:|---:|---| kulekhani-cascade | ~220 | 22 | ~17 MWp | Operating; pilot-ready | tanahu-hydropower | ~700 | 70 | ~56 MWp | Under construction; design in now | budhigandaki | ~6,300 | 630 | ~500 MWp | Proposed; 10+ year horizon | dudhkoshi-storage | ~1,800 | 180 | ~144 MWp | Proposed | mugu-karnali-storage | ~9,000 | 900 | ~720 MWp | Proposed | uttarganga-storage | ~2,400 | 240 | ~192 MWp | Proposed | Even at conservative 5% coverage and discounting the long-dated projects, the near-term-buildable floating PV at Kulekhani + Tanahu is ~70–90 MWp — more than the entire operating utility-scale solar fleet as of FY 2024/25. The design move that matters most: require floating-PV integration in the tender documents for every new reservoir project, starting with Tanahu. Retrofitting is ~2× more expensive than designing it in. # The siting-cost stack, one table Archetype | Land cost | Grid cost | GHI (typical) | LCOE index (Terai greenfield = 100) | ---|---|---|---|---:| Hydro co-location | 0 (already owned) | 0 (spare headroom) | 4.5–5.5 | 60–70 | Substation-adjacent Terai | 15–25 | 5–10 | 4.8–5.3 | 100 | Floating PV | 0 | low | 4.5–5.5 | 75–85 | Trans-Himalayan (Mustang) | low | very high | 6.0–6.5 | 180–250 | Rooftop (Kathmandu Valley) | 0 (existing) | net-metering | 4.2–4.6 | 90–110 | Hill greenfield | 10–20 | 30–60 | 4.3–4.8 | 140–180 | Grid cost is the single widest column. In a country with stranded-generation as a current, real constraint, archetypes that spend zero new transmission (hydro co-location, floating PV, rooftop) are worth their ~5% higher module-side costs many times over. # The portfolio rule Over 2026–2035, roughly: ~60% of solar MW should be substation-adjacent Terai greenfield (Archetype 2), with ~70% of that as agrivoltaics. ~20% as hydro co-location (Archetype 1), increasingly standard in the next NEA tender batches. ~10% as floating PV on Kulekhani, Tanahu, and the earliest-operating reservoir sites (Archetype 3), scaling to more as reservoirs commission. ~10% as rooftop / distributed + off-grid mini-grids (see rooftop-minigrid-offgrid), which is a separate political track. This is the sort of portfolio a competent NEA + ERC could produce in a 10-year plan. Nothing in the 2024/25 annual report refutes it; the infrastructure for all four archetypes is under way. The missing piece is an explicit portfolio rule that treats the four archetypes as complements rather than competitors. # Common Misunderstandings Best solar resource does not automatically mean best project site. Grid, land, roads, and permitting can dominate the economics. Hydro co-location does not mean solar replaces hydropower. It uses existing infrastructure and dry-season spare evacuation to complement hydro output. Floating PV is not only a land-saving trick. It also interacts with reservoir evaporation, interconnection, and storage-project design. # Related solar-hydro-complementarity — why these sites are valuable solar-resource-geography-nepal — which zones suit which archetype solar-lcoe-crossover — the price argument each archetype compounds agrivoltaics-and-land — the political condition for Archetype 2 rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the fourth archetype, treated separately kulekhani-cascade, tanahu-hydropower, budhigandaki, dudhkoshi-storage — floating PV candidates nea-960mw-solar-tender — the first portfolio-scale test of Archetype 2

pages.title: Hydro-Geopolitics
headings: Downstream scale: why Nepal's choices ripple
India as decisive actor; China as absent partner
pages.excerpt: Hydro-geopolitics is the intersection of transboundary river geography, bilateral energy trade, and sovereignty questions that shapes Nepal's hydropower strategy and project siting. It treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems — a
pages.body_text: Hydro-Geopolitics # Summary Hydro-geopolitics is the intersection of transboundary river geography, bilateral energy trade, and sovereignty questions that shapes Nepal's hydropower strategy and project siting. It treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems — and therefore as objects of bargaining, not merely engineering inputs. # Simple Explanation Nepal's rivers don't stop at the border. What Nepal builds upstream affects irrigation, floods, and water supply for hundreds of millions of people downstream — mostly in India. This means every dam, reservoir, or power line is also a diplomatic negotiation. "Hydro-geopolitics" is the name for the fact that Nepal's electricity strategy cannot be separated from its relationship with its downstream neighbors. # Common Misunderstandings "Hydro-geopolitics means India is the enemy." It does not. The concept includes cooperation, market integration, and treaty negotiation — not just conflict. "Technical optimization is enough." Ignoring the geopolitical layer turns technically optimal projects into politically unrealizable ones. "Bhutan is a model Nepal can copy." Bhutan's export-led hydro works because of a specific patron relationship and fiscal design; Nepal's larger population and different downstream geometry make copy-paste misleading. Hydro-geopolitics is the lens that treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems—and therefore as objects of bargaining, not merely as engineering inputs. Electricity is one slice of a larger portfolio that includes irrigation, flood management, navigation where relevant, ecosystem services, and disaster risk. Ignoring this layer turns technically "optimal" projects into politically unrealizable ones. # Downstream scale: why Nepal's choices ripple Nepal-origin rivers contribute a large share of Ganges annual discharge (commonly cited ~40–45%) and an even larger share of dry-season flow (~70–80% in Farakka-style accounting used in basin assessments). Those percentages imply hundreds of millions of people and many million hectares of irrigated command indirectly indexed to Nepal-influenced regimes. Illustrative orders of magnitude appear repeatedly in basin literature: Koshi irrigation on the order of 500–600 thousand hectares in Bihar; Gandak systems on the order of 1.5–2 million hectares across Bihar/UP; Karnali/Ghaghara complexes affecting roughly 2–3 million hectares in UP. The exact numbers shift with dataset and boundary definition; the strategic fact is extreme downstream dependence on upstream timing and quality of flows—developed analytically in ganges-contribution. # Treaties, asymmetry, and unfinished business Historical agreements (Koshi, Gandak, Mahakali) are often described as asymmetric in implementation experience: formal principles of equity and benefit sharing collide with as-built financing, maintenance, and interpretation disputes. pancheshwar remains the emblematic large joint project whose stall shows how sovereignty, resettlement, benefit splits, and India's internal federal politics can freeze decades of studies into zero concrete storage. # India as decisive actor; China as absent partner india-energy-relationship is decisive for cross-border trade, transmission corridors, grid codes, and perceptions of security. China's role in Nepal hydro has been receding, not growing: China Three Gorges withdrew from west-seti in 2018; China Gezhouba was blocked from budhigandaki on political grounds. No major Chinese-linked storage project is currently under active construction in Nepal. India, meanwhile, has expanded its presence: NHPC took over West Seti (2022), SJVN is building the 900 MW Arun-3, and India's Power Grid Corporation agreed in April 2025 to build high-capacity cross-border transmission. The triangulation is not symmetric: India can veto or complicate Chinese-backed projects through market access, transmission denial, and geopolitical pressure, while China has no equivalent lever over India-backed schemes. Nepal's ability to play one against the other is limited in practice — a finding that tempers the "strategic leverage" narrative. # Bhutan as comparator, not clone bhutan-hydropower-model illustrates how export-led hydro can work when fiscal rules, load management, and a patron relationship align. Nepal's larger population, internal political fragmentation, and different downstream co-riparian geometry mean copy-paste is misleading—but the comparison clarifies that governance is where opportunity is won or lost. # Basin anchors Transboundary technical narratives often anchor on koshi-basin as the hazard–sediment–irrigation nexus par excellence. Hydro-geopolitics is therefore not a "soft" add-on to power-sector economics; it is frequently the binding constraint on what can be built, financed, and operated.

pages.body_text: Hydro Insurance # Summary The insurance market for Nepal's hydropower sector — coverage requirements, premium costs, exclusions and claim settlement. The current wiki record does not yet establish a sector-wide premium increase, settlement-delay rate or the contractual outcome of an insured outage under a PPA. # Simple Explanation Hydropower projects need insurance because floods, landslides, GLOFs, and equipment failures can stop generation. The concept matters because insurance is not just a safety net: rising premiums, delayed claims, and lender requirements can become a major financial stress for IPPs. # Current Evidence Boundary One primary filing now supports a bounded project-level observation: Project and period | Electricity-sales revenue | Insurance expense | Insurance / revenue | Source | ---|---:|---:|---:|---| Upper Tamakoshi, FY 2080/81 | NPR 8.679 billion | NPR 99.3 million | 1.14% | utkhpl-disclosures-2026 | This ratio is a single-project-year observation, not evidence of a sector-wide premium burden or a trend. Comparable audited statements are needed before generalizing it. # Market Evidence Needed The former assertions about premium floors, reinsurance withdrawal, market concentration and percentage increases did not have linked primary source pages in the current wiki. They are therefore not retained as findings. The next source pass should obtain the Nepal Insurance Authority directive, insurer annual reports, reinsurance terms where public, and named project claim records. # Market Concentration No market-concentration finding is currently made. It requires a complete insurer premium, exposure and reinsurance dataset with a defined period and methodology. # Claim Settlement Delays The "90% claim settlement delays" claim is not verified. Upper Tamakoshi's FY 2080/81 statements record that property and lost-revenue claims were lodged after the September 2024 flood and remained in settlement processing at that report date; they do not give a later settlement outcome or a comparable market-wide delay measure. [Under research — obtain named cases and Nepal Insurance Authority settlement data.] # Interaction with AD Penalties and Force Majeure The current secondary analysis of a standard PPA reports that force-majeure energy is included in the AD-penalty formula and that force majeure is narrowly defined. It does not establish whether a particular physical-damage loss qualifies, how an insurer's coverage decision affects it, or how NEA settled any resulting shortfall. Those questions require the signed PPA, policy wording, claim correspondence and settlement record for a named project. [Under research.] # Analytical links ad-penalties — the penalty mechanism that may compound insurance gaps nea-triple-authority — the institutional framework of NEA as off-taker and penalty administrator # Common Misunderstandings Insurance does not remove project risk. It can shift some losses, but premium cost, exclusions, and settlement delays still affect cash flow. A claim is not the same as cash in hand. Delayed settlement can matter as much as the covered amount. Hydro insurance is not separate from PPA risk. Physical damage can interact with AD penalties, debt service, and off-taker receivables.

pages.title: Hydropower Potential Categories
pages.excerpt: “Nepal has 83,000 MW” is a political slogan and a methodological landmine. Hydropower potential categories exist precisely because theoretical river power is not the same as financeable capacity, buildable projects, or firm winter electricity (see firm-power).
pages.body_text: Hydropower Potential Categories # Summary “Nepal has 83,000 MW” is a political slogan and a methodological landmine. Hydropower potential categories exist precisely because theoretical river power is not the same as financeable capacity, buildable projects, or firm winter electricity (see firm-power). # Simple Explanation Hydropower potential is a stack of increasingly strict filters. A river may have theoretical energy, but that does not mean a project can be engineered, financed, permitted, connected to the grid, or depended on in the dry season. # The reduction pyramid (conceptual chain) Think of a pyramid—quantified in data-potential-pyramid—where each step applies filters the previous step ignores: 1. Theoretical / gross potential — legacy national figures near ~83,000 MW appear in older discourse; WECS (2019) reframed theoretical potential around ~72,500 MW depending on methodological choices. 2. Technical potential — what is physically plausible with conventional technology; commonly discussed in the ~42,000–46,000 MW range in national studies (exact bounds depend on site database and assumptions). 3. Techno-economic potential — WECS (2019) reports 32,680 MW at this layer: sites that meet engineering and economic screening rules as modeled. 4. Economically viable (market window) — often discussed as ~25,000–35,000 MW under price and financing assumptions that move with interest rates, carbon policy, and India import terms. 5. Realistically developable by ~2040 — planning horizons frequently land around ~10,000–15,000 MW once execution risk, transmission, and social license are acknowledged. 6. Installed — roughly ~3,591 MW hydro installed (order-of-magnitude anchor for “today”). These categories are not interchangeable. Moving down the chain is not “being conservative”; it is changing the question. # Basin concentration A large share of gross potential concentrates in three major basins—koshi-basin, karnali-basin, and gandaki-basin—often cited on the order of ~94% of national potential. That concentration matters for cascade externalities, sediment, and geopolitical export corridors: “national potential” is geographically lumpy. # Why this matters for analysis Potential-category discipline prevents two common failures: inflating creditworthiness with theoretical MW, and confusing annual energy with dry-season dependability. Primary methodology and citations live under wecs-hydropower-potential-2019. # Common Misunderstandings Theoretical MW is not a build plan. It is the least filtered number in the chain. Technical potential is not the same as bankable potential. Financing, transmission, social license, and market value still apply. Installed MW is not firm winter power. Seasonal output and dispatchability determine how much capacity actually helps in dry months.

pages.title: IPO Hydropower Bailout
pages.excerpt: How Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and rights share issuances can shift hydropower-project financing risk onto retail investors — and what the public record can, and cannot, demonstrate about that pattern in Nepal.
pages.body_text: IPO Hydropower Bailout # Summary How Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and rights share issuances can shift hydropower-project financing risk onto retail investors — and what the public record can, and cannot, demonstrate about that pattern in Nepal. This page is under research. The current evidence establishes a set of official offering records, not a verified sector-wide "bailout" inventory. SEBON's scans and Nepali-language PDFs make extraction laborious, but they are a research task rather than a basis for treating the evidence as unavailable. # Simple Explanation The concept is a testable financing-risk question: when a hydropower company raises public equity before stable earnings, or later seeks rights capital, are investors funding productive expansion, balance-sheet repair, or both? The answer must be established issuer by issuer from prospectuses, financial statements and post-offer disclosures. # What SEBON's records establish SEBON has official records for a partial cohort of hydropower IPOs and rights-share filings. Issuer financial statements now provide post-offer evidence for three of the four rights issues; the table distinguishes prospectus plans from later reported outcomes. Issuer | Official record located | What the records establish | Remaining limitation | ---|---|---|---| Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut | IPO, approved prospectus and audited FY 2081/82 statements | NPR 1.20 billion rights cash plus NPR 134.642 million auction premium; net borrowing repayment NPR 482.416 million; total borrowings fell by NPR 498.474 million | The audited statements do not trace the full planned NPR 800 million Ankhu Khola-2 equity allocation; other-equity investments rose by NPR 135.225 million | Joshi Hydropower | IPO and approved right-issue prospectus | 1:0.65; NPR 241.41 million planned: NPR 155.71 million bank principal/interest, NPR 56.835195 million promoter advance, NPR 28.864805 million repairs | Final allotment, actual application and subsequent audited balances remain unreconciled | People's Power | Approved prospectus, closure notice and issuer Q3 FY 2082/83 statement | Paid-up capital rose by the full NPR 316.3 million offer amount; reported long-term borrowing fell from NPR 318.024 million to zero | The post-offer statement is unaudited and has no separate proceeds-application schedule | Terhathum Power | Approved prospectus and issuer Q3 FY 2082/83 statement | Issuer says the 1:1 issue completed and proceeds repaid long-term bank debt; paid-up capital doubled to NPR 800 million and long-term borrowings fell by NPR 540.032 million | The statement is unaudited; the debt reduction exceeds the offer amount and cannot all be attributed to rights cash | Rasuwagadhi | Local-offering record | A SEBON prospectus record exists | A comparable IPO amount, a rights issue, and a use-of-proceeds finding | The earlier five-row inventory has been retired. It referred to six companies while listing five, did not provide row-level primary documents, and treated pipeline values as completed-rights-issue amounts in several cases. sebon-hydropower-offering-records preserves the official regulatory trail now available in the wiki. Ankhu Khola is now the first issuer in this cohort with a primary prospectus-level proceeds allocation: one-third of the planned NPR 1.20 billion was earmarked for partial bank-loan repayment and two-thirds for investment in a second project. That is evidence of a mixed expansion-and-balance-sheet transaction, not proof that the whole issue was a debt bailout. Claims about NEPSE suspensions, insider trading, promoter sales or debt-repayment outcomes are not retained here until an official NEPSE notice, issuer filing or audited statement is linked. # The Chilime contrast Chilime Hydropower's 2010 IPO occurred after seven years of profitable operations and distributed a 35% dividend within a year. This is a documented contrast case, but whether newer issuers were pre-revenue, distressed or using equity for debt retirement must be established from each issuer's own record. See chilime for the pre-IPO profitability context. # The triple-authority blindspot The interaction between offering disclosures, PPA tariff assumptions and ad-penalties is a research question, not a current finding. The prospectuses in the first SEBON pass have not yet been extracted and coded for hydrology, curtailment, tariff or AD-penalty risk disclosure. See nea-triple-authority for the institutional context. # What is missing The approved-prospectus extraction is complete for Ankhu Khola, Joshi Hydropower, People's Power and Terhathum Power. Across this bounded four-issuer cohort, each prospectus assigns some rights proceeds to bank or other financing liabilities, but the allocations differ: Ankhu Khola combines expansion equity with partial bank repayment; Joshi combines bank debt, a promoter advance and repairs; People's Power and Terhathum direct the stated proceeds to bank debt. This establishes planned uses, not actual cash application or a representative sector-wide rate. Post-offer reconciliation is now substantially complete for Ankhu Khola, People's Power and Terhathum Power. The records show that public equity did fund balance-sheet repair in all three, but they do not support one uniform transaction type or a sector-wide rate. Ankhu Khola mixed debt reduction with a stated project-investment purpose; People's Power and Terhathum show post-offer debt reductions consistent with their stated bank-repayment purposes. Only Ankhu Khola's outcome is audited. The remaining bounded gaps are: What was Joshi Hydropower's final allotment and actual split between bank debt, promoter advance and repairs? Where is Ankhu Khola's full planned NPR 800 million Ankhu Khola-2 equity allocation reflected after the offer? Can audited FY 2082/83 statements confirm the People's Power and Terhathum quarterly outcomes? What risk disclosures about hydrological underperformance, PPA rate risk, and AD penalty exposure appear in hydro IPO prospectuses? What is the full list of NEPSE-listed hydropower companies whose rights issues completed within three years of IPO? What is NRB's specialized hydro loan book — the true extent of off-balance-sheet restructuring and informal forbearance? Next evidence steps: obtain Joshi's allotment and post-offer financial statement; trace Ankhu Khola-2 investment through the issuer's investment notes; capture audited FY 2082/83 statements for People's Power and Terhathum; then expand beyond this selected cohort using a declared sampling rule. Only after that audit can the page quantify a debt-retirement or "bailout" pattern. # Common Misunderstandings An IPO is not automatically a growth investment. In distressed hydro cases, proceeds or later rights shares may function as balance-sheet repair. The Chilime example is not automatically replicable. Chilime listed after profitable operations; many newer projects list before stable earnings. A SEBON pipeline entry is not a completed issue. Review-stage terms cannot be treated as cash raised or debt repaid. # Sources sebon-hydropower-offering-records chilime-annual-report-fy2078-79

pages.title: Kosi-Ganges Merge
pages.excerpt: This marker explains where the koshi-basin route reaches the Ganges trunk after crossing the North Bihar floodplain.
pages.body_text: Kosi-Ganges Merge # Summary This marker explains where the koshi-basin route reaches the Ganges trunk after crossing the North Bihar floodplain. # Simple Explanation The Koshi route is one of the clearest examples of a Nepal-linked river becoming a downstream plains issue. This marker helps readers follow the route from Himalayan basin geography into the Ganges trunk. # Why It Matters Koshi is the clearest hazard and sediment case in the Nepal-linked downstream story. Its route matters because flood memory, embankment politics, sediment behavior, and dense settlement all meet in North Bihar before the system enters the lower Ganges. # How To Read The Marker Read it together with north-bihar-kosi-gandak-floodplain. The merge point is the route handoff; the floodplain zone is the human and agricultural exposure context. # Caveat This is not a claim that Nepal alone determines Kosi or Ganges outcomes. It is a route and exposure marker for a shared river system. # Common Misunderstandings This is not a flow-control claim. It marks a route connection, not Nepalese control over downstream outcomes. It is not a flood model. Flood memory and sediment context matter, but the marker does not simulate inundation. It should be read with the floodplain zone. The merge point alone does not show the human exposure geography. # Related koshi-basin north-bihar-kosi-gandak-floodplain ganges-contribution how-to-read-geopolitics-map

pages.title: Lower Delta And Bay Interface
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone marks the coastal-delta context where river timing, sediment, salinity, and Bay of Bengal exposure meet.
pages.body_text: Lower Delta And Bay Interface # Summary This dependency zone marks the coastal-delta context where river timing, sediment, salinity, and Bay of Bengal exposure meet. # Simple Explanation It is the map layer for the place where upstream river behavior meets coastal risk. The concept connects Nepal-linked route tracing to the lower delta, where flow timing and sediment delivery matter alongside sea, storm, and salinity pressures. # Why It Matters The lower delta is not just the end of a river. It is where upstream flow timing interacts with sediment delivery, coastal risk, storm exposure, and salinity pressure. That makes it relevant to a strategic map of Nepal-linked routes, even though it is far outside Nepal. # How To Read The Zone Read it after padma-meghna-delta-dependency and before bay-of-bengal-terminal. The route reaches the ocean; the dependency zone explains why the coastal endpoint is more than a cartographic endpoint. # Caveat The polygon is low-to-medium confidence context. It is not a salinity-front model, sediment budget, storm-surge model, or tidal channel map. # Common Misunderstandings The layer is not a coastal hazard model. It does not predict salinity, storm surge, or channel migration. It is not Nepal-specific control geography. It is downstream dependency context for a route-to-ocean map. It is not a precise delta boundary. It marks strategic context, not detailed geomorphology. # Related padma-meghna-delta padma-meghna-delta-dependency bay-of-bengal-terminal how-to-read-geopolitics-map

pages.title: Mahakali/Sharda Handoff
pages.excerpt: This marker explains where the far-western Nepal-linked route stops being only a border-river story and starts becoming part of the wider downstream Ganges geography.
pages.body_text: Mahakali/Sharda Handoff # Summary This marker explains where the far-western Nepal-linked route stops being only a border-river story and starts becoming part of the wider downstream Ganges geography. # Simple Explanation The Mahakali/Sharda route begins as a highly political Nepal-India border river. This marker shows how that western route continues into the downstream plains system instead of remaining only a bilateral border issue. # Why It Matters The mahakali-basin is already politically sensitive because it is a border river tied to sovereignty, irrigation, and the Pancheshwar/Mahakali treaty frame. Downstream, the route joins the Sharda-Ghaghara-Ganges logic rather than staying a self-contained Nepal-India border question. # How To Read The Marker Use it as an orientation point for data-layer-nepal-origin-ocean-routes, not as a surveyed confluence coordinate. Its job is to show the western handoff from Nepal-linked hydrology into the northern plains. # Caveat This is a strategic route marker. It does not model local withdrawals, barrages, canals, or exact flow contribution. # Common Misunderstandings The marker is not a surveyed confluence coordinate. It is an orientation point for the downstream route. It does not model treaty allocation or canal operations. Those questions sit outside this map marker. It does not make the western route identical to the central and eastern routes. It only shows where the downstream geography starts to overlap. # Related mahakali-basin ghaghara-ganges-merge downstream-river-geopolitics how-to-read-geopolitics-map

pages.title: NEA Triple-Authority Conflict
pages.excerpt: A governance concept describing the conflict risk created when dispatch, purchasing and penalty administration are concentrated around one utility; public evidence does not establish discriminatory dispatch or a proven Barahi outcome.
pages.body_text: NEA Triple-Authority Conflict # Summary The NEA Triple-Authority Conflict is an analytical description of the governance risk created when the Nepal Electricity Authority is involved in dispatch, electricity purchasing and administration of contractual deductions. Concentrating these functions can create conflicts of interest and weak appeal pathways. It does not, by itself, prove discriminatory dispatch, unlawful deductions or a particular project's loss. # Simple Explanation The concern is procedural: a generator may depend on the same utility for dispatch instructions, payment and application of contractual penalties. A credible system therefore needs transparent rules, auditable records and a review mechanism that affected parties can use. # What the Current Evidence Establishes nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 records electricity supplied by NEA and its subsidiaries, independent producers and imports, while NEA operates central parts of the transmission and distribution system. nea-standard-ppa-clauses and ad-penalty-clause-research report availability-declaration, reserve-margin and curtailment provisions through secondary legal analysis. They are not a corpus of signed project PPAs and are not a formal legal opinion. Public reporting indexed at erc-open-access-directive-2082 states that ERC issued Open Access Directive 2082. The official directive and implementing manuals are not archived in the current corpus, and issuance does not demonstrate operational third-party trading. The available evidence is sufficient to identify a structural conflict risk. It is not sufficient to measure how dispatch or deductions are applied across projects. # What Is Not Established A project-level pattern of dispatch discrimination after controlling for plant availability, location, network constraints and contract terms. A public merit-order, dispatch-instruction or accepted-energy dataset that permits ownership comparisons. A representative set of signed PPAs showing whether curtailment relief and dispute clauses vary by project. A project-by-project ledger of penalties assessed, waived, disputed, adjudicated or recovered. A primary audited filing, ERC decision or court record establishing the reported Barahi Hydropower outcome. # The Barahi Research Lead Legacy pages treated barahi-hydropower as an audited demonstration of the conflict. The audited statement, fiscal year, applicable PPA and regulatory or adjudication record are not present in the current corpus. Barahi must therefore remain a research lead, not proof of the mechanism in operation. No sector-wide penalty share should be inferred from the reported case or from the standard-contract formula. The public evidence needed for such a measure is not available here. # Governance Options Possible responses include publishing dispatch and penalty records, operationalising open access under current institutions, ring-fencing dispatch functions, creating an independent operator, or establishing a neutral penalty-review pathway. Their legal requirements, cost and effectiveness have not been compared in the current source set. See intervention-nea-structural-separation for the evidence-led Decision Dossier, including response options, trade-offs and the visibly labelled TransparentGov assessment. # Common Misunderstandings A structural conflict is not proof of misconduct. The institutional arrangement creates a risk that needs controls and evidence. A complaint recorded in an academic or industry report is not a dispatch audit. It can identify an issue for investigation without establishing its frequency or cause. Secondary standard-PPA analysis is not a signed-contract census. Clause wording and enforcement may vary. Barahi is not currently an audited case in this wiki. The primary filing and adjudication trail are missing. # Related intervention-nea-structural-separation ad-penalties stranded-generation claim-governance-binding institutions-finance-and-project-delivery

pages.title: Nepal Power Trade Schemes
headings: Generator-facing wholesale channels named in the IPSDP
Commercial modes layered on top of those channels
Why this matters to the wiki
pages.excerpt: In Section 2.4 of moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, the IPSDP does two different but related things. It names three generator-facing wholesale customer categories, and it separately describes the commercial modes those channels may use, including exchange-market sales and long-term
pages.body_text: Nepal Power Trade Schemes # Summary In Section 2.4 of moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, the IPSDP does two different but related things. It names three generator-facing wholesale customer categories, and it separately describes the commercial modes those channels may use, including exchange-market sales and long-term PPAs. # Simple Explanation Nepal power trade is not one single export mechanism. The IPSDP describes a mixed structure where power can move through NEA, trading companies, or direct overseas buyers, and those channels can use either long-term PPAs or more market-linked sales. # Generator-facing wholesale channels named in the IPSDP Channel | Buyer | How the PDF frames it | ---------|-------|------------------------| NEA default | nea | Conventional domestic trade. NEA buys power, serves the domestic market, and exports surplus itself. Lowest administrative burden for smaller projects. | Power-trading company | Nepal trading company such as NPTCL | A future channel in which trading companies intermediate between generators and markets. The PDF explicitly says sales may be either PPA-based or market-linked. | Direct overseas trade | DISCOs or large customers in India/Bangladesh | A generator deals directly with overseas buyers. The PDF ties this to larger projects, investor participation, and more complex transmission and contracting requirements. | # Commercial modes layered on top of those channels The executive summary then adds a second distinction that should not be collapsed into the buyer categories above: Long-term PPA mode: PPAs with NEA, with a trading company, or directly with foreign distribution companies / major customers. Market-linked mode: power sold through trading-company arrangements into exchange-style markets such as IEX, including the green-market discussion in the surrounding text. That is why the section reads as more than a simple "three-scheme" menu. The PDF clearly names three buyer categories, but it also makes room for multiple price-setting and dispatch arrangements inside them. # Why this matters to the wiki It clarifies that Nepal is not moving from one monolithic single-buyer system to one monolithic export system. The IPSDP is imagining a mixed commercial stack. It sharpens india-energy-relationship and bangladesh-trade-route by showing that cross-border trade is not just a transmission problem; it is also a buyer-structure and contract-structure problem. It explains why niettp and other interconnection corridors are enabling infrastructure rather than the whole trade model by themselves. # Confidence boundary This page sticks to what the executive summary says explicitly on pages 24-26. It does not claim that Nepal has already implemented this market structure. The document is a planning frame, not proof of execution. # Common Misunderstandings Trade schemes are not the same as transmission corridors. Lines enable trade, but buyer structure and contract mode determine how trade works. Direct overseas trade is not already normal practice. In this page it is an IPSDP planning category, not proof of implementation. Market-linked sales and long-term PPAs are different commercial modes. They should not be collapsed into one generic export bucket. # Related india-energy-relationship bangladesh-trade-route niettp seasonal-arbitrage-trap

pages.title: North Bihar Kosi-Gandak Floodplain
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone explains why the Kosi and Gandak routes cannot be read as simple blue lines. They pass into one of the most sensitive floodplain and agricultural geographies in the downstream story.
pages.body_text: North Bihar Kosi-Gandak Floodplain # Summary This dependency zone explains why the Kosi and Gandak routes cannot be read as simple blue lines. They pass into one of the most sensitive floodplain and agricultural geographies in the downstream story. # Simple Explanation The zone marks the downstream plain where Nepal-linked rivers meet dense settlement, agriculture, embankment systems, and flood memory. It is there to show exposure context, not to model flood depths or assign control. # Why It Matters North Bihar is central to the geopolitics map because dense settlement, agriculture, sediment, embankments, and flood memory sit directly downstream of Nepal-linked river systems. # How To Read The Zone Read it with kosi-ganges-merge and gandak-ganges-merge. The zone explains exposure; the merge markers explain route handoff. # Caveat This is not a hydrodynamic or flood-risk model. It does not say Nepal controls North Bihar water outcomes. It says Nepal-linked routes pass through a high-sensitivity downstream geography. # Common Misunderstandings This is not a flood-inundation map. It marks strategic exposure, not modeled water depth or return periods. It is not a claim that Nepal controls North Bihar outcomes. The layer shows route dependency within a shared river system. It should not be read without the merge markers. The floodplain zone explains exposure; kosi-ganges-merge and gandak-ganges-merge explain route handoff. # Related koshi-basin gandaki-basin kosi-ganges-merge gandak-ganges-merge data-layer-future-regulation-scenario

pages.title: Padma-Meghna Delta Dependency
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone explains why the geopolitics map follows Nepal-linked routes into Bangladesh.
pages.body_text: Padma-Meghna Delta Dependency # Summary This dependency zone explains why the geopolitics map follows Nepal-linked routes into Bangladesh. # Simple Explanation The delta dependency layer shows that upstream river timing eventually becomes part of a downstream Bangladesh story. It is not saying Nepal determines delta outcomes; it is showing why route-to-ocean context matters. # Why It Matters The lower delta is sensitive to flood timing, dry-season flow, sediment delivery, salinity pressure, and population exposure. Nepal is not the sole driver of any of these outcomes, but Nepal-linked river timing is part of the larger Ganges/Padma/Meghna system. # How To Read The Zone Read it with ganges-padma-transition and padma-meghna-delta. The transition marker explains route naming and border geography; the dependency zone explains why the downstream context matters. # Caveat This zone is strategic context. It is not a distributary map, salinity model, flood model, or Bangladesh water-allocation claim. # Common Misunderstandings The zone is not a Bangladesh water-allocation claim. It provides downstream context for Nepal-linked routes. It is not a salinity or sediment model. It flags sensitivity rather than quantifying it. It does not make Nepal the sole upstream driver. The Ganges/Padma/Meghna system has many contributors and controls. # Related ganges-padma-transition padma-meghna-delta lower-delta-bay-interface bangladesh-trade-route how-to-read-geopolitics-map
