pages.title: Decision Dossier — Electric-Cooking Evidence Gate and Pilot
headings: Decision Dossier — Electric-Cooking Evidence Gate and Pilot
pages.excerpt: An evidence-led comparison of research, pilot and scale-up options for electric cooking; national adoption, feeder readiness, load timing, appliance costs and LPG fiscal effects remain incompletely measured.
pages.body_text: Decision Dossier — Electric-Cooking Evidence Gate and Pilot [!important] TransparentGov assessment, not settled fact: Electric cooking is a credible electrification pathway, but the current evidence is not sufficient to specify a national adoption target, subsidy, tariff window or grid-investment envelope. # Decision Question What evidence and pilot design would allow Nepal to test electric cooking without shifting unreliable service, appliance costs or peak demand risks onto households? # Established Facts wb-household-electric-cooking-nepal-2025 describes electricity use for cooking as below one percent of Nepali households and biomass as the primary cooking fuel for about 60 percent. It is a cost-economics study, not a programme evaluation or annual adoption series. The World Bank study finds electricity cheaper than fossil fuels on average in its modelled comparison. It does not establish current retail appliance prices, household financing terms, feeder reliability, cooking-hour load shapes or the outcome of a national programme. wecs-energy-synopsis-2024 places grid electricity at 7.23 percent of final energy in FY 2079/80 and traditional biomass at 63.87 percent. These are economy-wide energy-balance shares, not electric-cooking adoption measures. nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 reports 97.6 percent national grid coverage and 12.26 percent total system loss at its reporting cutoff. Grid coverage does not establish continuous, cooking-grade service at a household or feeder. # Unknowns A current annual series for electric-cooking adoption and continued use, including fuel stacking. Household cooking times and appliance load profiles by season, geography and income group. Feeder and transformer headroom, outage duration and voltage quality in candidate locations. Current induction-appliance prices, compatible cookware costs, repair access and household finance terms. Current LPG tax, price-support and subsidy incidence, including who would gain or lose from a policy change. Distributional effects for renters, low-income households and households that cannot rely on electricity at meal times. # Comparable Cases No comparable implementation case is included in the current evidence set. The World Bank Nepal paper compares costs across cooking technologies, but it does not evaluate a municipal or national electric-cooking programme. Transfer limitation: programme results from another country or from a short equipment-distribution pilot should not be transferred to Nepal without checking feeder reliability, tariff structure, cooking practices, appliance persistence and fuel stacking. # Response Options and Trade-offs Option | What it would involve | Potential advantage | Material limitation or risk | ---|---|---|---| Build the evidence baseline first | Publish adoption, load-shape, appliance-market, LPG-fiscal and feeder-readiness evidence | Reduces the risk of designing around national averages that do not describe household service | Delays direct implementation and still requires access to utility and household data | Run a bounded local pilot after feeder screening | Select locations using service-quality evidence; test appliances, finance, tariffs and measured use | Produces Nepal-specific adoption, reliability and load evidence | Pilot results may not transfer nationally; selection can favour unusually strong feeders | Target existing reliable customers | Offer support only where household service and wiring meet defined thresholds | Lower initial grid risk and faster learning | Can exclude poorer or weakly served households and widen service inequality | Begin broad national support now | Offer a national appliance or tariff programme before local evidence is complete | Signals policy commitment and may accelerate uptake | Unknown peak effects, fiscal exposure, feeder constraints and sustained-use rates make benefits difficult to estimate | # TransparentGov Assessment Preferred evidence-led sequence: publish the missing baseline, screen candidate feeders, and run a bounded pilot with pre-declared measures for reliability, sustained appliance use, fuel stacking, household cost and hourly demand. A national target or fiscal saving should follow measured results rather than substitute for them. The assessment would change if Nepal publishes a current household adoption series, feeder-level reliability and capacity data, a cooking-load study, and a documented LPG fiscal ledger. # Monitoring Triggers A current national household energy-use survey with electric-cooking variables. Public feeder reliability or transformer-capacity data for candidate locations. A programme evaluation reporting sustained use, fuel stacking and household costs. A residential time-of-use tariff or metering decision with implementation evidence. A current official LPG price-support, tax and subsidy account. # Related energy-substitution-pathway data-domestic-demand distribution-and-reliability seasonal-mismatch demand-and-electrification

pages.title: Decision Dossier — Power-System Role Separation and Open Access
headings: Decision Dossier — Power-System Role Separation and Open Access
pages.excerpt: An evidence-led comparison of transparency, open-access implementation, ring-fenced dispatch and institutional-separation options; public records do not yet establish discriminatory dispatch or the benefits of a particular reform model.
pages.body_text: Decision Dossier — Power-System Role Separation and Open Access [!important] TransparentGov assessment, not settled fact: Better disclosure and operational rules are immediately testable. A separate system operator or penalty authority remains a policy option requiring legal, institutional and cost analysis; this dossier does not treat it as a proven cure. # Decision Question Which changes to dispatch governance, open-access implementation and penalty administration would improve neutrality and accountability without weakening system reliability or creating an institution that Nepal cannot yet operate effectively? # Established Facts nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 records electricity supplied by NEA and its subsidiaries, independent producers and imports, while NEA operates central parts of the transmission and distribution system. The reviewed PPA analysis also identifies NEA as the off-taker under standard hydropower contracting. Public reporting indexed at erc-open-access-directive-2082 states that ERC issued the Open Access Directive 2082 in January 2026. The official directive text and implementing manuals are not archived in the current corpus, and issuance does not establish operational use. nea-standard-ppa-clauses and ad-penalty-clause-research describe availability-declaration and curtailment provisions through secondary legal analysis. They are not a complete corpus of signed PPAs or a formal legal opinion. The reviewed public corpus does not contain project-level dispatch instructions, accepted-energy records, reason codes, penalty ledgers or adjudication outcomes sufficient to measure discriminatory dispatch or sector-wide penalty exposure. The frequently repeated 16 percent penalty figure has no identified basis in the reviewed standard-PPA analysis and must not be used as a sector aggregate. # Unknowns The official text, current implementing rules and observed transactions under Open Access Directive 2082. Whether project-level dispatch differs systematically by ownership after controlling for location, grid conditions, contract terms and plant availability. The content and variation of representative signed PPAs, including curtailment and dispute provisions. Penalties assessed, waived, disputed and recovered by project and year. The statutory amendments, staffing, systems and recurring cost required for a separate operator or penalty authority. Whether a ring-fenced unit inside NEA could deliver adequate independence, and how its performance would be audited. # Comparable Cases No sourced comparable institutional-reform case is included in the current corpus. International system-operator models vary in legal mandate, market design, utility ownership, metering and settlement capability. Transfer limitation: the existence of an independent operator elsewhere does not show that separation would produce neutral dispatch in Nepal, nor that Nepal currently has the data, staffing and legal framework needed to operate that model. The Barahi material is not used as a proven comparison: the current source record does not include a primary audited statement or adjudication record sufficient to establish the claimed penalty outcome. # Response Options and Trade-offs Option | What it would involve | Potential advantage | Material limitation or risk | ---|---|---|---| Publish operational evidence | Release dispatch instructions, accepted energy, reason codes, constraints and penalty outcomes with contract-sensitive redactions | Makes the problem measurable and supports later institutional design | Disclosure requires data standards, audit controls and legitimate confidentiality rules | Operationalise open access within current institutions | Publish the official directive, eligibility, wheeling charges, metering, scheduling, settlement and dispute procedures | Tests third-party access before a larger institutional redesign | Formal rules may not alter practice without enforcement, capable metering and settlement systems | Ring-fence dispatch inside NEA | Separate staff, accounts and decision criteria; publish performance and conflict-of-interest controls | Potentially faster than creating a new statutory body | Formal separation inside one organisation may not create practical independence | Create an independent system operator | Transfer dispatch functions to a legally separate, governed institution | Creates a clearer institutional separation if mandate and capability are credible | Requires legislation, transition design, funding, technical capacity and accountability safeguards | Separate penalty calculation or appeals | Give ERC or another neutral body a defined review or adjudication role | Could strengthen procedural fairness | Jurisdiction, evidence standards, appeal rights and administrative capacity remain unresolved | # TransparentGov Assessment Preferred evidence-led sequence: publish the official open-access instrument and its implementation rules, establish auditable dispatch and penalty records, and test the current framework before choosing a permanent institutional model. Ring-fencing and independent operation should be compared through a published legal and capability assessment. This assessment would change if primary dispatch and penalty evidence demonstrates a systematic conflict that cannot be controlled inside the current structure, or if official open-access implementation records show that the present model works in practice. # Monitoring Triggers An official archived copy of Open Access Directive 2082 and its implementing manuals. A completed third-party transaction using the open-access framework. Publication of project-level dispatch, constraint and penalty records. A bill, regulation or government decision on system-operator or penalty-administration roles. A primary PPA corpus or authoritative legal interpretation. # Related nea-triple-authority claim-governance-binding ad-penalties stranded-generation institutions-finance-and-project-delivery

pages.title: Decision Dossier — Climate-Risk Requirements in Hydropower Studies
headings: Decision Dossier — Climate-Risk Requirements in Hydropower Studies
pages.excerpt: An evidence-led comparison of disclosure, pilot and mandate options for climate and hazard analysis in hydropower studies; the current corpus does not support a universal Q-design decrement or a claimed published national guideline.
pages.body_text: Decision Dossier — Climate-Risk Requirements in Hydropower Studies [!important] TransparentGov assessment, not settled fact: Hydropower studies should make climate and hazard assumptions visible and testable. The evidence does not justify applying one forward-looking discharge decrement to every basin or project. # Decision Question What climate-risk, hydrological-sensitivity and hazard information should DoED require in hydropower studies, and should any requirement begin as disclosure, a pilot standard or an immediate mandate? # Established Facts doed-licensing-directive-2075 records a Q45 design-discharge requirement in the current amended licensing directive and states that the directive does not mandate climate-adjusted hydrology. It does not show how individual applicants implement the rule. wecs-river-basin-plan-2024 documents strong wet–dry seasonality using model-derived basin flows and warns that those values can differ from gauges and project studies. icimod-hkh-glacier-change provides regional evidence of glacier loss and scenario-dependent long-term change. Its regional aggregates cannot be converted directly into a project-specific design-discharge factor. aiib-dudhkoshi-project-2026 identifies GLOF, sediment, slope stability, seismic and dam-safety risks for a proposed large storage project and says assessment instruments remain under preparation or review. This establishes the relevance of multi-hazard assessment, not a completed national standard. The current source corpus does not establish the publication and formal adoption of a final ICIMOD climate-resilient hydropower guideline. It also does not provide a census of modelling methods used in domestic feasibility studies. # Unknowns Which climate, hydrology and hazard methods recent project studies actually use, by basin, project size and financing source. Whether DoED is preparing a revised study guideline, the draft text, or an implementation timetable. The sensitivity of project economics and safety outcomes to specific hydrology datasets, scenarios and bias-correction methods. The staff, data and modelling capability available to DoED and domestic developers. The cost and delay associated with different study requirements. Whether a size threshold is appropriate; small projects can face serious local hazard exposure even when modelling budgets are limited. # Comparable Cases The current corpus provides project-specific context rather than a comparable national regulation. Dudhkoshi's lender record identifies a broad hazard set; uahel-upper-arun-project records current project parameters and preparation status but does not, on its own, establish a climate-adjusted method. Transfer limitations: large projects with multilateral financing have different budgets, safeguard processes and review capacity from domestically financed projects. Project-specific assessment does not prove that the same method, scenario or cost is appropriate as a universal licensing rule. # Response Options and Trade-offs Option | What it would involve | Potential advantage | Material limitation or risk | ---|---|---|---| Standard disclosure and sensitivity tests | Require every study to identify data periods, stationarity assumptions, climate scenarios, uncertainty ranges and hazard screens | Makes assumptions comparable without imposing one model result | Disclosure can become procedural unless DoED can review quality and require revisions | Pilot a technical standard | Apply a draft method to selected basins or project types and publish lessons | Tests data, cost and review capacity before scaling | Pilot projects may not represent Nepal's full basin and project diversity | Phase requirements by risk | Begin with larger or higher-hazard projects, then expand after capacity review | Focuses early effort where consequences may be larger | Size is an imperfect proxy for local hazard and can leave smaller projects under-screened | Immediate universal decrement factor | Apply one forward-looking reduction to design discharge across projects | Simple to administer and easy to compare | Creates false precision, can misstate basin-specific conditions and may shift rather than reduce risk | Retain current rules | Continue Q45 licensing without additional climate disclosure | Avoids new compliance cost and review burden | Leaves assumptions and climate-risk treatment difficult to compare or audit | # TransparentGov Assessment Preferred evidence-led sequence: require transparent data, uncertainty and hazard disclosure; then pilot a reviewable technical standard before deciding whether any method should become mandatory. A fixed national decrement should not be adopted without basin-specific validation and an implementation-capacity assessment. The assessment would change if DoED publishes an adopted method with technical annexes, consultation evidence and an implementation plan, or if a representative project-study review establishes a consistent, material gap that a specific standard can correct. # Monitoring Triggers A final DoED or ICIMOD hydropower study guideline with a stable official record. A DoED circular, amendment or consultation on climate-risk requirements. A representative review of feasibility-study methods by project size and financing source. Public project sensitivity tests connecting climate assumptions to design and financial outcomes. Evidence on compliance cost and regulator review capacity. # Related q-design-discharge claim-climate-harder-not-easier glof-risk sediment-as-design-constraint climate-resilience-and-decarbonization

pages.title: Decision Dossier — Hydropower Securities Disclosure
pages.excerpt: An evidence-led comparison of bounded civic data, minimum machine-readable annexes and fuller structured filing for hydropower securities; the current evidence covers four issuers, not the sector.
pages.body_text: Decision Dossier — Hydropower Securities Disclosure [!important] TransparentGov assessment, not settled fact: A minimum machine-readable data annex is a proportionate near-term option, but the current four-issuer evidence does not establish a sector-wide bailout pattern or prove that XBRL is Nepal's only suitable filing system. # Decision Question What disclosure format and minimum data fields would let investors and regulators compare hydropower offering plans with post-offer outcomes without imposing an unusable reporting system on issuers or SEBON? # Established Facts sebon-hydropower-offering-records documents approved rights-offer prospectuses for a bounded four-issuer cohort: Ankhu Khola, Joshi Hydropower, People's Power and Terhathum Power. Each prospectus assigns at least some proceeds to financing liabilities, but the mixes differ: project investment, bank repayment, promoter-advance repayment, and repair and maintenance appear in different combinations. Ankhu Khola's audited FY 2081/82 statements establish completion of its rights issue and substantial debt reduction, but do not reconcile the full planned investment in Ankhu Khola-2. People's Power and Terhathum have issuer-published post-offer evidence consistent with capital increases and debt reduction, but the current records are unaudited. Joshi's final allotment and post-offer application of proceeds remain unverified in the source record. A SEBON pipeline record or approved prospectus establishes a filing stage or planned use of proceeds; it does not by itself establish completion, allotment or actual use. # Unknowns A declared sampling frame and complete census of hydropower IPOs and rights issues. Final allotment and post-offer outcomes for Joshi Hydropower. Audited FY 2082/83 confirmation for People's Power and Terhathum. Full reconciliation of Ankhu Khola's planned project investment. SEBON's current structured-data policy, technical capability, cost constraints and any prior pilot. Which fields investors, supervisors and issuers consider decision-useful, and which require confidentiality or legal interpretation. Aggregate banking exposure and whether public securities data can be reconciled with NRB supervisory records. # Comparable Cases No sourced comparable securities-regulation case is included in the current corpus. The legacy page's references to foreign XBRL programmes were not supported by source pages and are not used here. Transfer limitation: a structured-filing system from another jurisdiction may rely on different accounting taxonomies, digital signatures, enforcement powers, issuer capacity and market infrastructure. Its existence would not establish the right format or implementation sequence for Nepal. # Response Options and Trade-offs Option | What it would involve | Potential advantage | Material limitation or risk | ---|---|---|---| Continue a bounded civic dataset | Publish issuer-level fields with source links, audit status, cutoffs and missing values | Can proceed with existing records and exposes evidence gaps | Remains incomplete, labour-intensive and non-authoritative | Require a minimum data annex | Add a downloadable CSV or JSON schedule for offering terms, planned proceeds, allotment and actual use | Lower implementation burden than a full filing platform; supports comparison | Requires stable field definitions, validation and enforcement | Phase a fuller structured-filing system | Develop a taxonomy, pilot with selected issuers, then expand | Could support more comprehensive automated analysis | Higher technical, training and compliance cost; poor taxonomy design can create false comparability | Standardise post-offer reconciliation only | Require a dated table comparing planned and actual use of proceeds, with audit status | Directly addresses the main evidence gap in the current cohort | Does not solve broader financial-statement or market-data accessibility | Retain PDF-only filing | Keep current public-document practice | Lowest transition cost | Preserves extraction burden and makes cross-issuer comparison difficult | # TransparentGov Assessment Preferred evidence-led sequence: complete the bounded four-issuer reconciliation, publish its sampling limits, and test a minimum machine-readable annex covering planned proceeds, allotment, actual use, debt balances and audit status. A fuller structured-filing mandate should follow a SEBON capacity and cost assessment. This assessment would change if SEBON publishes an existing data standard or pilot, if issuers demonstrate that a minimum annex is impractical, or if a broader sample shows that different fields are more decision-useful. # Monitoring Triggers Joshi Hydropower final allotment and audited post-offer accounts. Audited FY 2082/83 statements for People's Power and Terhathum. Ankhu Khola-2 investment reconciliation. A SEBON consultation, filing specification or structured-data pilot. Publication of a declared broader sampling rule and issuer census. # Related ipo-hydropower-bailout ad-penalties q-design-discharge institutions-finance-and-project-delivery unresolved-questions

pages.title: Decision Dossier — Hetauda–Dhalkebar Completion and Community Resolution
headings: Decision Dossier — Hetauda–Dhalkebar Completion and Community Resolution
pages.excerpt: An evidence-led assessment of options for completing and commissioning Hetauda–Dhalkebar while resolving community and right-of-way concerns; current completion and remaining-tower counts are not verified.
pages.body_text: Decision Dossier — Hetauda–Dhalkebar Completion and Community Resolution [!important] TransparentGov assessment, not settled fact: Completion of the Hetauda–Dhalkebar section remains a high-value system objective, but the public evidence is insufficient to publish a current completion percentage, remaining-tower count, commissioning date or national curtailment benefit. # Decision Question What combination of construction management, public disclosure, compensation and dispute-resolution measures can complete and commission the Hetauda–Dhalkebar section while addressing affected communities' right-of-way concerns? # Established Facts nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 reports that, at its July 2025 cutoff, 773 of 792 tower foundations were complete, 770 towers had been erected and more than 534 circuit-kilometres of conductor had been strung across the wider Hetauda–Dhalkebar–Inaruwa project. It also reports the Dhalkebar–Inaruwa section charged since June 2024. nea-hddi-construction-notices-july-2026 records NEA local-outage notices on 3 and 5 July 2026 associated with conductor-stringing work on the Hetauda–Dhalkebar section. The notices establish active work, not completion or energisation. world-bank-hddi-rap documents the corridor's right-of-way, land and structure impacts. These are material project-delivery issues, not merely a construction scheduling problem. The public operational corpus does not contain the plant-level availability and dispatch data required to estimate national curtailed energy or attribute it to this corridor. See stranded-generation and nea-operational-reporting-portals-2026. # Unknowns Current erected-tower, foundation, stringing and testing totals after the July 2026 work. Whether all required land, right-of-way and compensation agreements are complete. A dated commissioning and energisation schedule issued by NEA. Transfer capacity and N-1 improvement under current network conditions. Avoided congestion, curtailment or export value attributable specifically to this section. Terms of any current community agreement and whether affected households consider it implemented. # Comparable Case ## Bharatpur–Bardaghat mediated settlement The world-bank-bharatpur-bardaghat-drs-2023 establishes that NEA and affected residents reached a mediated agreement in 2023 after the last two towers of the Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV line had been delayed. The process used separate meetings, facilitated joint meetings, information exchange and negotiated options. Transfer limitations: this was a different 220 kV line, alignment and community; it had access to a World Bank accountability mechanism; and the detailed settlement terms are confidential. It supports independent mediation as a demonstrated process option in Nepal. It does not show that Hetauda–Dhalkebar can use the same compensation terms, institution or timeline. # Response Options and Trade-offs Option | What it would involve | Potential advantage | Material limitation or risk | ---|---|---|---| Publish and execute a dated completion plan | NEA publishes remaining works, testing stages, responsible units and milestone updates | Creates a common factual baseline and makes slippage visible | Disclosure alone does not resolve disputed land, compensation or trust | Independent facilitated mediation | A mutually accepted mediator structures information exchange and negotiation with affected communities | Nepal has one documented transmission precedent | Participation, authority and funding arrangements are not currently public; results cannot be guaranteed | Technical and social disclosure package | Publish alignment impacts, compensation basis, EMF standards, grievance channels and implementation status in accessible language | Addresses information asymmetry and permits claims to be checked | May expose unresolved disagreement and require additional surveys or compensation review | Construction-led completion under existing authority | Continue works wherever legal access and agreements are already in place | May preserve momentum on uncontested spans | Can deepen conflict if it is used in place of consultation, remedy or lawful compensation | Phased commissioning with published constraints | Commission technically complete elements where system studies permit and disclose residual limits | Could deliver partial operational value earlier | Feasibility depends on engineering and protection studies not present in the public corpus | # TransparentGov Assessment Preferred evidence-led sequence: NEA should first publish a dated, segment-specific status and completion plan; then pair construction on uncontested works with an independent, documented process for unresolved community issues. The Bharatpur–Bardaghat case makes mediation a credible option, but not a proven template for the outcome. This assessment would change if NEA publishes a commissioning certificate, an implemented settlement record, a revised route or a current works inventory. It does not assign a monetary benefit because the required load-flow and plant-level dispatch evidence is unavailable. # Monitoring Triggers NEA energisation or commissioning notice for Hetauda–Dhalkebar. Dated project inventory of foundations, towers, stringing, testing and substations. Public compensation or grievance-resolution record. Load-flow or transfer-capacity study. Plant-level curtailment and dispatch dataset response. # Related hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone claim-transmission-immediate-blocker stranded-generation world-bank-bharatpur-bardaghat-drs-2023 data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network
